entries.name: Lata Mangeshkar
entries.desc: Lata Mangeshkar, born Hemalata in Indore, was an Indian playback singer whose career in film music spanned eight decades and who recorded songs in more than thirty-six Indian languages. The daughter of the classical singer and actor Deenanath Mangeshkar, she began working after his death in 1942 and moved to Mumbai in 1945; her song Aayega Aanewaala in the film Mahal (1949) helped win recognition for playback singers, until then uncredited. In 1963, during the Sino-Indian War, she sang Aye Mere Watan Ke Logo before Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. She received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1989 and the Bharat Ratna in 2001, and died in 2022 after treatment for COVID-19 and pneumonia.

entries.name: M. S. Subbulakshmi
entries.desc: M. S. Subbulakshmi was an Indian Carnatic singer from Madurai and in 1998 the first musician to be awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour. The daughter of the veena player Shanmukhavadivu Ammal, of the devadasi community, she first performed in public in 1927 at the Rockfort Temple in Tiruchirappalli and sang at the Madras Music Academy in 1929, at 13. Her title role in the Tamil film Meera (1945) brought her national prominence. Her concerts abroad included the United Nations General Assembly in 1966, and in 1974 she received the Ramon Magsaysay Award. She stopped performing after her husband Kalki Sadasivam died in 1997, and died in Chennai in 2004.

entries.name: Umm Kulthum
entries.desc: Umm Kulthum, born Fatima Ibrahim es-Sayyid el-Beltagi in the village of Tamay al-Zahayra in Egypt's Dakahlia Governorate, was an Egyptian singer and film actress known by the honorific Kawkab el-Sharq, Planet of the East. The daughter of a rural imam, she sang religious hymns in her father's ensemble as a child, dressed as a boy, and moved to Cairo in the early 1920s, working with the poet Ahmed Rami and composers such as Mohammed Abdel Wahab. From 1934 she gave a broadcast concert on the first Thursday of every month for forty years, and after the 1967 war she sang abroad to raise funds for the Egyptian war effort. Her funeral in Cairo in 1975 drew a crowd of over 4 million people.

entries.name: Sayed Darwish
entries.desc: Sayed Darwish was an Egyptian singer and composer from Alexandria, considered the father of Egyptian popular music, who set to music Bilady, Bilady, Bilady, the song that became Egypt's national anthem. Trained in Quran recitation and for two years at al-Azhar, he worked as a bricklayer and café singer before turning in 1918 to musical theatre in Cairo, composing operettas for Naguib el-Rihani's company, for Munira al-Mahdiyya and others. His songs of the 1919 revolt against British occupation, mostly with words by the poet Badi' Khayri, voiced national feeling, and light melodies such as Salma ya Salama passed into Egyptian folklore. He died in September 1923, aged thirty-one.

entries.name: Ahmed Shawqi
entries.desc: Ahmed Shawqi was an Egyptian poet and linguist, born in Cairo in 1868, whom his peers crowned Amir al-Shu'ara, the Prince of Poets, in 1927. After studying law at Montpellier and Paris, he served at the court of the Khedive Abbas II, and his early verse praised the Khedive. Exiled to Andalusia in Spain in 1914 for his opposition to the British, he wrote patriotic poems on Egypt and the Arab world until his return in 1920. He was the first in modern Arabic literature to write poetic plays, among them Majnun Laila and The Death of Cleopatra, and scholars count him the leading poet of Arabic Neoclassicism. He died in 1932.

entries.name: Tian Han
entries.desc: Tian Han was a Chinese playwright, translator and poet and a leader of left-wing drama, music and film, counted by drama historians among the three founders of Chinese spoken drama. After studying in Japan from 1916 to 1922, he founded the Southern Society in Shanghai, joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1932 and wrote plays on workers' struggles and resistance to Japan. In 1934 he wrote the lyrics of March of the Volunteers, set to music by Nie Er, which was adopted as the provisional national anthem of the People's Republic of China in 1949. Denounced and jailed in the Cultural Revolution, he died in 1968; he was rehabilitated in 1979, and his words were restored to the anthem in 1982.

entries.name: Enoch Sontonga
entries.desc: Enoch Sontonga was a Xhosa composer and teacher, born in Uitenhage in the Eastern Cape Colony, who wrote the hymn Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika (God Bless Africa). Trained at the Lovedale Institution, he taught and led the choir at a Methodist mission school in Nancefield, near Johannesburg, and composed the first verse and chorus in 1897 as a school anthem; the poet Samuel Mqhayi later added seven verses. The African National Congress adopted it as its closing anthem in 1925, Tanganyika and Zambia took versions of it as national anthems, and since 1994 it has formed the first half of South Africa's anthem. Sontonga died in 1905, and his grave was declared a national monument in 1996.

entries.name: Solomon Linda
entries.desc: Solomon Linda was a South African singer and composer from Natal whose song Mbube, improvised in a Johannesburg recording studio in 1939 with his group the Evening Birds, reshaped the isicathamiya style of choral singing. A migrant worker in Johannesburg, he introduced a falsetto lead voice over several bass singers. Mbube reportedly sold more than 100,000 copies in South Africa, but Linda had sold his rights to Eric Gallo for ten shillings. The Weavers recorded it as Wimoweh in 1951 and the Tokens as The Lion Sleeps Tonight in 1961, neither crediting him. He died poor in 1962; after his family sued Disney in 2004, a settlement gave them royalties and him a cowriting credit.

entries.name: Feodor Chaliapin
entries.desc: Feodor Chaliapin was a Russian bass singer, born into a peasant family in Kazan in 1873, who is often credited with establishing the tradition of naturalistic acting in opera. After success as Mephistopheles at the Mamontov Private Opera, he sang at Moscow's Bolshoi Theatre from 1899 to 1914, and the title role of Mussorgsky's Boris Godunov became his signature part. From 1901 he sang abroad, at La Scala and later the Metropolitan Opera, and his advocacy made Russian operas such as Khovanshchina and Prince Igor well known in the West. He remained outside Russia after 1921, settled in Paris and died there in 1938; his remains were moved to Moscow in 1984.

credit.artist: Unknown (Bibliothèque nationale et universitaire de Strasbourg, France)

entries.name: Arturo Toscanini
entries.desc: Arturo Toscanini was an Italian conductor, born in Parma in 1867, who began as a cellist and first conducted in Rio de Janeiro in 1886, leading Aida from memory at the age of 19. He conducted the world premieres of Leoncavallo's Pagliacci and Puccini's La bohème, was principal conductor and later music director of La Scala, and led the Metropolitan Opera and the New York Philharmonic. An opponent of Mussolini, he refused to conduct the Fascist anthem Giovinezza and was beaten by Blackshirts in Bologna in 1931. From 1937 to 1954 he was the first music director of the NBC Symphony Orchestra, whose broadcasts and recordings reached a mass audience. He died in New York in 1957.

entries.name: Marian Anderson
entries.desc: Marian Anderson was an American contralto from Philadelphia who sang music from opera to spirituals with leading orchestras in the United States and Europe between 1925 and 1965. In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let her sing to an integrated audience in Constitution Hall in Washington, D.C.; with the help of Eleanor and Franklin D. Roosevelt she sang instead on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial on Easter Sunday, before more than 75,000 people. In 1955 she became the first Black American singer to perform at the Metropolitan Opera. She later served as a delegate to the United Nations Human Rights Committee, sang at the March on Washington in 1963 and died in 1993.

entries.name: Mahalia Jackson
entries.desc: Mahalia Jackson was an American gospel singer, born in poverty in New Orleans in 1911, the granddaughter of enslaved people, who was central to the development and spread of gospel blues in Black churches. In Chicago she sang with the Johnson Singers and drew on Thomas Dorsey and Bessie Smith; her 1947 recording Move On Up a Little Higher sold two million copies, a first for gospel music. She became the first gospel recording artist to tour Europe, turned down offers to record secular music, and is credited with influencing rhythm and blues, soul and rock and roll singing. A supporter of Martin Luther King Jr., she sang at the March on Washington in 1963. She died in 1972.

entries.name: Francis James Child
entries.desc: Francis James Child was an American scholar and folklorist at Harvard University, known for The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, the collection now called the Child Ballads. He became Boylston Professor of Rhetoric and Oratory in 1851, and in 1876 Harvard made him its first professor of English to keep him from Johns Hopkins. Using the methods of comparative philology and corresponding with the Danish scholar Svend Grundtvig, he gathered some 305 ballads with their variants, published in parts from 1882 to 1898, the last after his death in 1896. His studies also shaped how Chaucer's grammar and pronunciation are understood, and in 1888 he founded the American Folklore Society.

entries.name: Allan Ramsay
entries.desc: Allan Ramsay was a Scottish poet, playwright, publisher and librarian of early Enlightenment Edinburgh, born at Leadhills in Lanarkshire, who worked as a wig-maker before turning bookseller around 1718. His collections The Tea-Table Miscellany (1723–37), of Scots and English songs, and The Ever Green (1724), of Scots poems written before 1600, revived interest in vernacular literature. His pastoral drama The Gentle Shepherd (1725) went through several editions, and he is credited with creating the first circulating library in Britain in 1726. He is seen as the link between the makars of the 15th and 16th centuries and the later poets Robert Fergusson and Robert Burns. He died in 1758.

entries.name: Louis Armstrong
entries.desc: Louis Armstrong was an American jazz trumpeter, cornetist and singer from New Orleans, among the most influential figures in jazz, who shifted the music's focus from collective improvisation to solo performance. Raised in poverty, he followed his mentor King Oliver to Chicago in 1922, and his Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings from 1925 showcased his solos. He was one of the first African-American entertainers to reach wide white and international audiences, toured Africa, Europe and Asia for the US State Department, and spoke out publicly during the Little Rock school desegregation crisis of 1957. His recording of Hello, Dolly! reached No. 1 in 1964. He died in Queens, New York, in 1971.

entries.name: Leonard Bernstein
entries.desc: Leonard Bernstein was an American conductor, composer, pianist and music educator, born in Lawrence, Massachusetts, in 1918 to Jewish immigrant parents, and the first American-born conductor to win international acclaim. His unrehearsed debut with the New York Philharmonic in 1943, broadcast nationwide, made him famous, and he was its music director from 1957, jointly at first, until 1969. He composed the musical West Side Story (1957), On the Town, Candide, the Chichester Psalms and the score of On the Waterfront, and he was central to the modern revival of Gustav Mahler's music. His Young People's Concerts brought classical music to television audiences. He died in New York in 1990.

entries.name: Mercedes Sosa
entries.desc: Mercedes Sosa was an Argentine singer from San Miguel de Tucumán, rooted in Argentine folk music, who became a leading voice of the nuevo cancionero movement and was called the voice of the voiceless. After a performance at the Cosquín folklore festival in 1965 brought her national attention, she recorded songs by many Latin American writers, among them Violeta Parra's Gracias a la vida. Under the military junta of Jorge Videla she received death threats, was arrested on stage at La Plata in 1979 along with her audience and was barred from performing, and she went into exile in Paris and Madrid. She returned to Argentina in 1982 and toured widely until her death in 2009.

entries.name: Teresa Teng
entries.desc: Teresa Teng was a Taiwanese singer, born in Yunlin County in 1953 to parents from the mainland, who is credited as a pioneer of modern Chinese popular music. She recorded more than 1,700 songs in Mandarin, Hokkien, Cantonese, Japanese and other languages, and built a second career in Japan from 1974. From the late 1970s her songs, among them The Moon Represents My Heart, spread through mainland China on cassettes; banned there for some years in the early 1980s as bourgeois, they circulated on the black market until the restrictions ended. She never performed on the mainland, supported the Tiananmen student protests of 1989, and died in Chiang Mai, Thailand, in 1995.

entries.name: Revolutions of 1848
entries.desc: The revolutions of 1848, also called the springtime of the peoples, were a wave of uprisings across Europe between January 1848 and October 1849, the most widespread in European history. Beginning in Sicily in January and spreading after the February Revolution in Paris overthrew the July Monarchy, they reached Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Buda and Pest and more than fifty countries. Coalitions of workers and middle-class reformers sought constitutions, nation states, a free press and economic rights, after a food crisis from 1845 to 1847. Most were soon suppressed, with tens of thousands killed, but serfdom was abolished in Austria and Hungary and absolute monarchy ended in Denmark.

entries.name: Oxford Movement
entries.desc: The Oxford Movement was a high-church movement within the Church of England, begun in the 1830s by clergy mostly associated with the University of Oxford, which developed into Anglo-Catholicism. Prompted by the Irish Church Temporalities Bill and John Keble's Assize Sermon of 1833, its leaders, among them Keble, John Henry Newman and Edward Bouverie Pusey, published the Tracts for the Times, arguing that the church's authority came from God through apostolic succession rather than from the state. Newman's reception into the Catholic Church in 1845 shook the movement, yet it led to Anglican religious orders, a more central place for the Eucharist and the wider use of vestments.

entries.name: Division of Korea
entries.desc: The division of Korea began at the end of the Second World War in 1945, when the peninsula, annexed by Japan in 1910, was split at the 38th parallel into a Soviet occupation zone in the north and a US zone in the south. Two American officers chose the line on 10 August 1945 using a National Geographic map, placing Seoul in the American zone, and a four-power trusteeship agreed in Moscow that December was never carried out. In 1948 the Republic of Korea and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea were founded, each claiming the whole peninsula. North Korea's invasion in 1950 began the Korean War, and the 1953 armistice left Korea divided along the Demilitarized Zone, as it remains.

entries.name: Powhatan
entries.desc: Powhatan, whose name is also rendered Wahunsenacawh or Wahunsunacock, was the mamanatowick, or leader, of the Powhatan Confederacy, a confederacy of Algonquian-speaking peoples living in Tsenacommacah, in the Tidewater region of Virginia. When English settlers landed at Jamestown in 1607 he led the main political and military power facing the colonists, who called him King or Chief Powhatan. He was the father of Matoaka (Pocahontas) and probably the older brother of Opechancanough, who led the attacks on the settlers in 1622 and 1644.

entries.name: Richard Rumbold
entries.desc: Richard Rumbold was an English Parliamentarian soldier and political radical. He served in the New Model Army during the Wars of the Three Kingdoms, was one of the guards at the execution of Charles I in January 1649 and reached the rank of captain before he was dismissed after the Restoration of 1660. Implicated in the Rye House Plot of 1683, an alleged plan to assassinate Charles II and his brother James, he escaped to the Dutch Republic, then joined Argyll's Rising of 1685. Captured after being badly wounded, he was executed at Edinburgh on 26 June 1685; words of his scaffold speech were later quoted by Thomas Jefferson.

entries.name: Canassatego
entries.desc: Canassatego was a leader of the Onondaga nation who became a prominent diplomat and spokesman of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy in the 1740s. He first appears in the records at a treaty conference in Philadelphia in 1742, and he was involved in several controversial land sales to British colonial officials. He is best known for a speech at the Treaty of Lancaster in 1744, in which he recommended that the British colonies form a confederacy as the Haudenosaunee had done. He was reportedly assassinated in 1750, perhaps by sympathizers or agents of New France.

entries.name: Logan the Orator
entries.desc: Logan the Orator was a Cayuga orator and war leader of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, a son of the diplomat Shikellamy. After moving to the Ohio Country in the 1760s he became affiliated with the Mingo. When members of his family were killed by Virginians in the Yellow Creek Massacre of 1774 he took revenge on the frontier, and his attacks helped spark Dunmore's War later that year. He became known for a speech, Logan's Lament, which he reportedly delivered after the war; scholars dispute his original name and whether its words were his.

entries.name: Robert Emmet
entries.desc: Robert Emmet was an Irish republican, orator and rebel leader. After the suppression of the United Irish uprising of 1798 he organised a renewed attempt to overthrow British rule and the Protestant Ascendancy in Ireland and to break the recent union with Great Britain. Hopes of French help faded, many veterans of 1798 held back, and his rising in Dublin in 1803 failed. He was hanged on 20 September 1803. His proclamation of a provisional government, his speech from the dock and his end on the gallows inspired later Irish republicans, among them Patrick Pearse in 1916.

entries.name: Daniel Webster
entries.desc: Daniel Webster was an American lawyer, statesman and diplomat who represented New Hampshire and Massachusetts in the United States Congress and served twice as secretary of state, under William Henry Harrison, John Tyler and Millard Fillmore. He argued over 200 cases before the Supreme Court, winning Dartmouth College v. Woodward, McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden. With Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun he formed the Great Triumvirate of the Senate. He opposed Andrew Jackson's domestic policies and Calhoun's theory of nullification, and his Second Reply to Hayne of 1830 was long studied by students of oratory.

entries.name: Black Hawk
entries.desc: Black Hawk, Mahkatêwe-meshi-kêhkêhkwa in Sauk, was a Sauk leader and warrior in what is now the Midwestern United States. Not a hereditary civil chief, he earned his standing as a war leader. In the War of 1812 he fought for the British against the United States, hoping to push American settlers away from Sauk land, and in 1832 he led the British Band of Sauk and Meskwaki warriors in the Black Hawk War in Illinois and present-day Wisconsin. Captured and taken on a tour of eastern cities, he told his story to an interpreter; published in 1833, it was the first Native American autobiography printed in the United States.

entries.name: Chief Seattle
entries.desc: Seattle, usually styled Chief Seattle, was a leader of the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples. Born around 1780 to a Suquamish father and a Duwamish mother, he became a leading figure among his people and pursued a path of accommodation with the white settlers, forming a personal relationship with Doc Maynard. He was baptised in 1852 as Noah Seattle. The city of Seattle, in the state of Washington, was named after him, and a widely publicised speech arguing for ecological responsibility and for respect for Native Americans' land rights has been attributed to him.

entries.name: Red Cloud
entries.desc: Red Cloud, Maȟpíya Lúta in Lakota, was a leader of the Oglala Lakota from 1865 to 1909. He led the Lakota to victory over the United States Army in Red Cloud's War, whose largest action, the Fetterman Fight of 1866, killed 81 American soldiers. After signing the Treaty of Fort Laramie in 1868 he led his people through the transition to reservation life. Some of his opponents wrongly took him for the overall leader of the Sioux, whose divisions were highly decentralised, with bands acting on their own under leaders respected as warriors, as he was.

entries.name: Booker T. Washington
entries.desc: Booker T. Washington was an American educator, author and orator, from 1890 to 1915 the foremost leader of the African-American community. Born into slavery in Hale's Ford, Virginia, he was freed when United States troops reached the area during the Civil War, worked his way through the Hampton Institute and in 1881 became the first leader of the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. His Atlanta Address of 1895 brought him national prominence. He promoted self-help, education and Black business, helping to found the National Negro Business League, and his autobiography Up from Slavery appeared in 1901.

entries.name: David Lloyd George
entries.desc: David Lloyd George was a Welsh Liberal politician and Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1916 to 1922. Member of Parliament for Caernarvon Boroughs for 55 years, he became Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1908 and proposed taxes on land ownership and high incomes in the People's Budget of 1909 to fund welfare reforms; its rejection by the House of Lords led to a constitutional crisis resolved by the Parliament Act 1911. His budget, the National Insurance Act 1911 and other measures helped establish the modern welfare state. He led the country through the later years of the First World War, took part in the Paris Peace Conference and negotiated the establishment of the Irish Free State.

entries.name: Patrick Pearse
entries.desc: Patrick Pearse was an Irish teacher, barrister, poet, writer, nationalist and republican revolutionary, born in Dublin, the son of a stonemason from Birmingham and a Dublin mother whose family were native Irish speakers. He was one of the leaders of the Easter Rising of 1916, in which a provisional government was proclaimed in Dublin. After the rising he was executed with 15 others, on 3 May 1916, and came to be seen by many as the embodiment of the rebellion.

entries.name: Eugene V. Debs
entries.desc: Eugene V. Debs was an American socialist activist and trade unionist, a founding member of the Industrial Workers of the World and five times the Socialist Party of America's candidate for president. He helped found the American Railway Union and led its boycott of trains with Pullman cars in the Pullman Strike of 1894, which affected more than 250,000 workers in 27 states until President Grover Cleveland used the army to break it. Jailed for six months for defying an injunction against the strike, he came out a committed socialist.

entries.name: George C. Marshall
entries.desc: George C. Marshall was an American soldier and diplomat. He rose to become Chief of Staff of the United States Army under Franklin D. Roosevelt and Harry S. Truman, and Winston Churchill called him the organizer of victory for his leadership in the Second World War. He then tried without success to end the Chinese Civil War, and served Truman as Secretary of State and Secretary of Defense. As Secretary of State he advocated an American commitment to Europe's recovery after the war, the Marshall Plan that bore his name, and he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953.

entries.name: Shadoof
entries.desc: The shadoof is a tool for lifting water from a well, river or pond onto land or into a channel: a long pole pivoted on an upright frame, with a bucket at one end and a counterweight of clay or stone at the other. The earliest evidence of it is a cylinder seal from Mesopotamia of about 2200 BCE; it appeared in Upper Egypt sometime after 2000 BCE and reached China around the same time. One man can lift 39 to 130 litres a minute with it, and it is still used for irrigation in Africa, Asia and parts of Europe.

entries.name: Noria
entries.desc: A noria is a water wheel turned by a river's current whose rim carries pots, buckets or compartments that lift water into a small aqueduct, for irrigation or to supply towns. Paddle-driven water-lifting wheels had appeared in Egypt by the 4th century BCE; the Roman architect Vitruvius described the noria in the 1st century BCE, and around 300 CE the Romans tied ceramic pots to an open-framed wheel. Muslim engineers adopted and improved it: Ibn Bassal of al-Andalus fitted a flywheel, and Ismail al-Jazari a crank in 1206. The norias of Hama in Syria were 20 metres across.

entries.name: Canning
entries.desc: Canning is a method of preserving food by processing it and sealing it in an airtight container, a glass jar or a steel or tin can. In 1809 the French confectioner and brewer Nicolas Appert, answering a government prize of 12,000 francs for preserved rations for the Grande Armée, developed a way of sealing food in glass jars, and was awarded the prize in 1810. In London Peter Durand patented the tin can process in 1810, and Bryan Donkin made sealed cans of tinned wrought iron, sold chiefly to the British Army and Royal Navy. Why the food kept was explained only when Louis Pasteur showed the role of microbes.

entries.name: Mechanical reaper
entries.desc: A mechanical reaper is a machine that cuts, and often gathers, grain crops at harvest. Patrick Bell built one in Scotland in 1828; in the United States Obed Hussey patented a reaper in 1833 and Cyrus McCormick a horse-drawn one in 1834, completing a design begun by his father Robert, with the aid of Jo Anderson, a man enslaved by the family. Reapers spread slowly until McCormick acquired the rights to Hussey's cutter bar around 1850. The reaper-binder of 1872 also bound the sheaves, and it was replaced in turn by the swather and the combine harvester.

entries.name: Tractor
entries.desc: A tractor is an engine-powered vehicle that pulls or drives farm machinery. The first tractors were steam ploughing engines, which followed the self-propelled traction engine Thomas Aveling made in 1859; in 1889 John Charter of Illinois built the first gasoline-powered tractors, and John Froelich built another in Iowa in 1892. Dan Albone's Ivel Agricultural Motor of 1901 was the first commercially successful light petrol tractor, and Henry Ford's mass-produced Fordson of 1917 held 77% of the US market by 1923. By 1935 nearly a million tractors were in use in the United States.

entries.name: Barbed wire
entries.desc: Barbed wire is steel fencing wire with sharp points set at intervals along its strands, used for cheap fences and, as a wire obstacle, in trench warfare. In France Leonce Eugene Grassin-Baledans proposed a fence of thin wire with bristling points in 1860, and Louis François Janin patented a double wire with diamond-shaped barbs in 1865. In the United States Lucien B. Smith of Kent, Ohio, received the first patent in 1867, and Joseph Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, patented the modern form in 1874. It made fencing the western plains cheap, and the open range was closed amid the Fence Cutting Wars of the 1880s.

entries.name: Aquaculture
entries.desc: Aquaculture is the farming of fish, crustaceans, molluscs, algae and other aquatic organisms under controlled or semi-natural conditions. Oral tradition in China places the culture of the common carp around 2000–2100 BCE, but the earliest significant evidence is The Classic of Fish Culture, a monograph by Fan Li written around 475 BCE. Romans bred fish in ponds and farmed oysters before 100 CE, medieval monasteries took up their methods, and Hawaiians built ocean fishponds. By 1866 artificial fish hatcheries operated in Canada and the United States, and world output reached 130.9 million tonnes in 2022.

entries.name: Wine
entries.desc: Wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting grapes. The earliest known traces of it, from about 6000 BCE, were found near Tbilisi in Georgia; jars from Hajj Firuz in Iran, of about 5000 BCE, held wine sealed with pine resin, and the Areni-1 cave in Armenia holds the oldest known winery, with a press, vats and jars from about 4100 BCE. Phoenicians and Greeks spread wine around the Mediterranean, the Romans enlarged its trade, and it became part of Jewish and Christian ritual. In the 19th century phylloxera forced the replanting of almost every vine in Europe.

entries.name: Cheese
entries.desc: Cheese is a food made by curdling milk. It was probably first made by accident, when milk was stored in bladders made of ruminants' stomachs, whose rennet curdles it. The earliest direct evidence is holed clay sieves more than seven thousand years old, from Kujawy in Poland and the Dalmatian coast of Croatia, where residues suggest cheese. Sumerian cuneiform texts of the Third Dynasty of Ur record it, remains were found in an Egyptian tomb of about 2900 BCE, the first cheese factory opened in Switzerland in 1815, and Jesse Williams began assembly-line production in New York in 1851.

entries.name: Coffee
entries.desc: Coffee is a drink brewed from the roasted seeds of the coffee plant, which grows wild in Ethiopia. There is no confirmed evidence of it being drunk before the 15th century, when Sufis in Yemen used it to stay alert during night prayers; Abd al-Qadir al-Jaziri reported that Jamal-al-Din al-Dhabhani, mufti of Aden, first adopted it around 1454. It reached Mecca, Cairo and Damascus, and the first coffeehouse in Istanbul opened in 1554. Until the end of the 17th century the Yemeni port of Mocha was its only gateway; by 1788 Saint-Domingue supplied half the world's coffee, and by 1852 Brazil was the largest producer.

entries.name: Kuk Swamp
entries.desc: Kuk Swamp is an archaeological site in the Wahgi Valley of the Papua New Guinea highlands, at about 1,550 metres, some 12–13 kilometres northeast of Mount Hagen. Drainage ditches dug there from about 9,000 years ago, from major disposal channels to small field ditches, turned the swamp into grassland where taro was grown, and bananas and sugar cane were cultivated from 6,900–6,400 years ago. Studied by the Australian archaeologist Jack Golson, it was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008 as one of the places where people developed agriculture independently. The Kawelka people live in the area today.

entries.name: Norfolk four-course system
entries.desc: The Norfolk four-course system is a method of crop rotation in which four crops follow one another over a four-year cycle: wheat, turnips, barley, and clover or ryegrass. Unlike the earlier three-field system, it has no fallow year. It was developed in the early 16th century in Waasland, in present-day northern Belgium, and popularised in the 18th century by the British agriculturist Charles Townshend. Its fodder crop, turnips, and its grazing crop, clover, allowed livestock to be kept year-round, and it was a key development in the British Agricultural Revolution.

entries.name: Seismoscope
entries.desc: A seismoscope is an instrument that shows that the ground has shaken, without the continuous record that a seismometer keeps. The earliest well-documented one was made in 132 CE by Zhang Heng of the Han dynasty in China and called Houfeng Didong Yi. According to the History of the Later Han Dynasty, it was a bronze vessel about 2 metres across, with eight dragon's heads that dropped a ball into a bronze toad to show the direction of a quake. Mercury and pendulum seismoscopes followed in 18th-century Europe, and the modern seismometer was developed in the 19th century.

entries.name: Water clock
entries.desc: A water clock, or clepsydra, measures time by the regulated flow of water into or out of a vessel. Its oldest documentation is the tomb inscription of the 16th-century BCE Egyptian court official Amenemhet, which names him as its inventor, and the oldest surviving one, from the reign of Amenhotep III (c. 1417–1379 BCE), was used at Karnak. Babylonian tablets record water clocks used for the night and day watches, and the oldest written reference in China dates to the 6th century BCE. Ctesibius and other Hellenistic engineers added feedback control, gearing and dials, and water clocks stayed in use until mechanical clocks replaced them in Europe around 1300.

entries.name: Sundial
entries.desc: A sundial tells the time of day from the apparent position of the Sun, usually by the shadow that a gnomon casts on a dial marked with hour-lines. The earliest sundials known from the archaeological record are shadow clocks of about 1500 BCE from ancient Egyptian and Babylonian astronomy. By 240 BCE Eratosthenes had used an obelisk and a water well to estimate the circumference of the world, and the Roman writer Vitruvius listed the dials known in his day in De architectura. Canonical sundials marked the liturgical hours of religious orders from the 7th to the 14th centuries, and Giovanni Padovani published a treatise on making sundials in 1570.

entries.name: Armillary sphere
entries.desc: An armillary sphere is a model of the sky made of rings that stand for the celestial equator, the ecliptic and other circles, centred on the Earth or the Sun. It was invented separately in ancient Greece and in China. Hipparchus credited Eratosthenes (276–194 BCE) with its invention, and Greek armillary spheres served as teaching tools in the 3rd century BCE. In China, Geng Shouchang introduced a fixed equatorial ring in 52 BCE, and Zhang Heng completed the sphere with horizon and meridian rings in 125 CE and turned it by water power. Islamic and medieval European astronomers took it up, and it remained the main instrument for finding celestial positions until the telescope.

credit.artist: physical object: Jost Bürgi, Antonius Eisenhoit Photograph: Chris Bainbridge

entries.name: Trigonometry
entries.desc: Trigonometry is the branch of mathematics that relates the angles of triangles to the lengths of their sides. It emerged in the Hellenistic world in the 3rd century BCE, when Euclid and Archimedes proved theorems on chords equivalent to later trigonometric formulae, and in 140 BCE Hipparchus gave the first tables of chords. Ptolemy set out detailed tables in his Almagest in the 2nd century CE, and the modern definition of the sine is first attested in the Indian Surya Siddhanta. Persian mathematicians such as Abu al-Wafa used all six trigonometric functions by the 10th century, and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi treated trigonometry as a discipline apart from astronomy.

entries.name: Barometer
entries.desc: A barometer is an instrument that measures air pressure, from which changes in the weather can be forecast. Evangelista Torricelli is usually credited with inventing it in 1643, though the historian W. E. Knowles Middleton holds 1644, when Torricelli first reported his experiments, the more likely date. After a water-tube experiment by Gasparo Berti and Raffaello Magiotti, Torricelli argued that the weight of the atmosphere, not the pull of a vacuum, held up the liquid, and he used mercury so that a tube of only 80 cm was needed. In September 1648 Florin Perier carried a barometer up the Puy de Dôme for Blaise Pascal and found that the mercury stood lower at altitude.

entries.name: Thermometer
entries.desc: A thermometer measures temperature through a change in a sensor that is read against a scale. Philo of Byzantium in the 3rd century BCE and Hero of Alexandria described devices in which heated and cooled air moved water, and in the late 16th and early 17th centuries Galileo Galilei and Santorio Santorio built thermoscopes, which had no scale. The first instrument shown with a scale, and so a thermometer, was Santorio's of 1625; in 1629 Joseph Solomon Delmedigo described a sealed liquid-in-glass thermometer. Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit made a reliable mercury thermometer in 1714, and Anders Celsius proposed his scale in 1742.

entries.name: Kite
entries.desc: A kite is a tethered craft heavier than air whose wing surfaces react against the wind to give lift. It was first made in China, where kites of silk and bamboo, and of paper after its invention in the Han dynasty, served to measure distances, test the wind, lift men and signal in war; by 549 CE a kite carried a message for a rescue mission. Kites spread to India, where the fighter kite developed, and across Polynesia, but reached Europe late: Konrad Kyeser described dragon kites about 1400. Benjamin Franklin published an account of a kite experiment on lightning in 1752, and kites served the research of the Wright brothers toward the first airplane.

entries.name: Lathe
entries.desc: A lathe is a machine tool that turns a workpiece about an axis while tools cut, sand, drill or shape it into a form symmetrical about that axis. Clear evidence of turning comes from the 6th century BCE: fragments of a wooden bowl in an Etruscan tomb in northern Italy and two wooden dishes with turned rims from present-day Turkey. A painting in the tomb of Petosiris in 4th-century BCE Egypt is the first known picture of a lathe, and in China rotary lathes sharpened tools and weapons by about 400 BCE. Andrey Nartov built a lathe with a tool-carrying carriage and gears in 1718, and by the 1770s precision lathes with a slide-rest had become practical.

entries.name: Screw
entries.desc: A screw is a helically threaded fastener tightened or released by twisting its head, and one of the six classical simple machines. It was one of the last simple machines to be invented, first appearing in Mesopotamia in the Neo-Assyrian period (911–609 BCE) and later in Ancient Egypt and Greece, where Archytas of Tarentum described it. By the 1st century BCE wooden screws drove the presses that pressed olive oil and grape juice around the Mediterranean. Metal screws became common fasteners only from the 1760s, when Job and William Wyatt patented a screw machine, and Jesse Ramsden made the first satisfactory screw-cutting lathe in 1777.

entries.name: Loom
entries.desc: A loom is a device for weaving cloth and tapestry that holds the warp threads under tension while the weft threads are passed over and under them. The earliest evidence of a horizontal loom is a picture on a pottery dish from ancient Egypt dated to 4400 BCE, showing a frame loom with treadles that left the weaver's hands free to pass and beat the weft. The warp-weighted loom, whose warp is kept taut by hanging weights, may go back to the Neolithic. The drawloom for patterned silk is first confirmed by fabrics from the State of Chu of about 400 BCE; it sped up Chinese silk weaving and was introduced to Persia, India and Europe.

entries.name: Sewing needle
entries.desc: A sewing needle is a slender pointed tool with an eye at one end to carry thread through material. A needle of bird bone found in Denisova Cave and attributed to the Denisovans is estimated to be about 50,000 years old, and a bone needle from Potok Cave in Slovenia dates to the Aurignacian, 47,000 to 41,000 years ago. Bone and ivory needles come from Xiaogushan in Liaoning and from Kostenki in Russia, and Flinders Petrie found copper sewing needles at Naqada in Egypt dating from 4400 to 3000 BCE. Iron needles are known from the third century BCE, and needle-making began at Redditch in England in 1639.

entries.name: Pencil
entries.desc: A pencil is a writing or drawing implement with a solid core of pigment, usually graphite, in a protective casing. Around 1560 the Italian couple Simonio and Lyndiana Bernacotti made what are likely the first plans for a wood-encased pencil, from a hollowed stick of juniper. In 1565 a large deposit of pure, solid graphite, then thought to be a form of lead and called plumbago, was found at Seathwaite in Borrowdale, Cumbria, England, and its sticks were at first wrapped in string or sheepskin. The first attempt to make graphite sticks from powder was in Nuremberg in 1662, and in 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté fired powdered graphite with clay, the method still in use.

entries.name: Wheelbarrow
entries.desc: A wheelbarrow is a small hand-propelled vehicle, usually with one wheel, pushed and guided by a single person using two handles at the rear. The earliest evidence comes from Han dynasty China: a painted tomb mural at Chengdu in Sichuan, dated to 118 CE, shows a man pushing one. The Records of the Three Kingdoms credit the minister Zhuge Liang with a 'wooden ox' that carried military supplies in 231 CE. Chinese wheelbarrows mostly carried the load over a large central wheel, while those that appeared in medieval Europe between 1170 and 1250 had the wheel at or near the front.

entries.name: Hot air balloon
entries.desc: A hot air balloon is a lighter-than-air aircraft whose envelope holds heated air, with a basket or gondola for passengers and a source of heat hung beneath it. The French brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier developed one at Annonay in Ardèche and flew it unmanned in public in September 1783. On 21 November 1783 Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier and François Laurent d'Arlandes made the first untethered manned flight, in Paris, in a Montgolfier balloon. The French used a balloon for observation at the battle of Fleurus in 1794, and Ed Yost and Jim Winker developed modern balloons with an onboard heat source from the 1950s.

entries.name: Parachute
entries.desc: A parachute is a device that slows an object's descent through an atmosphere by creating drag. The oldest known design appears in a manuscript of the 1470s attributed to Francesco di Giorgio Martini, a man hanging from a conical canopy, and Leonardo da Vinci sketched a pyramidal one about 1485. Louis-Sébastien Lenormand made the first recorded public jump, in France in 1783, and coined the word in 1785. André Garnerin made the first descent under a frameless silk canopy in 1797, Gleb Kotelnikov invented the knapsack parachute in 1911, and in World War I observers escaped from tethered balloons by parachute.

entries.name: Helicopter
entries.desc: A helicopter is a rotorcraft whose lift and thrust come from horizontally spinning rotors, so that it can take off and land vertically and hover. Chinese children played with bamboo flying toys from around 400 BCE, and Leonardo da Vinci designed an 'aerial screw' in the early 1480s. In 1907 the Breguet brothers' Gyroplane No. 1 lifted its pilot about 0.6 metres while men held it steady, and on 13 November 1907 Paul Cornu's machine made the first free flight with a pilot, in France. The Focke-Wulf Fw 61 of 1936 was the first practical helicopter, and Igor Sikorsky's R-4 of 1942 the first in full-scale production.

entries.name: Junk
entries.desc: A junk is a Chinese sailing ship with a central rudder, an overhanging flat transom, watertight bulkheads and a flat bottom, built with iron nails and clamps. It grew from tapering rafts rather than dugout canoes, and Chinese junks were at first river craft with square sails. Under the Song dynasty (960–1279) they took up ocean-going features from Southeast Asian ships: Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Table Talks, published by 1119, describes hulls divided by bulkheads, and the battened junk sail was adopted around the 12th century. Under the Yuan, Chinese trade ships displaced Southeast Asian ones on their Indian Ocean routes.

entries.name: Dugout canoe
entries.desc: A dugout canoe, or logboat, is a boat made from a hollowed-out tree, and the oldest boat type archaeologists have found. Before metal tools the log was hollowed with controlled fires and the burnt wood removed with an adze. The Pesse canoe from the Netherlands, carbon dated to between 8040 and 7510 BCE, is believed to be the world's oldest boat; the Dufuna canoe of Nigeria and a dugout from Kuahuqiao in Zhejiang, China, are both about 8,000 years old. Dugouts could be fitted with outriggers for rougher water, and they are still paddled and punted on lakes and rivers in Africa and Asia.

entries.name: Horseshoe
entries.desc: A horseshoe is a piece of equipment, usually nailed through the hoof wall, that protects a horse's hoof from wear. Its origin is uncertain, since worn iron was usually reforged: bronze shoes with apparent nail holes come from an Etruscan tomb of around 400 BCE, iron remnants from tombs in northeast China of the Goguryeo period dated to 414 CE, and a shoe with its nails from the tomb of the Frankish king Childeric I at Tournai. Written records of nailed shoes begin around 900 CE; by the Crusades horseshoes were widespread in Europe, and in China iron shoes became common under the Yuan dynasty.

entries.name: Spear-thrower
entries.desc: A spear-thrower, or atlatl, is a lever, usually about as long as the user's arm or forearm, with a cup or spur that holds the butt of a dart or javelin and throws it faster than the arm alone could. It is believed to have been used by Homo sapiens since the Upper Paleolithic, and the earliest known example is a Solutrean spear-thrower of reindeer antler, 17,500 years old, from Combe Saunière in the Dordogne, France. Ice Age hunters used it against megafauna; in Europe the bow and arrow supplemented it, while it stayed in use in the Americas, where Teotihuacan's warriors carried it, and in Australia as the woomera.

entries.name: Bayonet
entries.desc: A bayonet is a knife, dagger, sword or spike mounted on the barrel of a musket or rifle, so that the gun can be used as a spear in close combat. The first recorded bayonet proper is the 'gun-knife' of the son-and-mother gun in the Chinese military treatise Binglu of 1606, a plug bayonet pushed into the barrel. Jean Martinet standardized plug bayonets for new French fusilier regiments in 1671; because they stopped the gun from firing, socket bayonets that fitted around the barrel replaced them, and by the mid-18th century most European armies had adopted these for massed infantry charges.

entries.name: Torpedo
entries.desc: A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater weapon with an explosive warhead that detonates on contact with or close to its target. The word first named mines and spar torpedoes, used by Cornelius Drebbel, Robert Fulton and in the American Civil War. In 1864 the naval officer Giovanni Luppis gave the English engineer Robert Whitehead plans for a floating weapon at Fiume, now Rijeka in Croatia; Whitehead made from it the first modern self-propelled torpedo, run underwater by compressed air, and presented it to the Austrian Imperial Naval commission on 21 December 1866. On 16 January 1878 the Turkish steamer Intibah became the first ship sunk by self-propelled torpedoes.

entries.name: Rifling
entries.desc: Rifling is the helical grooving cut inside a gun barrel to spin the projectile, steadying its flight and making it more accurate. Its inventor is not known: straight 'soot grooves' were cut in small arms from at least 1480, and among the earliest recorded spiral-grooved barrels are those of the Vienna gunsmith Gaspard Kollner in 1498 and of Augustus Kotter of Nuremberg in 1520. Because the grooves had to be engraved by hand, rifled guns were at first used mostly by wealthy hunters, and they became common only in the mid-19th century; the first practical military rifled weapons were breech-loaders such as the Queen Anne pistol.

entries.name: Crane
entries.desc: A crane is a machine that lifts and moves loads with a boom, hoist, ropes or chains and sheaves, using levers and pulleys for mechanical advantage. The shaduf, a crane-like lever for lifting irrigation water, was used in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, but building cranes appear in Greece in the late 6th century BCE, attested by cuttings for lifting tongs and Lewis irons on temple blocks. The Romans added pulleys and treadwheels: a polyspastos worked by four men could lift 3,000 kg. Treadwheel cranes returned to Europe in the High Middle Ages for Gothic cathedrals and harbours, and steam engines, then internal combustion engines and electric motors, later powered them.

entries.name: Typewriter
entries.desc: The typewriter is a mechanical or electromechanical machine that prints characters on paper when a key is pressed, a type element striking an inked ribbon against the page. Its invention was incremental: Rasmus Malling-Hansen of Denmark invented the Hansen Writing Ball in 1865, and it went into commercial production in 1870 as the first typewriter sold. The first commercially successful model was patented in 1868 by Christopher Latham Sholes and others in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and made by E. Remington and Sons from 1873 with the QWERTY layout, still the standard for English computer keyboards. Personal computers largely replaced typewriters after the 1980s.

entries.name: Phonograph
entries.desc: The phonograph is a device for the mechanical and analogue recording and reproduction of sound, in which a stylus traces a groove cut into a rotating cylinder or disc. Thomas Edison, working to play back recorded telegraph messages and to automate speech for the telephone, announced it in November 1877 and patented it in 1878; his first machines recorded on tinfoil wrapped round a grooved cylinder. Alexander Graham Bell's Volta Laboratory improved it in the 1880s with the graphophone and wax-coated cylinders, and in the 1890s Emile Berliner moved from cylinders to flat discs, naming his machine the gramophone. The disc record was the main commercial audio format for most of the 20th century.

entries.name: Lithography
entries.desc: Lithography is a planographic method of printing based on the immiscibility of oil and water: an image drawn with a greasy substance on smooth limestone or a metal plate takes the oily ink, while the wetted, etched surface around it repels it. The German author and actor Alois Senefelder invented it in the Electorate of Bavaria in 1796, and it was first used mostly for musical scores and maps. Godefroy Engelmann introduced multicolour printing, chromolithography, in 1837, and offset lithography, in which a rubber cylinder carries the ink from plate to paper, has printed most books and magazines since the 1960s.

credit.artist: Pierre Puvis de Chavannes. Imprimerie Lemercier, 57 Rue de Seine, Paris.

entries.name: Morse code
entries.desc: Morse code is a method of telecommunication that encodes letters, numerals and punctuation as standard sequences of two signal durations, dots and dashes. Around 1837 the American artist Samuel Morse devised a code of numerals for the electrical telegraph he was developing with Joseph Henry and Alfred Vail; in 1840 Vail extended it to letters, giving the shortest signs to the commonest ones, and this code was first used in 1844. Friedrich Gerke's simpler Hamburg alphabet of 1848, adopted in Germany and Austria in 1851, led to the International Morse code of 1865, which also carried early radio communication from the 1890s.

entries.name: Braille
entries.desc: Braille is a tactile writing system used by blind and visually impaired people, in which characters are formed by six raised dots arranged in two columns of three, the braille cell. Louis Braille, a Frenchman who had lost his sight in a childhood accident, developed it in 1824 at the age of fifteen as an improvement on Charles Barbier's night writing, whose sets of 12 embossed dots encoded 36 sounds; Braille's cells stood for the letters of the French alphabet and added numerals and punctuation. He published the system, with musical notation, in 1829. Braille codes now exist for over 133 languages.

entries.name: Radar
entries.desc: Radar is a system that uses radio waves to find the distance, direction and speed of objects such as aircraft, ships and weather formations; the United States Navy coined the name in 1940 from radio detection and ranging. In 1904 the German inventor Christian Hülsmeyer detected a ship in dense fog with his telemobiloscope, but German military officials rejected it. Pulsed radar was first shown in December 1934 by Robert M. Page at the Naval Research Laboratory, and in Britain Robert Watson-Watt's team built the Chain Home stations, operational from 1936, which helped the Royal Air Force win the Battle of Britain. The cavity magnetron made small sets possible.

entries.name: Personal computer
entries.desc: A personal computer is a computer designed to be operated directly by one user, rather than shared by many through time-sharing like a minicomputer or mainframe. It was made possible by the integrated circuit and the microprocessor, the first single-chip one being the Intel 4004 of 1971; the Micral N, built from 1972, was the earliest commercial, non-kit microcomputer based on a microprocessor. The Altair 8800 of 1974 was the first commercially successful personal computer, the Commodore PET, Apple II and TRS-80 brought ready-assembled machines to a mass market in 1977, and the IBM Personal Computer of 1981 set the standard its compatibles followed.

entries.name: Email
entries.desc: Email, or electronic mail, is a method of sending and receiving digital messages over a computer network, on a store-and-forward model in which servers accept, forward, deliver and store messages. Messaging between users of the same computer became possible with time-sharing in the early 1960s, with a notable implementation in MIT's CTSS project in 1965. In 1971 the first network mail was sent over the ARPANET, introducing addresses with the @ symbol for the user's system; the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol was implemented on the ARPANET in 1983, and after 1995 SMTP, POP3 and IMAP became the standard.

entries.name: Transatlantic telegraph cable
entries.desc: The transatlantic telegraph cables were undersea cables laid across the Atlantic Ocean for telegraph communication between Europe and the Americas. The Atlantic Telegraph Company, led by Cyrus West Field, laid the first from Valentia Island off Ireland to Trinity Bay, Newfoundland, and it carried its first messages on August 16, 1858, among them Queen Victoria's congratulations to President James Buchanan, but it failed after three weeks. Cables laid from the SS Great Eastern in 1865 and 1866 proved durable, and since 1866 the continents have been linked, so that a message could be answered on the same day rather than after weeks by ship.

entries.name: Mercator projection
entries.desc: The Mercator projection is a way of drawing the globe on a flat map in which courses of constant compass bearing, rhumb lines, appear as straight lines, so that a chart serves sailors directly. Gerardus Mercator introduced it on his world map of 1569, printed from 18 copper plates he engraved himself, by increasing the degrees of latitude towards each pole as the parallels lengthen. He left no account of his method, and Edward Wright and others later showed how to calculate the latitude scale exactly. Acceptance was slow and came only with the French sea atlas Le Neptune Francois at the end of the seventeenth century; the projection is still the basis of navigation charts.

entries.name: Library of Ashurbanipal
entries.desc: The Library of Ashurbanipal is a collection of more than 30,000 clay tablets and fragments of the 7th century BCE, gathered at Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, by Ashurbanipal, king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 668 to 627 BCE. He had cities and centres of learning across Mesopotamia send him copies of their texts, sent scribes to collect them and took tablets as war loot; the texts, mostly Akkadian in cuneiform, were placed in rooms by subject and marked with coloured signs or their first words. The fire that destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE baked the tablets, among them the Epic of Gilgamesh. Most are now in the British Museum.

entries.name: Fired brick
entries.desc: Fired brick is brick of clay and shale baked in a kiln, harder and longer-lasting than the older sun-dried mudbrick. Mesopotamia had discovered it between 5000 and 4500 BCE, and the earliest fired bricks of China appeared around 4400 BCE at Chengtoushan, a walled settlement of the Daxi culture, where they paved house floors. Indus Valley cities such as Kalibangan used it by 3000 BCE, and the Roman legions stamped the bricks of their mobile kilns across the empire. The first brick-making machine was patented in 1852, as the Industrial Revolution multiplied production.

entries.name: Flying buttress
entries.desc: A flying buttress is a ramping arch that carries the outward thrust of a stone vault or roof from the upper part of a wall across open space to a massive pier standing away from it. Ancient examples survive on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and the Rotunda of Galerius in Thessaloniki, and Romanesque churches such as Durham Cathedral hid similar arches under their gallery roofs. By the 1160s builders in the Île-de-France ran longer, visible arches over the aisles, as at Saint-Germain-des-Prés, completed in 1163, and Notre Dame de Paris in 1180. Walls could then be thinner, with larger windows of stained glass, and the flying buttress became a defining feature of Gothic architecture.

entries.name: Reinforced concrete
entries.desc: Reinforced concrete is concrete with embedded iron or steel bars or mesh, which take the tension plain concrete cannot bear while the concrete resists compression. It was developed in parallel in England and France in the mid-19th century. The French builder François Coignet built the first iron-reinforced concrete structure, a four-story house in the suburbs of Paris, in 1853–55, and in 1854 the English builder William B. Wilkinson reinforced the roof and floors of a house with knowledge of tensile stresses. Joseph Monier patented reinforced flowerpots in 1867 and columns and girders in 1877, and the firm Wayss & Freytag made the first commercial use of it in 1884.

entries.name: Portland cement
entries.desc: Portland cement is a hydraulic cement made by heating limestone and clay minerals in a kiln to form clinker, then grinding it with a little gypsum; it is the most common cement and the basic ingredient of concrete and mortar. Joseph Aspdin patented it in England in 1824 and named it after Portland stone, quarried on the Isle of Portland in Dorset. It grew out of the natural cements made in Britain from the middle of the 18th century, John Smeaton’s experiments of 1756 and Louis Vicat’s artificial hydraulic lime. His son William Aspdin improved it in the 1840s at Rotherhithe, and the rotary kiln, patented in 1885, allowed continuous manufacture.

entries.name: Hypocaust
entries.desc: A hypocaust is a system of central heating in which hot air and smoke from a furnace circulate beneath a floor raised on stacks of tiles, the pilae, and rise through clay or tile flues in the walls. Vitruvius attributes its invention to Sergius Orata around 80 BCE, and described its construction in his De architectura of about 15 BCE. Hypocausts heated public baths and the villas of the wealthy throughout the Roman Empire, and their remains survive across Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. The system fell out of use in the western provinces as the empire declined, but lived on in the Eastern Roman Empire and in the baths of Al Andalus.

entries.name: Vulcanization
entries.desc: Vulcanization is the hardening of rubber, originally of natural rubber treated with sulfur and heat, which forms cross-links between its polymer chains and makes it firmer and more durable. Ancient Mesoamerican cultures already cured rubber with sulfur-rich plant juices, an early form of the process. Charles Goodyear, who worked in the 1830s to strengthen rubber, found in 1839 that a mixture of rubber and sulfur dropped on a hot pan hardened instead of melting, and by 1844 he had patented the process and produced the rubber on an industrial scale. Thomas Hancock had taken out a British patent eight weeks earlier, in November 1843.

entries.name: Friction match
entries.desc: A friction match is a small stick tipped with a mixture that ignites when struck against a rough surface. Pinewood sticks tipped with sulfur, lit from a flame, are described in China around 950, and in 1805 Jean Chancel of Paris made a match lit by dipping it in sulfuric acid. The first commercially successful friction match was made by John Walker, a chemist and pharmacist of Stockton-on-Tees, England, and first recorded in April 1827: sticks tipped with antimony trisulfide and potassium chlorate. Samuel Jones sold an improved version as the lucifer, and Gustaf Erik Pasch’s striking surface of red phosphorus of 1844 led to the safety match.

entries.name: Egyptian blue
entries.desc: Egyptian blue, a calcium copper silicate, is a pigment made by heating silica, lime, a copper compound and an alkali, and is considered the first synthetic pigment. The earliest evidence of its use is on an alabaster bowl of the late pre-dynastic period, Naqada III, about 3250 BCE, excavated at Hierakonpolis. Egyptians made it to imitate turquoise and lapis lazuli and painted it on tombs, wall paintings, furnishings and statues; it is also found in the Near East, the Eastern Mediterranean and the Roman Empire. Vitruvius described how it was made in the first century BCE, but its use died out in the fourth century CE and the method was forgotten until modern analysis.

entries.name: Lacquerware
entries.desc: Lacquerware consists of objects coated with lacquer, in East Asia an urushiol-based lacquer from the dried sap of the lacquer tree, Toxicodendron vernicifluum. The oldest known lacquerware, burial ornaments from an Initial Jōmon pit grave at the Kakinoshima site in Hakodate, Hokkaido, Japan, is about 9,000 years old, and the earliest in China is a red wooden bowl from a Hemudu culture site in Zhejiang. Chinese lacquer became a decorative art under the Shang dynasty and a commercial industry in the state of Chu under the Eastern Zhou, and spread to Korea and Japan; the traditions of Southeast Asia, South Asia and the Americas arose independently.

entries.name: Sulfuric acid
entries.desc: Sulfuric acid, called oil of vitriol by medieval alchemists, is a strong acid first made by distilling vitriols, the hydrated sulfates of metals. The Jabirian authors and Abu Bakr al-Razi distilled vitriols, and al-Razi may have made the acid unknowingly; according to Ahmad Y. al-Hassan, an anonymous Garshuni manuscript from before c. 1100 holds three recipes for it. European works first allude to it in the thirteenth century. Joshua Ward of London began large-scale production in 1736, John Roebuck’s lead chamber process of 1746 in Birmingham industrialised it, and Peregrine Phillips patented the contact process in 1831, by which nearly all of it is made today.

entries.name: Electrolysis
entries.desc: Electrolysis is the use of a direct electric current to drive a chemical reaction that would not otherwise occur, as in separating elements from ores and compounds. In 1800 William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle, furthering Volta’s experiments, placed the wires of a voltaic pile in water and saw hydrogen and oxygen bubble from them. Humphry Davy discovered potassium, sodium, barium, calcium and magnesium by electrolysis by 1808, and his assistant Michael Faraday published two laws of electrolysis and introduced the word in 1834. The method later yielded gallium in 1875, fluorine in 1886 and, through the Hall–Héroult process of the same year, aluminium.

entries.name: Hall–Héroult process
entries.desc: The Hall–Héroult process is the major industrial process for smelting aluminium: alumina, obtained most often from bauxite, is dissolved in molten cryolite and the bath is electrolysed at 940–980 °C, giving metal of 99.5–99.8% purity. It was discovered independently and almost simultaneously in 1886 by the American chemist Charles Martin Hall and the Frenchman Paul Héroult, both 22 years old. Before it, aluminium was made with sodium or potassium and cost more than gold; Hall opened the first large-scale plant in Pittsburgh in 1888, later Alcoa, and with cheaper electric power the metal became an inexpensive commodity. The process uses much electricity and can emit much carbon dioxide.

entries.name: Stethoscope
entries.desc: The stethoscope is a medical device for listening to the sounds of the heart, lungs and intestines and to blood flow, a practice called auscultation. René Laennec invented it in 1816 at the Necker-Enfants Malades Hospital in Paris: a monaural wooden tube, devised after he found that a rolled piece of paper carried heart sounds without his ear touching the patient's chest. Golding Bird described one with a flexible tube in 1840, and Arthur Leared made a binaural stethoscope in 1851. George Philip Cammann's design of the following year, with a plug for each ear, has remained essentially unchanged since.

entries.name: Blood transfusion
entries.desc: Blood transfusion is the transfer of blood or its components into the veins of a human or other animal. The physician Richard Lower performed the first reliably documented successful transfusion, between two dogs, in February 1665, and described it to the Royal Society that December. On 15 June 1667 Jean-Baptiste Denys transfused a sheep's blood into a 15-year-old boy, but deaths after such experiments led to bans in 1668. James Blundell performed the first successful transfusion of human blood, for bleeding after childbirth, in 1818 at Guy's Hospital in London, and Karl Landsteiner's discovery of blood groups in 1901 gave the practice a scientific basis.

entries.name: Prosthesis
entries.desc: A prosthesis is an artificial device that replaces a missing body part lost through injury, disease or a condition present at birth. The earliest archaeological evidence is an eye prosthesis, probably of bitumen paste covered with a thin layer of gold, buried with a woman at Shahr-i Shōkhta in Iran about 3000 to 2800 BCE. A wood and leather artificial big toe found on a mummy near Thebes, dated 950 to 710 BCE, shows signs of use. Ambroise Paré, considered the father of modern prosthetics, designed an above-knee device, and functional prostheses appeared in the 1500s.

entries.name: Sulfonamide
entries.desc: Sulfonamides, or sulfa drugs, were the first broadly effective antibacterial medicines used systemically. Experiments began in 1932 in the laboratories of Bayer AG, then part of IG Farben, where a team led by Gerhard Domagk found that Prontosil, a red dye synthesised by Josef Klarer, stopped some bacterial infections in mice; the first report appeared in 1935. A team at the Pasteur Institute showed that the body breaks Prontosil down into sulfanilamide, a compound first made in 1906 whose patent had expired. Between 1937 and 1943 sulfa drugs lowered maternal mortality in the United States by 25–40%.

entries.name: Artificial cardiac pacemaker
entries.desc: An artificial cardiac pacemaker is a medical device that sends electrical pulses through electrodes to the chambers of the heart to keep an even heart rate. The first fully implantable pacemaker, designed by the inventor Rune Elmqvist and the surgeon Åke Senning, was implanted on 8 October 1958 at the Karolinska Institute in Solna, Sweden; it failed after three hours, and its patient, Arne Larsson, went on to receive 26 pacemakers. Earlier devices were external, from Mark C Lidwill's apparatus of 1926 in Sydney to John Hopps's of 1950. Wilson Greatbatch's lithium iodide cell of 1971 led to pacemakers lasting up to eleven years.

entries.name: Organ transplantation
entries.desc: Organ transplantation is the removal of an organ or tissue from one body and its placement in another, to replace a damaged or missing function. The first transplant in the modern sense was performed in 1883 by the Swiss surgeon Theodor Kocher, who reversed the symptoms that followed the complete removal of the thyroid by implanting thyroid tissue. Alexis Carrel's techniques for joining blood vessels, from the early 1900s, laid the groundwork for later transplant surgery, but rejection defeated most attempts until Joseph Murray's kidney transplant between identical twins in Boston in 1954. Christiaan Barnard performed the first human-to-human heart transplant in 1967.

entries.name: Electric motor
entries.desc: An electric motor is a machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy, usually through the interaction of a magnetic field and the current in a wire winding. Michael Faraday first showed electromagnetic rotation on 3 September 1821 at the Royal Institution, where a wire carrying a current turned around a magnet in a pool of mercury. Ányos Jedlik built a device with a stator, rotor and commutator in 1828, William Sturgeon a DC motor able to turn machinery in 1832, and Frank Julian Sprague the first practical DC motor in 1886. Galileo Ferraris and Nikola Tesla invented AC induction motors in 1885 and 1887.

entries.name: Diesel engine
entries.desc: A diesel engine is an internal combustion engine in which the fuel is ignited by the heat of air compressed in the cylinder, without a spark plug. The German engineer Rudolf Diesel published his idea in 1893 in Theory and Construction of a Rational Heat Motor, and his first prototype was built that summer at the Maschinenfabrik Augsburg, with the first ignition on 10 August 1893. A redesigned engine ran for 88 revolutions in February 1894, and the third prototype, tested on 17 February 1897, reached an effective efficiency of 26.2%, against the 6–10% of steam engines that Diesel had learned of as a student.

entries.name: Hydroelectricity
entries.desc: Hydroelectricity is electricity generated from hydropower, the energy of moving water. Water had long driven machinery, but the first hydroelectric power scheme was developed in 1878 by William Armstrong at Cragside in Northumberland, England, where it powered a single arc lamp in his art gallery. The Schoelkopf Power Station No. 1 near Niagara Falls began to produce electricity in 1881, and by 1889 there were 200 hydroelectric power stations in the United States alone. Dams grew larger through the 20th century, to the Three Gorges Dam in China at 22.5 GW, and hydropower supplied 15% of the world's electricity in 2023.

entries.name: Alternating current
entries.desc: Alternating current is an electric current that periodically reverses direction, the form in which electric power is delivered to homes and businesses. The French instrument maker Hippolyte Pixii built the first alternator to produce it in 1832, on Michael Faraday's principles. In 1885 Károly Zipernowsky, Ottó Bláthy and Miksa Déri of the Ganz Works in Budapest patented closed-core transformers, and their system of 75 transformers supplied 1,067 lamps at the Hungarian National Exhibition that May. Westinghouse then built AC systems across the United States, and the first three-phase system was established in Frankfurt in 1891.

entries.name: Lithium-ion battery
entries.desc: A lithium-ion battery is a rechargeable battery that stores energy by moving lithium ions in and out of electronically conducting solids. M. Stanley Whittingham conceived intercalation electrodes in the 1970s and made the first rechargeable lithium-ion battery, with a titanium disulfide cathode, though safety problems kept it from being commercialized. John Goodenough used lithium cobalt oxide as a cathode in 1980, and Akira Yoshino developed the first prototype of the modern battery, with a carbonaceous anode, in 1985. A Sony and Asahi Kasei team led by Yoshio Nishi brought it to market in 1991, and the three inventors shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

entries.name: Wind turbine
entries.desc: A wind turbine is a device that converts the kinetic energy of wind into electrical energy. The first to generate electricity was installed by the Austrian Josef Friedländer at the Vienna International Electrical Exhibition in 1883: a Halladay wind motor 6.6 m across, whose 3.7 kW drove a dynamo that charged batteries. James Blyth lit his holiday home in Marykirk, Scotland, with one in July 1887, and Charles F. Brush built the first automatically operated wind turbine some months later. A 100 kW forerunner of modern horizontal-axis machines ran at Yalta in 1931, and by 2024 turbines generated over 1,136 gigawatts.

entries.name: One Thousand and One Nights
entries.desc: One Thousand and One Nights grew over many centuries from Persian and Indian roots into a large and changing Arabic collection of tales, framed by Scheherazade's storytelling to save her life.

entries.name: The Tale of Genji
entries.desc: The Tale of Genji, attributed to the lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu and finished by about 1021, follows a prince's loves and fortunes at the Heian court and then his heirs, in a vernacular prose rich in poetry.

entries.name: Terracotta Army
entries.desc: The Terracotta Army is a collection of life-sized terracotta figures of soldiers, chariots and horses buried with Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China, in 210–209 BCE to protect him in the afterlife.

entries.name: McCarthyism
entries.desc: McCarthyism was the practice of accusing and investigating left-wing Americans for communist and Soviet influence on American institutions and for Soviet espionage, from the late 1940s through the 1950s. It began before Senator Joseph McCarthy's fame, with President Harry S. Truman's 1947 order screening federal employees for loyalty, and its best-known forms were McCarthy's own investigations and the hearings of the House Un-American Activities Committee. Many lives were ruined by blacklists, dismissals and verdicts later overturned. In 1954 the Senate voted 67 to 22 to condemn McCarthy, and rulings of the Supreme Court under Earl Warren helped bring the Second Red Scare to an end.

entries.name: De-Stalinization
entries.desc: De-Stalinization was a series of political reforms in the Soviet Union after the death of Joseph Stalin on 5 March 1953. It began quietly, with the release of Gulag prisoners and unpublicised rehabilitations, and became official on 25 February 1956, when Khrushchev's speech to a closed session of the 20th Party Congress laid out some of Stalin's crimes and denounced his cult of personality. Monuments to Stalin were removed, his name was taken off places and out of the state anthem, and on 31 October 1961 his body was moved from the Lenin Mausoleum. China and Albania, which condemned Khrushchev as a revisionist, cited it as a major cause of the Sino-Soviet split.

entries.name: The Exodus
entries.desc: The Exodus is the founding myth of the Israelites, told over four of the five books of the Pentateuch: Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. It tells of the Israelites' bondage in Egypt, the plagues, their departure through a passage in the Red Sea under the leadership of Moses and the wanderings in the wilderness up to the borders of Canaan. The story is central in Judaism, recounted daily in prayer and at Passover; early Christians read it as a prefiguration of salvation by Jesus, and the Quran recounts it in the life of Moses. Modern scholars hold that the Pentateuch does not give an accurate account of Israelite origins, though some elements may have a historical basis.

entries.name: Adolf Hitler's rise to power
entries.desc: Adolf Hitler's rise to power began in the Weimar Republic in September 1919, when he joined the German Workers' Party, soon renamed the Nazi Party, which he led from 1921. After the failed Beer Hall Putsch of 1923 and nine months in prison, where he wrote Mein Kampf, he sought power by legal means on a platform of anti-communism, antisemitism and ultranationalism. In July 1932, during the Great Depression, the Nazis became the largest party in the Reichstag. President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933; the Reichstag Fire Decree and the Enabling Act gave him dictatorial powers, and in August 1934 he merged the chancellery and the presidency as Führer.

entries.name: Orange Revolution
entries.desc: The Orange Revolution was a series of protests in Ukraine from late November 2004 to January 2005, set off by the presidential run-off of 21 November 2004 between Viktor Yushchenko and Viktor Yanukovych, which election monitors and much of the public held to have been rigged in Yanukovych's favour. Kyiv was the centre of a campaign of civil resistance, with daily demonstrations, sit-ins and general strikes across the country. Ukraine's Supreme Court annulled the result and ordered a new vote for 26 December 2004, which observers judged free and fair; Yushchenko won about 52% to Yanukovych's 44% and was inaugurated on 23 January 2005, ending the revolution.

entries.name: Hawaiian sovereignty movement
entries.desc: The Hawaiian sovereignty movement (ke ea Hawaiʻi) is a grassroots political and cultural campaign to re-establish an autonomous or independent Hawaiian nation or kingdom. It generally holds both the overthrow of Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893 and the United States' annexation of 1898 to have been illegal, and some groups seek redress. Led by Native Hawaiian organisations and activists since the 1960s and 1970s, it has opposed commercial development, the appropriation of burial grounds and sacred places and the bombing of Kahoʻolawe. In 1993 the United States Congress passed the Apology Resolution, acknowledging that the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom was illegal.

entries.name: Proclamation of the People's Republic of China
aka: founding of the People's Republic of China
entries.desc: The People's Republic of China was proclaimed by Mao Zedong, chairman of the Chinese Communist Party, on 1 October 1949 in Tiananmen Square in Beijing, a ceremony that also proclaimed the Central People's Government and marked the foundation of contemporary China. It came as the Communists won the final phase of the Chinese Civil War against the Kuomintang-led Nationalist government of the Republic of China, which retreated to Taiwan by December 1949. At the ceremony the March of the Volunteers was played as the national anthem, the Five-starred Red Flag was raised for the first time to a 21-gun salute, and the People's Liberation Army held its first public parade.
links: proclamation of the People's Republic of China

entries.name: Meiji era
entries.desc: The Meiji era was the period of Japanese history from 23 October 1868 to 30 July 1912, the reign of Emperor Meiji. In it Japan moved from an isolated feudal society at risk of colonisation by Western powers to an industrialised nation-state and emerging great power, adopting Western science, technology, law and political ideas; it opened with the Charter Oath of 1868 and gave Japan the Meiji Constitution of 1889. Former samurai rebelled against the changes in the 1870s, most notably in Saigō Takamori's Satsuma Rebellion. Victories over Qing China in 1894–1895 and over Russia in 1904–1905 made Japan an international power. It was followed by the Taishō era.

entries.name: Marquis de Lafayette
entries.desc: Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de La Fayette, was a French military officer and politician who volunteered to serve in the Continental Army under George Washington in the American Revolutionary War, commanding troops at the siege of Yorktown in 1781.
