Back in France he helped write the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen and commanded the National Guard after the storming of the Bastille, but fled in 1792 and spent more than five years in Austrian prisons. He later sat as a liberal in the Chamber of Deputies, toured all 24 American states in 1824 and, in the July Revolution of 1830, supported Louis-Philippe as king. He is known as the Hero of the Two Worlds.

entries.name: Joe Hill
entries.desc: Joe Hill, born Joel Emmanuel Hägglund in Gävle, Sweden, was a Swedish-American labour activist, poet and songwriter. After his mother died in 1902 he emigrated to the United States, worked odd jobs across North America and organised for the Industrial Workers of the World, becoming its most prolific songwriter with songs such as The Preacher and the Slave, There Is Power in a Union and The Rebel Girl. Convicted in 1914 of the murder of a Salt Lake City grocer and his son on questionable evidence, he was executed by firing squad on 19 November 1915 despite calls for clemency, including from President Woodrow Wilson. He became a folk hero of the American labour movement.

entries.name: Kayak
entries.desc: A kayak is a small, narrow boat with an enclosed deck, propelled by a long double-bladed paddle; its name comes from the Inuktitut word qajaq. It was first used by Aleut, Inuit and Yupik hunters, and possibly the Ainu, in the subarctic, and is believed to be at least 4,000 years old. The first kayaks were made of stitched seal or other animal skins stretched over a frame of wood or whalebone, each built by the man who used it to fit his own body. Hunters used them for seals above all, and in some areas for whales and caribou; skin-on-frame kayaks are still used for hunting by Inuit in Greenland.

entries.name: Umiak
entries.desc: The umiak is an open skin boat of the Yupik and Inuit, once found along all the coasts from Siberia to Greenland and first used in Thule times. Its frame of driftwood or whalebone, pegged and lashed together, was covered with walrus or bearded seal skins, about seven for a large boat of 9.1 metres. Much larger than the kayak, it could carry up to 15 passengers yet was light enough for a few people to carry over the ice to open water. It was used in summer to move people and their belongings to seasonal hunting grounds and to hunt whales and walrus, rowed by women or paddled by men.

entries.name: Inuit art
entries.desc: Inuit art is the art made by the Inuit and related peoples of the circumpolar north. Its oldest forebears are the small carvings of the Dorset culture, which from around 600 BCE worked walrus ivory, bone and caribou antler into birds, bears, walruses, seals, human figures and tiny masks, often worn as amulets. For centuries walrus ivory remained the favoured material. Since markets for Inuit art opened in the south in 1945, prints and figures carved in soft stone such as soapstone, serpentinite and argillite have also become popular. The Winnipeg Art Gallery holds the largest public collection of contemporary Inuit art.

credit.artist: Palaya Qiatsuq (Cape Dorset, Nunavut Territory, Canada)

entries.name: Amesbury Archer
entries.desc: The Amesbury Archer was an early Bronze Age man of the Bell Beaker culture whose grave was found in May 2002 at Amesbury, near Stonehenge in England. He died in middle age around 2300 BCE and is named for the sixteen barbed flint arrowheads buried with him. His grave held more objects than any other early Bronze Age burial in Britain, including five Beaker pots, three copper knives, a stone wrist-guard, metalworking tools that suggest he was a coppersmith, and the earliest known gold objects found in England. Isotope analysis of his teeth shows that he spent his childhood in Central Europe, probably in the Western Alps.

entries.name: Clovis point
entries.desc: Clovis points are the fluted stone projectile points of the Clovis culture of prehistoric North America, all dated to roughly 13,400 to 12,700 years ago. A typical point is a lance-shaped blade about 10 centimetres long, shaped by careful pressure flaking, with a concave base from which grooves, called flutes, were removed on one or both faces so that it could be hafted. They are found in dense concentrations across much of North America. They are named after Clovis, New Mexico, where examples were first found in 1929. Whether they tipped thrusting spears, thrown darts or were also used for butchering is debated.

entries.name: Sumatralith
entries.desc: A sumatralith is a stone tool made by flaking one face of a rounded river cobble around its edge, leaving the other side unworked. Made from quartzite or andesite by hunter-gatherers of Southeast Asia from the late Pleistocene to the middle Holocene, it is the tool most closely associated with the Hoabinhian, and archaeologists treat it as the chief sign of a Hoabinhian site. The name comes from North Sumatra in Indonesia, where J. Neumann first recovered such tools from a shell midden at Batu Kenong in 1920. Because so little of the cobble is shaped, a sumatralith could be resharpened again and again.

credit.source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:临沧考古博物馆-旧石器时代-农克硝洞遗址-苏门答腊器1.jpg

entries.name: Nuraghe
entries.desc: The nuraghe is the main type of ancient megalithic building of Sardinia, raised during the Nuragic Age between 1900 and 730 BCE and today the symbol of the island and its Nuragic civilisation. A typical nuraghe is a tower shaped like a cone with its top cut off, built of layers of stones that grow smaller towards the top, with a corridor leading to a round chamber roofed by a corbelled dome. More than 7,000 have been found, and archaeologists believe there were once more than 10,000. Their purpose is still debated: fortresses, religious places, refuges or the seats of village chiefs.

entries.name: Nuragic bronze statuettes
entries.desc: The Nuragic bronze statuettes, bronzetti in Italian, are small bronze sculptures made in Sardinia at the end of the Bronze Age and in the early Iron Age. More than 500 have been found, mostly in places of worship such as holy wells and temples, but also in villages and nuraghes, and some in Etruscan tombs of central Italy. Probably cast by the lost-wax method and up to 39 centimetres tall, they show chiefs, warriors, divinities, people of every rank, animals, everyday objects and ships. They were long dated to the 9th to 6th centuries BCE, but fragments found at Orroli and Ballao have called that into question.

entries.name: Heuneburg
entries.desc: The Heuneburg is a prehistoric Celtic hillfort above the Danube near Herbertingen in Baden-Württemberg, southern Germany, one of the most important early Celtic centres of Central Europe in the time of the Hallstatt culture. Its citadel, about 300 by 150 metres, stood on a spur 40 metres above the river and is thought to have controlled more than 1,000 square kilometres of settlements, roads and cemeteries. For a time it was walled with sun-dried mudbrick on a limestone base, a wall destroyed in 530 BCE. Called the oldest city north of the Alps, it has been identified with Pyrene, the Celtic city named by Herodotus.

entries.name: Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites
entries.desc: The Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites in South Korea hold more than 1,000 stone dolmens, used as grave markers and for rituals during the first millennium BCE. The Korean Peninsula has over 35,000 dolmens, about 40% of all in the world. They mark the graves of the ruling elite, and pottery, comma-shaped jewels, bronzes and stone tools have been excavated from them. Dolmens in Korea date from the seventh century BCE, at places such as Gochang, until around the third century BCE. Excavation began in 1965, and the sites were made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.
links: Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites

entries.name: Ain Sakhri figurine
entries.desc: The Ain Sakhri figurine, or Ain Sakhri Lovers, is a Natufian stone sculpture of a couple, about 11,000 years old, found in one of the Ain Sakhri caves near Bethlehem. Carved from a single calcite cobble and without faces or other details, it is thought to be the oldest known representation of two people in sexual intercourse. The prehistorian René Neuville identified it in 1933 among finds kept by the French Fathers at Bethlehem and traced it to the caves, which had been lived in during the Natufian period. The British Museum bought it in 1958.

entries.name: Makassan contact with Australia
entries.desc: From around the middle of the 18th century, Makassarese merchants and Sama-Bajau fishermen from southern Sulawesi in Indonesia sailed each year to the coast of northern Australia, first to the Kimberley region and some decades later to Arnhem Land. They came to gather and process trepang, the sea cucumber, which was boiled, dried and smoked for sale in Chinese markets. The visits left their mark on the Aboriginal peoples of the coast: the Makassar word for trepang, for one, entered the Aboriginal languages of the Cobourg Peninsula. The name Makassan is used for all the trepangers who came to northern Australia.

entries.name: Su Nuraxi
entries.desc: Su Nuraxi is a Nuragic archaeological site at Barumini in Sardinia, whose name means simply "the nuraghe" in Campidanese Sardinian. Its oldest part is a central tower of basalt blocks with three chambers one above another, 18.6 metres high, built between the 17th and 13th centuries BCE; in the Late Bronze Age four corner towers joined by a wall were built around it, and a village inhabited from the 13th to the 6th century BCE grew up around the whole. First explored by the archaeologist Giovanni Lilliu, its discoverer, it is considered the most impressive expression of the Nuragic civilisation and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

entries.name: Dogū
entries.desc: Dogū, "earthen figures", are small clay figurines of people and animals made in the later part of the Jōmon period of prehistoric Japan and no longer made in the Yayoi period that followed. Typically 10 to 30 centimetres high, most appear to be female, with big eyes, small waists and wide hips, and many take them to represent goddesses. Some 15,000 to 18,000 are known, from all of Japan except Okinawa and mostly from the east. Their purpose is unknown; some scholars suggest that illnesses were thought to pass into them before they were broken. They are not to be confused with the later haniwa.

entries.name: Dong Son drum
entries.desc: The Dong Son drums are ancient bronze drums made by the Dong Son culture of the Red River Delta in what is now Vietnam, from about 600 BCE or earlier until the third century CE. Cast by the lost-wax method, they stand up to a metre high and weigh up to 100 kilograms, and seem to have been both musical instruments and objects of worship. Their surfaces show geometric patterns, scenes of daily life, farming and war, animals, birds such as the Lạc bird, and boats. More than 200 have been found, from eastern Indonesia to Vietnam and parts of southern China, carried as trade goods and kept as heirlooms.

entries.name: Samos
entries.desc: Samos is a Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea, separated from Anatolia by the Mycale Strait. In ancient times it was a rich and powerful city-state, known for its vineyards and wine, and it reached the height of its prosperity under the tyrant Polycrates in the 6th century BCE, when the engineer Eupalinos dug a tunnel through a mountain to bring water to the city. The Heraion of Samos, a temple of Hera, and the Eupalinian aqueduct are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Pythagoras, Epicurus and the astronomer Aristarchus of Samos were born there. From 1835 the island was a semi-autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty, until it joined Greece in 1913.

entries.name: Ifá
entries.desc: Ifá is a system of divination that originated in Yorubaland in West Africa, within the traditional religion of the Yoruba people. According to Ifá teaching it is overseen by the orisha Orunmila, who is believed to have given it to humanity. Its initiates, called babaláwo if male and ìyánífá if female, consult a body of 256 signs, the Odù, using a divining chain or palm nuts on a wooden divination tray, the ọpọ́n Ifá. Yoruba influence spread Ifá to neighbouring peoples such as the Fon, and the Atlantic slave trade carried it to the Americas, where it survived in Cuba alongside Santería.

entries.name: Orisha
entries.desc: The orishas are the divine spirits of the Yoruba religion of West Africa and of the religions of the African diaspora that derive from it, among them Haitian Vodou, Cuban Santería and Brazilian Candomblé. According to these traditions they are spirits sent by the supreme creator, Olodumare, to help humanity on Earth, and many are held to have lived first in the spirit realm and then as humans. The Atlantic slave trade carried their worship to the Americas. In the Lucumí tradition of Cuba the orishas were identified with Catholic saints, which let enslaved Africans keep their faith under colonial persecution.

entries.name: Oshun
entries.desc: Oshun is the orisha of love, fertility, water, divination, wealth and beauty in the Yoruba religion, and the patron of the Osun River in Nigeria, which bears her name; she is one of the most popular and venerated of the orishas. According to traditional beliefs she was once a queen of King Shango of Oyo and was deified after her death. In the Ifá literary corpus she is the only female primordial spirit sent by Olodumare to help create the world. She is honoured each August at the two-week Osun-Osogbo Festival in the sacred grove at Osogbo, and her worship continues in the Americas.

entries.name: Shango
entries.desc: Shango is the orisha of fire, thunder, lightning, drumming, dance, strength and justice in the Yoruba religion. Tradition holds that he was the third Alaafin, or king, of the Oyo Empire, after Oranmiyan and Ajaka, a warlike ruler whose seven-year reign ended when lightning destroyed his palace, and who was deified after his death; his wives are named as Oshun, Oba and Oya. He is known for his double-headed axe, the oṣé. Enslaved Yoruba carried his worship to the Americas, where as Xangô in Candomblé and Changó in Santería he is identified with Saint Barbara or Saint Jerome.

entries.name: Ogun
entries.desc: Ogun is the deity of iron, metalworking and war in the traditional religions of several West African peoples, among them the Yoruba, Edo and Itsekiri. In Yoruba religion he is a primordial orisha who, in some traditions, cleared a path for the other orishas to come to Earth with a metal machete, helped by a dog. Scholars trace his worship to the Yoruba, but the historian Sandra T. Barnes holds that the time and place of his emergence are uncertain and the evidence circumstantial. His worship spread to the Americas, where in Brazilian Candomblé he is known as Ogum and identified with Saint George.

entries.name: Yemọja
entries.desc: Yemọja is a major water deity of the Yoruba religion, the patron spirit of rivers, above all the Ogun River in Nigeria, and of the oceans in the orisha religions of Cuba and Brazil. She is said to be motherly and protective, the protector of women and the one who can cure infertility, while her anger is likened to the floodwaters of turbulent rivers. Some of her priests hold that she lent her fresh water to Ọbàtálá as he moulded human beings from clay. Many devotees depict her as a mermaid, and since the era of the Atlantic slave trade she has been identified with Our Lady of Regla and other figures of the Virgin Mary.

entries.name: Eshu
entries.desc: Eshu is the orisha of trickery, chance, crossroads, judgement and languages in the Yoruba religion. According to Yoruba belief he is a primordial divinity sent by Olodumare and the chief enforcer of natural and divine law, the messenger between the orishas, the malevolent spirits and human beings, who oversees the sacrifices people offer. Unlike the other divinities, every day of the four-day Yoruba week is held to be his day of worship. As Yoruba religion spread his name changed from place to place, among them Exu in Brazilian Candomblé, while the beliefs about him stayed much the same.

entries.name: Obatala
entries.desc: Obatala, King of White Cloth, also called Oriṣanla, the Great Orisha, is the king of the orishas in the Yoruba religion, believed to have created the Earth and human beings. In some versions of the story he failed to finish creating the Earth after drinking palm wine and was outdone by his younger brother Oduduwa, and was given instead the task of moulding humans from clay, into whom Olorun breathed life; he is thus held to be the father of humanity. In the oral traditions of Ife a mortal Obatala was the city's founder and king, who defeated Oduduwa's challenge, and was later merged with the deity.

entries.name: Olorun
entries.desc: Olorun, also called Olodumare, is the supreme being of the Yoruba religion and of related religions, the ruler of the heavens and creator of the universe; the name joins words meaning owner and the heavens. Olorun is held to be compassionate, all-powerful and present everywhere, yet distant: people do not worship Olorun directly, and there are no shrines, sacred places or images. The world is governed instead by the orishas, divine beings sent by Olorun, of whom Obatala is king. In some belief systems the different names refer to particular deities or aspects of the one deity.

entries.name: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove
entries.desc: The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove is a forest along the Osun River just outside Osogbo in Osun State, Nigeria, sacred to the orisha Oshun. Several centuries old, it is among the last of the sacred forests that once bordered most Yoruba cities. In the 1950s its shrines were neglected and it was fished, hunted and felled, until the Austrian artist Susanne Wenger, with the support of the Ataoja, the king of Osogbo, and local people, founded the New Sacred Art movement to restore and protect it. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005, and the Osun-Osogbo Festival is held there every August.

entries.name: Aedui
entries.desc: The Aedui or Haedui were a Gallic people of central-eastern Gaul, living between the Loire and the Saône in modern Burgundy during the Iron Age and the Roman period. Their civitas was an oligarchy run by a senate and an annual magistrate, the vergobret. From the middle of the 2nd century BCE they were allies of Rome, the first people of inner Gaul to make a formal treaty with the Republic. They gave Caesar uneven support in the Gallic Wars before briefly joining the revolt of Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. In 48 CE they became the first Gauls admitted to the Roman Senate, and their capital moved from Bibracte to Augustodunum (Autun).

entries.name: Ahir
entries.desc: The Ahirs are a community of India, traditionally non-elite pastoralists whose occupations were cattle-herding and agriculture, variously described as a caste, a clan, a race or a tribe. Their name is believed to derive from the Sanskrit abhira, though the origins of the ancient Abhira are disputed. From the 1920s many adopted the name Yadav and claimed descent from the mythological king Yadu, part of a movement for higher status in the caste hierarchy under the influence of the Arya Samaj. The British raised four Ahir army companies in 1898 and in the 1920s classed the Ahirs of Punjab as an agricultural tribe, then synonymous with a martial race.

credit.artist: J. Forbes Watson and John William Kaye

entries.name: Aitchison College
entries.desc: Aitchison College is a day and boarding school for boys in Lahore, Pakistan, founded in British India as the Punjab Chiefs' College on 2 January 1886 and renamed after the Lieutenant Governor of the Punjab, Sir Charles Umpherston Aitchison, that November. It grew out of the Wards School at Ambala, established in 1868 to educate young princes and widened in 1874 to the heirs of the princely states of the Punjab. Admission was opened to ordinary boys from the surrounding areas in 1935. The college has since educated prime ministers of Pakistan, among them Imran Khan, as well as presidents, lawyers and cricketers.

entries.name: Ammi-saduqa
entries.desc: Ammi-saduqa was a king of the First Dynasty of Babylon, who ruled in 1646–1626 BCE by the High Middle Chronology or 1638–1618 BCE by the Low Middle Chronology. He was the eldest son and successor of Ammi-ditana, probably born of Queen Šamuḫtum. Some twenty-one year-names survive for his reign, including the first seventeen, and they suggest fairly peaceful years in which he was chiefly occupied with enriching and enlarging the temples, as well as other building, such as a wall at the mouth of the Euphrates. His son Samsu-ditana, the last king of the Amorite dynasty, succeeded him.

entries.name: Andrea Gritti
entries.desc: Andrea Gritti was Doge of the Venetian Republic from 1523 to 1538. A grain merchant in Constantinople for almost twenty years, he represented Venice at the Ottoman court and in 1499 was imprisoned for sending coded reports on the Ottoman navy, escaping execution through his friendship with the grand vizier. As provveditore generale in the War of the League of Cambrai he recaptured Padua in July 1509, a feat that opened his way to the dogeship. As doge he made a treaty with Charles V that ended Venice's active part in the Italian Wars, but could not keep the Republic out of a new Ottoman war after Suleiman I attacked Corfu in 1537.

entries.name: Annual Customs of Dahomey
entries.desc: The Annual Customs of Dahomey were the main yearly celebration of the Kingdom of Dahomey, held at its capital, Abomey, and largely begun under King Agaja around 1730. Every family lineage was expected to bring gifts and tribute to the king, who displayed the wealth and then redistributed much of it. The ceremony honoured the royal ancestors with human sacrifice: captives from war and criminals were killed, around 500 at a time, mostly by decapitation, and as many as 4,000 were reported killed in 1727. The Customs also held military parades and the Great Council, where leaders, women among them, debated policy until the king declared consensus.

entries.name: Arsinoe II
entries.desc: Arsinoe II was a Hellenistic queen, daughter of Ptolemy I Soter, who was successively the wife of King Lysimachus of Thrace, of her half-brother Ptolemy Keraunos and of her brother Ptolemy II Philadelphus of Egypt. As queen of Egypt she shared in all her brother's titles, acted alongside him in ritual, appeared on coinage and took part in foreign policy, a role that became a model for later Ptolemaic queens. She died in 270 or 268 BCE, and Ptolemy II made her a goddess: every temple in Egypt had to hold her cult statue, and the Fayyum became the Arsinoite nome, with Arsinoe as its patron goddess.

entries.name: Article 58
entries.desc: Article 58 of the Penal Code of the Russian SFSR, in force from 25 February 1927, was the law under which people suspected of counter-revolutionary activity were prosecuted in the Soviet Union. Its sections punished treason, espionage, wrecking, terrorism, anti-Soviet propaganda and agitation, and even the failure to report such acts, many of them by death with confiscation of property. Sentences ran up to 25 years and were often extended without trial, and those convicted were known as political prisoners, apart from common criminals. In effect it allowed the secret police to arrest anyone deemed suspicious; the code was rewritten after Khrushchev denounced Stalinism.

entries.name: Arverni
entries.desc: The Arverni were a Gallic people of the late Iron Age and the Roman period whose territory lay in the Massif Central, the later Auvergne. One of the most powerful peoples of Gaul, they contested primacy with the neighbouring Aedui, and under their chiefs Luernius and Bituitus they dominated many neighbours until Bituitus was defeated by the Romans in 121 BCE. In 52 BCE the Arvernian chief Vercingetorix led the Gallic revolt against Caesar, winning at Gergovia before his defeat at Alesia. Under Rome they formed one of the largest civitates of Aquitania, with its capital at Augustonemetum, the later Clermont-Ferrand, until their land was ceded to the Visigoths in 475.

entries.name: Assegai
entries.desc: An assegai is a polearm used for throwing, usually a light spear or javelin with a wooden handle and an iron tip. Various types were used all over Africa, and it was the most common weapon there before the introduction of firearms; the Zulu, Xhosa and other Nguni peoples of South Africa were noted for their use of it. Dingiswayo, the Zulu ruler whose chief lieutenant was Shaka, popularised in war a shorter stabbing spear, traditionally a hunting spear, with a 610 mm shaft and a broad blade 300 mm long, known as the iklwa. The throwing spear was kept and hurled at enemy formations before close combat with the iklwa and a cowhide shield.

entries.name: Avalokiteśvara
entries.desc: Avalokiteśvara, the Lord who looks down, is a bodhisattva of Buddhism associated with great compassion, known in Tibetan as Chenrezig and in East Asia as Guanyin, Kannon or Gwaneum. Chapter 25 of the Lotus Sutra describes him as a bodhisattva who hears the cries of beings and helps all who call on his name, in 33 manifestations, some of them female. He is depicted in a vast number of forms across Buddhist cultures, and his mantra, Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ, is the most popular in Tibetan Buddhism. He is the only Mahayana figure who entered the worship of ordinary Buddhists in Theravada countries, and many Tibetan Buddhists hold the Dalai Lamas to be his manifestations.

entries.name: Avogadoria de Comùn
entries.desc: The Avogadori de Comùn, the state attorneys, were an institution of the Republic of Venice charged with defending the interests of the Commune Veneciarum, the union of noble families that governed the state, in a manner similar to a modern state attorney. They could supervise the accounts of the Camerlenghi, prosecute breaches of the naval laws reported by crews, investigate corruption and negligence among judges and officials, and take part in the Council of Forty's proceedings wherever the commune's interests were at stake. Their main task was to guard constitutional legality, with the power to suspend unconstitutional measures, and from 1400 even the Doge could be taken to court.

entries.name: Baha al-Din al-Amili
entries.desc: Baha al-Din al-Amili, commonly known as Sheikh Bahāʾī, was a Twelver Shia scholar and polymath of Safavid Iran, closely tied to the court of Shah Abbas I. Born near Baalbek in Ottoman Syria, he moved as a child to Iran, where his father served as shaykh al-Islam in several cities to spread Twelver Shi'ism. He wrote over a hundred treatises in Arabic and Persian on jurisprudence, logic, astronomy, mathematics and theology, as well as Persian verse, and seventy-seven scholars are counted among his students. As chief advisor to Abbas I he conceived the urban vision behind Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan and helped begin the planning of the Shah Mosque and the Ali Qapu Palace.

entries.name: Banteay Kdei
entries.desc: Banteay Kdei, the Citadel of Chambers, is a Buddhist temple in Angkor, Cambodia, southeast of Ta Prohm and east of Angkor Thom, built between the mid-12th and early 13th centuries during the reign of Jayavarman VII. A monastic complex in the Bayon style, similar in plan to Ta Prohm and Preah Khan but smaller and less complex, it stands on the site of a 10th-century temple of Rajendravarman, and inscriptions record its building by Jayavarman VII and the royal architect Kavindrarimathana. Monks occupied it at intervals over the centuries until the 1960s. Faulty construction and poor sandstone have left it dilapidated, and it is now under renovation.

entries.name: Baray
entries.desc: A baray is an artificial body of water, a common element of the architecture of the Khmer Empire of Southeast Asia. The largest are the East Baray and the West Baray in the Angkor area, each rectangular, oriented east to west and measuring roughly five by one and a half miles. Historians are divided on what barays meant and what they were for. Some hold that their purpose was mainly spiritual, symbolising the Sea of Creation that surrounds Mount Meru, the centre of the Hindu cosmos; others that it was mainly practical, holding water for drinking or for irrigating fields; their function may have combined these or other purposes.

entries.name: Booi Aha
entries.desc: Booi aha, a Manchu phrase meaning household person, referred to the hereditarily servile people of the Eight Banner system in 17th-century Qing China, often translated as bondservant. They fell into three groups: company servants, half-company servants and estate bannermen. Booi usually meant household servants doing domestic service, aha the servile people working in the fields. The historian Mark C. Elliott warns that calling them slaves conveys the wrong meaning, since booi often held powerful positions and were sometimes intimates of the emperor; according to Pamela Kyle Crossley, all enrolled in the banners called themselves the emperor's slaves when addressing him.

entries.name: Boyar
entries.desc: A boyar or bolyar was a member of the highest rank of the feudal nobility in many Eastern European states, among them Bulgaria, Kievan Rus' and later Russia, Moldavia, Wallachia and Lithuania, second only to the ruling princes, grand princes or tsars from the 10th to the 17th centuries. In Kievan Rus' the boyars held the highest state offices and, as members of the Boyars' Duma, advised the grand prince and were the main legislators. In Muscovy their power declined from the reign of Ivan III, and by the end of the Time of Troubles they had lost nearly all independent power. Peter the Great replaced their old council with an appointed senate.

entries.name: Braccae
entries.desc: Braccae or bracae is the Latin word for trousers, used today for a style of woollen trousers that, according to the Romans, originated among the Gauls. They were usually held up by a drawstring and reached from just above the knee to the ankles, generally longer among the peoples living further north. Roman men typically wore tunics ending at or above the knee, and in the time of Pompey and Horace binding the legs and thighs with bands was taken as a sign of ill health and effeminacy. The word comes from Gaulish and is related to the English breeches.

entries.name: Bucentaur
entries.desc: The bucentaur was the ceremonial barge of the doges of Venice, used every year on Ascension Day up to 1798 to carry the doge out to the Adriatic for the Marriage of the Sea, a ceremony that symbolically wedded Venice to the sea. Scholars believe there were four major barges, the first significant one built in 1311 at public expense. The last, launched in 1729 under Doge Alvise III Sebastiano Mocenigo, was a two-deck floating palace 35 m long, with the doge's throne in the stern, rowed by 168 oarsmen. It was destroyed in 1798 on Napoleon's orders to mark his conquest of Venice, and work on a reconstruction began at the Arsenale in 2008.

credit.artist: After Giovanni Antonio Canal / Francesco Guardi

entries.name: Callimachus
entries.desc: Callimachus was a Greek poet, scholar and librarian of the 3rd century BCE, born into a prominent family of Cyrene and active in Alexandria under the Ptolemies. Under the patronage of Ptolemy II Philadelphus he worked at the Library of Alexandria, where he compiled the Pinakes, a catalogue of all Greek literature in 120 volumes. Of his more than 800 works only a few survive, chief among them the Aetia, six hymns, around 60 epigrams, the Iambs and the Hecale. Favouring short, learned and refined poems over long epic, he became a principal model for Catullus, Horace, Vergil, Propertius and Ovid, and through them influenced later Western literature.

entries.name: Carnutes
entries.desc: The Carnutes were a Gallic people of the middle Loire basin, in what is now the Centre-Val de Loire region of France, whose two chief centres were Cenabum (Orléans) and Autricum (Chartres), the city named after them. Caesar placed in their land the yearly assembly of the druids, held at a consecrated place reckoned the centre of Gaul, where people with disputes came to accept their judgements. In 52 BCE the Carnutes killed the Roman traders settled at Cenabum, giving the signal for the great revolt; Caesar took the town and burned it, but they still sent 12,000 men to relieve Alesia. Under Rome, Autricum became the capital of their civitas.

entries.name: Cetbang
entries.desc: Cetbang were cannons made and used by the Majapahit Empire (1293–1527) and other kingdoms of the Indonesian archipelago, known in Old Javanese as bedil or warastra. The eastern style, descended from guns brought by Kublai Khan's army when it sought to invade Java in 1293, resembled Chinese cannons and was loaded from the front; the western style, a breech-loading swivel gun derived from the Turkish prangi, reached the archipelago after 1460. Majapahit under its prime minister Gajah Mada used gunpowder weapons in its fleet, and when Malacca fell to the Portuguese in 1511 they captured cetbang there; the Javanese were then known as expert gun casters.

entries.name: Chakravarti
entries.desc: A chakravarti, one who moves the wheels, is the ideal universal ruler of the historiography and religion of India, a concept that may have developed by the time of the early Maurya kings in the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE. Tradition distinguishes three kinds: the emperor of all four continents, the ruler of one, and the king of only part of one. In Buddhism the chakravarti is the secular counterpart of a buddha, and in Buddhism and Hinduism alike he upholds dharma. Rulers associated with the title include Ashoka, Kanishka and Samudragupta. The idea later evolved into the devaraja, the divinity of kings, adopted by Majapahit, the Khmer Empire and the Thai monarchs.

entries.name: Chamar
entries.desc: The Chamars are a community of the Indian subcontinent, classified as a Scheduled Caste in modern India, traditionally associated with leather tanning and shoemaking, though the historian Ramnarayan Rawat holds that this association was constructed and that they were historically agriculturists. By the late 19th century Chamars had begun to rewrite their caste histories to claim Kshatriya descent. In the later 20th century the Bahujan Samaj Party, led by the Chamar leaders Kanshi Ram and Mayawati, drew on their votes. The name is now often used as a casteist slur, and the Supreme Court of India has ruled it highly offensive.

entries.name: Chatusadom
entries.desc: Chatusadom, the Four Pillars, was the Thai system of central government of the Ayutthaya, Thonburi and Rattanakosin kingdoms from 1454 to 1892. King Trailokanat set it out in his Palatine Law of 1454, organising four existing ministries under ministers of the rank of Phraya, with two prime ministers, the Samuhanayok for civil and the Samuhakalahom for military affairs, ruling on the king's behalf. Over time the line between civil and military officials blurred, and the Samuhakalahom grew so powerful that one of them seized the throne as King Prasat Thong in 1629. King Chulalongkorn reorganised the system into modern ministries and established the Cabinet in 1892.

entries.name: Cleruchy
entries.desc: A cleruchy was a type of colony established by Athens in Classical Greece, whose settlers, the cleruchs or lot-holders, kept their Athenian citizenship while the community remained a political dependency of Athens. According to Plutarch the lots went to poor citizens, but inscriptions suggest the cleruchs were more often wealthy men who stayed in Athens while slaves worked their overseas estates. The network was lost at the end of the Peloponnesian War. Hellenistic kingdoms, above all the Ptolemies, also granted land to soldiers as cleruchies, and by the mid-3rd century BCE they and their descendants made up up to 29% of the adults of the Faiyum.

entries.name: Cloistered rule
entries.desc: Cloistered rule, or insei, was a form of government in Heian Japan in which an emperor abdicated but kept power, while his chosen successor performed the ceremonial duties of the monarchy. As a system it usually refers to the practice begun by Emperor Shirakawa, who abdicated in 1086 in favour of his four-year-old son, and followed by his successors until the rise of the Kamakura shogunate in 1192. The retired emperors, some of whom entered Buddhist monastic life, acted to counterbalance the Fujiwara regents and the warrior class, and kept courts and troops of their own. Their military units helped the Taira clan rise to power, and the system lingered formally long after the Jōkyū War.

credit.artist: 高階隆兼（模写：板橋貫雄）

entries.name: Clotilda
entries.desc: The Clotilda was a two-masted schooner and the last known American slave ship to bring enslaved Africans to the United States, landing 110 men, women and children at Mobile Bay, Alabama, in autumn 1859 or on 9 July 1860, long after Congress had banned the trade in 1807. Built for the Mobile shipyard owner Timothy Meaher and commanded by William Foster, it bought its captives at Whydah in Dahomey, whose forces had raided communities in the interior. The ship was then burned and scuttled to destroy the evidence. After the Civil War, Oluale Kossola (Cudjo Lewis) and 31 other survivors founded Africatown north of Mobile; the wreck was identified in 2019.

entries.name: Collectivization in the Soviet Union
entries.desc: Collectivization was the Soviet policy, carried out between 1928 and 1940 as part of the first five-year plan, of merging individual peasant holdings and labour into collective and state farms, the kolkhozes and sovkhozes, to secure grain for the cities, industry and export. Joining was not voluntary: from about 1% of farmland in 1928, the share rose to about 90% of agriculture by 1936. Peasants resisted with protests and armed revolt and slaughtered their livestock. Stalin resolved to eliminate the kulaks as a class by dispossession, deportation and execution, and the famine of 1932–33, in which an estimated 5.7 to 8.7 million people starved, followed the collapse of production.

entries.name: Communal Award
entries.desc: The Communal Award was announced by the British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald on 16 August 1932, after the Round Table Conferences, and extended separate electorates in British India to the Depressed Classes, now known as the Scheduled Castes, alongside Muslims, Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans. B. R. Ambedkar supported separate electorates for the Scheduled Castes, but Mahatma Gandhi, who feared that the award would break up Hindu society, declared a fast unto death from Yerwada Jail in September 1932. After long negotiations Gandhi and Ambedkar agreed in the Poona Pact on a single Hindu electorate with seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes.

entries.name: Council of Ten
entries.desc: The Council of Ten was one of the major governing bodies of the Republic of Venice from 1310 to 1797, created by Doge Pietro Gradenigo as a temporary body to investigate the plot of Bajamonte Tiepolo and Marco Querini and made permanent in 1455. Its ten patrician members, elected by the Great Council for one year, held broad powers over state security and could punish nobles with banishment or death; on its orders Doge Marino Faliero was executed in 1355. With secret funds, anonymous informers and police powers, the Ten and the Collegio formed the inner circle of patricians who in effect ruled the republic, and by the end of the 16th century the Ten oversaw its large intelligence network.

entries.name: Criminal Tribes Act
entries.desc: The Criminal Tribes Act was the name given to a series of colonial laws in British India, from 1871 to 1924, that criminalised entire communities by designating them and their members as habitual criminals. Once notified, a community had no legal recourse, and its members were bound to compulsory registration and a pass system that limited where they could travel and live. At independence in 1947 thirteen million people in 127 communities were subject to it. The act was repealed in August 1949 and the communities denotified in 1952, but the Habitual Offenders Act that replaced it re-stigmatised them, and the denotified tribes still face its legacy.

entries.name: Cudjoe Lewis
entries.desc: Cudjoe Lewis, born Oluale Kossola in West Africa, was one of the last survivors of the Atlantic slave trade to the Americas. According to the historian Sylviane Diouf a Yoruba from the Banté region of Benin, he was captured in 1860 in a dry-season raid by the female warriors of King Glele of Dahomey, sold at Ouidah and carried to Alabama on the Clotilda. He worked as a de facto slave of the Meaher family until the end of the Civil War, then helped found the community at Magazine Point north of Mobile, now the Africatown Historic District. In old age he told the history of the Clotilda captives to visitors, among them Emma Langdon Roche and Zora Neale Hurston.

entries.name: Dalit
entries.desc: Dalit, from a Sanskrit word meaning broken or scattered, is the name of the people once called untouchables and outcastes, the lowest stratum of the castes of the Indian subcontinent, excluded from the fourfold varna of Hindu caste hierarchy and seen as a fifth, the Panchama. Jyotirao Phule used the word in the late 1880s, and B. R. Ambedkar, himself a Dalit, popularised it. India's 1950 Constitution abolished untouchability and created reservations for the Scheduled Castes in legislatures, government jobs and education, and in 1997 K. R. Narayanan became the first Dalit president. Caste discrimination nonetheless remains widespread, above all in rural India.

entries.name: Dasa
entries.desc: Dasa is a Sanskrit word of the Rigveda, the Pali canon and the Arthashastra whose meaning varies with its context and with its translators. In the Vedic texts it can mean an enemy, a people opposed to the Vedic Aryans, or demonic forces, and scholars have identified those people variously as indigenous inhabitants of South Asia or as Iranian or Central Asian peoples. In Pali texts it denotes a slave or servant, and the Arthashastra of the Maurya period gives a chapter to dasas, translated as slaves, with rights to wages, inheritance and freedom on payment. Elsewhere dasa means a devotee or servant of god, and it is widely used today as a surname and an honorific.

entries.name: Decree of Canopus
entries.desc: The Decree of Canopus is a trilingual inscription of Ptolemaic Egypt, written in Egyptian hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, that records an assembly of priests held at Canopus in March 238 BCE in honour of Ptolemy III Euergetes, Queen Berenice and Princess Berenice. It lists the king's gifts to the temples, the return of divine statues carried off by Cambyses, the suppression of native Egyptian revolts and grain imported in a year of low flood, deifies the dead princess, and introduces a calendar of 365 and a quarter days, a reform that failed until Augustus. Copies have been found at Tanis in 1866 and elsewhere since, and its many signs helped decipher hieroglyphs.

entries.name: Dekulakization
entries.desc: Dekulakization was a campaign of repression in the Soviet Union against the so-called kulaks, a loosely defined category of supposedly wealthy or exploitative peasants, begun after Stalin announced the liquidation of the kulaks as a class on 27 December 1929. It aimed to break resistance to collectivization and to supply forced labour for Siberia, the Urals, Kazakhstan and the North. Between 2.1 and 2.3 million people were deported to special settlements in 1930–1933 and 20,000 to 30,000 executed by troiki; Manfred Hildermeier estimates 530,000 to 600,000 deaths, excluding the famine. The deportations became a cornerstone of the Gulag and helped bring about the famine of 1930–1933.

credit.artist: Unknown. Thanks to Lewis H. Siegelbaum and Andrej K. Sokolov

entries.name: Doctrine of lapse
entries.desc: The doctrine of lapse was an annexation policy of the British East India Company in India, under which a princely state under its suzerainty was annexed to directly ruled British India if its ruler was manifestly incompetent or died without a male heir, overriding the long-established right of an heirless Indian sovereign to choose a successor. Articulated by the Company's directors as early as 1834, it is chiefly associated with Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General from 1848 to 1856, who took Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Tanjore and other states by it. Widely considered illegitimate, it was one of the causes of the rebellion of 1857 and was renounced when Crown rule replaced the Company in 1858.

entries.name: Doge of Venice
entries.desc: The doge of Venice was the highest authority of the Republic of Venice (697–1797), head of state and of the Venetian oligarchy, elected for life. The title comes from the Latin dux, leader, and grew out of the offices of Byzantine Venetia; the first historically attested doge was Orso Ipato in the first half of the 8th century. From 1268 the doge was chosen by a complex machinery of lots and nominating committees in the Great Council, meant to limit the influence of the great families, and he was kept under strict surveillance. As the oligarchy took over his functions the office became mostly representative. The last doge, Ludovico Manin, abdicated in 1797 after Napoleon's conquest.

entries.name: Druid
entries.desc: A druid was a member of the learned class of the ancient Celtic peoples of Gaul and Britain, described by Greek and Roman writers as priest, teacher, judge and keeper of religious and legal tradition. According to Julius Caesar, the druids were one of the two honoured classes of Gaul beside the horsemen; they conducted sacrifices, judged nearly all disputes, were exempt from tax and military service, and met yearly in the land of the Carnutes. Because they wrote nothing down, almost all that is known of them comes from outsiders. They declined after the Roman conquest and were the object of prohibitions under Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius.

entries.name: Druzhina
entries.desc: A druzhina was the retinue in the service of a Slavic chieftain or prince (knyaz). In Kievan Rus' the word meant at its core the prince's permanent bodyguard and more widely his extended household, his closest group after his kin and the protective and coercive basis of his power; a prince was expected to feast with it, consult it and reward it. As principalities grew more complex it developed its own hierarchy, with rank-and-file youths in the junior druzhina and boyars as its senior members holding military, domestic and urban offices. In Poland the traveller Ibrahim ibn Yaqub reported that the druzhina of Duke Mieszko I numbered 3,000 paid men in 961–962.

entries.name: Eastern Depot
entries.desc: The Eastern Depot was a spy and secret police agency of the Ming dynasty run by eunuchs, created in 1420 by the Yongle Emperor, who had usurped the throne from his nephew in 1402, to suppress political opposition. Named for its place east of the imperial palace, it spied on officials of every rank, military officers, scholars, rebels and the general populace, and handed those it arrested to the Jinyiwei for interrogation. In the late Ming it had its own forces and prisons and grew so powerful that even officials were ordered to kowtow to its leaders. It lasted until the end of the dynasty in 1644; its chiefs included Wang Zhen, Liu Jin and Wei Zhongxian.

entries.name: Eight-legged essay
entries.desc: The eight-legged essay was the style of essay written in the imperial examinations of the Ming and Qing dynasties in China, intended to test candidates' merits for government service through Confucian thought and knowledge of the Four Books and Five Classics. Its eight legs were the sections of a fixed structure, from breaking open the topic to the conclusion, with rules for the number of sentences and words. The term first appeared in the early reign of the Chenghua Emperor, and the form was required in the examinations from the 1480s. Widely criticised under the Qing for its rigid, formulaic character, it was permanently abolished in 1905 by the Guangxu Emperor.

entries.name: Embroidered Uniform Guard
entries.desc: The Embroidered Uniform Guard, or Jinyiwei, was the imperial secret police of the Ming dynasty in China, founded by the Hongwu Emperor in 1368 as his personal bodyguard and formally established in 1382 with about 500 members, who grew to around 14,000 in three years. Taking orders from the emperor alone, it could overrule judicial proceedings and arrest, interrogate, detain without trial and punish anyone. Its duties were curtailed in 1393 after it allegedly abused its authority in the case of the general Lan Yu, in which about 40,000 people were executed, and restored by the Yongle Emperor. It was disbanded when Li Zicheng's rebels overthrew the Ming in 1644.

entries.name: Emperor Daigo
entries.desc: Emperor Daigo was the 60th emperor of Japan according to the traditional order of succession, reigning from 897 to 930. The eldest son of Emperor Uda, he was born a subject named Minamoto no Korezane, because his grandfather Emperor Kōkō had demoted his sons from the imperial ranks, and became an imperial prince only in 887. The highlight of his 34-year reign was that he ruled by himself without a Fujiwara regent, though he was part Fujiwara himself; in his reign Ki no Tsurayuki presented the Kokin Wakashū. Falling ill in 930, he abdicated, became a monk and died, and was buried at Daigo-ji, which gave him his posthumous name.

entries.name: Emperor Go-Sanjō
entries.desc: Emperor Go-Sanjō was the 71st emperor of Japan according to the traditional order of succession, reigning from 1068 to 1073. A son of Emperor Go-Suzaku and Princess Sadako, he was the first emperor in 170 years whose mother was not of Fujiwara descent paternally, so he owed the Fujiwara regents no special loyalty and was determined to rule personally. In 1069 he issued the Enkyū Shōen Regulation Decree and set up an office to certify the records of the shōen estates. It was during and due to his reign that the Fujiwara grip on power was broken. He abdicated in favour of his son Shirakawa in 1073, became a monk and died the same year.

entries.name: Emperor Shirakawa
entries.desc: Emperor Shirakawa was the 72nd emperor of Japan according to the traditional order of succession, reigning from 1073 to 1087. The eldest son of Emperor Go-Sanjō, he tried like his father to rule directly, regulating the shōen manor system and weakening the regents' lines. In 1087 he abdicated in favour of his son Horikawa but went on exercising broad powers from his residence, the Shirakawa-in, becoming the first to practise what came to be known as cloistered rule. In 1096 he entered the Buddhist priesthood. By his death in 1129 he had ruled as cloistered emperor through the reigns of three emperors who were effectively little more than figureheads.

entries.name: Emperor Uda
entries.desc: Emperor Uda was the 59th emperor of Japan according to the traditional order of succession, reigning from 887 to 897. A son of Emperor Kōkō, he had been demoted to commoner status as Minamoto no Sadami in 884 and was restored as an imperial prince only in 887, just before his father's death. His attempt in the Akō controversy to make the regent Fujiwara no Mototsune's office merely honorific failed, and only after Mototsune died in 891 could he rule directly, promoting men outside the main Fujiwara line such as Sugawara no Michizane and ending missions to Tang China. He abdicated in 897 in favour of his son Daigo, became a monk and died in 931.

credit.artist: Emperor_Uda_large.jpg : unknown derivative work: bamse ( talk )

entries.name: Empress Xiaoyichun
entries.desc: Empress Xiaoyichun was an imperial consort of the Qing dynasty and one of the most favoured consorts of the Qianlong Emperor, with whom she had seven children. Of Han Chinese origin, she was born into a bondservant family of the Imperial Household Department, a class excluded from the imperial draft, and probably entered the palace as a maid before rising from noble lady in 1745 to imperial noble consort in 1765. After Empress Nara's fall she ran the palace as de facto empress. She died in 1775; her son Yongyan, chosen in secret as heir, became the Jiaqing Emperor, and she was named empress posthumously in 1796 and given her full title in 1799.

credit.source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:清人画孝仪纯皇后朝服像轴2.png

entries.name: Empress Xiaozhuangwen
entries.desc: Empress Xiaozhuangwen, born Bumbutai of the Khorchin Mongol Borjigit clan, was a consort of the Manchu ruler Hong Taiji, whom she married in 1625 as one of his several wives. Her son Fulin became the Shunzhi Emperor in 1643, and she was honoured as Empress Dowager Zhaosheng, then as Grand Empress Dowager under her grandson, the Kangxi Emperor. She took charge of the young Kangxi Emperor's upbringing and in 1669 helped him remove the regent Oboi from power. Respected for her political wisdom, she died in 1688 and was named Empress Xiaozhuangwen posthumously, though she never held the rank of empress consort in her lifetime.

entries.name: Endybis
entries.desc: Endybis or Endubis was a late-3rd-century king of Aksum in East Africa, in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea. He was among the earliest rulers in Africa to mint his own coins, issued in gold, silver and bronze or copper with inscriptions in Koine Greek. Dated to about 295 to 310, they are the oldest known Aksumite coins, and their weights follow the Roman gold coinage of the period. They show the king's bust in profile between stalks of two-row barley, under a crescent and disc that may stand for the Moon-god and the Sun-goddess, and call him king of the Aksumites and bisi Dakhu, the first appearance of the title bisi. His successors largely kept his design.

entries.name: Epona
entries.desc: Epona was the goddess of horses and ponies in Gallo-Roman religion, and also a fertility and mother goddess. Her name, from Gaulish, means 'Great Mare'. In Roman Gaul she watched over horses, donkeys, mules and their riders, and she was often shown riding sidesaddle or seated between horses or foals, holding a cornucopia, fruit or grain. Cavalry units recruited from Gaul, Lower Germany and Pannonia spread her cult across the Roman Empire, where she was widely worshipped as patroness of cavalry between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. She was the only Celtic divinity ultimately worshipped in Rome itself, invoked for the emperor as Epona Augusta or Epona Regina.

entries.name: Erie people
entries.desc: The Erie were an Iroquoian people who lived southeast of Lake Erie, in what became western New York and northwestern Pennsylvania, until the mid-17th century. A matrilineal, clan-based society living in palisaded villages of bark longhouses and farming maize, beans and squash, they formed a loose confederacy of three settlement clusters, estimated at roughly 12,000 people before smallpox and measles halved their numbers. In the 1650s the Seneca and Onondaga made war on the Erie, storming their fort in 1654. By 1656 the confederacy was gone; most captives were taken into Haudenosaunee families, and some survivors may have become the Westo.

entries.name: False Face Society
entries.desc: The False Face Society is a spiritual and medicinal society of the Haudenosaunee, known especially for its wooden masks. It cures ailments through ritual, with power over illnesses of the teeth, ears and joints, inflammation and nosebleeds. Members join by being cured by the society or by dreaming that they have the power to cure; they were men, but the society's leader was always a woman. According to Haudenosaunee oral tradition, the masks represent a being whose face was broken by a mountain and who promised to heal the people. The masks are held to be living, and in 1995 the Haudenosaunee Grand Council condemned their exhibition and called for their return from collectors and museums.

entries.name: Fondaco dei Turchi
aka: Palace of the Dukes of Ferrara
entries.desc: The Fondaco dei Turchi is a palazzo on the Grand Canal of Venice whose façade combines Islamic, Renaissance and Byzantine elements. Built as a private palace, it was acquired by the Republic of Venice in 1381 and given to Nicolò II d'Este, and for over two centuries it housed the ambassadors of Ferrara. After its sale to the senator Antonio Priuli in 1602 it became a fondaco, a combined home, warehouse and market for the Ottoman merchants the Venetians called Turks, who lived there under set hours and trading rules until 1838. The government mostly rebuilt it in 1869, keeping only the canal façade, and it now houses Venice's Natural History Museum.

entries.name: Foot binding
entries.desc: Foot binding was the Chinese custom of breaking and tightly binding the feet of young girls to change their shape and size, a painful practice that limited women's mobility and left lifelong disabilities. It may have begun among court dancers in the 10th century and spread among the elite under the Song dynasty, the earliest archaeological evidence coming from tombs of 1243 and 1274. It later spread to lower classes, and Manchu bans of 1636 to 1664 failed. In late imperial China bound feet were a status symbol and a mark of beauty; by the 19th century perhaps 40 to 50% of Chinese women had them. Reformers and missionaries campaigned against it, and it died out in the early 20th century.

entries.name: Forbidden City
aka: Imperial Palace of the Ming and Qing Dynasties
entries.desc: The Forbidden City is the imperial palace complex at the centre of the Imperial City in Beijing, built from 1406 to 1420 after the Yongle Emperor moved the capital from Nanjing, with more than a million workers. It was home to 24 Ming and Qing emperors and the centre of political power in China from 1420 to 1924; its name reflects its access, severely restricted to all but the emperor, his family and their eunuch servants. The Outer Court served ceremony, while the Inner Court housed the emperor, the empress and the consorts by rank. After Puyi's eviction in 1924 the Palace Museum was founded there in 1925, and the complex has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

entries.name: François-Timoléon de Choisy
entries.desc: François-Timoléon de Choisy was a French abbé, writer and member of the Académie Française, known for his memoirs, historical and religious writings and travel accounts. Born in Paris to a family attached to the court, he was made an abbé in childhood. In 1676 he went to Rome with the cardinal de Bouillon, and in 1685 he accompanied the Chevalier de Chaumont on a diplomatic mission to the Kingdom of Siam; David Hume later owned his account of Siam. He entered the Académie in 1687 and wrote an eleven-volume history of the Church. His gossiping Mémoires of 1727 and his autobiographical writings, which describe his wearing of women's clothing, are of questioned reliability.

entries.name: Fujiwara no Michinaga
entries.desc: Fujiwara no Michinaga was a Japanese statesman under whom the Fujiwara clan's control over Japan and its politics reached its zenith. A son of the regent Kaneie, he outmanoeuvred his nephew Korechika after his elder brothers died in 995, becoming Minister of the Right that year and Minister of the Left in 996. Called the Mido Kampaku, regent in all but name, he married four daughters to emperors and future emperors, among them Ichijō, Sanjō, Go-Ichijō and Go-Suzaku. He pressed Sanjō to retire in 1016 and ruled as regent for the young Go-Ichijō, then handed the office to his son Yorimichi. He became a monk in 1019, and his diary records the Heian court at the height of Fujiwara power.

entries.name: Fujiwara no Mototsune
entries.desc: Fujiwara no Mototsune was a Japanese statesman, courtier and aristocrat of the early Heian period and the first kampaku, a regent for an adult emperor, in Japanese history. Born the third son of Fujiwara no Nagara, he was adopted by his powerful uncle Fujiwara no Yoshifusa, who had no sons, and followed him as regent, holding power at court for four successive emperors. Named sesshō in 876 and Daijō Daijin in 880, he invented the office of kampaku for himself so that he could stay in power after an emperor came of age, receiving the title first in 884. The innovation let the Fujiwara tighten their grip on power throughout an emperor's reign. He died in 891.

entries.name: Fujiwara no Sumitomo
entries.desc: Fujiwara no Sumitomo was a Japanese court noble and warrior of the Heian era who led a revolt in western Japan from 939 to 941. Having built a power base in northern Kyushu and made a secret agreement with Taira no Masakado, who was in revolt in Shimōsa Province, he rose in Iyo Province in 939 and invaded Harima and Bizen, and the revolt spread through the whole San'yō region. Pursued by imperial forces under Ono no Yoshifuru and Minamoto no Tsunemoto, he fled to Dazaifu and burned its headquarters before being defeated at Hakata Bay. He was captured in Iyo and executed in 941 by Tachibana no Tōyasu. He was the ancestor of the Arima clan of Hizen.

entries.name: Fujiwara no Yoshifusa
entries.desc: Fujiwara no Yoshifusa was a Japanese statesman and courtier of the Heian period who served as a minister under the emperors Ninmyō, Montoku and Seiwa. Made Daijō Daijin in 857, he became regent, sesshō, in 858 for his young grandson, Emperor Seiwa, the first sesshō in Japanese history who was not himself of imperial rank and the first of a series of Fujiwara regents. He conceived the programme of boy-sovereigns guided by Fujiwara regents, which his adopted son and nephew Fujiwara no Mototsune carried out. Married to a daughter of Emperor Saga, he edited the Shoku Nihon Kōki, one of the Six National Histories of Japan, and died in 872.

entries.name: Garima Gospels
entries.desc: The Garima Gospels are three Geʽez manuscripts of the four Gospels kept at the Abba Garima Monastery in Ethiopia. Monastic tradition ascribes them to Saint Abba Garima, one of the Nine Saints, who is said to have written and illustrated them in a single day. Radiocarbon analysis dated samples from Garima 2 to about 390–570 and from Garima 1 to about 530–660, making them the oldest surviving Ethiopian manuscripts of any kind, and Garima 2 is believed to be the earliest surviving complete illuminated Christian manuscript; the third book is later. Their Evangelist portraits and canon tables are in a broadly Byzantine style, and they are the major witness to the Ethiopic version of the Gospels.

entries.name: Gayatri Rajapatni
entries.desc: Gayatri Rajapatni was the queen consort of Kertarajasa Jayawardhana, founder and first king of Majapahit in East Java, and the mother of its queen regnant Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi. The youngest daughter of King Kertanegara of Singhasari, she escaped the sack of her father's palace in 1292 by hiding among captured servants, and after Raden Wijaya defeated Jayakatwang in 1293 she became one of his five wives, by tradition his favourite. As dowager she was the matriarch of the Rajasa dynasty and probably the patron of Gajah Mada and Adityawarman. A devout Buddhist, she became a nun, had her daughter rule on her behalf from 1329, and died in 1350; she was enshrined as Prajnaparamita.

entries.name: Geji
entries.desc: Geji, literally 'singer-performers', were female Chinese performing artists and courtesans trained in singing and dancing. A legendary singer of the Warring States period, Han'e of the Taoist Liezi is held to be the first. Like other entertainers in ancient China they had low social standing, though some contributed to dance, poetry, painting and literature, and under the Tang and Song they sang poems that helped spread them. They were sought chiefly for their artistic talents and sometimes provided sexual services. Under the Ming their accomplishments were cultivated to set them apart from common prostitutes, and the Qing later banned such courtesans from performing at official functions.

entries.name: Genrikh Yagoda
entries.desc: Genrikh Yagoda was a Soviet secret police official who headed the NKVD, the Soviet Union's security and intelligence agency, from 1934 to 1936. Born in Rybinsk into a Jewish family, he rose through the Cheka and became the real head of the OGPU by the late 1920s. He organised the building of the White Sea–Baltic Canal with forced labour from 1931 to 1933, at a cost of 12,000 to 25,000 lives, and the camps he supervised grew into the Gulag. Appointed by Stalin, he prepared the first Moscow show trial, which led to the execution of Zinoviev and Kamenev in 1936 and began the Great Purge. Replaced by Nikolai Yezhov, he was arrested in 1937, tried with twenty others and shot in 1938.

entries.name: Gopal Krishna Gokhale
entries.desc: Gopal Krishna Gokhale was an Indian political leader and social reformer of the independence movement, a senior leader of the Indian National Congress and the political guru of Mahatma Gandhi. Born into a Chitpavan Brahmin family, he graduated from Elphinstone College in 1884 and joined the Congress in 1889 as a protégé of Mahadev Govind Ranade. He led its moderate faction, which sought reform through existing institutions, against Bal Gangadhar Tilak's agitation, a rivalry that split the party at Surat in 1907. As Congress president in 1905 he founded the Servants of India Society to expand Indian education, and he played a leading role in the Morley-Minto Reforms.

entries.name: Great Council of Venice
entries.desc: The Great Council was the chief political assembly of the Republic of Venice from 1172 to 1797, electing most magistracies and senior councils, passing laws and exercising judicial oversight. At first relatively open, it was reshaped by the Serrata, or lock-out, of 28 February 1297, which kept existing members and more than doubled the council to over 1,100 men by 1300; from 1323 membership was restricted to men whose ancestors had held high office, making it hereditary. Its members thus became the nobility of Venice, almost 200 families, later recorded in the Golden Book, while a class of citizens stood between them and the common people. On 12 May 1797 it voted to end the Republic.

entries.name: Great Theban Revolt
entries.desc: The Great Theban Revolt was an uprising in the Thebaid against the Ptolemaic dynasty, lasting from 206 to 186 BCE. Driven by heavy taxes and a devalued currency after the Fourth Syrian War, Theban autonomist feeling and anti-Greek sentiment, the rebels seized the Temple of Edfu and Thebes, and their leader was crowned pharaoh as Haronnophris in 205 BCE. Ptolemy V's army retook Thebes in 199 BCE, but a successor, Chaonnophris, fought on until his defeat south of Aswan in 186 BCE and his execution at Memphis. The revolt pushed later Ptolemies to court the Egyptian clergy and play the role of pharaoh, though a Greco-Macedonian elite still dominated.

entries.name: Halāyudha
entries.desc: Halāyudha was an Indian mathematician and poet of the 10th century, best known for the Mṛtasañjīvanī, a commentary on Piṅgala's Chandaḥśāstra, a work on arranging long and short syllables into metres and counting them. As Halāyudha interpreted and elaborated it, his 'method of pyramidal expansion' (meru-prastāra) for counting metres is equivalent to Pascal's triangle. He first lived at the Rashtrakuta capital Manyakheta, in present-day Karnataka, under the patronage of Emperor Krishna III, whom his Kavi-Rahasya on poetics praises. He later moved to Ujjain in the Paramara kingdom, where he wrote the Mṛtasañjīvanī in honour of King Munja; he also compiled a lexicon and a dictionary.

entries.name: Hangbe
entries.desc: Hangbe was a woman who ruled the Kingdom of Dahomey for a brief period before Agaja came to power in 1718; oral traditions describe her variously as a regent or as a ruler in her own right. The twin sister of King Akaba, she is said to have taken power on his sudden death in 1716, when his eldest son Agbo Sassa was not yet of age, and in one version she wore his armour to continue his war. Her rule is said to have lasted three months or three years. She backed Agbo Sassa against her younger brother Agaja, who became king, and she was left out of the court king lists by a thorough damnatio memoriae; her descendants still live beside the Royal Palaces of Abomey.

entries.name: Hanlin Academy
aka: Academy of the Forest of Pencils
entries.desc: The Hanlin Academy was an academic and administrative institution founded in the 8th century in Chang'an by Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty. Its membership was confined to an elite group of scholars who did secretarial and literary work for the court, and one of its main duties was to settle the interpretation of the Chinese classics on which the imperial examinations for higher government posts were based. Court painters were attached to it, and its members included Li Bai, Su Shi and Ouyang Xiu. From 1407 the Ming attached to it a Bureau of Translators for foreign languages. Its Beijing buildings and library burned in 1900, and it operated until the Xinhai Revolution of 1911.

credit.artist: Jin Kun, Sun Hu, Lu Zhan, Wu Yu, and Zhang Qi

entries.name: He Chaozong
entries.desc: He Chaozong was a Chinese potter of the early 17th century who made mainly Buddhist statues in white porcelain in the tradition of the Dehua kilns in Fujian Province, known in the West as Blanc-de-Chine. Little documentary evidence of him survives beyond his works, though a gazetteer entry of 1763 names him among the art notables of the Ming dynasty. The figures identified by his seal are thickly potted and more expressive than the thinner, standardised unsigned works of the kilns, and he was one of the few named artists in a ceramic history otherwise marked by anonymous, industrial production. A revival of his manner in the late 19th and early 20th centuries produced works bearing his seal.

entries.name: Helvetii
entries.desc: The Helvetii were a Celtic tribe or tribal confederation that occupied most of the Swiss Plateau when they came into contact with the Roman Republic in the 1st century BCE. They had no kings but seem to have been ruled by a class of noblemen. In 58 BCE they burned their homes and set out to settle in southwestern Gaul, a migration that served as a catalyst for Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul; defeated near Bibracte, they were sent back to rebuild their homes, and Caesar's own figures, which modern scholars think too high, claim only about 30 percent survived. Subjugated after 52 BCE and largely Romanised by the 2nd century, they were later assimilated by the Alemanni and Burgundians.

entries.name: Heshen
entries.desc: Heshen was a Manchu official of the Qing dynasty, of the Niohuru clan and the Plain Red Banner, who rose from imperial bodyguard to become the Qianlong Emperor's favourite, holding several top posts at once. His son married the emperor's favourite daughter in 1790, and by Qianlong's abdication in 1796 he had become practically a regent. He extorted gifts, filled posts with his own men and stole public and military funds, and has been described as the most corrupt official in Chinese history. After Qianlong died in 1799 the Jiaqing Emperor charged him with 20 crimes, confiscated a fortune estimated at 60 to 80 million taels and ordered him to hang himself.

entries.name: History of the Haudenosaunee
entries.desc: The history of the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois, goes back to the formation of their league, which many scholars date to about 1450, when the Mohawk, Onondaga, Oneida, Cayuga and Seneca accepted the Peacemaker's Great Law of Peace; the Tuscarora joined in the 18th century. A Council of Fifty sought consensus, clan mothers held considerable power, and captives of mourning wars were adopted to replace the dead or enslaved. From 1609 the Beaver Wars brought the defeat and absorption of the Huron, Neutral and Erie. The American Revolution split the confederacy, and after it much of its homeland was ceded in treaties of 1784 and 1794, while many followed Joseph Brant to the Grand River in Canada.

entries.name: Hōgen rebellion
entries.desc: The Hōgen rebellion was a short civil war fought in Kyoto in 1156 over the Japanese imperial succession and the power of the Fujiwara regents. After the death of the cloistered emperor Toba, his sons, the reigning Emperor Go-Shirakawa and the retired Emperor Sutoku, contested the throne, and the Fujiwara, Minamoto and Taira houses split between them. In a night attack Taira no Kiyomori and Minamoto no Yoshitomo set fire to Sutoku's palace and won for Go-Shirakawa, who went on to rule as cloistered emperor until 1192. Sutoku was banished and Fujiwara no Yorinaga was killed. The war made the samurai clans major political powers and led to the Heiji Rebellion of 1159.

entries.name: Honorary citizenship
entries.desc: Honorary citizenship is a status that a city or other government bestows on a foreign or native individual it considers especially admirable or worthy of the distinction. It is usually symbolic and changes no one's citizenship or nationality, though in Ireland it gives full legal citizenship. In the Russian Empire, by contrast, honorary citizens formed a social estate (sosloviye), a privileged subcategory of the estate of urban dwellers. In German municipalities it is the highest distinction a town can award and outlasts the honoree's death. The United States has granted it to only eight people since 1963 and Canada to seven since 1985, while San Marino offered it to Abraham Lincoln in 1861.

entries.name: Horwennefer
entries.desc: Horwennefer, in Greek Haronnophris, was an Egyptian who led Upper Egypt in secession from the rule of Ptolemy IV Philopator in 205 BCE and ruled as a rebel pharaoh. Together with his successor Ankhwennefer, or Chaonnophris, he held a large part of Egypt until 186 BCE. No monuments of his are known, but a demotic document is dated to his Year 1, and a graffito of about 201 BCE in the mortuary Temple of Seti I at Abydos attests the reach of his rule. Written in Egyptian with Greek letters, it is the oldest testimony of the development that ended with Coptic replacing demotic. He appears to have died before 197 BCE; both rebel kings stressed their strong ties to Thebes.

entries.name: House of Aisin Gioro
entries.desc: The House of Aisin Gioro is the Manchu clan that ruled the Later Jin dynasty from 1616, the Qing dynasty from 1636 to 1912 and Manchukuo from 1932 to 1945. Under the Ming its members were chiefs of the Jianzhou Jurchens; Nurhaci created the clan as part of his reorganisation of Jurchen society in 1601, naming the descendants of his father Taksi Aisin, 'gold'. It had no fixed rule of succession: an emperor named his heir in a secret edict. Princely titles fell by one rank with each generation, except for twelve 'iron-cap' peerages that passed on undiminished. The clan had 29,000 members when the Qing fell in 1912, and Puyi kept his title in the Forbidden City until 1924.

entries.name: Hugh Tinker
entries.desc: Hugh Tinker was a British historian whom the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography called Britain's foremost historian of modern Burma. Born in Westcliff-on-Sea, he served in the Royal Armoured Corps in the Second World War, then read history at Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, and from 1948 taught the modern history of Southeast Asia at SOAS, where Aung San Suu Kyi was at one point his student. His first book, of 1954, dealt with the government of India, Pakistan and Burma. He directed the Institute of Race Relations from 1970 to 1972, then researched the Indian diaspora at the Institute of Commonwealth Studies, and taught politics at Lancaster University from 1977 to 1982.

entries.name: Huibin Jang
entries.desc: Huibin Jang, personal name Jang Ok-jeong, was a consort of King Sukjong of Joseon Korea and the mother of King Gyeongjong. Born into the jungin class from a long line of interpreters and tied to the Namin faction, she entered the palace as a lady-in-waiting and rose through the ranks of royal consort from 1686, bearing the king's first son in 1688. She was made queen in 1689, when Queen Min was deposed, but lost the king's favour and was demoted in 1694. Accused of cursing Queen Min, who died in 1701, she was executed by poisoning that year, and Sukjong forbade any royal consort from becoming queen.

entries.name: Hwanjile
entries.desc: Hwanjile was a high priest and kpojito, or "reign mate", of the Kingdom of Dahomey, in what is now Benin. An Aja woman brought to the palace at Abomey, reportedly as a war captive or trader, she helped Tegbesu take the throne over his older brother and was named kpojito, which made her the richest and most powerful woman in the kingdom. She imported the creator gods Mawu and Lisa, proclaimed them rulers of the Dahomean pantheon and served as their high priest beside the palace. After her death a descendant took her name and functions, a succession that still continues.

entries.name: Ilbert Bill
entries.desc: The Ilbert Bill was a bill introduced to the Imperial Legislative Council of British India in February 1883 that would have let senior Indian judges try cases involving white plaintiffs or defendants. Drafted by Sir Courtenay Ilbert and backed by the Governor-General, Lord Ripon, it met fierce opposition from the European community, including plantation owners, whose protests and press drew on openly racist tropes. A compromise passed in January 1884 gave European defendants the right to a jury at least half European. The controversy strengthened Indian national awareness, and the Indian National Congress was formed a year later.

entries.name: Imperial Clan Court
entries.desc: The Imperial Clan Court was the institution responsible for all matters concerning the imperial family under the Ming and Qing dynasties of China, and later the Nguyễn dynasty of Vietnam. The Hongwu Emperor established it in 1389, drawing on earlier Tang, Song and Yuan offices. Staffed by members of the imperial clan, it came under the Ministry of Rites in the Ming and stood outside the regular bureaucracy in the Qing. Imperial clansmen who committed crimes were not tried in the regular courts. From reports of births, marriages and deaths the Court compiled the imperial genealogy, revised 28 times under the Qing.

entries.name: Imperial Household Department
entries.desc: The Imperial Household Department was the Qing dynasty institution that managed the internal affairs of the imperial family and the inner palace, tasks in which it largely replaced eunuchs. Founded before the Qing conquest of 1644, it matured after 1661 under the Kangxi Emperor. It was staffed by booi, bondservants of the upper three banners, among them Manchu, Han Chinese, Korean and Muslim companies, with the sinjeku as the lowest class of bondservants. Beyond palace works, ceremonies and the imperial mausoleums, it traded in jade, ginseng, salt and furs, ran textile factories in Jiangnan and by the nineteenth century oversaw more than 56 subagencies.

entries.name: Impi
entries.desc: Impi is a Nguni word meaning war or combat, and by extension any body of men gathered for war; in English it usually means a Zulu regiment, an ibutho, or the army of the Zulu Kingdom. It grew out of older age-grade customs, which the Mthethwa chief Dingiswayo began to use as military drafts and which Shaka reorganised radically.
