Young men were formed into regiments by age rather than clan, served the king until he allowed them to marry, and fought with the short stabbing spear and large shield in the buffalo horns formation. The impi defeated the British at Isandlwana in 1879.

entries.name: Indian indenture system
entries.desc: The Indian indenture system was a system of indentured servitude that carried more than 1.6 million workers from India to European colonies after the abolition of slavery. Described by colonial authorities as free migration, it relied on recruits who were often deceived, coerced or kidnapped, and the historian Hugh Tinker called it a new form of slavery. It began with the Atlas voyage to Mauritius in 1834 and spread to the Caribbean, Natal, Réunion and Fiji, where labourers worked sugar plantations under harsh discipline and criminal penalties. Export to Natal ended in 1911 and to the other colonies in 1917, leaving large Indian diasporas.

entries.name: Indravarman II
entries.desc: Indravarman II was a ruler of the Khmer Empire and the son of Jayavarman VII. The years of his reign are disputed, partly because his successor, Jayavarman VIII, probably destroyed the records about him; the only inscription that names him directly reports that he died in 1243. A Buddhist, he is credited with enlarging or completing some of his father's temples. During his peaceful reign the Khmers lost control of Champa, and the new Sukhothai Kingdom under Indraditya took some of their western territories. The historian David P. Chandler suggested that he may have been the Leper King of Khmer legend.

entries.name: Indravarman III
entries.desc: Indravarman III, also titled Srindravarman, ruled the Khmer Empire from 1295 to 1308. A commander of the army, he took power when his father-in-law Jayavarman VIII abdicated: the king's daughter gave him the Sacred Sword, and he seized the crown prince, had his toes cut off and imprisoned him before being crowned. A follower of Theravada Buddhism, he made it the state religion. The Chinese diplomat Zhou Daguan stayed at his court from August 1296 to July 1297 and recorded that a recent war with the Siamese had devastated the country; his report is today one of the most important sources on life in Angkor.

entries.name: Induna
entries.desc: Induna, plural iziNduna, is a Zulu and Xhosa title meaning advisor, headman, ambassador or commander of a group of warriors. It was reserved for senior officials appointed by the king or chief for their leadership, bravery or service, and the iziNduna often acted as a bridge between the people and the king, gathering in an indaba to discuss important matters. Among other Bantu peoples of South Africa a nduna was the monarch's political representative and royal councillor. Notable holders include Ndlela kaSompisi, chief advisor to Dingane, and Ntshingwayo kaMahole, who commanded at Isandlwana. The word survives in South African English for a boss.

entries.name: Internal passport
entries.desc: An internal or domestic passport is an identity document in passport form, used variously for identification, civil registration, recording ethnicity or status, and controlling internal migration. France required one to leave one's canton from 1795, and former convicts carried a yellow passport that made them outcasts. The Russian Empire's system was abandoned after 1917, but the Soviet Union reintroduced the passport regime in 1932, binding people to their place of residence through the propiska. Others served discrimination: passes for African Americans in the slave states, Canada's pass system for First Nations people from 1885, and apartheid South Africa's pass books.

entries.name: Ivor Wilks
entries.desc: Ivor Wilks was a British Africanist and historian of Ghana, considered one of the founders of modern African historiography. After service in the British Army in Palestine and studies at Bangor and Oxford, he went in 1953 to the University College of the Gold Coast, now the University of Ghana, where he devoted his career to what he called the decolonisation of West African history and helped set up the Institute of African Studies at Legon. In 1966 he moved to Northwestern University. His 1975 book on Asante in the nineteenth century remains a standard text on the Ashanti Empire; he also wrote on the Welsh working-class movement.

entries.name: Iyoba of Benin
entries.desc: The Iyoba, known in English as the Queen Mother, is an important female titleholder in the chieftaincy system of the Kingdom of Benin, in present-day Nigeria. According to tradition, King Esigie created the office for his mother Idia, who had rallied the Binis to his side in a civil war with his brother and against the rebel Igala. Ranking equal to the senior chiefs, the Iyoba held the town of Uselu as a perpetual fief, where she lived after her son's coronation, forbidden to see him again yet serving as his chief advisor. She commanded her own regiment in war, and after death was honoured as her son's patron goddess in the shrine of the kings.

entries.name: Jacob Cats
entries.desc: Jacob Cats was a Dutch poet, humorist, jurist and politician, best known for his moralistic emblem books. Born in Brouwershaven, he studied law in Rotterdam and Paris, practised in The Hague and later farmed and wrote in Zeeland. He became pensionary of Middelburg and then Dordrecht, was knighted by Charles I of England in 1627, and served as Grand Pensionary of Holland from 1636 until he resigned in 1651, though he left little mark on the office. His collected poems are said to have sold around 50,000 copies, often the only book besides the Bible in Dutch homes. His villa near The Hague, the Catshuis, is now the Dutch Prime Minister's residence.

entries.name: Jahriyya revolt
entries.desc: The Jahriyya revolt of 1781 was a rebellion in Qing China that grew out of sectarian violence between two Naqshbandi Sufi orders, the Jahriyya and their rivals the Khafiyya. After street fighting and lawsuits between them, the Qing arrested the Jahriyya leader Ma Mingxin; his followers tried to free him by force, which led to his execution and the crushing of the rebels with the help of the Khafiyya and Muslim loyalists. Salar and other Jahriyya rebels, labelled the New Teaching, were deported to Xinjiang, Guizhou and Yunnan. The Dungan Revolt of 1895–96 broke out in the same place for very similar reasons.

entries.name: Jamsetji Tata
entries.desc: Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata was an Indian industrialist and philanthropist who founded the Tata Group, India's largest conglomerate. Born in Navsari into a poor Parsi family of Zoroastrian priests, he broke with the priestly tradition, joined his father's trading firm and founded his own trading company in 1868. He built cotton mills in Bombay, Nagpur and Ahmedabad and opened the Taj Mahal Hotel in Mumbai in 1903, India's first hotel with electricity. His plans for an iron and steel company, a hydroelectric plant and a research institute were realised after his death as Tata Steel, Tata Power and the Indian Institute of Science, and the city of Jamshedpur bears his name.

entries.name: Japanese Village (Ayutthaya)
entries.desc: The Japanese Village, Ban Yipun in Thai, was a Japanese enclave just outside Ayutthaya, the capital of the Ayutthaya Kingdom, that flourished from the 17th century to the mid-18th century. Its people, perhaps 1,000 to 1,500, were mercenaries, traders and Christians fleeing persecution in Japan, along with Thai and Chinese slaves. Ayutthaya hired Japanese soldiers against the Burmese, and their leaders could hold the Phraya rank, third highest in the Siamese hierarchy, as Yamada Nagamasa did. In 1630, after Nagamasa's assassination, the settlement was burned and its residents killed; refounded in 1633, it gradually merged into the Thai population.

credit.artist: กสิณธร ราชโอรส
credit.source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:หมู่บ้านญี่ปุ่น_อ.พระนครศรีอยุธยา_จ.พระนครศรีอยุธยา_(2).jpg

entries.name: Jayanegara
entries.desc: Jayanegara was the second monarch of the Majapahit Empire in Java, ruling from 1309 until his death in 1328, and the only son of its founder, Raden Wijaya. Accounts differ over his mother: inscriptions name Queen Tribhuwana, while the Pararaton and the Nagarakretagama name the Malayu princess Dara Petak. His reign was troubled by rebellions, above all that of Kuti in 1319, which seized the capital until Gajah Mada, commander of the palace guard, crushed it and began his rise at court. The Pararaton calls him Kala Gemet, the weak villain. He was killed by his doctor Tanca in 1328, and the true nature of the murder remains unknown.

entries.name: Jayavarman VIII
entries.desc: Jayavarman VIII was a king of the Khmer Empire who ruled from 1243 until his abdication in 1295. A Shaivite, he turned from his father's Buddhism to Hinduism and tried to destroy Buddhism: Buddha images at temples such as Preah Khan were defaced, and the Bayon was made a temple of Shiva, its central Buddha statue thrown into a well. Faced with the Mongols of Kublai Khan, whose envoys he had imprisoned in 1281, he chose to pay tribute and so kept his throne, while the Lavo kingdom threw off Khmer overlordship in 1290. He was overthrown by his Buddhist son-in-law, Indravarman III, and the kingdom returned to Buddhism.

entries.name: Jiajing Emperor
entries.desc: The Jiajing Emperor, personal name Zhu Houcong, was the 12th emperor of the Ming dynasty of China, reigning from 1521 to 1567. A cousin of the Zhengde Emperor, who died without an heir, he came to the throne unexpectedly and at once clashed with his officials in the Great Rites Controversy, from which he emerged victorious after three years. From 1542 he lived in the West Park outside the Forbidden City among Taoist temples, eunuchs and trusted advisers, and his pursuit of immortality led him to elixirs containing arsenic, lead and mercury. His reign saw Altan Khan's raids, which reached the outskirts of Beijing in 1550, and wokou piracy that peaked in the 1550s.

entries.name: Jige
entries.desc: A jige is a traditional Korean pack frame for carrying heavy loads on the back. Used for centuries in farming communities, it carried compost, grain, wood and grass, and its easy making and the mountainous Korean terrain made it widespread; designs varied by region. The name jige is first known from a book of 1690 and was established by the 18th century. Its frame of pine wood stands on two legs with upward-angled branches to hold the load, straw shoulder straps and a loose stick for propping it up and walking. During the Korean War of 1950–1953 it still carried supplies and ammunition in the mountains, and American soldiers called it the A-frame.

entries.name: Jigonhsasee
entries.desc: Jigonhsasee was an Iroquoian woman considered, with the Great Peacemaker and Hiawatha, a co-founder of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, dated by some between 1142 and 1450 and by others to about 1570–1600. According to Haudenosaunee oral tradition, she lived beside the warriors' path and gave warriors of every faction food and counsel at her hearth. She joined the Peacemaker's vision of a league in the form of a longhouse, and at the peace gathering he gave her the task of assigning men to the Grand Council and gave women the power to choose the chiefs. Called the Mother of Nations, she became the Head Clan Mother, a name passed to her successors until the 1800s.

entries.name: Jingdezhen
entries.desc: Jingdezhen is a city in eastern Jiangxi province, China, known as the Porcelain Capital for producing ceramics for at least 1,000 years. Founded as Changnan under the Jin dynasty, it took its present name in 1004 from the era name of Emperor Zhenzong of Song, under whom its porcelain first rose to fame. Close to deposits of pottery stone and kaolin and to pine forests for fuel, it was the largest centre of Chinese porcelain by the 14th century, making qingbai ware, blue and white from the 1330s and famille rose under the Qing. From the Ming onwards its official kilns made imperial porcelain for the court. Taiping forces destroyed its 9,000 kilns in 1855.

entries.name: Johann and Wendelin of Speyer
entries.desc: Johann and Wendelin of Speyer were German brothers who worked as printers in Venice from 1468 to 1477, among the first to bring printing from Mainz to Italy. The Venetian Senate granted Johann a five-year monopoly of printing, and he began in 1469 with a hundred copies of Cicero's letters, followed by the first printed edition of Pliny the Elder's Natural History and an edition of Livy. Johann died of the plague in 1470 while printing Augustine's City of God, and Wendelin finished it and issued over seventy major works until 1477. Johann is credited with the first numbering of leaves in Arabic numerals, and the brothers are sometimes named as originators of roman type.

entries.name: Jūnihitoe
entries.desc: The jūnihitoe, literally twelve layers, is a style of formal court dress first worn in the Heian period by noblewomen and ladies-in-waiting at the Japanese Imperial Court. It consisted of many layered silk robes, the outer ones cut larger and thinner to show those beneath, over an innermost kosode and long red hakama, with a short coat and a train for formal occasions; early versions could weigh as much as 20 kilograms. The colour combinations of the layers, kasane no irome, were named for and evoked the seasons. It first appeared around the 10th century, and its layers were much reduced by the Kamakura period. Members of the Imperial House still wear it on important occasions.

entries.name: Juren
entries.desc: Juren, literally recommended man, was the rank won by passing the provincial examination, the xiangshi, in the imperial examination system of China: above the shengyuan and below the jinshi, the highest degree. In the Ming and Qing dynasties candidates who already held the shengyuan rank sat the examination every three years in their provincial capital, under strict rules against favour; quotas kept success rare, and by 1630 about 49,200 candidates competed for 1,279 degrees. Women, clergy and merchants were excluded. The rank could also be bought, and it brought gentry status and its privileges. The title ended with the abolition of the examinations in 1904.

entries.name: Jyotirao Phule
entries.desc: Jyotirao Phule was an Indian social activist, businessman, anti-caste reformer and writer from Maharashtra. Born into the Mali caste of flower growers, placed among the Shudras in the caste hierarchy, he was insulted at a Brahmin friend's wedding in 1848, an event that shaped his view of caste injustice. That year he and his wife Savitribai opened the first indigenously run school for girls in Pune, and later schools for children of the untouchable castes. In 1873 he founded the Satyashodhak Samaj to win equal rights for lower castes and women and published Gulamgiri, on slavery and caste. He received the title Mahatma in 1888 and died in Pune in 1890.

entries.name: Kagerō Nikki
entries.desc: Kagerō Nikki, known in English as The Gossamer Years, is a work of classical Japanese diary literature written around 974 by a Heian noblewoman known only as the Mother of Michitsuna. Mixing waka poems and prose, it records her marriage to the courtier Fujiwara no Kaneie, her anguish as his visits to her dwindled, her pilgrimages, and her devotion to her son and adopted daughter. She probably began it around 971, during one of her marriage crises. Its frank first-person exploration of feeling expanded the possibilities of kana prose and influenced later women's writing, including The Tale of Genji.

entries.name: Kakawin Sutasoma
entries.desc: Kakawin Sutasoma is an Old Javanese poem in Sanskrit-derived metres, written by Mpu Tantular in the 14th century during the golden age of the Majapahit Empire, most probably between 1365 and 1389. Based on the Mahasutasoma Jataka, it tells of Sutasoma, a Bodhisattva born as the son of the king of Hastinapura, and it is the only Buddhist kakawin in Javanese literature. Teaching tolerance between Hindus and Buddhists, it is the source of Indonesia's motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, usually translated as Unity in Diversity. Nearly all surviving manuscripts, on lontar and paper, come from Bali, where it is still well known and played in wayang theatre.

entries.name: Kakawin
entries.desc: Kakawin are long narrative poems in Old Javanese, also called Kawi, written in metres derived from Sanskrit prosody. Poets used a formal literary language rather than the vernacular, and composed and performed the poems at the courts of central and east Javanese kings between the 9th and 16th centuries, and in Bali. Each stanza has four lines with a fixed number of syllables arranged in patterns of heavy and light syllables, guru and laghu. Although the poems depict characters and events from Hindu mythology, their stories are set in the landscapes of the islands, which makes them rich sources on courtly society in Java and Bali.

entries.name: Kana
entries.desc: Kana are syllabaries used to write the morae of Japanese: today hiragana and katakana, and historically also man'yōgana, Chinese characters used for their sounds, and hentaigana, older variants of hiragana. The name means borrowed name, in contrast to kanji used for their meaning. Each kana stands for a vowel, a consonant and vowel, or the final nasal n, so the system represents spoken Japanese closely. Phonetic kanji were once called men's kana, while hiragana, derived from cursive man'yōgana, was called women's script. Tradition credits the priest Kūkai with inventing kana in the ninth century, and katakana are also used to write Ainu.

entries.name: Kassi
entries.desc: Kassi, also called Qasa, meaning the Queen, was an empress of Mali, principal wife and paternal cousin of Mansa Suleyman, who reigned from 1341 to 1360. As was traditional she ruled jointly with her husband, and Ibn Battuta recorded that her name was mentioned in the pulpit, an honour due only to a sovereign. Suleyman later divorced her for a commoner, Bendjou, but the noblewomen of the court kept honouring Kassi, who took sanctuary in the mosque and encouraged her relatives to revolt with the sons of the former ruler Maghan. Suleyman defeated them in 1352 or 1353. Her son Kassa briefly succeeded him.

entries.name: Kholop
entries.desc: A kholop was an unfree dependant in Kievan Rus' and later Muscovy; in the 11th and 12th centuries the term covered several categories of dependent people, especially slaves. The Russkaya Pravda set out their status: a master could kill or sell his kholop but answered for his acts. People became kholops through capture, selling themselves, debt, crime or marriage to a kholop. In 16th-century Russia their status was essentially that of slaves; some served as armed retainers of landowners, and many fell into debt bondage as kabala kholops. Those who were house serfs became liable to the poll tax in 1722–1724 and were thereafter treated as ordinary serfs.

entries.name: Khusrau Khan
entries.desc: Khusrau Khan, regnal name Nasir ud-Din Khusrau Shah, was the sixteenth Sultan of Delhi for about two months in 1320. Born among the Baradus of Gujarat, a Hindu military group, he was captured in Alauddin Khalji's conquest of Malwa in 1305, brought to Delhi as a slave and converted to Islam. Sultan Mubarak Shah, whose favourite he became, gave him his title and made him vazir; he retook Devagiri in 1317 and forced the Kakatiya ruler of Warangal to resume tribute in 1318. In 1320 he led Baradus and discontented nobles in killing Mubarak Shah and took the throne, but Ghazi Malik's rebels defeated him, and he was captured and killed.

entries.name: Kolkhoz
entries.desc: A kolkhoz was a collective farm in the Soviet Union, the main form of Soviet agriculture alongside the state farms, or sovkhozes. The first were organised soon after 1918, and after forced collectivisation the agricultural artel became the only form by 1938. Legally a cooperative, in practice it was run by district and provincial authorities, and membership was neither voluntary nor freely left. Members, kolkhozniki, were paid by labour days, often in little or no cash, while the farm sold its produce to the state at very low fixed prices, a major source of state income. Private plots of about one acre produced a large share of output. Their number declined rapidly after 1992.

credit.artist: Неизвестный художник (не указан в выходных данных плаката; отсутствует авторская монограмма или подпись)

entries.name: Kolyma
entries.desc: Kolyma is a historical region of the Russian Far East covering the basin of the Kolyma River and the northern shores of the Sea of Okhotsk, with a subarctic climate of permafrost and tundra and rich gold deposits. Its indigenous peoples include the Evens, Koryaks, Yakuts, Chukchis and Yukaghirs. From 1932 the trust Dalstroy built Magadan and some 80 camps with forced labour, many of the prisoners swept up in the campaigns against the kulaks, and they mined gold and built the Kolyma Highway, the Road of Bones. Solzhenitsyn called Kolyma the pole of cold and cruelty in the Gulag. Estimates of the dead up to the mid-1950s range from 250,000 to over a million.

credit.artist: The original uploader was Oxonhutch at English Wikipedia .

entries.name: Kris
entries.desc: The kris or keris is an asymmetrical Javanese dagger whose blade is patterned by laminations of iron and nickelous iron, called pamor; many have a wavy blade, though older ones were mostly straight. Its development most probably took place in Java, and a Chinese account of the Majapahit Empire describes men from the king to commoners carrying such daggers; the oldest known surviving kris, the Kris of Knaud, bears a date corresponding to 1342. Both weapon and spiritual object, it served as a talisman, an heirloom, part of ceremonial dress and an indicator of social status, and was forged by master smiths called empu. UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2005.

entries.name: Kugyō
entries.desc: Kugyō was the collective term for the most important officials of the Japanese imperial court before the Meiji era, the upper court nobility holding court rank between the First and Third Ranks under the Ritsuryō system, as opposed to the lower nobility. They comprised the Kō, the Chancellor of the Realm and the Ministers of the Left and Right, and the Kei, the counsellors of Third Rank or higher; later the regents, the Inner Minister, the Middle Counsellors and some holders of the Fourth Rank were included. The model was the Three Lords and Nine Ministers of Qin China. In 1869 the court nobility and the daimyo were merged into the new peerage, the kazoku.

entries.name: Kūkai
entries.desc: Kūkai, posthumously called Kōbō Daishi, was a Japanese Buddhist monk, calligrapher and poet who founded the esoteric Shingon school. Born into the aristocratic Saeki family on Shikoku, he left his Confucian studies for Buddhist practice and in 804 joined an official mission to China, where he studied esoteric Buddhism under the monk Huiguo; he returned in 806 with many texts new to Japan. With the support of emperors, especially Saga, he founded a retreat on Mount Kōya and was given Tō-ji in Kyoto, which became the first Shingon centre. In 828 he opened a school open to all regardless of rank. Legend credits him with inventing kana.

entries.name: Kulak
entries.desc: A kulak was a peasant who owned over 3 hectares of land at the end of the Russian Empire, a pejorative term from the 19th century for wealthier peasants who owned land and lent to poorer ones; the class grew after the abolition of serfdom in 1861 and the Stolypin reform. The Bolsheviks branded kulaks class enemies, and the label spread to peasants with only a little more than their neighbours. From 1930 Stalin's campaign to liquidate them as a class seized their farms, executed many and deported others: Soviet archives record 1,803,392 people sent to labour colonies and camps in 1930 and 1931. Estimates of the deaths vary widely.

credit.artist: Credited to U. Druzhelubov. The date of death is impossible to determine therefore PMA is not known.

entries.name: Kurmi
entries.desc: The Kurmi are a traditionally non-elite caste of tillers in the lower Gangetic plain of India, especially southern Awadh, eastern Uttar Pradesh and parts of Bihar and Jharkhand. Mughal and British administrators praised them for their work ethic and superior tillage and manuring, which let them grow market crops; in 18th-century Awadh the gentry let them clear jungle at low rents and then raised the rent well above the going rate. Landed elites who claimed twice-born status demanded unpaid labour of them as supposedly servile. In response Kurmi caste associations, the first formed at Lucknow in 1894, campaigned for Kshatriya status and in 1910 founded the All India Kurmi Kshatriya Mahasabha.

entries.name: Kusi Obodom
entries.desc: Kusi Obodom was the third Asantehene of the Ashanti Empire, ruling from 1750 to 1764. The kingmakers elected him over Darko, the successor named by Opoku Ware I, which set off a civil war until his rule was affirmed in 1751. At home he restored the full constitutional powers of the chiefs that his predecessor had limited, banned human sacrifice, though the practice continued after him, and is said to have formed the Akwanmofo to keep the roads. Abroad he faced an alliance of rebel provinces and the Fante that blocked Ashanti's way to the coast. In 1764 his army was defeated by Dahomey and Oyo at Atakpamé, and his unpopularity and failing health led to his removal.

entries.name: Kwaku Dua I
entries.desc: Kwaku Dua I, also Kwaku Dua Panin and born Fredua Agyeman, was the eighth Asantehene of the Asante Empire, from 1834 until his death in 1867. He had fought against Gyaman and commanded a division at the battle of Katamanso in 1826. As king he pursued mercantilism, enlarged the state's share of the economy, extorted payments from wealthy Asante to build the reserves, and created the Manwere fekuo, the last of Kumasi's administrative units. He rebuilt Kumasi's streets and the great roads. In 1837 he agreed with William I of the Netherlands to supply recruits for the Dutch East Indies Army in exchange for guns, and sent his son Kwasi Boachi to be educated in the Netherlands.

entries.name: Kwasi Boachi
entries.desc: Kwasi Boachi, or Kwasi Boakye, was a prince of the Ashanti Empire, son of King Kwaku Dua I, sent to the Netherlands with his cousin Kwame Poku in 1837 as part of negotiations over the recruitment of Ashanti soldiers for the Dutch East Indies Army. Unlike his cousin, who returned to the Gold Coast, he stayed in Europe, graduating as a mining engineer from the Royal Academy in Delft in 1847 and attending lectures at the Freiberg Mining Academy. Sent to the Dutch East Indies in 1850, he suffered discrimination from his superior and in 1857 received compensation, including an estate south of Buitenzorg, where he died in 1904.

credit.artist: Possibly made by C. Vogel von Vogelstein

entries.name: Lady Hyegyeong
entries.desc: Lady Hyegyeong of the Pungsan Hong clan was a Korean writer and Crown Princess of Joseon, the wife of Crown Prince Sado and mother of King Jeongjo. Chosen at the age of nine as the Crown Prince's bride, she married him in 1744 and bore him sons and daughters while his mental illness grew ever more violent. In 1762 King Yeongjo sentenced Sado, and he died that year. Between 1795 and 1806 she wrote, in Hangul rather than literary Chinese, the four narratives known as The Memoirs of Lady Hyegyeong, or A Record of Sorrowful Days, recounting her life and her family's story. Emperor Gojong gave her a posthumous title as empress in 1903.

entries.name: Law of Spikelets
entries.desc: The Law of Spikelets was a decree of the Soviet Union, dated 7 August 1932, that protected the property of kolkhozes, the collective farms, and especially their grain, from theft, largely by desperate peasants during the Soviet famine of 1932–33. Theft of collective or cooperative property was punished by execution with confiscation of all property, or in mitigating circumstances by at least 10 years of imprisonment, and amnesty was forbidden. Its common name came from Prosecutor General Vyshinsky's condemnation of prosecuting peasants who gleaned the spikelets left in the fields. There were 181,827 sentences under it in 1932–1939; in 1936 a review found most applications incorrect.

entries.name: Leonardo Loredan
entries.desc: Leonardo Loredan was a Venetian nobleman and statesman who reigned as the 75th Doge of Venice from 1501 until his death in 1521. Born into the noble Loredan family, he traded in North Africa and the Levant before rising through the Republic's magistracies, among them Savio del Consiglio, podestà of Padua, ducal councillor and, from 1492, Procurator of Saint Mark, one of the highest offices of the state. As doge he led Venice through the War of the League of Cambrai, in which the Republic was defeated in 1509 before a new alliance with Louis XII of France in 1513. Under his rule, in 1516, a decree isolated the Jews of Venice in the first Ghetto.

entries.name: Lingam
entries.desc: A lingam, Sanskrit for sign or mark, is an abstract or aniconic representation of the Hindu god Shiva in Shaivism, usually a short cylindrical pillar of stone, metal, wood, clay or precious stone. It often stands within a disc-shaped platform, the yoni, its feminine counterpart, shaped to let liquid offerings drain away. Though rooted in representations of the male organ, it is regarded in Shaivism as the outward symbol of formless reality, and with the yoni as the union of the feminine and masculine that recreates all existence. It is typically the main devotional image in temples of Shiva; the Gudimallam Lingam, one of the oldest, is mostly dated to the 3rd to 1st century BCE.

entries.name: Lishenets
entries.desc: A lishenets, plural lishentsy, was a disenfranchised person in Soviet Russia from 1918 to 1936. The 1918 Constitution of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic listed the categories stripped of the vote, among them those who used hired labour for profit, those living on unearned income, private merchants, monks and clergy, and former policemen and military officers. The Bolsheviks used disenfranchisement as repression against people classed as enemies of the working people: a lishenets could hold no government post, receive no higher education and join no kolkhoz or cooperative. The 1936 Constitution brought universal suffrage and ended the category.

entries.name: Lit de justice
entries.desc: The lit de justice, or bed of justice, was a formal session of the Parlement of Paris under the presidency of the King of France in the Ancien Régime, held to compel the registration of royal edicts and impose the king's sovereignty. It took its name from the throne of five cushions under a canopy on which the king sat, surrounded by princes of the blood, peers and prelates. In the Middle Ages it was the setting for trials of great aristocrats; from the 16th century it enforced edicts on a reluctant court, since in the king's presence the parlement lost its role of judge. It was revived under Louis XV, and the last session was held at Versailles in 1788.

entries.name: Liu Jin
entries.desc: Liu Jin was a Chinese eunuch of the Ming dynasty who dominated the government of the Zhengde Emperor from 1506 to 1510. Castrated as a boy and adopted by a palace eunuch, he served the future emperor from 1492 as one of the eunuchs later called the Eight Tigers. As head of the Directorate of Ceremonial, the most influential eunuch office, he pressed officials with fear and fines to raise state revenue, raised eunuch intendants to equal footing with provincial officials, and changed the examination quotas in favour of the north. His reforms provoked unrest and mutinies; in 1510 the other Tigers accused him of treason, and he was executed by slow slicing.

entries.name: Machimoi
entries.desc: The machimoi, a Greek word meaning pugnacious, were a broad category of low-ranked ancient Egyptian soldiers of the Late Period (664–332 BCE) and, more prominently, the Ptolemaic dynasty. Herodotus described them as a closed caste of warriors, forbidden other work and granted twelve arourai of tax-free land, in two groups, the hermotybies and kalasiries. Under the Ptolemies they appear in documents as guards and soldiers, taking on larger roles likely from the Battle of Raphia in 217 BCE; the Rosetta Stone mentions an amnesty for deserters among them. Christelle Fischer-Bovet argued in 2013 that they formed the lowest level of the military hierarchy, yet stood above the average peasant.

entries.name: Marriage of the Sea ceremony
entries.desc: The Marriage of the Sea was a maritime ceremony of the Republic of Venice, held on Ascension Day, in which the doge threw a golden ring into the Adriatic Sea as a sign of Venice's dominion over it. According to most authors it first appeared around the year 1000, at the time of the Venetian conquest of Dalmatia under Doge Pietro II Orseolo; it was fixed on Ascension Day in 1173 under Doge Sebastiano Ziani. The doge sailed out on the state galley, the bucentaur, with the Senate, and the Patriarch of Venice pronounced a nuptial blessing. It lasted until the fall of the Republic in 1797, and the mayor of Venice has re-enacted it since 1965.

entries.name: Matteo Ricci
entries.desc: Matteo Ricci was an Italian Jesuit, born in Macerata in the Papal States, who served at the court of Ming dynasty China and was one of the founders of the Jesuit China missions. Arriving at Macau in 1582, he mastered the Chinese language and script, settled in Zhaoqing and later reached Nanjing, and in 1601 became the first European invited into the Forbidden City, valued for his predictions of solar eclipses. He stressed parallels between Catholicism and Confucianism, converted several officials, and with Xu Guangqi translated Euclid's Elements into Chinese. He made the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu world map of 1602, and died in Beijing in 1610, where the Wanli Emperor granted him a burial place.

credit.artist: Chinese brother Emmanuel Pereira (born Yu Wen-hui 游文辉)

entries.name: Mayo College
entries.desc: Mayo College is a boys-only private boarding school in Ajmer, Rajasthan, India, founded in 1875 and named after the 6th Earl of Mayo, Viceroy of India from 1869 to 1872. Proposed in 1869 by Colonel Walter, it was meant to be an Eton of India: the British built it for the sons of the Indian upper classes, particularly the princes and nobles, to give the rulers of the princely states an education like that of Eton College. Its first student, Maharaja Mangal Singh of Alwar, arrived in October 1875 on an elephant with 300 retainers. Its coat of arms, designed by Lockwood Kipling, carries Rajput emblems, and it has educated many members of India's royal families.

entries.name: Mehu
entries.desc: Mehu was an ancient Egyptian vizier of the Sixth Dynasty, holder of the most important office at the royal court. He is known mainly from his monumental mastaba at Saqqara, not far from the Pyramid of Unas. His exact date is disputed: Hartwig Altenmüller, who published the tomb's reliefs, places him under Teti, while others date him slightly later, under Pepi I. Besides the vizierate he held titles such as overseer of the treasuries, overseer of the double granary, overseer of Upper Egypt and overseer of all royal works. His parents are unknown, but he very likely came from Mendes; parts of his mastaba were reserved for a vizier named Hetepka, possibly his son.

entries.name: Milovan Djilas
entries.desc: Milovan Djilas was a Yugoslav communist politician, theorist and author, born near Mojkovac in the Kingdom of Montenegro. Jailed and tortured as a student radical in the 1930s, he joined the politburo of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia in 1939, helped Josip Broz Tito build the Partisan resistance in the Second World War, and became vice-president in Tito's government. Once regarded as Tito's possible successor, he was expelled from the Central Committee in January 1954 after articles arguing against the one-party state. In The New Class, published abroad in 1957, he argued that communism had created a privileged class of party bureaucracy, and he spent years in prison for his writings.

entries.name: Minamoto clan
entries.desc: Minamoto was a noble surname that the Emperors of Japan gave, from 814, to members of the imperial family excluded from the succession and demoted into the nobility; Emperor Saga first granted it to his seventh son. The Minamoto were one of the four great clans of Heian politics, with the Fujiwara, Taira and Tachibana. Their most notable line, the Seiwa Genji, became a warrior dynasty that restored order for the Fujiwara. After defeats in 1156 and 1160, Minamoto no Yoritomo rose against the Taira in the Genpei War of 1180–1185, destroyed them, and in 1192 became shōgun, founding Japan's first shogunate at Kamakura. The Ashikaga and Tokugawa claimed Minamoto descent.

entries.name: Mir Damad
entries.desc: Mir Damad, born Seyyed Mir Mohammad Baqer Astarabadi, was an Iranian Twelver Shia philosopher in the tradition of Avicenna, who died in 1631 or 1632. With his student Mulla Sadra he was the foremost figure of the cultural renaissance of Iran under the Safavid dynasty, and he is regarded as the founder of the School of Isfahan; admirers called him the Third Teacher after Aristotle and al-Farabi. His chief idea was atemporal origination, which sought to resolve whether the world was created in time. His name, Groom of the King, came from his marriage to a daughter of Shah Abbas. He wrote 134 known works, some of them poetry under the pen name Ishraq.

entries.name: Mohawk
entries.desc: The Mohawk, in their own language Kanienʼkehá꞉ka, People of the Flint Place, are an Indigenous people of the Northeastern Woodlands and the easternmost nation of the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy, known as the Keepers of the Eastern Door. Their homeland centred on the Mohawk Valley of present-day New York. Their society rests on three matrilineal clans, Bear, Turtle and Wolf, led by women; children belong to their mother's clan, and Clan Mothers nominate the hereditary chiefs. Smallpox reduced them from 7,740 to 2,830 in 1635. They sided with the British in the American Revolutionary War and today live in communities in New York, Quebec and Ontario.

entries.name: Mortmain
entries.desc: Mortmain, from the Medieval Latin mortua manus, dead hand, is the perpetual and inalienable ownership of land by a corporation or institution, usually spoken of in the context of its prohibition. In medieval Western Europe the Church and religious orders were legal persons that never died, so land given to them never escheated or passed by inheritance, unlike the land nobles held from the king in return for service, especially in war. As the Church gained a large share of land, tension grew with the Crown. In England the Statutes of Mortmain of 1279 and 1290, under Edward I, required the Crown's authorisation before land could vest perpetually in a corporation.

entries.name: Mount Kōya
entries.desc: Mount Kōya is a large temple settlement in Wakayama Prefecture, Japan, south of Osaka, and the headquarters of the Kōyasan sect of Shingon Buddhism, whose head temple is Kongōbu-ji. It was first settled in 819 by the monk Kūkai, on an 800-metre plain among eight peaks said to resemble a lotus. The original monastery has grown into the town of Kōya, with a university of religious studies and 120 sub-temples, many of which lodge pilgrims. Its Okunoin holds Kūkai's mausoleum within the largest graveyard in Japan, and the third shōgun Iemitsu built a tomb there for the Tokugawa family. In 2004 it became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

entries.name: Mu
entries.desc: Mu is the Korean term for a shaman in Korean shamanism; shamans hold rites called gut for the welfare of individuals and of society. Female shamans are mostly called mudang and male shamans baksu, while tangol are hereditary shamans, concentrated in the south, whose families held exclusive rights to perform rites in their districts; others become shamans through initiation. In the Joseon dynasty, which made Confucianism the state religion, shamans were ridiculed and mistreated yet still consulted in famines and natural disasters. In more recent Korean history they were regarded as belonging to the lowest class of society, the cheonmin.

entries.name: Murasaki Shikibu
entries.desc: Murasaki Shikibu was a Japanese novelist, poet and lady-in-waiting at the Imperial court in the Heian period, author of The Tale of Genji, widely considered one of the world's first novels, written between about 1000 and 1012. Born into a branch of the northern Fujiwara clan that had fallen to the middle and lower ranks of the aristocracy, the level of provincial governors, she learned the Chinese classics in her father's household, though Heian women were traditionally excluded from Chinese. In about 1005 Fujiwara no Michinaga invited her to serve Empress Shōshi. Her personal name is unknown; most scholars date her death to 1014, others think she was alive in 1025.

entries.name: Naftaly Frenkel
entries.desc: Naftaly Frenkel was a Soviet security officer of the secret police, best known for organising labour in the Gulag. His origins are uncertain; his prisoner card gives his birthplace as Haifa. Arrested in 1923 and sentenced to 10 years at the Solovki camp, he rose from prisoner to camp commander and developed the nourishment scale, which divided prisoners by their capacity for work and fed them accordingly, so that in practice it sorted those who would survive from those who would die. He then directed the daily work on the White Sea–Baltic Canal from November 1931, headed the BAMlag railway camp by 1937, and led the railway construction directorate from 1937 to 1947.

entries.name: Nathaniel Isaacs
entries.desc: Nathaniel Isaacs was an English adventurer, born in Canterbury into a Jewish family, who played an important part in the history of Natal. Stranded at Port Natal in 1825 when his ship foundered, he lived among the Zulu, met King Shaka regularly and fought in the ranks of his warriors, and was rewarded with land near present-day Durban and made an induna, a headman, under Shaka. His Travels and Adventures in Eastern Africa (1836), whose accuracy is often disputed, became a principal source for the history of Natal. He left in 1831, later built a business from Freetown and ruled Matakong Island, and in 1854 was accused of slave-trading but escaped prosecution.

entries.name: Ndlela kaSompisi
entries.desc: Ndlela kaSompisi was a general of the Zulu kings Shaka and Dingane, who died in February 1840. Of non-Zulu, Ntuli origin, he distinguished himself in the Ndwandwe–Zulu War and rose quickly under Shaka, who was said to promote soldiers on merit whatever their origin. Under Dingane he was the highest political and military officer of the kingdom: inDuna or chief adviser, prime minister and commander-in-chief of the army. He commanded at the Battle of Blood River in 1838, a significant Zulu defeat by the Boers of Andries Pretorius. He refused to kill Dingane's half-brother Mpande, and after defeat at Maqongqo in 1840 Dingane had him executed by strangulation.

entries.name: Neak Pean
entries.desc: Neak Pean, the entwined serpents, is an artificial island at Angkor, Cambodia, with a Mahayana Buddhist temple on a circular island in the Jayatataka Baray, the reservoir of the Preah Khan temple, built in the reign of King Jayavarman VII. Its name comes from the sculpted nagas around the base of the temple, and some historians believe it represents Anavatapta, a mythical Himalayan lake whose waters cure illness. It was one of the many hospitals Jayavarman VII built: four pools, standing for water, earth, fire and wind, were fed from the main tank through conduits shaped as heads. The temple was dedicated to Avalokitesvara, and Zhou Daguan mentioned it in the late 13th century.

entries.name: Neutral Confederacy
entries.desc: The Neutral Confederacy was a confederation of Iroquoian peoples in what is now southern Ontario, along the Grand River and the north shore of Lake Erie to the Niagara River. The French called them Neutral because they tried to stay out of the wars between the Wendat and the Haudenosaunee, though they fought the Mascouten, or Fire Nation. Skilled hunters, they traded furs and deerskins to the Wendat for European goods, and their flint deposits let them trade with both rival confederacies. In 1641, after an epidemic, the Jesuits counted 40 villages and about 12,000 people. After Haudenosaunee attacks in the Beaver Wars they dispersed in 1651 and joined other Iroquoian nations.

entries.name: Nicolas Jenson
entries.desc: Nicolas Jenson was a French engraver, printer and type designer who did most of his work in Venice. While Master of the French Royal Mint at Tours, he was sent by King Charles VII to Mainz in 1458 to study metal movable type. He went to Venice in 1468 and opened a printing shop in 1470, producing around 150 titles; his roman type, first used in his 1470 edition of Eusebius, is credited as one of the finest early roman typefaces. By 1477 he ran as many as twelve presses, helping make Venice Italy's publishing capital. In 1480 he formed a syndicate with John of Cologne, and he died that year, a wealthy man.

entries.name: Nikolai Yezhov
entries.desc: Nikolai Yezhov was a Soviet secret police official who served under Joseph Stalin as head of the NKVD from 1936 to 1938, at the height of the Great Purge. A former tailor's assistant and factory worker who joined the Bolsheviks in 1917, he rose through the Party's personnel apparatus to the Central Committee. As head of the NKVD he organised mass arrests, torture and executions: local troikas condemned ordinary citizens to fill arbitrary quotas, and he purged the security organs themselves. Lavrenty Beria, named his deputy in August 1938, took control of the NKVD and succeeded him that November. Yezhov was arrested in April 1939 and executed in 1940.

entries.name: NKVD Order No. 00447
entries.desc: NKVD Order No. 00447 of 30 July 1937 was signed by Nikolai Yezhov and approved by the Politburo during the Great Purge of the Soviet Union. It ordered kulaks and other so-called anti-Soviet elements to be divided into two categories, the first to be shot and the second sent to Gulag labour camps, and set quotas for each territory, to be met in a speedy and simplified way. Sentences were passed by troikas of the regional NKVD chief, the prosecutor and the Party secretary, and executions were held in secret. The quotas were exceeded many times over: by the end of 1938 the NKVD had executed 386,798 Soviet citizens under the order.

entries.name: NKVD troika
entries.desc: The NKVD troikas, or special troikas, were quasi-judicial commissions of three officials of the Soviet security police that sentenced people after simplified, speedy investigations and without a public trial, as an instrument of quick and secret execution or imprisonment. The first was set up in 1918 under the Cheka. From 1930 regional troikas of a police officer, a local party secretary and a procurator decided the fate of peasants branded kulaks, without appeal. Under NKVD Order No. 00447 of 1937 they condemned people to fill target numbers; when the operation was stopped in November 1938, up to 767,000 people had been condemned, of whom 387,000 were shot.

entries.name: Nomenklatura
entries.desc: The nomenklatura were the elite of the Soviet Union and other Eastern Bloc countries who held the key administrative posts in government, industry, agriculture, education and other spheres, posts granted only with the approval of the communist party. The word referred to the party's lists: one of key positions it filled and one of vetted candidates for them, kept by every party committee from the Politburo down to the district level. The system arose early in Soviet history and was built up by Joseph Stalin as a patronage network. Milovan Đilas described the nomenklatura as a new class, a bureaucratic elite with special privileges that had replaced the old wealthy elites.

entries.name: Oboi
entries.desc: Oboi was a Manchu military commander and courtier of the Gūwalgiya clan who served three emperors of the early Qing dynasty. Registered under the Bordered Yellow Banner, he won a hereditary captaincy and the honorific Baturu, brave warrior, in the wars against the Ming, and fought in the Qing conquest of China from 1644. In 1661 the dying Shunzhi Emperor named him one of four regents for the young Kangxi Emperor; Oboi reversed Shunzhi's policies and pushed to reassert Manchu power over the Han Chinese. In 1669 the Kangxi Emperor had him arrested on 30 charges and imprisoned, and he died that year; he was later rehabilitated, with a pardon in 1713.

entries.name: Odoric of Pordenone
entries.desc: Odoric of Pordenone was a Franciscan friar and missionary explorer from Friuli in northeast Italy. Leaving Venice sometime after 1318, he travelled through India, Sumatra, Java and China, where he spent three years in the Yuan capital Khanbaliq, now Beijing, between 1323 and 1328. After more than ten years of travel he returned home and dictated an account, the Relatio, describing the customs, religions and societies of Asia. Copied many times in Latin and in Italian, French and German, it added much to Europe's knowledge of the Far East and was a primary source for Mandeville's Travels. He died in Friuli in 1331 and was beatified in 1755.

entries.name: Oikonomos
entries.desc: Oikonomos, household manager, was the ancient Greek word for the person in charge of all the affairs of an oikos, the household, the base unit of Greek social and economic life. Usually the husband, he made its economic decisions and acted as kyrios, legal guardian, of his wife, unmarried women and males under 18, arranging marriages and representing them at law; to the household's slaves he was not kyrios but despotes, master. He also directed the labour of any metics and represented the household in the polis. In Byzantine times the word became a title for the manager or treasurer of an organisation, and it is still a title in the Orthodox and Catholic churches.

entries.name: Oneida
entries.desc: The Oneida, People of the Standing Stone, are an Indigenous people of the Northeastern Woodlands and one of the five founding nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, traditionally living between the Mohawk and the Onondaga around Oneida Lake in present-day New York. In the early 17th century they held about 6 million acres. In the American Revolution, after the Confederacy's neutrality broke down, most Oneida sided with the revolutionaries, unlike most of the other nations, and about fifty fought at Oriskany in 1777. After the war New York reduced their land drastically, and many moved to Wisconsin and Canada; today there are Oneida nations in New York, Wisconsin and Ontario.

entries.name: Onondaga
entries.desc: The Onondaga, People of the Hills, are one of the five original nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, with their homeland in and around present-day Onondaga County, New York. As the most central nation they are the Keepers of the Fire, and Onondaga is regarded as the Confederacy's capital, where the Grand Council meets; the title of Tadodaho, its presiding officer, is always held by an Onondaga chief. Their nine clans, led by Clan Mothers, descend through the mother, and the chiefs serve at the pleasure of their Clan Mothers, who can recall them. In 1779 the Sullivan Expedition devastated them, and many later followed Joseph Brant to Six Nations in Upper Canada.

entries.name: Oppidum
entries.desc: An oppidum, plural oppida, is a large fortified settlement or town of the European Iron Age, associated above all with the Celtic late La Tène culture of the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, from Britain and Iberia to the edge of the Hungarian Plain. The Latin word meant a defended administrative centre or town. Julius Caesar used it for the larger settlements he met in Gaul in the Gallic Wars of 58 to 52 BCE: places where goods were made, stored and traded, and seats of the authorities who decided matters for many people. Often called the first cities north of the Alps, many became Roman towns after the conquest, while others were abandoned.

entries.name: Osei Bonsu
entries.desc: Osei Bonsu, also known as Osei Tutu Kwame, was the Asantehene, King of the Ashanti, from either 1800 or 1804 until his death in Kumasi in 1824. His name means whale in Akan, a symbol of his extension of the Ashanti Empire to the coast. Early in his reign he suppressed a rebellion of Muslim subjects in the north-west who wanted to restore Osei Kwame Panyin. He led wars against the Fante of the southern Gold Coast in 1806–07 and against Gyaman in 1818–19, and the Ashanti came to dominate the Gold Coast trade. He rebuilt the great roads, began the Aban Palace in Kumasi, and brought literate Muslims into the Ashanti bureaucracy.

entries.name: Osei Kwame Panyin
entries.desc: Osei Kwame Panyin was the ruler of the Ashanti Empire with the title of Asantehene from 1777 to 1801. Born between 1762 and 1765 to Akyaama and Safo Kantanka, King of Mampong, he had been named successor by Osei Kwadwo, but his accession in 1777 was contested by the late king's family and councillors, and Atakora Kwame rose against him before he was made Asantehene. Through the 1780s he removed former councillors and had some executed. The former Queen Mother Konadu Yaadom, accusing him of poisoning her son, rose against him and placed him under house arrest. When she gathered most of the Ashanti clans against him in 1803, he killed himself rather than start a civil war.

entries.name: Otrok
entries.desc: Otrok, known in Georgia as Atraka, was an early 12th-century Cuman-Kipchak khan of the Sarukhanids, one of the ruling houses of the Kipchak confederation that the Rus' called the Wild Cumans. After the victories of the Rus' Grand Prince Vladimir II Monomakh in 1109 he fled to Georgia with some 40,000 followers, was baptised and entered the service of King David IV, who had married his daughter Gurandukht. His Kipchaks helped David against the Seljuk Turks and in the Georgian victory at Didgori in 1121, making Georgia the most powerful kingdom of the region. According to the Hypatian Codex, he returned to the steppe after Monomakh's death in 1125.

entries.name: Ousanas
entries.desc: Ousanas was the ruler of the Kingdom of Aksum in the 320s CE, known in Eritrean and Ethiopian tradition as Ella Allada or Ella Amida. Little is known of his life: he may have invaded Nubia and imposed tribute on it, and his reign may have been briefly interrupted by the usurper Wazeba. Stuart Munro-Hay thought it very likely that he was the king to whom Aedesius and Frumentius were brought. His sons Ezana and Saizana probably lie behind Abreha and Atsbeha, whom Ethiopian tradition credits as the first Christian kings. His coins, in gold, silver and copper, name him King Ousanas of the Aksumites, and some have been found at sites in India.

entries.name: Pandita Ramabai
entries.desc: Pandita Ramabai Sarasvati was an Indian social reformer and Christian missionary, born Ramabai Dongre into a Marathi-speaking Chitpavan Brahmin family. Taught Sanskrit by her father, she was the first woman to receive the titles Pandita and Sarasvati from the University of Calcutta, in 1878. Widowed after an inter-caste marriage considered improper at the time, she founded the Arya Mahila Samaj in Pune to promote women's education and oppose child marriage, and gave evidence before the Hunter Commission. She converted to Christianity in England, raised funds in the United States, and founded the Sharada Sadan for child widows in 1889 and the Mukti Mission at Kedgaon.

entries.name: Patriarchate of Venice
entries.desc: The Patriarchate of Venice, sometimes called the Archdiocese of Venice, is a patriarchate of the Latin Church of the Catholic Church, with its episcopal seat in the Cathedral Basilica of St. Mark in Venice. It was formed in 1451, when the Patriarchate of Grado was merged with the Bishopric of Castello and Venice. It is one of only four patriarchates of the Latin Church that still exist. Its ordinary, the Patriarch of Venice, is traditionally created a cardinal by the pope and may wear scarlet from his installation, and as metropolitan he heads the Ecclesiastical Province of Venice, whose suffragan dioceses include Padova, Treviso, Verona and Vicenza.

entries.name: Permanent Settlement
entries.desc: The Permanent Settlement, or Permanent Settlement of Bengal, was an agreement concluded in 1793 by the East India Company administration under Charles, Earl Cornwallis, with the landlords of Bengal, fixing for good the revenue to be raised from land. Part of the Cornwallis Code, it made the zamindars, who under the Mughals had collected revenue under supervision, into holders treated as landowners who paid a fixed sum in perpetuity, creating an Indian landed class that supported British authority. Introduced in Bengal and Bihar and later elsewhere, it lowered the Company's income over time, while the peasantry suffered as landlords pressed them to grow cash crops.

entries.name: Pierre-Esprit Radisson
entries.desc: Pierre-Esprit Radisson was a French coureur des bois and explorer in New France, born between 1636 and 1640. Captured by a Mohawk raiding party near Trois-Rivières in 1651 or 1652, he was adopted into a Mohawk family, following the custom of adopting young captives to replace lost relatives; after a failed escape he was tortured and saved by his adoptive family. With his brother-in-law Médard des Groseilliers he traded and explored around Lake Superior, and after quarrels with the governor of New France the two entered English service. In 1670 they received a royal charter and founded the Hudson's Bay Company; Radisson later changed sides between England and France more than once.

entries.name: Pillai Lokacharya
entries.desc: Pillai Lokacharya, also called Vāraṇādrīśa, was a Sri Vaishnava leader and philosopher of Tiruvarangam in southern India whose works are central to Vishishtadvaita thought. He taught that God's grace is spontaneous and is met by prapatti, a passive surrender, comparing the devotee to a kitten carried in its mother's mouth. His eighteen texts, the Ashtadasa Rahasyangal, mostly in Manipravalam, include the Srivachana Bhushana of 484 sentences, and his teachings shaped the Tenkalai school. When Malik Kafur's invasion struck Tiruvarangam he left the town to protect the image of the Aranganatha temple, and he died in 1311 near Madurai.

entries.name: Poliudie
entries.desc: The poliudie was the practice by which the rulers of Kievan Rus' collected tribute from their East Slavic subjects. In the mid-10th century the Byzantine emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus described how, from November to April, the Rus' chiefs left Kiev on these 'rounds' among the tributary Slavs, who paid in money, furs, other goods or slaves. The Primary Chronicle relates that Olga of Kiev changed the method of collection after the Drevlians killed her husband Igor in 945 for demanding more than had been agreed. Collection later moved to stations called pogosty, and from the 12th to the 16th centuries the term denoted a fixed tax, usually paid in furs or money.

entries.name: Poll tax
entries.desc: A poll tax, also called a head tax or capitation, is a tax of a fixed sum levied on every liable individual, usually every adult, without regard to income or resources. Such taxes were important sources of revenue from ancient times until the 19th century: the Romans levied a tributum capitis on their provincial subjects, Islamic law imposed the jizya on non-Muslims, and Louis XIV's capitation of 1695 divided French society into twenty-two classes for assessment. Because the tax is regressive, high rates provoked revolts such as the Peasants' Revolt in England in 1381, and in the United States poll taxes were used to keep poor and African-American voters from the polls.

entries.name: Poona Pact
entries.desc: The Poona Pact was an agreement of 24 September 1932 between Mahatma Gandhi and B. R. Ambedkar on the political representation of the depressed classes of British India, now known as the Scheduled Castes. It answered the Communal Award of August 1932, which had granted the depressed classes separate electorates; Gandhi, imprisoned in Yerwada Central Jail in Poona, began a fast unto death against it, seeing it as a British attempt to divide the Hindus. The pact, signed by 23 people, replaced separate electorates with 148 seats reserved for the depressed classes within joint electorates, nearly twice what the Award had offered. Its reserved seats endure in India's legislatures.

entries.name: Potin
entries.desc: Potin is a base metal alloy used for coins, usually a mixture of copper, tin and lead in varying proportions without significant precious metal; the term is applied above all to Celtic coinage. In 1890 'potin lumps' made of some 18,000 fused Celtic coins mixed with charcoal were found at the Alpenquai pile-dwelling settlement in Zürich, the largest weighing 59.2 kilograms; some of the coins are of the Zürich type, dated to around 100 BCE and attributed to the Helvetii, and the lumps may have been meant as cult offerings. In Britain the Kentish cast bronzes of the late 2nd century BCE appear to have been the first coins made on the island.

credit.artist: Rèmes (peuple celtique de Gaule). Autorité émettrice de monnaie

entries.name: Prahok
entries.desc: Prahok is a salted and fermented fish paste, usually of mudfish, used in Cambodian cuisine as a seasoning or condiment. It began as a way of preserving fish for the part of the year when fresh fish was scarce. The fish are trampled to remove scales and entrails, salted, sun-dried and pounded, then left to ripen in open earthenware jars for about a month, the liquid drawn off each day serving as fish sauce. Its strong smell has earned it the nickname 'Cambodian cheese'. In rural Cambodia it is commonly eaten with steamed rice as an important source of protein, and it flavours soups, sauces and fish amok.

entries.name: Pre Rup
entries.desc: Pre Rup is a Hindu temple at Angkor in Cambodia, built as the state temple of the Khmer king Rajendravarman and dedicated in 961 or early 962. A temple mountain of brick, laterite and sandstone, it rises in three steep tiers to a summit platform with five towers set in a quincunx, and stands just south of the East Baray, aligned with the East Mebon of the same reign. It was dedicated to Shiva and probably occupies the site of an earlier Shaivite ashram built by Yasovarman I. Its modern name, meaning 'turn the body', reflects a common belief among Cambodians that funerals were held there.

entries.name: Preah Khan
entries.desc: Preah Khan is a Buddhist temple at Angkor in Cambodia, built in the 12th century for King Jayavarman VII to honour his father, on the site of his victory over the invading Chams in 1181. Its main image, the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara in the form of the king's father, was dedicated in 1191, and its foundation stela records an institution that combined city, temple and Buddhist university, with 97,840 attendants and servants, among them 1000 dancers and 1000 teachers. Royal support ended around the 15th century and the complex slowly declined. Like Ta Prohm it has been left largely unrestored, and since 1991 the World Monuments Fund has maintained it.

entries.name: Ptolemais Hermiou
entries.desc: Ptolemais Hermiou, or Ptolemais in the Thebaid, was a city of Greco-Roman Egypt founded by Ptolemy I Soter on the west bank of the Nile, at the Egyptian village of Psoï, sometime after 312 BCE. Strabo called it the largest city of the Thebaid, equal in size to Memphis. With Alexandria and Naukratis it was one of only three cities with full Greek city status, with its own constitution, assembly and elected magistrates; its settlers came from the Peloponnese and northern Greece, and it had temples to Greek and Egyptian gods, a cult of the Ptolemies and a theatre. It later became the metropolitan see of Thebais Secunda, and El Mansha now stands on its site.

entries.name: Ptolemais Theron
entries.desc: Ptolemais Theron, 'Ptolemais of the Hunts', was a marketplace on the African coast of the Red Sea founded, according to Strabo, by Eumedes, whom Ptolemy II Philadelphus sent there to support the hunting of elephants. The early Ptolemies, cut off from Indian elephants, sought African ones for war; the animals served at the Battle of Raphia but proved unstable and were eventually abandoned. Unlike most such stations Ptolemais had enough fertile land to sustain a town, but by the mid-1st century CE the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes it as having no harbour. Its site remains unidentified: Arqiqo, Suakin and Trinkitat have all been proposed.

entries.name: Pu Songling
entries.desc: Pu Songling was a Chinese writer of the Qing dynasty, best known as the author of Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio (Liaozhai zhiyi). Born into a poor merchant family in Zichuan, Shandong, he gained the xiucai degree in the imperial examinations at 18, but received the gongsheng degree only at 71, for his literary achievement rather than for passing the examination. He spent most of his life as a private tutor, collecting the stories that were published in 1740, after his death. Some critics also attribute to him the vernacular novel Xingshi Yinyuan Zhuan, and his tales have been translated many times since Herbert A. Giles's version of 1880.

entries.name: Qaba
entries.desc: A qaba is a long coat with sleeves and buttons, open at the front and similar to a cassock, whose name comes from the Middle Persian kabāh. It was worn in Egypt, Turkey, the Levant and Persia, among other places, and is named in the Baburnama among the garments of the Mughal emperors Babur and Humayun. Arab sources distinguished a Turkish style, favoured by the Seljuks and Ayyubids, from a Tatar or Mongolian style fastened on the wearer's right side, which Mamluk amirs preferred. Henry II, Count of Champagne and king of Jerusalem, asked Saladin for a qaba as a gift and wore it in Acre. The coat remains part of the dress of clerics and mosque leaders.

entries.name: Queue
entries.desc: The queue was a male hairstyle of the Jurchen and Manchu peoples of Manchuria, in which the front of the scalp was shaved and the rest of the hair grown long and braided. Under the Qing dynasty it was imposed on male Chinese subjects as a sign of submission: in July 1645 the regent Dorgon ordered all Han men to shave their foreheads and wear the queue within ten days or face death, and resistance was crushed in massacres such as those at Jiading and Jiangyin. Refusal was punished as treason. After the fall of the Qing in 1912 the queue was no longer required, and most men gave it up after the last emperor, Puyi, cut his own in 1922.

entries.name: Ramathibodi II
entries.desc: Ramathibodi II, born Prince Chettathirat, was King of Sukhothai from 1485 and King of Ayutthaya from 1491 to 1529. The youngest son of Trailokanat, he succeeded his brother Borommaracha III and so reunified the two kingdoms. In 1500 he sent forces against the Sultanate of Malacca, which failed to subdue it but gained tribute from it and its neighbours. In 1518 a Portuguese embassy under Duarte Fernandes made the first European contact with Siam, and he granted the Portuguese commercial freedom and leave to build churches. The same year he instituted the corvée system, under which commoners, the phrai, owed the state lifelong labour, until Chulalongkorn abolished it in 1905.

entries.name: Raphia Decree
entries.desc: The Raphia Decree is an inscribed stone stela of ancient Egypt, the second of the Ptolemaic Decrees issued by a synod of Egyptian priests meeting at Memphis under Ptolemy IV of the Ptolemaic dynasty. Dated to 217 BCE, it celebrates the king's victory at the Battle of Raphia. Like the Rosetta Stone, it is bilingual, in the Egyptian language and Greek, and is written in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. A partial copy survives on the stone known as the Memphis Stele, and a nearly complete one on the Pithom Stele II.

entries.name: Razia Sultan
entries.desc: Razia Sultan was Sultan of Delhi from 1236 to 1240, the first female Muslim ruler of the Indian subcontinent and the only one of Delhi. A daughter of the Mamluk sultan Iltutmish, she ran Delhi while he campaigned at Gwalior in 1231–1232, and by a possibly apocryphal account he then named her his heir. She took the throne after rousing the people of Delhi against her half-brother Ruknuddin Firuz and his mother. Turkic nobles who had expected a figurehead resented her assertiveness and her appointment of non-Turkic officers such as the Abyssinian Yaqut. Deposed in April 1240, she married the rebel Altunia and tried to regain the throne, but was defeated in October and killed soon after.

entries.name: Regenten
entries.desc: The regenten were the ruling elite of the Dutch Republic from the 16th to the 18th century: the leaders of its cities and the heads of institutions such as orphanages. Not formally a hereditary class, they were in practice patricians, drawn from the rich merchant families who had run the cities since the late Middle Ages. Co-opted for life into the town councils they nominated the burgomasters and voted for their cities in the provincial states, and from 1588 they were the republic's rulers in fact and law. Contracts of correspondence later reserved offices to allied families, and only upheavals of 1672, 1747 and 1785 dislodged them, until the revolution of 1795 ended their oligarchy.

entries.name: Remi
entries.desc: The Remi were a Belgic tribe of the Iron Age and Roman period in the valleys of the Aisne, Vesle and Suippe, roughly the modern Marne and Ardennes. Their Gaulish name means 'the first ones', that is, 'the princes'. Enriched by farming and by trade with the Mediterranean, they were the first people of Gallia Belgica to issue coins, in the second half of the 2nd century BCE. In 57 BCE their leaders Iccius and Andecombogius placed them under Caesar's protection, ending a union with the Suessiones, and they stayed loyal to Rome throughout the Gallic Wars, refusing to join Vercingetorix. Their town Durocortorum became the capital of their civitas, and Reims is named after them.

entries.name: Richard Pipes
entries.desc: Richard Pipes was an American historian of Russia and the Soviet Union. Born in Cieszyn, Poland, to an assimilated Jewish family, he fled occupied Poland in 1939, reached the United States in 1940 and taught at Harvard from 1958 to 1996. In 1976 he headed Team B, a group of outside analysts organised by the CIA, which the journalist Fred Kaplan judged wrong on nearly every point, and in 1981–1982 he served on Ronald Reagan's National Security Council. In books such as Russia under the Old Regime (1974) and The Russian Revolution (1990) he traced Soviet rule to Muscovy's patrimonial state and described the October Revolution as a coup by a small group of radical intellectuals.

entries.name: Ridder
entries.desc: Ridder, meaning knight, is a noble title in Belgium, Denmark and the Netherlands, a literal translation of the Latin eques, originally 'horseman' or 'rider'. Before 1814 it was the highest rank of the nobility in the Low Countries, below only the head of state, and the knights of each province formed a ridderschap, which after the abjuration of Philip II in 1581 held much executive and legislative power. The revolution of 1798 ended that power. In modern usage ridder is the second lowest rank, below baron and above the untitled jonkheer; it has no female form in the Netherlands or Belgium, and the title descends either to all male-line descendants or to the eldest alone.

entries.name: Ritsuryō
entries.desc: Ritsuryō was the legal system of early Japan, based on Confucianism and Chinese Legalism, which joined a criminal code (ritsu) and an administrative code (ryō). Copying Tang China's system, the imperial court issued a series of codes in the late Asuka and Nara periods; the Taihō code of 701 was the most influential. It set up central departments under the emperor, more than 30 court ranks, a periodic redistribution of rice fields, and a division of the people into ryōmin and senmin, the latter close to slaves. Its land and caste rules had largely lapsed by the early 10th century, while hereditary high ranks left the chief posts to a few families such as the Fujiwara.

entries.name: Robert Conquest
entries.desc: Robert Conquest was a British and American historian, poet and novelist, one of the leading Western Sovietologists of the Cold War. After briefly joining the Communist Party as an Oxford student, he served in Bulgaria at the end of the Second World War and from 1948 to 1956 worked in the Foreign Office's anticommunist Information Research Department. His The Great Terror (1968), the first comprehensive study of the Soviet purges of 1936–1938, estimated that they caused some 20 million deaths; in 2008 he put the total at no lower than thirteen to fifteen million. The Harvest of Sorrow (1986) dealt with collectivisation and the famine that followed it.

entries.name: Royal Pragmatic on Marriage
entries.desc: The Royal Pragmatic on Marriage (Real Pragmática) was legislation by which the Spanish Crown sought to control marriage, requiring children to obtain their parents' permission before marrying and allowing parents to disinherit those who disobeyed. The first Royal Pragmatic was passed on 23 March 1776. It rested on the idea that a family might object to a match with a spouse of unequal social standing. The historian Jeffrey M. Shumway has traced the legal backing it gave to that idea through much of Argentina's history, in his histories of love, gender and nation in Buenos Aires from 1776 to 1870.

entries.name: Ryotwari
entries.desc: The ryotwari system was a land revenue system of British India, associated with Sir Thomas Munro, under which the colonial government collected revenue directly from the ryots, the individual cultivators, rather than through zamindars. As John Stuart Mill described it in 1857, each registered holder was recognised as proprietor, could sublet, sell or mortgage his land, and could not be ejected while he paid a fixed money assessment. Used in the Madras Presidency, where Munro became governor in 1820, it was extended to Bombay. Munro cut the demand from a half to a third of the gross produce, and payment in cash left cultivators at the mercy of moneylenders when crops failed.

entries.name: Saichō
entries.desc: Saichō was a Japanese Buddhist monk credited with founding the Tendai school, posthumously titled Dengyō Daishi. Fully ordained at Tōdai-ji, he withdrew to Mount Hiei, where his community became Enryaku-ji, and in 804 he travelled to Tang China to study the Tiantai school. On his return he made Enryaku-ji the centre of Tendai, joining Tiantai meditation, study, precepts and ritual with esoteric practices. He sought an ordination based on the bodhisattva precepts rather than the traditional Vinaya; the Buddhist establishment protested, and his request was granted only seven days after his death in 822. His school laid the ground for later Pure Land and Zen traditions.

entries.name: Sak Kʼukʼ
entries.desc: Sak Kʼukʼ, also known as Muwaan Mat and Lady Beastie, was queen of the Maya city-state of Palenque. The daughter of Janahb Pakal, who seems to have had no male heirs, she took the throne on 19 October 612, a few months after his death, and ruled until 615, when her son Kʼinich Janaab Pakal I succeeded her on reaching maturity. She seems to have kept considerable influence over Palenque in the early decades of his reign: Pakal's sarcophagus lid records her as the ruler who celebrated the sealing of the kʼatun in 633. She was probably also the mother of Ajen Yohl Mat, and she died in 640.

entries.name: Sakdina
entries.desc: Sakdina was a system of social hierarchy in Thailand from the Ayutthaya to the early Rattanakosin period, assigning each person a numerical rank by status that set their precedence in society, above all among the nobility. The numbers stood for the rai of land a person was entitled to own, the word meaning 'field prestige', though there is no evidence that it was applied literally: the Three Seals Law gives 100,000 for the Maha Uparat, 600 for learned monks, 20 for commoners and 5 for slaves. Borommatrailokkanat fixed the scale by law in 1454. Since 1945 the word has served as a critique of Thai political authority, and protesters in 2020–2021 used it against authoritarian values.

entries.name: Sampot
entries.desc: The sampot is the traditional lower garment of Cambodia, a cloth wrapped around the body; the Khmer word comes from a root meaning 'to encircle'. It dates back to the Funan era, when third-century Chinese envoys reported that the king ordered the men of Funan to wear cloth wraps, and in the late 13th century Zhou Daguan saw the king and ordinary people alike at Angkor wrapped in cloth from the waist. Its styles include the chong kben, comparable to the dhoti, and pleated forms seen on Angkorian carvings, and the Siamese court bestowed such cloths, as sompak, on its nobles. Royalty and officials wore the chong kben with a formal jacket, and Cambodians still wear it on special occasions.

credit.artist: Cambodia4kids.org Beth Kanter from Massachusetts, USA

entries.name: San Giorgio dei Greci
entries.desc: San Giorgio dei Greci is a church in the Castello district of Venice, built for the city's Greek community and the centre of its Confraternity of the Greeks. Although Venice had close ties to the Byzantine world, the Greek Orthodox rite was long not permitted there; in 1498 the Greeks gained the right to found a confraternity, and in 1539 the papacy allowed the church to be built, paid for by a tax on all ships from the Orthodox world. Begun by Sante Lombardo, it received a bell tower in 1592 and a dome painted with the Last Judgement. Its treasures include icons by Michael Damaskinos and three that Anna Notaras brought to Italy before 1453.

entries.name: Sangha
entries.desc: Sangha is a term meaning association, assembly or community. Historically it denoted the governing assembly of a republic or a kingdom, and it has long been used by religious associations, among them Buddhists, Jains, Hindus and Sikhs. In Buddhism it refers above all to the monastic communities of monks (bhikkhu) and nuns (bhikkhuni), established by Gautama Buddha in the fifth century BCE for those who wished to practise full-time, free of household life. Members follow the vinaya, whose 227 main rules include complete chastity and eating only before noon. The sangha is the third of the Three Refuges, and it has preserved, translated and spread the Buddha's teachings.

entries.name: Sanskritisation
entries.desc: Sanskritisation is the process by which castes and tribal groups in India adopt the customs, rituals, values and way of life of the dominant upper castes in order to rise in the caste hierarchy. The term was popularised in the 1950s by the sociologist M. N. Srinivas, who first set out the idea in his Oxford thesis on the Kodava of Karnataka, showing that a caste could rise within a generation or two by taking up vegetarianism, teetotalism and Brahmin rites.
