His work challenged the view of caste as rigid and unchanging. It has been observed especially among mid-ranked castes, as when pastoral communities such as the Ahir took the name Yadav in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

entries.name: Sarah Forbes Bonetta
entries.desc: Sarah Forbes Bonetta, born Aina, was a Yoruba girl enslaved in West Africa who became the ward of Queen Victoria. In 1848 the army of Dahomey captured her village, Oke-Odan, and killed her parents, and she spent two years as a child slave at King Gezo's court. In 1850 Gezo gave her as a diplomatic gift to Captain Frederick E. Forbes of the Royal Navy, who had failed to persuade him to end the slave trade; Forbes named her after himself and his ship and presented her to the Queen, who paid for her education in Sierra Leone and England. In 1862 she married the Lagos merchant James Pinson Labulo Davies. She died of tuberculosis at Funchal, Madeira, in 1880.

entries.name: Schutterij
entries.desc: A schutterij was a voluntary city guard or citizen militia of the medieval and early modern Netherlands, meant to defend a town against attack and to act in case of revolt or fire. Its members, grouped by district and by weapon, bought their own arms and kept the night watch at the gates; its officers were wealthy citizens appointed by the magistrates, and in the north after the Reformation they had to belong to the Dutch Reformed Church. The ruling regenten were members, and the guards' group portraits, among them Rembrandt's Night Watch of 1642, rank among the grandest of Dutch Golden Age painting. Inactive by the 18th century, the schutterijen were abolished in 1901.

entries.name: Second Franco-Dahomean War
entries.desc: The Second Franco-Dahomean War of 1892–1894 was fought between France, led by Alfred-Amédée Dodds, and the Kingdom of Dahomey under King Béhanzin. After Dahomey re-armed and resumed raids in the Ouémé Valley, France blockaded its coast in June 1892 and Dodds marched inland with 2,164 men armed with Lebel rifles. The Fon army, with its women soldiers, the Amazons or Mino, attacked again and again at Dogba, Poguessa, Adégon and Cana, but lost heavily to French bayonet charges. Béhanzin burned and abandoned Abomey before the French entered it on 17 November 1892; he surrendered on 15 January 1894 and was exiled to Martinique, and Dahomey was incorporated into French West Africa.

entries.name: Secretary of State for India
aka: Secretary of State for India and Burma
entries.desc: The Secretary of State for India was the British Cabinet minister in charge of the India Office in Whitehall, which oversaw relations with and the administration of the Indian subcontinent under the British Raj. The post was created in 1858, when the East India Company's rule ended and India, apart from the princely states, was brought officially under the British Crown. After the reorganisation of 1937, which placed Burma and Aden under a new Burma Office, the same minister headed both departments as Secretary of State for India and Burma. The office was abolished in August 1947, when the Indian Independence Act created the independent dominions of India and Pakistan.

entries.name: Sei Shōnagon
entries.desc: Sei Shōnagon was a Japanese author, poet and court lady of the middle Heian period, the author of The Pillow Book. The daughter of the scholar and waka poet Kiyohara no Motosuke, of a middle-ranking court family, she served Empress Teishi, consort of Emperor Ichijō, from 993; her name is a court nickname, and her given name is unknown. The Pillow Book, a collection of lists, observations, poems and gossip in the zuihitsu genre, describes the customs and affairs of Teishi's court with wit while passing over harsh realities such as the empress's death in childbirth. Her rival Murasaki Shikibu wrote of her scathingly, and by one tradition she ended her days in poverty as a Buddhist nun.

entries.name: Seneca
entries.desc: The Seneca are an Iroquoian-speaking Indigenous people who historically lived south of Lake Ontario, the westernmost nation of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois League), called the Keepers of the Western Door; their own name, Onödowaʼga꞉ʼ, means Great Hill People. The most populous Haudenosaunee nation, about four thousand in the 17th century, they lived in palisaded villages where women owned the land and homes and grew maize, beans and squash. Their society is matrilineal: children belong to their mother's clan, and Clan Mothers can depose chiefs. Allies of the British in the American Revolution, they were forced to cede much of their land; over 10,000 Seneca live in the United States today.

entries.name: Serfdom in Russia
entries.desc: In tsarist Russia a serf was an unfree peasant who originally could be sold only together with the land to which he was attached, though by the 19th century serfs were practically indistinguishable from slaves. The Sudebnik of 1497 limited peasants' right to leave their masters to the days around Yuri's Day, and the law code of 1649 bound serfs to the estates; serfdom became the dominant relation between peasants and nobility in the 17th century and spread to Ukraine under Catherine the Great. By the census of 1857 private serfs numbered 23.1 million of 62.5 million subjects. Alexander II abolished serfdom in 1861, but most former serfs had to make redemption payments until 1907.

entries.name: Servants of India Society
entries.desc: The Servants of India Society is a social reform organisation founded in Pune in 1905 by Gopal Krishna Gokhale to train young Indians for patriotic service. Its members took vows of renunciation and worked as nationalist missionaries, campaigning for education, sanitation and health care and against untouchability, alcoholism, poverty and the oppression of women. It is regarded as the country's first secular organisation devoted to the underprivileged, rural and tribal communities, and it kept apart from bodies such as the Indian National Congress. It began publishing The Hitavada in 1911, founded the Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics in 1930, and continues with a small membership.

entries.name: Shahsevan
entries.desc: The Shahsevan are Turkic groups of northwestern Iran, living mainly in the districts of Mughan, Ardabil, Kharaqan and Khamsa; their name means 'those who love the shah'. Shia Muslims who speak Azerbaijani, they were pastoral nomads who wintered in Mughan and summered on the Sabalan range. A story told by John Malcolm made them a tribe created by Shah Abbas I to curb the Qizilbash, but Vladimir Minorsky and Richard Tapper doubted it, and conclusive evidence of a Shahsevan tribe or confederacy dates only from the 18th century. Their chiefs opposed the Constitutional Revolution in 1909, Reza Khan's army disarmed them in 1922–1923, and in 1986 they numbered about 6,000 families.

entries.name: Shaykh al-Islam
entries.desc: Shaykh al-Islam, 'elder of Islam', was an honorific title for outstanding scholars of the Islamic sciences that first emerged in Khurasan in the 10th century. In the central and western Islamic lands it was given informally to jurists whose fatwas were especially influential, while in the east rulers such as the Ilkhans, the Delhi sultans and the Timurids conferred it on high-ranking ulama. In the Ottoman Empire it came to designate the chief mufti, who headed the hierarchy of state-appointed ulama, issued fatwas, advised the sultan, confirmed new sultans and appointed judges. The Ottoman office was abolished in 1924 together with the Caliphate.

entries.name: Shingon Buddhism
entries.desc: Shingon, the 'True Word' or mantra school, is one of the major schools of Buddhism in Japan and one of the few surviving Vajrayana lineages of East Asia. It descends from the Zhenyan lineage founded in China by Indian masters such as Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra, whose teachings the monk Kūkai received from Huiguo in Chang'an after sailing to China in 804. Back in Japan Kūkai founded the monastic centre on Mount Kōya, still Shingon's main pilgrimage site, and gained Tō-ji in the capital. Shingon teaches that buddhahood can be attained in this very body through the three mysteries of mudra, mantra and mandala, and it influenced Tendai, Shugendo, Shinto and Japanese art.

entries.name: Shōen
entries.desc: A shōen was a private estate or manor in Japan from about the 8th to the 15th century, often tax-free and autonomous, whose rise undermined the power of the emperor. The estates grew from lands assigned to shrines and temples or granted by the emperor, and from fields reclaimed under laws of 723 and 743 that let reclaimers keep them, eroding the ritsuryō system. Peasants commended their land to temples, shrines and court nobles to escape taxes, and by the end of the Heian period virtually all land in Japan was shōen. The estates fostered a local military class; stewards appointed under the Kamakura shogunate weakened their lords, and the system ended as villages came under daimyō.

entries.name: Signoria of Venice
entries.desc: The Signoria of Venice was the supreme governing body of the Republic of Venice, replacing the older Commune of Venice from 1423 and adopted officially in the Promissione Ducale of Doge Cristoforo Moro in 1462. It joined the doge with those commissioned to rule beside him: the six councillors of the Minor Council, created in 1175, and the three heads of the Quarantia, the supreme tribunal, created in 1179. Over time these officials became the doge's partners in power, and the Signoria was held to matter more than the doge himself, as the words spoken at a doge's death declared: the doge is dead, but not the Signoria.

entries.name: Simon de la Loubère
entries.desc: Simon de la Loubère was a French diplomat, writer, mathematician and poet who led an embassy to the Ayutthaya Kingdom of Siam in 1687. The mission, of five warships, reached Bangkok in October 1687, and he sailed home in January 1688 with the Jesuit Guy Tachard and a Siamese embassy. At the request of Louis XIV he described the country in Du Royaume de Siam (1691), which included the astronomer Jean Dominique Cassini's reading of a Siamese manuscript of Indian origin, the first foundation of European scholarship on Indian astronomy. He also brought back the 'Siamese method' of making magic squares, and sat in the Académie française from 1693.

entries.name: Smerd
entries.desc: A smerd was a free peasant, and later a feudal-dependent serf, in the medieval Slavic states of eastern Europe, recorded in 11th- and 12th-century sources such as the Russkaya Pravda in Kievan Rus' and, as smerdones, in Poland. In Kievan Rus' smerdy owned property and paid fines for their offences, but never had full rights: killing one was fined like killing a kholop, and the prince (knyaz) inherited a dead smerd's property. In 14th- and 15th-century Novgorod and Pskov they held land but could not seek a new master, and owed labour and tribute to the city. From the 14th century the word gave way in Russia to krestyanin, peasant, and lived on as a term of contempt.

entries.name: Solovki prison camp
entries.desc: The Solovki prison camp was a Soviet place of detention on the Solovetsky Islands in the White Sea, set up in 1923 in the Solovetsky Monastery, at first chiefly for socialist opponents of the Bolshevik regime. One of the first forced labour camps, known by the acronym SLON, it was the nucleus from which the whole Gulag grew: from no more than 3,000 prisoners in 1923 it held about 50,000 by 1930, many of them later sent to build the White Sea–Baltic Canal. As a special prison from 1936 it held many who were executed in the Great Terror; all but five of the 1,116 prisoners shipped to the mainland in October 1937 were shot at Sandarmokh. It closed in 1939.

entries.name: Songtham
entries.desc: Songtham, also known as Borommaracha I, was king of the Ayutthaya Kingdom of Siam from 1611 to 1628, of the Sukhothai dynasty. A son of King Ekathotsarot who had spent eight years in the priesthood, he took the throne after the murder of King Si Saowaphak. His reign was a time of prosperity and of growing overseas trade, above all with the Dutch, with whom he signed a treaty in 1617, and the Japanese; Japanese mercenaries under Yamada Nagamasa served as his royal guards. He had Wat Phra Phutthabat built over the Buddha's Footprint found at Saraburi, but his invasions of Cambodia in 1621 and 1622 failed, and Cambodia and Lanna regained their independence.

entries.name: Stadtholder
entries.desc: A stadtholder, in Dutch stadhouder or 'stead holder', was a steward in the Low Countries, first a medieval official who stood in for an absent duke or count and later a provincial and national leader. Under the Burgundian and Habsburg rulers each province had its own. After the Act of Abjuration of 1581 the office survived in the Dutch Republic as the highest executive official of each province, appointed by its States and commander of the armed forces. Usually held by the Princes of Orange, the stadtholdership of Holland at times made its holder the de facto head of state; it became hereditary in 1747 and was abolished in 1795, when William V fled the French.

entries.name: Suhita
entries.desc: Suhita was a Javanese queen regnant, the sixth monarch of the Majapahit empire, who ruled from 1429 until her death in 1447. She was the daughter of her predecessor, King Wikramawardhana, very probably by his principal wife Kusumawardhani; her two elder brothers died during their father's reign. The Pararaton records that the empire was ruled by a queen regnant after 1429, and Suhita is thought to have been that queen. She married her relative Prince Ratnapangkaja and was succeeded by her younger brother Dyah Kertawijaya. The Damarwulan legend of a maiden queen is associated with her reign, which saw a war with Blambangan.

entries.name: Sullivan Expedition
entries.desc: The Sullivan Expedition was a United States military campaign of the American Revolutionary War, from June to October 1779, against the four British-allied nations of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy in what is now New York. Ordered by George Washington after Haudenosaunee and Loyalist raids on the Wyoming Valley and Cherry Valley, four Continental Army brigades under John Sullivan and James Clinton carried out a scorched-earth campaign, razing 40 villages with their crops and food stores. Just over 5,000 Haudenosaunee fled to Fort Niagara, where many starved or froze to death that winter. Some scholars describe the campaign as a genocide, a term that is disputed.

entries.name: Susquehannock
entries.desc: The Susquehannock, also known as the Conestoga, Minquas and Andaste, were an Iroquoian people of the lower Susquehanna River in what is now Pennsylvania, whose name means 'people of the muddy river'. First described by John Smith in 1608, they traded furs with Virginia, New Sweden and New Netherland, and made peace with Maryland in 1652, while suffering intermittent attacks by the Haudenosaunee. By the 1670s disease and war had sharply reduced them; in 1675 militias from Maryland and Virginia besieged their fort on Piscataway Creek, and the survivors scattered, many joining the Haudenosaunee. The last community, at Conestoga Town, was massacred by the Paxton Boys in 1763.

entries.name: Taira clan
entries.desc: The Taira, also called the Heishi or Heike, were one of the four great clans that dominated Japanese politics in the Heian period, with the Minamoto, the Fujiwara and the Tachibana. Taira was one of the surnames the Heian emperors gave to descendants not eligible for the throne, first borne by grandsons of Emperor Kanmu after 825. A branch of the Kanmu Heishi settled in Ise rose to power under Taira no Kiyomori, who became Daijō Daijin and in 1180 put his grandson Antoku on the throne. The Minamoto rose against them in the Genpei War of 1180–1185, which ended with the Taira's destruction at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura, a story told in The Tale of the Heike.

entries.name: Taira no Kiyomori
entries.desc: Taira no Kiyomori was a Japanese military leader and court noble of the late Heian period who, as Daijō-daijin, was the de facto ruler of Japan from 1167 until his death, and established the first samurai-dominated administrative government in Japanese history. Head of the Taira clan from 1153, he helped put down the Hōgen Rebellion in 1156 and defeated Minamoto no Yoshitomo in the Heiji Rebellion of 1160, but only exiled Yoshitomo's sons Yoritomo and Yoshitsune. In 1167 he became the first courtier of a warrior family made chief minister; in 1179 he staged a coup, and in 1180 he put his grandson Antoku on the throne. The Genpei War began that year, and he died of sickness in 1181.

entries.name: Tajlu Khanum
entries.desc: Tajlu Khanum, also known by her title Shah-Begi Khanum, was a Turkoman princess of the Mawsillu tribe of the Aq Qoyunlu confederation who became the principal wife of Shah Ismail I of the Safavid Empire and the mother of Tahmasp I. Married to Ismail in 1503 or 1504, she was his most favoured wife and an adviser to whom nobles in disgrace turned for help. When Ismail died in 1524 she helped the Qizilbash leaders enthrone the ten-year-old Tahmasp, became queen mother and held power behind the throne for at least eight years, even sending an envoy to the governor of Baghdad. Suspected of favouring her son Bahram Mirza, she was exiled to Shiraz, where she died in 1540.

entries.name: Taranis
entries.desc: Taranis, sometimes Taranus or Tanarus, was a Celtic thunder god known from literary sources and from inscriptions dating between the 4th century BCE and the 3rd century CE; his name comes from Proto-Celtic *torano-, thunder. The Roman poet Lucan names him with Esus and Teutates as gods to whom the Gauls sacrificed humans, and early medieval scholia on Lucan add that his victims were burned in a hollow wooden container, a rite compared with the wicker man described by Caesar. The Romans equated him with Jupiter, as inscriptions confirm. Some scholars identify him with the Celtic wheel god, though no direct evidence links the two.

entries.name: Teganissorens
entries.desc: Teganissorens, also known as Decanesora, was an Onondaga chief, orator and diplomat who played a leading part in relations between the Haudenosaunee, the French and the English from the 1680s to the 1710s. Strongly attached to the French, he led Haudenosaunee deputations to Montreal in 1682 and 1688; on the second journey the Huron chief Kondiaronk took him prisoner. He became a Christian in 1693, and in 1694 proposed to Governor Frontenac that Catarocouy (Kingston) be restored. Later he received both French and English agents at Onondaga, and in 1703 protested in Montreal against plans to draw his people into attacks on the English, declaring that they would take neither side.

entries.name: Temple of Edfu
entries.desc: The Temple of Edfu is an Egyptian temple on the west bank of the Nile at Edfu in Upper Egypt, built under the Ptolemaic Kingdom between 237 and 57 BCE and dedicated to Horus. Begun under Ptolemy III Euergetes and completed under Ptolemy XII Auletes on the site of an earlier temple of Horus, it is one of the best preserved shrines in Egypt and the largest temple dedicated to Horus and Hathor of Dendera. Its inscribed walls record its building, its creation myth and the conflict between Horus and Seth, and each year Hathor's journey from Dendera to Edfu was marked by a great festival. Buried up to 12 metres deep in sand and silt, it was cleared from 1860 by Auguste Mariette.

entries.name: Tenant farmer
entries.desc: A tenant farmer is a farmer or farmworker who lives and works on land owned by a landlord, paying rent in a fixed share of the produce, in cash or in both, with rights that have varied widely: some could be evicted at will, others held contracts for a fixed number of years. In England, where tenants under Anglo-Norman law were almost all bound to the land as villeins, free tenancy grew after the Black Death, and by the 19th century about 90% of farmland was tenanted. In Ireland landlords held as much as 97% of the land in 1870, until the Land Acts let tenants buy their holdings. Norway's tenant farmers, the husmenn, were about a quarter of its people in the mid-19th century.

entries.name: Tendai
entries.desc: Tendai is a Mahāyāna Buddhist school with significant esoteric elements, officially established in Japan in 806 by the monk Saichō and based since then on Mount Hiei, where he founded Enryaku-ji. Drawn from the Chinese Tiantai tradition and its patriarch Zhiyi, it emphasises the Lotus Sutra and holds that all the Buddha's teachings can be unified in one perfect system. In the Heian period it eclipsed the Hossō school and rivalled Shingon as the most influential sect at the imperial court, and by the Kamakura period its temples held vast lands and fielded warrior monks. Hōnen, Shinran, Nichiren and Dōgen all trained as Tendai monks. Oda Nobunaga destroyed Enryaku-ji in 1571.

entries.name: The Pillow Book
entries.desc: The Pillow Book is a collection of observations, anecdotes, lists, poems and essays written by Sei Shōnagon while she was a lady at the court of Empress Consort Fujiwara no Teishi in Heian Japan, completed in 1002. Written for her own enjoyment and chiefly in hiragana, the script women then used while men typically wrote in Chinese, it mixes accounts of life at court, her opinions on many matters and 164 lists such as 'hateful things'. It is one of the best sources for the court society of the 10th century and a landmark of Japanese literature, which shaped the genre of zuihitsu, assorted writings. It circulated in manuscript until it was first printed in the 17th century.

entries.name: Theocritus
entries.desc: Theocritus was a Greek poet from Sicily, in Magna Graecia, and the creator of ancient Greek pastoral poetry. Little is known of his life beyond what his poems suggest: an ancient epigram makes him a Syracusan, the son of Praxagoras and Philinna, and he probably lived for a time in Alexandria, and perhaps on the island of Kos. His Idylls, written in the Doric dialect, include bucolic poems set in the country, such as the death of the herdsman Daphnis and the Cyclops Polyphemus's love for the sea-nymph Galatea, and mimes of town life. His poems praising Hiero II of Syracuse and Ptolemy Philadelphus are the only ones that can be dated. Virgil knew his work.

entries.name: Theophilos the Indian
entries.desc: Theophilos the Indian was a 4th-century Heteroousian bishop, of the Arian school of Aëtius, who came from an island in the Indian Ocean, perhaps Socotra, the Maldives or an island at the mouth of the Indus, and fell in and out of favour at the court of the Roman emperor Constantius II. Ordained a deacon by Eusebius of Nicomedia, he was known as a healer and is said to have cured the empress Eusebia. Around 354 Constantius sent him to south Asia by way of Arabia, where he is said to have converted the Himyarites and built three churches, one of them at Zafar. In about 356 the emperor asked Ezana of Aksum to replace Bishop Frumentius with him, a request that was turned down.

entries.name: Three Seals Law
entries.desc: The Three Seals Law is a collection of law texts compiled in 1805 on the orders of King Rama I of Siam, most of them laws of the Ayutthaya era that had survived the destruction of Ayutthaya in 1767. After a divorce case made the king suspect that the laws had been altered, a commission of judges, scribes and officials revised them in 11 months, producing 27 laws in 41 volumes, each stamped with the seals of the three ministries of Mahatthai, Kalahom and Phrakhlang. It remained the working law of Siam until modern codes partly replaced it from 1908. Under a 1978 Supreme Court ruling, its parts not since replaced are still in force.

entries.name: Torc
entries.desc: A torc is a large rigid neck ring of metal, made as a single piece or from twisted strands and usually open at the front, worn in the Scythian, Illyrian, Thracian, Celtic and other cultures of the European Iron Age from around the 8th century BCE to the 3rd century CE. Among the Iron Age Celts the gold torc seems to have been a key object, marking its wearer as a person of high rank: apparently usually a woman until the 3rd century BCE, and thereafter usually, though not only, a man. Celtic gods were shown wearing or holding torcs, and many of the finest works of ancient Celtic art are torcs, such as the Snettisham Torc. The Romans took them up as decorations for distinguished soldiers.

entries.name: Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi
entries.desc: Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi, also known as Dyah Gitarja, was a Javanese queen regnant and the third monarch of the Majapahit empire, reigning from 1328 to 1350. A daughter of the empire's founder, Kertarajasa Jayawardhana, and his principal wife Gayatri, she had been confined in the palace by her half-brother King Jayanegara, and came to the throne at her mother's order after he was murdered in 1328. In 1331 she led the army against rebels in Sadeng and Keta, and in 1334 she made Gajah Mada her prime minister; with him she pursued a great expansion of the empire, which conquered Bali in 1343. On her mother's death in 1350 she abdicated in favour of her son Hayam Wuruk.

entries.name: Umm al-walad
entries.desc: Umm al-walad, Arabic for 'mother of the child', was the title given in the Islamic world to an enslaved concubine who had borne a child that her master acknowledged as his. The caliph Umar forbade owners to sell or give away such women and had them freed at their master's death, a rule all the prominent Sunni legal schools adopted; Ali later declared that they could still be sold, a view that passed into Shi'ism. Their children by the master were born free and legitimate. From Yazid III in 744 the last Umayyad caliphs and most of the Abbasids were sons of slave mothers, and dynasties such as the Ottomans routinely had their heirs by concubines until slavery was abolished in the 20th century.

entries.name: Uparaja
entries.desc: Uparaja, from the Sanskrit upa-rāja, vice king, was a noble title for the viceroy in India, where the viceroy of the Magadha Empire bore it, and in the Buddhist dynasties of Burma, Cambodia, Laos and Thailand and some of their tributary kingdoms. In Burma the Maha Uparaja, or Ainshe Min, was the highest rank among the princes of the royal blood, though Europeans wrongly took it for crown prince: it carried no sure promise of succession, which was usually settled by a struggle for power. In Siam the Uparat, more often called the Front Palace or Second King, was discontinued in 1876 by King Chulalongkorn after the Front Palace Crisis of 1874, in favour of a crown prince.

entries.name: Vasily Grossman
entries.desc: Vasily Grossman was a Soviet writer and journalist, born to a Jewish family in Berdychiv in Ukraine, then part of the Russian Empire, who trained as a chemical engineer before writing full-time in the 1930s. As a war correspondent for the Red Army newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda he reported the battles of Moscow, Stalingrad, Kursk and Berlin, and his article The Hell of Treblinka (1944), among the earliest reports of a Nazi death camp, was used at the Nuremberg Trials. His novels Life and Fate and Everything Flows were suppressed as anti-Soviet, and the KGB seized the manuscripts of Life and Fate. Smuggled abroad after his death, they were first published in the West in 1980.

entries.name: Vates
entries.desc: The vates were a class of seers and sacrificers among the ancient Gauls, described by Greek and Roman writers as one of three specially honoured groups in Gaulish society, beside the bards and the druids. They conducted sacrifices, foretold the future and concerned themselves with the natural world. The account goes back to the lost Gaulish ethnography of the Greek philosopher Posidonius and survives in Diodorus Siculus, Strabo and Ammianus Marcellinus, who name and describe the class in terms that do not fully agree: only Strabo gives what appears to be its native name, ouáteis. The word is reconstructed as Proto-Celtic *wātis, seer, which also lives on in Old Irish fáith.

entries.name: Vedanta Desika
entries.desc: Vedanta Desika was a Sri Vaishnava guru, philosopher and poet of southern India who wrote in Sanskrit, Manipravalam, Tamil and Prakrit, and is revered as the most important guru of the Vadakalai sect. Born at Tūppul in present-day Tamil Nadu, he studied until the age of 20 under his maternal uncle Ātreya Rāmānuja, of the lineage of disciples that began with Ramanuja. More than 100 works are attributed to him, among them the Tattvamuktākalāpa and the Śatadūṣaṇī, besides 862 verses in 22 metres on the deities of temples. He shaped Vishishtadvaita Vedanta by joining Purva Mimamsa to Vedanta, and made prapatti, complete surrender to God, a path to liberation of its own, open to all.

entries.name: Venetian Arsenal
entries.desc: The Venetian Arsenal is a complex of former state shipyards and armouries in the Castello district of Venice that built most of the Venetian Republic's naval power from the Late Middle Ages to the early modern period. Usually said to have been begun in 1104, it was greatly enlarged with the Arsenale Nuovo of 1320 and became the largest industrial complex in Europe before the Industrial Revolution, covering about 45 hectares, some 15 percent of the city. At its peak in the early 16th century some 16,000 workers built galleys from standardised parts at a rate of nearly one a day. Galileo advised it from 1593. It served the Republic until its fall to Napoleon in 1797 and is now a naval base.

entries.name: Venetian Ghetto
entries.desc: The Venetian Ghetto was the area of Venice's Cannaregio district in which the government of the Venetian Republic forced Jews to live, and the origin of the English word ghetto. A decree of Doge Leonardo Loredan and the Senate of 29 March 1516 ordered all Jews in the city into the Ghetto Nuovo, where they were locked in at night under Christian surveillance, paid rents a third higher than before and could not own property. Its German, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese and Levantine communities kept synagogues of their own. In 1797 the French army under Napoleon Bonaparte ended its separation from the city. It remains a centre of Venice's Jewish community of about 450 people.

entries.name: Venetian nobility
entries.desc: The Venetian patriciate was the hereditary nobility that ruled the Republic of Venice, one of the three bodies into which its society was divided, with the citizens and the foreigners. From the Great Council Lockout (Serrata) of 1297 and a law of 1320, only the men of families registered in the Golden Book could sit in the Great Council, where every vote, the Doge's included, counted the same. Unlike a feudal nobility, the patricians drew their wealth from trade with the East, served as galley captains, merchants, ambassadors and governors, and could marry only within their class. New families were admitted for service in the War of Chioggia in 1381 and, from the 17th century, for payment.

entries.name: Vergobret
entries.desc: The vergobret was the chief magistrate among certain Gallic peoples, described by Caesar among the Aedui in 58 and 52 BCE and attested after the Roman conquest on coins and in inscriptions; it is the only Gaulish magistracy recorded at once in texts, on coins and in inscriptions. Among the Aedui the vergobret was elected for one year with regal authority, and Caesar says he held the power of life and death, though major decisions likely rested with a council of nobles. Two living members of one family could not both hold the office, and the holder could not leave the tribe's territory. In 52 BCE Caesar settled a disputed election in favour of Convictolitavis.

credit.artist: Lexoviens (peuple celtique de Gaule). Autorité émettrice de monnaie

entries.name: Vikramavardhana
entries.desc: Vikramavardhana, known by his regnal name Bhra Hyang Wisesa, was a Javanese ruler who succeeded Hayam Wuruk as the fifth monarch of the Majapahit empire, reigning from 1389 to 1429. Nephew and son-in-law of Hayam Wuruk, he took the throne through his wife Kusumawardhani, the late king's only child by his queen, but was challenged by Bhre Wirabhumi, Hayam Wuruk's son by a concubine, who ruled a rival eastern court. In 1398 his navy sacked the Kingdom of Singapura. He won the Regreg War against Bhre Wirabhumi, which broke out in 1406, but the civil war gravely weakened Majapahit's hold over its far-flung vassal kingdoms.

entries.name: Vroedschap
entries.desc: The vroedschap was the all-male city council of the early modern Netherlands, its members called vroedmannen, wise men. In the Dutch Republic it was drawn from the regent class, the burgher elite that had shut artisans out of city government since the late Middle Ages and become a kind of hereditary city nobility. Its ten to forty members sat for life, joined by co-optation and family standing, and had to be men, members of the Calvinist church and house owners. The council appointed the magistrate of burgomasters and aldermen, often from its own ranks,. In times of crisis the stadtholder replaced its members with his followers, as in 1619, 1672, 1748 and 1787.

entries.name: Wei Zhongxian
entries.desc: Wei Zhongxian was a Chinese court eunuch of the late Ming dynasty, considered by most historians the most notorious eunuch in Chinese history, whose power under the Tianqi Emperor (r. 1620–1627) came to appear to rival the emperor's. Illiterate and perhaps of peasant or merchant birth, he entered palace service and grew close to the young Zhu Youjiao and his wet nurse, Madame Ke. As head of the Eastern Depot and bearer of the emperor's edicts, he promoted and demoted hundreds of officials, while in 1625–1626 the Embroidered Uniform Guard tortured and killed leaders of the Donglin movement. Exiled by the Chongzhen Emperor in 1627, he hanged himself when he learned he was to be arrested.

entries.name: West African Vodún
entries.desc: West African Vodún is an African traditional religion of the Aja, Ewe and Fon peoples of Benin, Togo, Ghana and Nigeria, with no central authority. It teaches a supreme creator under whom are lesser spirits, the vodúns, who are believed to manifest in shrines and receive offerings, often animal sacrifices; divination, chiefly Fá, is used to gain knowledge from them. While the kingdom of Dahomey was a vassal of the Oyo Empire, from about 1727 to 1823, the Fon adopted Fá and other Yoruba cults, and kings who introduced new deities were believed to enhance their own power. Enslaved practitioners carried it to the Americas, where it shaped Haitian Vodou. About 17% of Benin's people follow it.

entries.name: White Sea–Baltic Canal
entries.desc: The White Sea–Baltic Canal is a ship canal in Russia, opened on 2 August 1933, that runs 227 kilometres from the White Sea to Lake Onega and so to the Baltic Sea. It was the first major Soviet project built with forced labour: Gulag inmates dug it in twenty months between 1931 and 1933, almost entirely by hand, and between 12,000 and 25,000 of them died according to official records. Presented as a showcase of the first five-year plan and of convicts 'reforging' themselves through labour, it was praised in a book compiled by a brigade of 120 writers and artists organised by Maxim Gorky. Yet at 3.5 metres deep it was too shallow for most seagoing ships.

entries.name: Xu Guangqi
entries.desc: Xu Guangqi was a Chinese agronomist, astronomer, mathematician, politician and writer of the late Ming dynasty, and one of the Three Pillars of Chinese Catholicism. Born in Shanghai, he met the Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci in 1600, was baptised as Paul in 1603, and in 1607 translated with Ricci the first parts of Euclid's Elements into Chinese. Rising to be Minister of Rites and Deputy Senior Grand Secretary, he was appointed in 1629 to lead a reform of the calendar with Jesuit help, completed after his death as the Chongzhen calendar. His Complete Treatise on Agriculture, of some 700,000 characters, was edited by Chen Zilong and published in 1639.

entries.name: Yevgenia Ginzburg
entries.desc: Yevgenia Ginzburg was a Soviet writer and Communist Party educator who served an 18-year sentence in the Kolyma Gulag and told of it in her memoir Journey into the Whirlwind. A docent in the history of the party at Kazan and wife of the city's mayor, Pavel Aksyonov, she was accused after the assassination of Sergei Kirov of belonging to a counter-revolutionary Trotskyist group, expelled from the party and arrested in February 1937. At a trial she later said took seven minutes, she was sentenced to ten years. Released in 1949 but kept in exile, she was rehabilitated in 1955. Her memoir, unpublishable in the USSR, was smuggled abroad and published in 1967.

entries.name: Yingya Shenglan
aka: The Overall Survey of the Ocean's Shores
entries.desc: The Yingya Shenglan, The Overall Survey of the Ocean's Shores, is a book by Ma Huan about the countries visited on the Ming treasure voyages led by Zheng He, published in 1451. Ma Huan served as an interpreter on the fourth, sixth and seventh voyages and wrote it with Guo Chongli, who sailed on three of them, from the notes they had kept; he began arranging them after his return in 1415 and wrote a foreword in 1416. He wrote in a colloquial style, which Zhang Sheng later rewrote in a literary one. No copy of the original edition survives: the text is known from later versions that differ from one another, among them those in the Guochao Diangu and the Jilu Huibian of about 1617.

entries.name: Zhang Juzheng
entries.desc: Zhang Juzheng was a Chinese scholar-official of the Ming dynasty who, as senior grand secretary from 1572 until his death, was the de facto ruler of China in the early reign of the young Wanli Emperor. Born in Jiangling in Huguang, he passed the palace examination in 1547 and became a grand secretary in 1567. With the support of the eunuch Feng Bao and the Empress Dowager Li he streamlined the administration, enforced the single whip reform of taxes paid in silver, began the first nationwide land survey since the Song and built up a surplus. After his death most of his reforms were reversed and in 1584 his family's property was confiscated; he was rehabilitated in 1622.

entries.name: Zhu Zaiyu
entries.desc: Zhu Zaiyu was a Chinese scholar, mathematician and music theorist, a prince of the Ming dynasty, who in 1584 described equal temperament by accurate mathematical calculation. Born in Qinyang, Henan, a sixth-generation descendant of the Hongxi Emperor, he inherited the title of Prince of Zheng in 1593 but soon gave it up to his cousin. He wrote treatises on music theory and history, dance, astronomy, mathematics and the calendar, calculated the magnetic declination of Peking and the length of the tropical year. His work on equal temperament won no official recognition under the Ming or the Qing, which favoured classical textual scholarship over empirical observation.

entries.name: Ziauddin Barani
entries.desc: Ziauddin Barani was a political thinker and historian of the Delhi Sultanate, best known for the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, a history of the sultanate to the early years of Firuz Shah Tughluq, and the Fatwa-i-Jahandari, advice for Muslim kings. Born at Baran (now Bulandshahr), he was for seventeen years a companion of Muhammad bin Tughluq. The Fatwa-i-Jahandari argued for a hierarchy of birth among Muslims, setting the ashraf upper castes apart from the ajlaf low castes, and urged kings to overpower and degrade the Hindus, while lamenting that the sultans in fact gave Hindus high posts. He fell out of favour after that sultan's death and died poor in 1357.

entries.name: Seneca the Younger
entries.desc: Lucius Annaeus Seneca, Seneca the Younger, was a Stoic philosopher, statesman and dramatist of Ancient Rome, born at Corduba in Hispania and trained in rhetoric and philosophy. Exiled to Corsica under the emperor Claudius in 41 CE, he was recalled in 49 to tutor the young Nero, and after Nero became emperor in 54 he served as his adviser, with the praetorian prefect Burrus. His influence waned, and in 65 he was forced to take his own life for alleged complicity in the Pisonian conspiracy, of which he may have been innocent. His essays and 124 letters are among the most important sources for ancient Stoicism, and his tragedies include Medea, Thyestes and Phaedra.

entries.name: Aspathines
entries.desc: Aspathines (Old Persian Aspacanā) was a senior official of Persia who served under Darius the Great and Xerxes I; he was born and died sometime between 550 and 450 BCE. He is depicted on the tomb of Darius I at Naqsh-e Rostam, where an inscription names him as the bowbearer who holds King Darius' battle-axe. The only other courtier named there with a dedication was Gobryas. His son Prexaspes became an admiral in the navy of Xerxes during the second Persian invasion of Greece.

entries.name: Maher
entries.desc: Maher, or Maḥrem, was a South Semitic god of the Aksumites and the Himyarites, worshipped as the deity of war. He was held to be the son of the main god Ashtar, and his counterpart was Beher, the god of the sea. As a god of war he was comparable to Mars or Ares. Maher held a place of special importance among the Aksumites: the kings of their pagan period were all called the "Sons of the Invincible Mahrem".

entries.name: Oba of Benin
entries.desc: The Oba, meaning 'king', is the traditional ruler of the Kingdom of Benin and the custodian of the culture of the Edo people and all Edoid people. The Oba dynasty is named after its first ruler, Eweka I, of around the 12th century, and followed the Ogiso monarchy; Ewuare the Great (1440–1473) heads the list of the imperial period. In 1897 a British force of about 1,200 men under Sir Harry Rawson captured, sacked and burned the capital, looted the Benin Bronzes from the palace and forced Oba Ovonramwen into exile; he died in 1914 without his throne. His line keeps the title as traditional rulers in modern-day Nigeria, Ewuare II since 2016.

entries.name: Paroikoi
entries.desc: Paroikoi (singular paroikos) was the Greek term that replaced "metic" in the Hellenistic and Roman periods for foreign residents, and the origin of the words parish and parochial. In the Byzantine Empire the paroikoi were peasants who did not own their land but held it by hereditary right, and could not be removed as long as they paid their rent. The status appears in the Justinian code, which prohibited it, so for a time it remained clandestine. Comparable to the serfs of the West, the paroikoi appear to have been widespread by the 13th century.

entries.name: Kpojito
entries.desc: The kpojito was the queen mother and consort of the pre-colonial West African kingdom of Dahomey, in present-day Benin. From the early eighteenth century she was a wife of the king's father, often of common birth or born into slavery, who rose in rank by merit to serve as coregent of the ruling king, and sometimes of his predecessor. A kpojito shared power with local princes, acting as their protégé and kingmaker, and as a priestess of the vodun, the gods, she had the authority to resolve religious disputes. The best known kpojito was Hwanjile, who reigned with King Tegbesu in the mid-eighteenth century.

entries.name: Malik Maqbul Tilangani
entries.desc: Malik Maqbul Tilangani was a commander of the Kakatiya Empire who, captured and converted to Islam, rose to become Wazir of the Delhi Sultanate under Firuz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351–1388). As Gannama Nayaka he commanded Warangal Fort under Prataparudra; after Ulugh Khan, later Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq, took Warangal in 1323, he was left in charge of the new province of Telangana until rebels retook it and he fled to Delhi. There he became finance minister and then Wazir, so trusted that Firuz Shah called him 'brother' and left the fiscal and general administration to him. He died in 1369, and his son Jauna Khan succeeded him as Wazir.

entries.name: Village accountant
entries.desc: A village accountant, known among other titles as patwari, karanam, talati or lekhpal, is a government official in rural areas of the Indian subcontinent who keeps land and agricultural records and collects taxes. Introduced in the early 16th century under Sher Shah Suri and improved by the Mughal emperor Akbar, the office was kept by the East India Company and the British Raj with some administrative changes. The 1882 Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency describes the talati as in charge of eight to ten villages for a yearly salary of Rs. 120–180. The official closest to the villagers, the accountant reports to the tehsildar and prepares the village land records, the jamabandi.

entries.name: Chamber of rhetoric
entries.desc: Chambers of rhetoric were dramatic societies of the Low Countries whose members, the rederijkers, took their name from the French rhétoricien and in the 15th and 16th centuries cultivated drama and lyric poetry. The first were founded in Flanders around the 15th century; they later flowered in Holland, where most cities sponsored one or more chambers that competed in prize contests, and De Egelantier in Amsterdam counted Coster, Bredero, Hooft and Roemer Visscher among its members. Closely tied to civic leaders, the chambers performed at civic festivities and, like guilds, attended members' funerals and collected for the sick and poor. The play Elckerlijc (Everyman) came from them.

entries.name: Bard
entries.desc: A bard was a poet and singer who composed and performed verse in the service of a patron, a calling attested among the ancient Celts and continued in the medieval Celtic-speaking world. Greek and Roman authors writing about Gaul between the 1st century BCE and the 4th century CE count the bards, with the druids and the vates, among its honoured learned orders, singing the praises of chieftains and the satire of their rivals to an instrument like the lyre. In medieval Wales bardd remained the usual word for a poet, while Ireland kept bard for a grade below the file; in both, praise and satire of rulers stayed central. The word now serves loosely for any poet.

entries.name: Alesia
entries.desc: Alesia was the capital of the Mandubii, a Gallic tribe allied with the Aedui, on Mont-Auxois near Alise-Sainte-Reine in Burgundy, France. The Celtic oppidum stood on a plateau of about 97 hectares, some 200 metres above the valley floor. In 52 BCE Julius Caesar besieged Vercingetorix there: in six weeks his troops built a ring of fortifications 15 km long around the town and another 21 km long to hold off relief, and the Roman victory decided the Gallic Wars and the fate of Gaul. Alesia then became a Gallo-Roman town with temples, a forum and a theatre. Its long-disputed site was confirmed by excavations in 1861–1865 and again in 1991–97.

entries.name: Yakoyaner
entries.desc: The Yakoyaner, also spelt Iakoiane, is the Kanien'kehá꞉ka (Mohawk) term for the clan mother of the Haudenosaunee, the senior woman responsible for the political, economic and social stability of her clan. In this matrilineal society the clan mothers chose the Royaner, the male chiefs, watched over them in council and could remove a chief who led poorly. They also named children, kept the order of the clan's names, adopted new members, among them prisoners of war, and passed on the Creation Story. In the Confederacy's history the first clan mother was Jigonsaseh, who with Hiawatha and the Great Peacemaker created its government around the 12th century.

entries.name: Three Sisters
entries.desc: The Three Sisters are squash, maize and climbing beans, the three main crops of various Indigenous peoples of Central and North America, grown together by companion planting. The maize stalk serves as a trellis for the beans, the beans fix nitrogen and steady the maize in high winds, and the wide leaves of the squash shade the ground, keep the soil moist and hold back weeds. The crops and their polyculture originated in Mesoamerica, where squash was domesticated first, about 10,000 years ago, followed by maize and then beans. Among the Haudenosaunee, where women grew and distributed them, the Three Sisters were the foundation of subsistence and appear in oral traditions and ceremonies.

entries.name: Sannyasa
entries.desc: Sannyasa is the fourth of the four Hindu life stages, the ashramas, after the celibate student, the householder and the forest dweller: a life of renunciation of material desires given to spiritual pursuits. A man in it is a sannyasi and a woman a sannyasini; they typically live simply, detached and itinerant, often in saffron or ochre clothes, alone or with fellow renunciates, seeking moksha, liberation. The term is rare in the earliest Vedic texts, and sannyasa became a recognised stage of life by about the 3rd and 4th century CE. From the 12th century through the British Raj, some Shaiva and Vaishnava ascetics also formed military orders and fought as guerrillas.

credit.artist: Unknown artist. Digitized by Davinder Singh Toor.

entries.name: Kū
entries.desc: Kū is one of the four great gods of Hawaiian religion, with Kanaloa, Kāne and Lono, the god of war, politics, farming and fishing. He was worshipped under many names that refer to his manifestations in forest and rain, husbandry, fishing, war and sorcery, among them Kūkāʻilimoku, the "Snatcher of Land", whose rituals included human sacrifice, which was not part of the worship of other gods. Kūkāʻilimoku was the guardian of Kamehameha I, who unified the Hawaiian archipelago under one ruler and raised monuments to him in Kona. Three colossal statues of Kū dedicated by Kamehameha were reunited at the Bishop Museum in Honolulu in 2010.

entries.name: Sesshō and Kampaku
entries.desc: Sesshō and Kampaku were the two regencies of the Japanese court, together called sekkan: the sesshō acted for a child emperor or an empress regnant, the kampaku assisted an adult emperor as chief adviser and regent. Fujiwara no Yoshifusa became the first sesshō from outside the imperial house in 858, and Fujiwara no Mototsune the first kampaku in 887. Marrying their daughters to emperors, the Fujiwara monopolised both offices from the 10th century and dominated the Heian court, until the cloistered rule of retired emperors from the 11th century left the titles without real power. Held in rotation by the five regent houses, they were abolished in 1868.

entries.name: Ryōmin and senmin
entries.desc: Under the Ritsuryō legal system, enforced in Japan from the end of the 7th century, the population was divided, as in Tang China, into two castes recorded in the citizen registers: the ryōmin, 'good citizens', and the senmin, 'low citizens'. The ryōmin comprised government officials, citizens, the shinabe who served the court's trades and the lower zakko tradesmen. The senmin, a minority, fell into five groups: caretakers of imperial tombs, the kanko of public ministries, the kenin servants of great families, and state and private slaves, who could be sold and had no registered family. Intercaste marriage was at first forbidden; from 789 children of mixed unions became ryōmin.

entries.name: Sati
entries.desc: Sati, or suttee, is a chiefly historical Hindu practice in which a widow burns alive on her dead husband's funeral pyre, voluntarily, by coercion, or for lack of acceptable options for living on. Greek sources of around 300 BCE mention it, Hindu inscriptions record it from 464 CE, and Brahmin law-books from the 7th century; by the 12th century it was widely recognised, though not universally accepted. In the Mughal period it was associated with Rajput elites. After campaigns by missionaries such as William Carey and reformers such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy, the Bengal Sati Regulation, 1829, made it punishable, and India's Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987, criminalised aiding or glorifying it.

entries.name: Blacksmiths of western Africa
entries.desc: Blacksmiths held a distinctive place in the societies of West Africa, where ironworking dates back to around 1500 BCE: their mastery of metal for tools, weapons and ceremonial objects was both revered and feared and often credited with magical power. Among the Mande, blacksmiths were held to control nyama, a force of energy and power; one family in the village produced them, and its boys were taught the secret knowledge of its use. In much of West Africa smiths formed endogamous castes, called numu in Mande, some of which became distinct ethnic groups with languages of their own, such as Ligbi. Among the Yoruba, the smith expressed the spirit of Ogun, god of iron.

entries.name: Sogolon Condé
entries.desc: Sogolon Condé was a 13th-century princess of Imperial Mali and one of the prominent women of the Epic of Sundiata, the second wife of King Naré Maghann Konaté and mother of Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire. The epic portrays her as the daughter, or in the griots of Guinea the younger sister, of the "buffalo woman" Dò Kamissa, ridiculed for her hunchback and for bearing a disabled son. After her husband's death, plots by his first wife Sassouma Bereté drove her into exile with her children until the King of Mema gave them asylum. She died in Mema before Sundiata returned to take the throne; griots praise him through her as Sogolon Djata.

entries.name: Wang Zhen
entries.desc: Wang Zhen was a Chinese court eunuch who, as tutor and adviser to the young Zhengtong Emperor, became the first eunuch of the Ming dynasty to wield significant political power, exercising dictatorial control over the court in the 1440s. Educated in the palace school for eunuchs founded in 1426, he joined the Directorate of Ceremonial in 1435, and after the death of Grand Empress Dowager Zhang in 1442 and the retirement of the elderly grand secretaries no official could check him; he imprisoned opponents and in some cases brought about their deaths. In 1449 he was killed in the Tumu Crisis, when Oirat Mongols defeated the army he had urged the emperor to lead and captured the emperor.

entries.name: Huiguan
entries.desc: A huiguan was a Chinese association, or its hall, of sojourners or migrants from the same native place. The first were founded by officials in Beijing in the Yongle era (1403–1424); under the Qing dynasty they were common across China and overseas, with at least 532 in Beijing and 2,000 in 300 other cities around 1900. Most were guilds of merchants or artisans, while most in Beijing lodged candidates for the imperial examinations. Huiguan kept temples, cemeteries and opera stages, held banquets, kept order among their members and represented them to the government, some acting almost as governments. In China they were dissolved in the 1950s; some overseas remain cultural organisations.

entries.name: Mughal karkhanas
entries.desc: Mughal karkhanas were the workshops and storehouses of craftsmen established by the Mughals in their empire to meet the needs of the state, the emperor's household and the army; karkhana is a Hindi and Marathi word meaning factory. Maintained by the state, nobles, mansabdars and zamindars, and headed for the emperor by the khan-i-saman, they made arms and armour, textiles, shawls, carpets, jewellery, perfumes and tents; the Ain-i-Akbari lists 36 classes. Artisans there worked under controllers' orders rather than on their own account, accounts were kept for each workshop, and skilled workers earned more in the imperial karkhanas. They declined with the Mughal Empire.

entries.name: Ankhwennefer
entries.desc: Ankhwennefer was a rebel pharaoh who held much of Upper Egypt against the Ptolemaic kings from about 200 to 186 BCE, succeeding the rebel ruler Horwennefer. His background is unknown; an inscription at Philae hints that he was Horwennefer's son, and historians disagree over whether the two were Nubian or native Egyptians. Having lost Thebes early in his reign, he raided north to cut Ptolemaic supply lines and, helped by the Ptolemaic defeat at Panium in 200 BCE, regained the Thebaid. The Ptolemies retook Thebes in 191, and about 186 BCE his Egyptian-Nubian army was decisively defeated; he was captured and may have been spared after Egyptian priests interceded.

entries.name: Zenon of Kaunos
entries.desc: Zenon of Kaunos was a Greek official in Ptolemaic Egypt around the 250s–230s BCE, known from the Zenon Papyri, an archive of over 2,000 documents in Greek and Demotic found near Kom el-Kharaba in the winter of 1914–1915. A native of Kaunos in Caria, he settled at Philadelphia on the edge of the Faiyum and became private secretary to Apollonius, finance minister to Ptolemy II and Ptolemy III. His letters record economic life in Egypt and Palestine, his travels through "Syria and Phoenicia" in 258–259 BCE, exports of grain, oil and asphalt, and the purchase and shipment of enslaved boys and girls, some of whom escaped.

entries.name: Demotic Egyptian script
entries.desc: Demotic is the ancient Egyptian script derived from northern forms of hieratic used in the Nile Delta, named 'popular' by the Greek historian Herodotus; the Egyptians called it 'document writing'. Written from right to left, it developed in Lower Egypt late in the Twenty-fifth Dynasty and became the official administrative and legal script under Amasis II. Used first for administrative, legal and commercial texts, in the Ptolemaic Kingdom it also served literature and religion, then declined in public life under Roman rule. The last dated example is a graffito at the temple of Isis at Philae from 452 CE. Its 32 lines on the Rosetta Stone were deciphered before the hieroglyphs.

entries.name: Iskandar Beg Munshi
entries.desc: Iskandar Beg Munshi was an Iranian court scribe and chronicler, author of the Tarikh-e Alam-ara-ye Abbasi, "The world-adorning history of Abbas", a history of the early Safavids and above all of the reign of Shah Abbas I (r. 1588–1629). Born in 1561 or 1562 into a Turkoman clan of the Qizilbash, the militant Shia group that had helped the Safavids to power, he joined the bureaucracy rather than the military elite, training as a pupil scribe of Mirza Ata-Allah Isfahani under Shah Tahmasp I. His chronicle, influenced by the Mughal Akbarnama, is considered the most significant work of Iranian historiography on Safavid Iran. He died in 1633 or 1634.

entries.name: Propiska
entries.desc: A propiska was a written residency permit and migration record used in the Russian Empire before 1917 and in the Soviet Union from 1932 until 1991, entered as a stamp in a citizen's internal passport. Passports were abolished after the October Revolution, but in December 1932 Stalin's government re-established a unified internal passport, above all to stop peasants flooding to the towns in the famine of 1930–1933; peasants could obtain passports only by special application. A permanent propiska confirmed the right to housing and was nearly impossible to revoke, while settling in Moscow or Leningrad without one was very hard. The system was ruled illegal and abolished on 11 October 1991.

entries.name: Special settlements in the Soviet Union
entries.desc: Special settlements were places of forced residence in the Soviet Union to which whole classes and nationalities were deported, a method of political repression separate from the Gulag labour camps. From 1930 peasants branded kulaks were sent with their families to remote parts of Siberia, Kazakhstan and Central Asia; from 1940 people from annexed Poland and the Baltic States followed, and in 1941–1944 whole peoples, among them Volga Germans, Chechens, Ingush, Kalmyks and Crimean Tatars. Settlers lived in families under NKVD watch, barred from many jobs and from going home. On 1 January 1953 there were 2,753,356 deported and special settlers; the system was abolished in the 1950s.

entries.name: Coartación
entries.desc: Coartación was a system of self-purchase in the slave societies of Ibero-America from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries, by which an enslaved person paid part of the price of freedom before a court and had the rest fixed, becoming a coartado. Growing from custom and slaves' petitions rather than from the Siete Partidas code, it entered Cuban law only in 1842. A new master could not raise the fixed price, and a coartado gained rights, among them to change masters without showing cause and to a share of the hire when rented out. Women, urban and American-born slaves gained freedom this way most often; it helped create a large population of free people of color in Spanish America.

entries.name: Gracias al Sacar
entries.desc: Gracias al Sacar, literally "Thanks for Removal", was a legal mechanism introduced by the Spanish Crown in 1795 by which colonial subjects of mixed ancestry could obtain official documents raising their racial classification. Arising in the Bourbon Reforms, as the Crown sought revenue and the loyalty of wealthy mixed-race subjects, it was standardised by José de Cistué y Coll, Crown Attorney on the Council of the Indies, and those approved were reclassified as español, with lower taxes and wider access to education and civil and religious rights. Only the wealthy could use it; the poor and the enslaved were excluded. The Peruvian physician José Manuel Valdés received such a decree in 1806.

entries.name: Ntshingwayo Khoza
entries.desc: Ntshingwayo kaMahole of the Khoza was the commanding general, inDuna, of King Cetshwayo's Zulu army in the Anglo-Zulu War of 1879. Given conflicting orders, to destroy the invading British centre column but first to seek a parley, he outmanoeuvred Lord Chelmsford, whose divided force left its camp poorly defended, and on 22 January 1879 his regiments virtually annihilated it at Isandlwana, where some 1,300 died in one of the worst British defeats of the Victorian era. Blamed for the heavy Zulu losses, he lost much of the acclaim due to him. On 21 July 1883 he was killed when Zibhebhu kaMaphitha attacked Cetshwayo's royal homestead at oNdini.

credit.artist: Unknown photographer (Life time: Unknown, but late 1800s.)

entries.name: Kallar
entries.desc: The Kallar are a caste of southern India, one of the three related castes, with the Maravar and Agamudayar, that form the Mukkulathor confederacy. The name, a Tamil word meaning thief, was according to the anthropologist Susan Bayly a title given by Tamil warrior-chiefs to pastoral peasants who served them as armed retainers; their identity as a caste took shape only from the late 18th century. Kallar chieftaincies controlled the country north and west of Madurai, Kallar watchmen served hundreds of villages, and from 1755 the East India Company campaigned against them. In 1918 the community was placed on the list of Criminal Tribes. The Thondaiman dynasty of Pudukkottai came from the Kallar.

entries.name: Li Zhi
entries.desc: Li Zhi was a Chinese philosopher, historian and writer of the late Ming dynasty, a critic of the Neo-Confucian views of Zhu Xi, then the orthodoxy of the Ming government. Born in Jinjiang in Fujian, he served as a teacher and official, as prefect of Yao'an in Yunnan from 1577, before leaving office; in 1588 he took the tonsure as a Buddhist monk without adopting a monk's ascetic life, and in Nanjing he met Matteo Ricci. He taught that the "childlike heart-mind", genuine and free of falsehood, should be preserved against borrowed doctrine, and denied that women were inferior to men in intelligence. Accused of heresy, he was imprisoned in 1602 and took his own life.

entries.name: Allahverdi Khan
entries.desc: Allahverdi Khan was a Safavid general and statesman of Georgian origin who rose from gholam, military slave, to high office in Safavid Iran. Born a Christian Georgian, he was taken prisoner in a Caucasian campaign of Shah Tahmasp I and converted to Islam to serve in the gholam army. After taking part in the killing of the kingmaker Morshed-Kholi Khan in 1589 he became commander of the gholams and governor of Fars, the first gholam to equal the Qizilbash emirs, and from 1600 he increased the gholam troops from 4,000 to 25,000. He led campaigns including the conquest of Bahrain in 1601–2. The Si-o-se-pol bridge in Isfahan still bears his name.

entries.name: Saturnalia
entries.desc: Saturnalia was an ancient Roman festival in honour of the god Saturn, held on 17 December in the Julian calendar and extended by the 1st century BCE to 23 December, seven days in all. It opened with a sacrifice at the Temple of Saturn in the Roman Forum and a public banquet, followed by gift-giving, gambling and a licence in which masters served their slaves at table and a "King of the Saturnalia" presided over the merrymaking. In 217 BCE, after the Roman defeat at the Battle of Lake Trasimene, the festival was reformed with sacrifices in the Greek manner. It remained popular into the 3rd and 4th centuries CE and may have influenced later midwinter customs of western Europe.

entries.name: Yule
entries.desc: Yule is a winter festival and time of the year observed by heathen Germanic peoples and later merged with Christmas during Christianisation. Its earliest record is a Gothic calendar in the Codex Ambrosianus of c. 350 CE, and the English historian Bede, writing c. 726 CE, recorded that the heathen Anglo-Saxons called both December and January Giuli. Old Norse sources describe a festival in which feasting, ceremonial drinking and oath swearing were central. According to Hákonar saga góða, Hákon the Good passed a law in Norway that set Yule at the time when Christians celebrated Christmas. Yule and its cognates still name Christmas in English and other Northern European languages.

entries.name: Dongzhi
entries.desc: Dongzhi is the 22nd solar term of the Chinese calendar, marking the winter solstice, and the festival that Chinese people observe at that time, around 21 to 23 December. Its origins are traced to the philosophy of yin and yang, the lengthening days representing positive energy. The festival was first celebrated during the Zhou dynasty (1045 BCE–256 BCE) and declared an official celebration during the Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE), when people took a break from work, worshipped heaven and honoured their ancestors. Families still gather to eat tangyuan, balls of glutinous rice that symbolize reunion, and dumplings; in Korea, where the day is called Dongji, porridge is made with red beans.

entries.name: Yalda Night
entries.desc: Yalda Night, also called Chilla Night, is an ancient festival celebrated on the winter solstice of the Northern Hemisphere in Iran, Kurdistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan. On the longest night of the year friends and family gather to eat, drink and read poetry, especially Hafez, late into the night; pomegranates and watermelons are particularly significant. In Zoroastrian tradition the night was inauspicious, and its customs were originally intended to protect people from evil. The name Yalda was borrowed from Syriac-speaking Christians, in whose language it means "birth". It was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage Lists in December 2022.

entries.name: Christmas
entries.desc: Christmas is a religious and cultural celebration commemorating the birth of Jesus Christ, observed primarily on 25 December; part of the Eastern Christian churches keep it on 25 December of the Julian calendar, which currently corresponds to 7 January. The Gospels of Luke and Matthew describe Jesus as born in Bethlehem to the Virgin Mary. The earliest document to place the birth on 25 December is the Chronograph of 354, in a part generally agreed to have been written in Rome in 336; the day was the traditional date of the winter solstice in the Roman Empire. Puritans prohibited the celebration in England from 1647 to 1660. Its customs mix pre-Christian, Christian and secular themes.

entries.name: Advent
entries.desc: Advent is a season observed in most Christian denominations as a time of waiting and preparation for the celebration of Jesus's birth at Christmas and for his return at the Second Coming. In Western Christianity it begins on the fourth Sunday before Christmas and opens the liturgical year; its name comes from the Latin adventus, "coming". When the season began is not known, though it existed from about 480, and the Council of Tours of 567 ordered monks to fast every day in December until Christmas. A fast kept from St. Martin's Day on 11 November, known as St Martin's Lent, was limited to the diocese of Tours until the sixth century. Practices today include Advent calendars and wreaths.

entries.name: Epiphany
entries.desc: Epiphany, known as Theophany in Eastern Christian tradition, is a Christian feast day commemorating the visit of the Magi, the baptism of Jesus and the wedding at Cana, traditionally on 6 January. It may have originated in the Greek-speaking east of the Roman Empire as a feast of the baptism of Jesus; the earliest reference to it as a Christian feast, by Ammianus Marcellinus, dates from 361. Western Christianity principally commemorates the Magi's visit to the Christ Child, seen as his manifestation to the Gentiles, while Eastern Christians commemorate his baptism in the River Jordan. Eastern Churches that follow the Julian calendar observe the feast on 19 January of the Gregorian calendar.

entries.name: Koliada
entries.desc: Koliada, or koleda, is the traditional Slavic name for the period from Christmas to Epiphany or, more generally, for Christmas-related rituals, some of which date to pre-Christian times. It denotes a festival held at the end of December to honour the sun at the winter solstice, and one theory derives it from the ancient calendae. The word originated in Old Church Slavonic, and in several Slavic languages its meaning has shifted to the custom of going from house to house on Christmas Eve, when groups of singers called koledari sing carols and receive gifts in return. The Dubrovnik kolenda, first mentioned in the 13th century, is one of the oldest recorded traditions of this kind in Croatia.

entries.name: Sol Invictus
entries.desc: Sol Invictus, the "Invincible" or "Unconquered Sun", was the official sun god of the late Roman Empire. The emperor Aurelian revived his cult in 274 CE, promoted him as the chief god of the empire and dedicated a new temple to him on 25 December 274; according to some scholars he also instituted on that day, the winter solstice of the Roman calendar, the festival Dies Natalis Solis Invicti. Scholars are divided on whether Sol Invictus was a Syrian sun god distinct from the old Latin god Sol or belonged to a single, continuous Roman cult of Sol. He often appeared on imperial coinage, and on that of Constantine I until 325/326. The last known inscription referring to him dates to 387 CE.

entries.name: Saint Lucy's Day
entries.desc: Saint Lucy's Day, also called the Feast of Saint Lucy, is a Christian feast day observed on 13 December in commemoration of Lucia of Syracuse, an early-fourth-century virgin martyr under the Diocletianic Persecution. According to legend she brought food to persecuted Christians hiding in the Roman catacombs, wearing a candle-lit wreath on her head to light her way. The feast became a universal feast of the Church in the 6th century. Because its date at one time coincided with the shortest day of the year, it is now widely celebrated as a festival of light, most widely in Scandinavia, Italy and Saint Lucia. The first modern-day Scandinavian celebration was held in 1928 in Stockholm.

entries.name: Hogmanay
entries.desc: Hogmanay is the Scots word for the last day of the old year and for the celebration of the New Year in the Scottish manner. The etymology of the word is obscure, the main modern theories deriving it from a French, Norse or Gaelic root; it is first recorded in a Latin entry of 1443 in the West Riding of Yorkshire and in Scots in 1604, in the records of Elgin. Its roots are speculated to reach back to the Norse celebration of the winter solstice and the Gaelic Samhain. The most widespread custom is first-footing, in which the first person to cross a friend's or neighbour's threshold after midnight brings symbolic gifts such as coal, shortbread, whisky and black bun.

entries.name: Twelfth Night
entries.desc: Twelfth Night, also known as Epiphany Eve, is a Christian festival on the last night of the Twelve Days of Christmas, marking the end of Christmastide and the coming of the Epiphany. Traditions place it on either 5 January or 6 January, depending on whether the counting begins on Christmas Day or on 26 December. In 567 the Council of Tours proclaimed the twelve days from Christmas to Epiphany a sacred and festive season. A popular custom was to hide a bean and a pea in a Twelfth-night cake, the man and the lady who found them becoming King and Queen for the night. Customs today include eating king cake, singing Christmas carols and chalking the door.

credit.artist: Hablot Knight Browne: scanned by Steven J Plunkett

entries.name: Christmas tree
entries.desc: A Christmas tree is a decorated tree, usually an evergreen conifer such as a spruce, pine or fir, set up for the celebration of Christmas. The custom developed in Central Europe, particularly Germany and Livonia (now Estonia and Latvia), and was first recorded among German Lutherans in the 16th century; records indicate that a tree was placed in the Cathedral of Strasbourg in 1539. Trees were hung with apples, wafers, paper roses and confectionery and lit with candles, which electric lights have often replaced. In Britain the German-born Queen Charlotte introduced a tree in 1800, and the custom spread more widely after Queen Victoria's marriage to Prince Albert.

entries.name: Santa Claus
entries.desc: Santa Claus is a legendary figure originating in Western Christian culture who is said to bring gifts on the night of Christmas Eve. The figure derives from folklore surrounding Saint Nicholas, the 4th-century Greek bishop of Myra and patron saint of children, and from the Dutch Sinterklaas, whose legend settlers brought to 17th-century New Amsterdam; it also merged with the English Father Christmas. The name was first used in the United States press in 1773. The 1823 poem "A Visit from St. Nicholas", with its sleigh pulled by flying reindeer, laid the foundation for the modern image, which the cartoonist Thomas Nast helped to define in Harper's Weekly from 1863.

entries.name: Sinterklaas
entries.desc: Sinterklaas is a legendary figure of Dutch tradition based on Saint Nicholas (270–343), a Greek bishop of Myra in present-day Turkey and patron saint of children. He is depicted as an elderly, stately man with a long beard, in a red cape and mitre, who traditionally arrives by steamboat from Spain in mid-November and rides a white horse. Gifts are given on St. Nicholas' Eve, 5 December, in the Netherlands and on the morning of 6 December in Belgium, Luxembourg, western Germany and northern France. His helper Zwarte Piet ("Black Pete"), who first appeared in print in 1850, has been the subject of debate and protest since the 2010s over his blackface appearance.

entries.name: Ded Moroz
entries.desc: Ded Moroz, whose name is traditionally translated as Father Frost, is a legendary figure of East Slavic tradition similar to Father Christmas and Santa Claus. His origins predate Christianity as a Slavic personification of winter, and since the 19th century his legend has been shaped by literature, among it Aleksandr Ostrovsky's play The Snow Maiden. He is depicted with a long white beard, a heel-length fur coat and a magic stick, bringing presents at New Year with his granddaughter Snegurochka. In 1928 he was declared an ally of the priest and kulak, but traditions were revived after a letter published in Pravda in 1935, and he became the main symbol of the Soviet New Year's holiday.

entries.name: Krampus
entries.desc: The Krampus is a horned figure of Central and Eastern Alpine folklore who is said to accompany Saint Nicholas on visits to children on the night of 5 December, Krampusnacht, before the Feast of St. Nicholas. In the tradition Saint Nicholas rewards well-behaved children with small gifts, while Krampus, hairy and carrying chains and birch rods, punishes badly behaved ones. The origin of the figure is unclear: some folklorists have proposed pre-Christian roots, but historians generally consider this unlikely, as it is not attested until the 16th century. The tradition was prohibited in Austria under the Dollfuss regime and saw a popular resurgence towards the end of the 20th century.

entries.name: Nativity of Jesus
entries.desc: The Nativity of Jesus is the birth of Jesus as told in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, the basis of the Christian holiday of Christmas. The two accounts agree that Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea in the reign of King Herod, to Mary, whose husband Joseph was descended from King David, and that the conception was divinely effected. Only Matthew has the wise men, the star of Bethlehem, the Massacre of the Innocents and the flight into Egypt; only Luke has the census of Quirinius and the adoration of the shepherds. The gospels state no date; reckoning from the death of Herod would place the birth between 6 and 4 BCE.

entries.name: Nativity scene
entries.desc: A nativity scene, also called a manger scene, crib or crèche, is a display, particularly during Christmastide, of figures representing the birth of Jesus. It shows Jesus, Mary and Joseph, usually with shepherds, angels, an ox and a donkey, and the Magi. The tradition comes from Italy: the first seasonal scene, which seems to have been enacted rather than sculpted, is attributed to Francis of Assisi, who is said to have staged it at Christmas 1223 in a cave near Greccio. Around 1290 Arnolfo di Cambio made a set of stone figures for Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome, and in the early modern period sculpted cribs, often exported from Italy, were set up in many churches and homes.

entries.name: Christmas carol
entries.desc: A Christmas carol is a song or hymn on the theme of Christmas, traditionally sung at Christmas or in the surrounding season. The first known Christmas hymns may be traced to 4th-century Rome, and by the 13th century popular Christmas songs in vernacular languages had developed in France, Germany and particularly Italy, under the influence of Francis of Assisi. The earliest English carols appear in a manuscript of 1426 by the Shropshire chaplain John Awdlay, who recorded twenty-five. Carols grew in popularity after the Protestant Reformation, when reformers such as Martin Luther promoted congregational singing, and printed collections of the 19th century widened their appeal.

entries.name: Wassail
entries.desc: Wassail is an English custom of Christmastide and the hot drink of mulled cider, ale or wine and spices that goes with it. The word was borrowed from the Old Norse salutation ves heill, 'be in good health'; its earliest record as a drinking formula is of around 1140, in Geoffrey of Monmouth, and by c. 1300 it also meant the drink itself. In the house-visiting wassail, traditionally on Twelfth Night (5 January), people go from door to door singing and offering a drink from the wassail bowl in exchange for gifts, a practice largely displaced by carol singing. In the orchard-visiting wassail of England's cider-producing regions, people sing to the trees to promote a good harvest.

entries.name: Winter solstice
entries.desc: The winter solstice is the moment when one of Earth's poles reaches its maximum tilt away from the Sun, giving that hemisphere its shortest day and longest night of the year.
