In the Northern Hemisphere it falls on 21 or 22 December and in the Southern on 20 or 21 June. Since prehistory it has been marked by festivals and rites in many cultures, as the point when daylight begins to increase again; monuments such as Newgrange in Ireland and Stonehenge in England are aligned with its sunrise or sunset. In the ancient Roman calendar the solstice was dated to 25 December, which the emperor Aurelian made the festival of the birthday of Sol Invictus in 274 CE.

entries.name: Lohri
entries.desc: Lohri is a midwinter folk and harvest festival of the Punjab region of India and Pakistan and other parts of northern India, marking the passing of the winter solstice and the end of winter. It falls on the night before Maghi (Makar Sankranti), commonly 13 January, and is celebrated by lighting bonfires, eating festive foods such as jaggery and gajak, singing, and dancing the bhangra and giddha. Many of its songs tell the legend of Dulla Bhatti, set in the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar and regarded in Punjab as a hero for rescuing girls from being sold in slave markets. European visitors mentioned the festival at the Lahore court of Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the 1830s.

entries.name: Makar Sankranti
entries.desc: Makar Sankranti is a Hindu observance and midwinter harvest festival in India and Nepal, typically celebrated on 14 January (15 January in a leap year). It marks the transition of the Sun from the zodiac sign of Sagittarius to Capricorn (makara), which coincides with its movement from south to north, and is dedicated to the solar deity Surya. The festival is known by many regional names, among them Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Magh Bihu in Assam and Uttarayana in Gujarat. It is observed with fairs, kite flying, bonfires and feasts, and many observers bathe in sacred rivers or lakes in thanks to the Sun. Every twelve years it is observed with the Kumbha Mela, a mass pilgrimage.

entries.name: Kwanzaa
entries.desc: Kwanzaa is an annual celebration of African-American culture held from 26 December to 1 January, culminating in a communal feast called Karamu, usually on the sixth day. The activist Maulana Karenga created it in 1966, in the aftermath of the Watts riots, drawing on his research into African harvest festival traditions; according to Karenga, the name derives from the Swahili phrase matunda ya kwanza, "first fruits". Each of its seven days is dedicated to one of the seven principles, the Nguzo Saba, and ceremonies include a candle-lighting ritual. Karenga at first meant it as an alternative to Christmas, but many African Americans who celebrate it also observe Christmas.

entries.name: Boxing Day
entries.desc: Boxing Day is a holiday celebrated on 26 December, the day after Christmas Day, which originated in the United Kingdom and is kept in several Commonwealth nations. It was once a day for giving gifts to those in need and usually coincides with the Christian festival of Saint Stephen's Day. The origin of the name is not definitive: it may refer to the alms boxes placed in churches, and in Britain tradesmen collected "Christmas boxes" of money or presents after Christmas, a custom mentioned in Samuel Pepys's diary in 1663. The Oxford English Dictionary gives the earliest attestation from Britain in 1743. In the United Kingdom outside Scotland, 26 December has been a bank holiday since 1871.

entries.name: Chinese New Year
entries.desc: Chinese New Year, also known as the Spring Festival, marks the beginning of a new year on the traditional lunisolar Chinese calendar, on the new moon that falls between 21 January and 20 February. The festival runs from New Year's Eve, when families gather for the reunion dinner, to the Lantern Festival on the 15th day of the year. Records of the first celebration can be traced to the Warring States period (475–221 BCE). Houses are cleaned, doors are decorated with red couplets, firecrackers are lit and money is given in red envelopes. It has influenced other new year celebrations, among them the Tết of Vietnam, the Seollal of Korea and the Losar of Tibet.

entries.name: Ōmisoka
entries.desc: Ōmisoka is the traditional Japanese celebration of the last day of the year. It was held on the final day of the 12th lunar month until Japan switched to the Gregorian calendar in 1873, when it was set as 31 December. Traditionally, house cleaning, the repaying of debts, purification and bathing were completed so that the new year could start fresh. About an hour before the New Year, people often eat a bowl of toshikoshi soba or udon, long noodles associated with crossing over from one year to the next. At midnight many visit a shrine or temple, and most Buddhist temples strike a large bell once for each of the 108 earthly temptations believed to cause human suffering.

entries.name: Maslenitsa
entries.desc: Maslenitsa is an Eastern Slavic religious and folk holiday celebrated during the last week before Great Lent, the eighth week before Eastern Orthodox Pascha. It has retained elements of Slavic mythology in its ritual and, according to archaeological evidence from the 2nd century CE, may be the oldest surviving Slavic holiday. Russians bake blini, and a straw effigy, Lady Maslenitsa, is paraded and then burned in a bonfire on Forgiveness Sunday, when relatives and friends ask each other for forgiveness. Large public celebrations became less common after the Russian Revolution in 1917 and under Soviet state atheism; since 2002 Moscow has staged a yearly festival next to the Red Square.

entries.name: Candlemas
aka: Feast of the Presentation of Jesus Christ
Feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary
entries.desc: Candlemas is a Christian feast day, kept on 2 February, that commemorates the presentation of Jesus at the Temple by Joseph and Mary, as told in the Gospel of Luke. It falls on what is traditionally the 40th day and the conclusion of the Christmas–Epiphany season. One of the oldest feasts of the church, it was recorded by the pilgrim Egeria as celebrated in Jerusalem in the 380s, and it was introduced to Rome and other places from the mid-7th century. Many Christians take candles to church to be blessed and use them for the rest of the year as a symbol of Jesus Christ, the "Light of the World". A German saying about a hedgehog's shadow on Candlemas was the origin of Groundhog Day.

entries.name: Thanksgiving
entries.desc: Thanksgiving is a national holiday celebrated on various dates in October and November in the United States, Canada, Saint Lucia and Liberia. It began as a day of giving thanks for the harvest, and its history in North America is rooted in English traditions of days of thanksgiving dating from the Protestant Reformation. A yearly thanksgiving is first documented in 1619 at Berkeley Hundred in Virginia; the 1621 harvest festival of Plymouth Colony, which the Wampanoag joined, was largely forgotten for hundreds of years and was termed "the first Thanksgiving" only in 1841. Abraham Lincoln made it a national holiday in 1863, and in 1941 Congress fixed it on the fourth Thursday in November.

entries.name: Day of the Dead
entries.desc: The Day of the Dead is a holiday traditionally celebrated on 1 and 2 November, widely observed in Mexico and among people of Mexican heritage elsewhere, in which family and friends gather to remember those who have died. Families build home altars called ofrendas with the favourite foods and beverages of the departed, and visit graves with calaveras and marigold flowers. Mexican academics are divided on whether it has indigenous pre-Hispanic roots or is a Spanish tradition recast in the 20th century, under the presidency of Lázaro Cárdenas, to encourage Mexican nationalism. In 2008 UNESCO added it to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

entries.name: Guy Fawkes Night
entries.desc: Guy Fawkes Night is an annual commemoration observed on 5 November, primarily in Great Britain, with bonfires and fireworks displays. It began in 1605, when Guy Fawkes, a member of the Gunpowder Plot, was arrested while guarding explosives placed beneath the House of Lords, and people lit bonfires around London to celebrate the survival of King James I. The Observance of 5th November Act 1605 mandated an annual public day of thanksgiving, and as Gunpowder Treason Day it became a focus for anti-Catholic sentiment, with effigies of the Pope burnt. Towards the end of the 18th century children began begging for money with effigies of Guy Fawkes. The Act was repealed in 1859.

entries.name: Gunpowder Plot
entries.desc: The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 was an unsuccessful attempt by a group of English Catholics, led by Robert Catesby, to kill King James VI of Scotland and I of England. The plan was to blow up the House of Lords on 5 November 1605, as the prelude to a revolt in the Midlands in which the king's nine-year-old daughter, Princess Elizabeth, was to be installed as head of state. After an anonymous letter of warning reached William Parker, 4th Baron Monteagle, a search on 4 November found Guy Fawkes guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder. Catesby was shot dead at Holbeche House; eight surviving conspirators, including Fawkes, were convicted in January 1606 and sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered.

credit.artist: Unknown (printed for P. Brooksby, I. Deacon, I. Blare, I. Back.)

entries.name: Diwali
entries.desc: Diwali, or Dipavali, is the Hindu festival of lights. It is celebrated over five or six days between around mid-October and mid-November and is associated with the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil; Hindus connect it with the day Rama returned to his kingdom in Ayodhya after defeating the demon king Ravana, and with Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity. Jains mark the final liberation of Mahavira, and Sikhs the release of Guru Hargobind from a Mughal prison. The festival originated in the Indian subcontinent, likely as a combination of harvest festivals of ancient India. Celebrants light their homes and temples with diyas, oil lamps.

entries.name: Christmas truce
entries.desc: The Christmas truce was a series of widespread unofficial ceasefires, mainly along the Western Front of the First World War around Christmas in 1914. Roughly 100,000 British and German troops were involved. In some areas men from both sides went into no man's land on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day to exchange food and souvenirs; there were joint burial ceremonies, carols and games of football, while hostilities continued in other sectors. Pope Benedict XV had begged the warring governments for an official truce on 7 December 1914, which both sides refused. The following year only a few units arranged ceasefires, in part because of orders from commanders prohibiting truces.

entries.name: Armistice Day
entries.desc: Armistice Day is commemorated every year on 11 November to mark the armistice signed between the Allies of World War I and Germany at Compiègne, France, which took effect at 11:00 am on that day in 1918 and ended hostilities on the Western Front. The first official Armistice Day events were held in the grounds of Buckingham Palace on the morning of 11 November 1919 and included a two-minute silence for those who died in the war. Around the Second World War many countries changed the holiday's name and several widened it to all veterans: most Commonwealth states adopted the name Remembrance Day, and the United States changed it in 1954. The date is a national holiday in France.

entries.name: Valley Forge
entries.desc: Valley Forge was the winter encampment of the Continental Army under George Washington in eastern Pennsylvania, along the Schuylkill River, during the Philadelphia campaign of the American Revolutionary War. Unable to defend Philadelphia after his defeat at the Battle of Brandywine, Washington led his 12,000-man army into winter quarters there in December 1777, approximately 18 miles northwest of the city. The army faced a disastrous supply crisis, and an estimated 1,700 to 2,000 soldiers died from disease, possibly made worse by malnutrition and cold, wet weather. Baron Friedrich von Steuben, a Prussian drill master, instituted a training program before the army marched out in June 1778.

entries.name: George Washington's crossing of the Delaware River
entries.desc: George Washington's crossing of the Delaware River, on the night of 25–26 December 1776, was the first move in a surprise attack by the Continental Army on the Hessian forces garrisoned at Trenton during the American Revolutionary War. Washington, the army's commander-in-chief, led a column from Pennsylvania across the icy river to New Jersey at McConkey's Ferry, in weather that turned from rain to sleet and snow. Other planned crossings in support were called off or ineffective, leaving about 2,400 men for the attack. After defeating the Hessians under Johann Rall in the Battle of Trenton, the army crossed back to Pennsylvania with its prisoners and captured stores.
links: George Washington's crossing of the Delaware River

entries.name: Battle of Trenton
entries.desc: The Battle of Trenton was a short American Revolutionary War battle fought on the morning of 26 December 1776, in Trenton, New Jersey. After crossing the icy Delaware River the previous night, George Washington led 2,400 men of the Continental Army against a garrison of about 1,400 Hessian auxiliaries commanded by Colonel Johann Rall. The Hessians, who had no long-distance outposts or patrols, were caught off guard; they lost 22 killed, including Rall, and 896 captured, while the Americans suffered two deaths on the march and five wounded. Coming after defeats in New York and a retreat through New Jersey, the victory raised the army's waning morale and inspired re-enlistments.

credit.artist: Published by U.S. Government Printing Office; painting by Hugh Charles McBarron, Jr. (1902-1992)

entries.name: Great Frost of 1709
entries.desc: The Great Frost, as it was known in England, or Le Grand Hiver in France, was an extraordinarily cold winter in Europe in 1708–1709, the coldest European winter of the past 500 years. William Derham recorded a low of −12 °C at Upminster, near London, on the night of 5 January 1709. France was particularly hard hit: the famine that followed is estimated to have caused 600,000 deaths by the end of 1710. During the Great Northern War, winter storms and frosts killed thousands in the Swedish army invading Russia, contributing to the Russian victory at Poltava the following summer.

entries.name: Siege of Leningrad
entries.desc: The siege of Leningrad was a military blockade of the Soviet city of Leningrad, present-day Saint Petersburg, by Germany and Finland on the Eastern Front of World War II; it lasted 872 days, and the city was never captured. Land routes to the rest of the Soviet Union were cut on 8 September 1941, and the Germans decided to bomb the city and starve its inhabitants. Many residents starved during the winter of 1941–1942; the siege caused an estimated 1.5 million deaths, from a prewar population of 3.2 million, and some historians have classified it as a genocide. Supplies came across Lake Ladoga, in winter over the Road of Life on the ice, until the siege was fully broken on 27 January 1944.

entries.name: River Thames frost fairs
entries.desc: The River Thames frost fairs were held on the frozen tideway of the River Thames in London in some winters, from at least the late 7th century until the early 19th. Most took place between the early 17th and early 19th centuries, during the Little Ice Age, when the river was wider and slower and was further impeded by the 19 piers of the medieval Old London Bridge. The first known fair was in 695, and the term was first used of the fair of 1608. During the Great Frost of 1683–84 the Thames was completely frozen for two months. The last fair began on 1 February 1814 and lasted four days, with printing presses on the ice; the old bridge was removed in 1831.

entries.name: Treaty of Ghent
entries.desc: The Treaty of Ghent was the peace treaty that ended the War of 1812 between the United States and the United Kingdom, signed on 24 December 1814, in the city of Ghent, now in Belgium. It restored the pre-war borders of June 1812. The five American commissioners were led by John Quincy Adams; the British at first demanded an Indigenous buffer state in the area from present-day Ohio to Wisconsin, which the Americans refused to consider. News of the treaty took a month to reach the United States, and in the meantime American forces under Andrew Jackson won the Battle of New Orleans on 8 January 1815. The treaty took effect in February 1815, when ratified copies were exchanged in Washington.

entries.name: Amundsen's South Pole expedition
entries.desc: Amundsen's South Pole expedition, led by the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen, was the first to reach the Geographic South Pole, on 14 December 1911. Amundsen had planned an Arctic drift in Fridtjof Nansen's ship Fram, but changed his goal in secret and revealed the Antarctic destination to his crew only on leaving Madeira in September 1910. From his base, Framheim, in the Bay of Whales, he set out in October 1911 with four companions, using skis and sled dogs and reaching the polar plateau by the Axel Heiberg Glacier. They arrived five weeks ahead of the British party led by Robert Falcon Scott, whose five men died on their return journey, and returned safely to their base in January 1912.

credit.artist: one of Amundsen's five-man polar party

entries.name: Apollo 8
entries.desc: Apollo 8 was the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and the first human spaceflight to reach the Moon, flown from 21 to 27 December 1968. Its three astronauts, Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and William Anders, travelled 68 hours to the Moon and orbited it ten times without landing; they were the first humans to see and photograph its far side and an Earthrise. On Christmas Eve they read the first ten verses of the Book of Genesis in a television broadcast. The mission, the first crewed launch of the Saturn V rocket, ended with a splashdown in the northern Pacific Ocean and paved the way for Apollo 11 in July 1969.

entries.name: A Christmas Carol
aka: A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas
entries.desc: A Christmas Carol is a novella by Charles Dickens, first published in London by Chapman & Hall in 1843 with illustrations by John Leech. It tells of Ebenezer Scrooge, an elderly miser who is visited by the ghost of his former business partner Jacob Marley and the spirits of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come, and becomes a kinder man. Dickens was inspired by a visit to the Field Lane Ragged School for London's street children. Published on 19 December, the first edition sold out by Christmas Eve, and thirteen editions had appeared by the end of 1844. The book has never been out of print, and Dickens gave public readings of it from 1849 until 1870, the year of his death.

entries.name: The Nutcracker
entries.desc: The Nutcracker is a two-act classical ballet by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, first performed on 18 December 1892 at the Imperial Mariinsky Theatre in Saint Petersburg, in a double premiere with his last opera, Iolanta. Its plot, set on Christmas Eve, adapts Alexandre Dumas's 1844 retelling of E. T. A. Hoffmann's 1816 story The Nutcracker and the Mouse King. The libretto was by Marius Petipa; whether he or his assistant Lev Ivanov choreographed the first production has been debated. The first performance was not deemed a success. Since the late 1960s the ballet has been danced by many companies, especially in North America; its score is noted for its use of the celesta.

entries.name: Wright Flyer
entries.desc: The Wright Flyer is the aircraft that made the first sustained flight by a manned, powered and controlled heavier-than-air machine, on 17 December 1903. Built and flown by Orville and Wilbur Wright, it is a single-place biplane with a 12 horsepower gasoline engine driving two pusher propellers. They flew it four times at what is now Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina: Orville's first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet, and the fourth, by Wilbur, covered 852 feet in 59 seconds before gusts wrecked the machine. After a long dispute between Orville and the Smithsonian Institution it joined the Institution's collection in 1948 and is displayed in Washington, D.C.

entries.name: Personent hodie
entries.dates: usually dated from a manuscript of 1360; first printed 1582
entries.desc: "Personent hodie" is a Christmas carol first published in 1582 in Piae Cantiones, a Finnish song book of 74 medieval songs with Latin texts, collected by Jacobus Finno (Jaakko Suomalainen), a Lutheran cleric, and published by T. P. Rutha.

entries.name: Wexford Carol
entries.desc: The Wexford Carol, also called the Enniscorthy Carol (in Irish Carúl Loch Garman or Carúl Inis Córthaidh), is a traditional Irish Christmas carol that comes from Enniscorthy in County Wexford. It is sometimes known by the opening of its first verse. Its subject is the nativity of Jesus Christ. Its origins are uncertain.

entries.name: I Saw Three Ships
aka: I Saw Three Ships (Come Sailing In)
entries.dates: earliest printed version 17th century; modern words published 1833
entries.desc: "I Saw Three Ships (Come Sailing In)" is an English Christmas carol, number 700 in the Roud Folk Song Index. The earliest printed version is from the 17th century, possibly from Derbyshire. The song was probably known traditionally as "As I Sat On a Sunny Bank", and it was particularly popular in Cornwall.

entries.name: Hark! The Herald Angels Sing
entries.desc: "Hark! The Herald Angels Sing" is an English Christmas carol written by Charles Wesley in 1739. It is based on Luke 2:8–14 and describes a chorus of angels singing of the birth of Christ. Wesley called it "Hymn for Christmas-Day", and it first appeared in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739), compiled by Charles and his brother John.

entries.name: Tu scendi dalle stelle
entries.desc: "Tu scendi dalle stelle" ("You Come Down from the Stars") is a Christmas carol from Italy, written in 1744 by Alphonsus Liguori in the musical style of a pastorale. Liguori was a prominent Neapolitan priest and scholastic philosopher, later canonised, who founded the Redemptorist missionary order. He wrote both the melody and the original words.

entries.name: The Twelve Days of Christmas
entries.desc: "The Twelve Days of Christmas" is an English Christmas carol and nursery rhyme, and a cumulative song: each of its twelve verses adds one new gift from "my true love" and then repeats all the earlier ones, so that each verse is one line longer than the last. The twelve days are those of the Christmas season, from Christmas Day to the day before Epiphany on 6 January.

entries.name: The First Nowell
entries.dates: most likely early modern, possibly earlier; current form first published 1823
entries.desc: "The First Nowell" (or "Nowel"), modernised as "The First Noel", is a traditional English Christmas carol of Cornish origin. It most likely dates from the early modern period, although it may be older.

entries.name: The Holly and the Ivy
entries.dates: traced to the early 19th century; the present version collected 1909, published 1911
entries.desc: "The Holly and the Ivy" is a traditional British folk Christmas carol, number 514 in the Roud Folk Song Index. The song itself can be traced only as far back as the early nineteenth century, but its words reflect a link between holly and Christmas that goes back at least to medieval times.

entries.name: Here We Come A-wassailing
entries.dates: at least the mid 19th century, probably much older
entries.desc: "Here We Come A-wassailing", also known as "Here We Come A-Caroling", "Here We Come A-Christmasing", "Wassail Song" and by many other names, is a traditional English Christmas carol and New Year song. It was typically sung while wassailing: going from door to door singing carols, wishing good health and exchanging gifts. It is number 209 in the Roud Folk Song Index.

entries.name: Good King Wenceslas
entries.desc: "Good King Wenceslas" is a Christmas carol that tells of a tenth-century ruler of Bohemia who goes out in harsh winter weather to give alms to a poor peasant on the Feast of Stephen, 26 December. The legend behind it is a story about Saint Wenceslaus I, Duke of Bohemia (907–935).

entries.name: Deck the Halls
entries.dates: English words 1862; melody published 1794, first found in a manuscript of the 1700s
entries.desc: "Deck the Halls" is a Christmas carol with a Welsh tune and English words. The melody belongs to "Nos Galan" ("New Year's Eve"), a traditional Welsh winter carol.

entries.name: We Wish You a Merry Christmas
entries.dates: date unknown; a closely related verse from the 1830s; the famous version published 1935
entries.desc: "We Wish You a Merry Christmas" is an English Christmas carol, and its famous version comes from the West Country of England. The greeting "A merry Christmas and a happy New Year" is recorded from the early 18th century, but the history of the carol itself has yet to be made clear.
links: We Wish You a Merry Christmas

entries.name: White Christmas
entries.dates: written c. 1940; first performed 25 December 1941; recorded 29 May 1942
entries.desc: "White Christmas" was written by Irving Berlin for the 1942 musical film Holiday Inn. Accounts differ as to when and where he wrote it. One story is that he wrote it in 1940 in warm La Quinta, California, while staying at the La Quinta Hotel, a retreat favoured by Hollywood; the Arizona Biltmore also claims the song was written there.

entries.name: Bible
entries.desc: The Bible is an anthology of religious texts central to Judaism and Christianity and important in other Abrahamic religions such as Islam, compiled by different religious communities into official collections called biblical canons. The Hebrew Bible, written in Hebrew with some parts in Aramaic, is divided into the Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim; its oldest parts may be as early as c. 1200 BCE. The Christian Bible joins the Old Testament, a reorganisation of the Hebrew Bible's books and the deuterocanonical books, to a New Testament written mostly in Koine Greek in the 1st century CE. With estimated sales of over five billion copies, it is the best-selling publication of all time.

entries.name: Marie Curie
entries.desc: Marie Curie, born Maria Salomea Skłodowska in Warsaw, was a Polish and naturalised-French physicist and chemist. She moved to Paris in 1891 and with her husband, Pierre Curie, carried out research on radioactivity, a term she coined, discovering the elements polonium and radium. She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics and won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win it in two scientific fields. She founded the Curie Institute in Paris in 1920 and died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, likely from exposure to radiation in her research.

entries.name: Thomas Edison
entries.desc: Thomas Edison was an American inventor and businessman known for his work on the incandescent light bulb, the phonograph, electric power distribution and early motion pictures. Born in Milan, Ohio, he worked as a railroad telegrapher before turning to invention, and developed Menlo Park, now considered the first industrial research laboratory. From 1878 he worked on an electrical lighting system to replace the gas lamp; competition with Westinghouse's AC system and the merger of Edison General Electric with Thomson-Houston led to the formation of General Electric. He registered 1,093 patents in the United States.

credit.artist: Louis Bachrach, Bachrach Studios , restored by Michel Vuijlsteke

entries.name: Easter
entries.desc: Easter, also called Pascha or Resurrection Sunday, is a Christian celebration and cultural holiday commemorating the resurrection of Jesus, which the New Testament describes as taking place on the third day after his crucifixion by the Romans at Calvary. It is preceded by Lent, a 40-day period of fasting, prayer and penance, and by Holy Week, and opens Eastertide, which lasts until Pentecost. A moveable feast, its date was set by the First Council of Nicaea (325) as the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the vernal equinox. It is linked to the Jewish Passover by its name, its origin and much of its symbolism.

entries.name: Franz Kafka
entries.desc: Franz Kafka was a German-language Jewish writer from Prague whose works fuse realism and the fantastique, typically with isolated protagonists facing bizarre predicaments and incomprehensible bureaucratic powers; the term Kafkaesque comes from them. He trained as a lawyer and worked in legal and insurance jobs, publishing only a minority of his works in his life, among them the collections Contemplation (1912) and A Country Doctor (1919) and the novella The Metamorphosis (1915). He died of tuberculosis in 1924, aged 40. His friend Max Brod ignored his wish that his remaining works be destroyed and published them, including The Trial (1925) and The Castle (1926).

entries.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
entries.desc: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher and writer who began as a classical philologist and in 1869, at 24, became Professor of Classical Philology at the University of Basel. Ill health made him resign in 1879, and he lived as an independent writer in Switzerland, Italy and southern France. His philosophy includes a critique of objective truth, a genealogical critique of Christian morality, and the concepts of the will to power, the Übermensch and eternal return. After his collapse in 1889 his sister, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, edited his manuscripts to fit her ultranationalist ideology, and his work became associated with fascism and Nazism.

entries.name: Nikola Tesla
entries.desc: Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist and inventor known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system. Born in Smiljan in the Austrian Empire, he migrated to the United States in 1884 and worked briefly at the Edison Machine Works before setting up his own laboratories in New York. His AC induction motor and polyphase patents, licensed by Westinghouse Electric in 1888, became the cornerstone of the polyphase system. His Wardenclyffe Tower project for wireless communication and power ran out of funding. He died in New York City in 1943; in 1960 the SI unit of magnetic flux density was named the tesla.

entries.name: Abraham
entries.desc: Abraham, originally Abram, is a foundational figure revered in the Abrahamic religions: in Judaism the first Hebrew patriarch, who began the covenant between the Jewish people and God; in Christianity the forebear of Jesus; and in Islam a link in the chain of prophets from Adam to Muhammad. According to the Book of Genesis, God called him to leave the house of his father Terah and settle in Canaan, promised to him and to his descendants through his son Isaac. Nearly all scholars view the patriarchal age as a late literary construct; many believe the traditions developed orally before being written into Genesis in the Persian period of Judah.

entries.name: Anton Chekhov
entries.desc: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright, short story writer and physician, born in Taganrog on the Sea of Azov. He began writing stories to earn money and made formal innovations that influenced the modern short story. After the reception of The Seagull in 1896 he renounced the theatre, but Konstantin Stanislavski's Moscow Art Theatre revived the play to acclaim in 1898, then staged Uncle Vanya and premiered Three Sisters and The Cherry Orchard. With Henrik Ibsen and August Strindberg he is often counted among the three seminal figures of early modernism in the theatre. He died of tuberculosis at Badenweiler in Germany in 1904, aged 44.

entries.name: Prehistory
entries.desc: Prehistory is the period of human history between the first known use of stone tools by hominins c. 3.3 million years ago and the beginning of recorded history with the invention of writing. The earliest known writing systems appeared c. 5,200 years ago, but writing spread gradually, so prehistory ended at different times in different places; the time when a culture is written about by others but has no writing of its own is often called its protohistory. Known only from archaeological and anthropological evidence, prehistory deals with archaeological cultures rather than named nations or individuals. The word first appeared in English in 1836.

entries.name: Francisco Goya
aka: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes
entries.desc: Francisco Goya was a Spanish romantic painter and printmaker, often called the last of the Old Masters and the first of the moderns. Born in Fuendetodos, Aragon, he became a court painter to the Spanish Crown in 1786 and in 1799 Primer Pintor de Cámara, the highest rank for a Spanish court painter. An illness in 1793 left him deaf, and his work grew darker, from the Caprichos and the Disasters of War prints to The Third of May 1808 and the Black Paintings of 1819–1823 on the walls of his house, the Quinta del Sordo. He left Spain in 1824 for Bordeaux, where he died in 1828.

entries.name: Mosque
entries.desc: A mosque, also called a masjid, is a place of worship for Muslims, usually a covered building but possibly any place where Islamic prayers are performed. Early mosques of the first stage of Islamic architecture (650–750 CE) were spaces enclosed by walls, often with minarets from which the call to prayer was issued. A mosque typically has a mihrab, a niche in the wall facing Mecca, a facility for ritual cleansing (wudu) and a minbar for the Friday sermon. Mosques have also served as community centres, courts of law and religious schools; the most important are al-Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, the Prophet's Mosque in Medina and al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem.

entries.name: Stone Age
entries.desc: The Stone Age was a broad prehistoric period during which stone was widely used to make tools with an edge, a point or a percussion surface. It lasted for roughly 3.4 million years, over 99% of human history, and ended between 4000 BCE and 2000 BCE with the melting and smelting of copper; in Western Asia bronze became widespread by about 3000 BCE. It is the first period of the three-age system, followed by the Bronze Age and the Iron Age, and is commonly divided into the Paleolithic, the Mesolithic and the Neolithic, when people began to leave hunting and gathering for settled life in towns and villages as agriculture spread.

entries.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
entries.desc: Carl Friedrich Gauss was a German polymath active as a mathematician, astronomer, geodesist and physicist, director of the Göttingen Observatory and professor of astronomy from 1807 until his death in 1855. A child prodigy, he proved at 19 the construction of the heptadecagon and wrote the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae and Theoria motus corporum coelestium. He introduced the normal or Gaussian distribution, the method of least squares and Gaussian curvature, helped identify Ceres, led the geodetic survey of the Kingdom of Hanover from 1820 to 1844, and with Wilhelm Eduard Weber built the first electromagnetic telegraph in 1833.

entries.name: Li Bai
entries.desc: Li Bai, also known by his courtesy name Taibai, was a Chinese poet counted among the most important of the Tang dynasty, whose poetry, with that of his friend Du Fu, is often called the Golden Age of Chinese Poetry. Around 1,000 poems attributed to him survive; some were collected in the Heyue yingling ji, compiled in 753 by Yin Fan, and thirty-four are in Three Hundred Tang Poems. His poems celebrate friendship, nature, solitude and drinking, and his later ones reflect the rebellion of An Lushan, which left most of Northern China devastated by war and famine. Ezra Pound's Cathay (1915) drew 11 of its 19 poems from him.

entries.name: Church building
entries.desc: A church, church building or church house is a building used for Christian worship services and other Christian religious activities. The earliest archaeologically identified Christian church is a house church at Dura-Europos, founded between 233 and 256 CE; purpose-built halls for worship began to be built in the second half of the third century, and larger churches appeared under Emperor Constantine the Great. In traditional Christian architecture the plan often forms a cross, with the altar in the chancel and a steeple that often houses church bells. From the 11th to the 14th century a wave of cathedral and parish church building took place in Western Europe.

entries.name: Ancient Greece
entries.desc: Ancient Greece was a civilisation of culturally and linguistically related but independent city-states and regions centred on the northeastern Mediterranean, lasting from the Greek Dark Ages of the 12th–9th centuries BCE to the end of classical antiquity (c. 600 CE). City-states, or poleis, formed in the 8th century BCE, opening the Archaic period and Greek colonisation of the Mediterranean Basin. The Classical period, from the Greco-Persian Wars to the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE, included the Golden Age of Athens and the Peloponnesian War. Alexander's conquests spread Greek culture in the Hellenistic period, which ended c. 30 BCE when Rome annexed Ptolemaic Egypt.

entries.name: Dmitri Mendeleev
entries.desc: Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist known for formulating the periodic law and creating a version of the periodic table of elements, which he presented to the Russian Chemical Society in 1869. Born in Verkhnie Aremzyani near Tobolsk in Siberia, he used the periodic law to correct the accepted properties of some known elements, such as the valence and atomic weight of uranium, and to predict the properties of three elements not yet discovered: germanium, gallium and scandium. He was one of the founders of the Russian Chemical Society in 1868 and also worked on protectionist trade and agriculture. The synthetic element mendelevium is named in his honour.

credit.artist: Original: Unknown author Unknown author Upload: Germansociety2014

entries.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
entries.desc: Frank Lloyd Wright was an American architect, designer, writer and educator who designed more than 1,000 structures over a creative period of 70 years. Raised in rural Wisconsin, he apprenticed in Chicago with Louis Sullivan at Adler & Sullivan, opened his own practice in 1893 and became a pioneer of the Prairie School movement. He called his philosophy of designing in harmony with humanity and the environment organic architecture, exemplified in Fallingwater (1935), and developed the Usonian home within Broadacre City, his vision for urban planning. In 2019 a selection of his work became a World Heritage Site as The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright.

credit.artist: New York World-Telegram and the Sun staff photographer: Al Ravenna

entries.name: Henry Ford
entries.desc: Henry Ford was an American industrialist and engineer who founded the Ford Motor Company in 1903 and is credited with making automobiles affordable for middle-class Americans through the system known as Fordism. Born on a farm in Greenfield Township, Michigan, he introduced the Ford Model T in 1908, credited with revolutionising transportation and American industry, and was among the pioneers of the five-day work-week. In the 1920s he promoted antisemitism through his newspaper The Dearborn Independent and the book The International Jew. He turned the company over to his grandson Henry Ford II in 1945 and left most of his wealth to the Ford Foundation.

entries.name: Old Testament
entries.desc: The Old Testament is the first division of the Christian Bible, based primarily upon the 24 books of the Hebrew Bible, or Tanakh, a collection of religious writings in Hebrew and occasionally Aramaic by the Israelites. It differs from the Jewish canon in order, textual tradition and, in some traditions, contents: the Catholic canon has 46 books, the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox Churches up to 49 and the Protestant Bible typically 39. Christians traditionally divide it into the Pentateuch, the Historical books, the Poetic Books and the Prophetic books. Books in the Christian Old Testament but not in the Hebrew canon, mostly from the Septuagint, are called deuterocanonical.

entries.name: Edgar Allan Poe
entries.desc: Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer, poet, editor and literary critic, known for his poetry and for short stories of mystery and the macabre. Born in Boston to the actors David and Eliza Poe, he was taken in by John and Frances Allan of Richmond, Virginia, after his mother's death. He published Tamerlane and Other Poems in 1827, worked for literary journals in Baltimore, Philadelphia and New York City, and in 1845 published "The Raven". One of the pioneers of detective fiction, he was the first well-known American writer to earn a living exclusively through writing. He died in Baltimore in 1849 of a cause that remains unknown.

credit.artist: Unknown author Unknown author ; Restored by Yann Forget and Adam Cuerden

entries.name: Ernest Hemingway
entries.desc: Ernest Miller Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer and journalist whose economical, understated style influenced later 20th-century writers. Raised in Oak Park, Illinois, he drove an ambulance for the Red Cross on the Italian Front in World War I and was seriously wounded in 1918. In Paris from 1921 he wrote for the Toronto Star, and he published The Sun Also Rises (1926), A Farewell to Arms (1929) and For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940), drawn from the Spanish Civil War. The Old Man and the Sea (1952) won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, and he received the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature. He died by suicide in Ketchum, Idaho, in 1961.

entries.name: September 11 attacks
entries.desc: The September 11 attacks were a coordinated series of suicide attacks carried out by al-Qaeda against the United States in 2001. A total of 19 hijackers seized four commercial airliners: two were flown into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York City, which both collapsed, a third into the Pentagon in Arlington County, Virginia, and the fourth, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, during a passenger revolt. The attacks killed 2,977 people. The United States responded by invading Afghanistan and launching its Global War on Terror, and NATO invoked Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty for the only time.

entries.name: Max Planck
entries.desc: Max Karl Ernst Ludwig Planck was a German theoretical physicist, the originator of quantum theory and one of the founders of modern physics. Born in Kiel, he studied in Berlin under Hermann von Helmholtz and Gustav Kirchhoff and in 1889 succeeded Kirchhoff at the Friedrich Wilhelm University of Berlin. On 14 December 1900 he presented a derivation resting on the supposition that electromagnetic energy could be emitted only as a multiple of an elementary unit, the origin of the Planck constant, h. He received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics and was twice President of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society, renamed the Max Planck Society in 1948.

entries.name: Marcel Proust
entries.desc: Marcel Proust was a French novelist, literary critic and essayist, author of À la recherche du temps perdu (In Search of Lost Time), published in seven volumes between 1913 and 1927 and totalling around 1.25 million words. Born in the Auteuil quarter of Paris to a wealthy bourgeois family, he suffered severe asthma from a young age and moved in the salons of Parisian high society, which gave material for the novel. He began it in 1908; the later volumes were revised and published after his death by his brother Robert. The work helped pioneer the stream of consciousness technique. He died of pneumonia in 1922, aged 51.

entries.name: Ernest Rutherford
entries.desc: Ernest Rutherford was a New Zealand physicist and chemist who did pioneering research in atomic and nuclear physics. Born in Spring Grove (now Brightwater), he named alpha and beta radiation, discovered radon and the concept of radioactive half-life, and received the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In 1911, from the gold foil experiment of Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, he proposed that an atom's charge is concentrated in a very small nucleus, and in 1917 he performed the first artificially induced nuclear reaction, which led to the discovery of the proton. From 1919 he directed the Cavendish Laboratory, and in 1937 he was buried in Westminster Abbey.

credit.artist: Bain News Service, publisher Restored by: Bammesk

entries.name: Igor Stravinsky
entries.desc: Igor Fyodorovich Stravinsky was a Russian composer and conductor, a French citizen from 1934 and an American one from 1945, and a central figure in modernist music. Born in Oranienbaum near Saint Petersburg, he studied under Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov until 1908. For Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes he wrote The Firebird (1910), Petrushka (1911) and The Rite of Spring (1913), whose premiere caused a near-riot. His career is divided into a Russian period, a neoclassical period (1920–1951) and a serial period (1954–1968), in which he took up Arnold Schoenberg's twelve-tone technique. He died in New York City in 1971.

entries.name: Erwin Schrödinger
entries.desc: Erwin Schrödinger was an Austrian theoretical physicist who devised the Schrödinger equation, which gives a way to calculate the wave function of a system and how it changes in time. Born in Vienna, he studied at the University of Vienna and served as an artillery officer from 1914 to 1918. He shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac and coined the term "quantum entanglement" in 1935. After the Nazi takeover of Austria he fled Graz in 1938 and settled in Dublin, where he remained until 1955. He returned to Vienna in 1956 and died of tuberculosis in 1961. In 1989 allegations of sexual abuse of several minors emerged.

entries.name: Wilhelm Röntgen
entries.desc: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German experimental physicist who produced and detected the radiation known as X-rays. Born in Lennep in the Rhine Province of Prussia, he studied in Zurich and held the chair of physics at the University of Giessen and, from 1888, at the University of Würzburg. In his laboratory at Würzburg, on 8 November 1895, he noticed a screen painted with barium platinocyanide shimmering near a covered Crookes–Hittorf tube, and in the following weeks studied the new rays, taking a radiograph of his wife Anna Bertha's hand. His paper appeared on 28 December 1895, and in 1901 he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics. He died in Munich in 1923.

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.desc: Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher and Catholic writer. Born in Clermont-Ferrand and taught by his father Étienne Pascal, he wrote a treatise on conic sections at the age of 16 and from 1642 worked on calculating machines, later called Pascalines. He clarified the concepts of pressure and vacuum, generalising the work of Evangelista Torricelli, and his correspondence with Pierre de Fermat in 1654 gave rise to the mathematical theory of probability. After a religious experience in late 1654 he wrote the Lettres provinciales, on the conflict between Jansenists and Jesuits, and the Pensées, which contains Pascal's wager. He died in Paris in 1662, aged 39.

credit.artist: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691 [réf. nécessaire] .

entries.name: Astrology
entries.desc: Astrology is a range of divinatory practices which propose that information about human affairs and events on earth can be discerned from the apparent positions of celestial objects; it has been recognised as pseudoscientific since the 18th century. Forms of it have been practised since at least the 2nd millennium BCE, and the Hindus, Chinese and the Maya developed elaborate systems. Western astrology traces its roots to Mesopotamia of the 19th–17th century BCE, from where it spread to Ancient Greece, Rome, the Islamic world and Europe. Before the Enlightenment it was a scholarly tradition close to astronomy, medicine and alchemy; it then lost that standing.

entries.name: Yoga
entries.desc: Yoga is a group of physical, mental and spiritual practices that originated in ancient India, aimed at controlling body and mind to attain liberation (moksha), as practised in the Hindu, Jain and Buddhist traditions. It may have pre-Vedic origins but is first attested in the early first millennium BCE, and systematic yoga concepts emerged in the fifth and sixth centuries BCE in the ascetic and Śramaṇa movements. The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, the classical text on Hindu yoga, date to the early centuries of the Common Era, and hatha yoga texts appeared between the ninth and 11th centuries. Modern forms, largely made up of asanas, spread worldwide after Swami Vivekananda's adaptation.

entries.name: David Hilbert
entries.desc: David Hilbert was a German mathematician and philosopher of mathematics. Born in or near Königsberg in the Province of Prussia, he studied and taught at the University of Königsberg and in 1895, through the intervention of Felix Klein, became Professor of Mathematics at the University of Göttingen, which became the leading institution in the mathematical world. He worked on invariant theory, algebraic number theory, the foundations of geometry, integral equations and the foundations of mathematics, and was a co-founder of proof theory and mathematical logic. He defended Georg Cantor's set theory, and in 1900 he presented a collection of problems that set a course for 20th-century research.

entries.name: Oscar Wilde
entries.desc: Oscar Wilde was an Irish author, poet and playwright and a key figure of the Aestheticism movement of the late 19th century. Born to Anglo-Irish intellectuals in Dublin, he studied at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford. He wrote his only novel, The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890), and four society comedies, among them The Importance of Being Earnest (1895). His libel suit against the Marquess of Queensberry, father of his lover Lord Alfred Douglas, led to his own conviction for gross indecency and two years' hard labour, served from 1895 to 1897. On his release he left for France, wrote The Ballad of Reading Gaol (1898) and died in Paris in 1900.

entries.name: James K. Polk
entries.desc: James Knox Polk was the 11th president of the United States, serving from 1845 to 1849. Born in Pineville, North Carolina, a protégé of Andrew Jackson and a Democrat, he became Speaker of the House in 1835 and won the 1844 presidential election as a dark-horse candidate, narrowly defeating Henry Clay. In office he saw Texas join the Union, settled the Oregon dispute with Great Britain largely along the 49th parallel and led the country to victory in the Mexican–American War, which brought the cession of the American Southwest. A slaveholder with a plantation in Mississippi, he deepened the divide between free and slave states. He served one term, as pledged, and died of cholera in 1849.

credit.artist: James_Polk.jpg : Brady, Mathew B., 1823 (ca.)-1896, photographer. derivative work: Superwikifan ( talk )

entries.name: Jules Verne
entries.desc: Jules Gabriel Verne was a French novelist, poet and playwright. Born in Nantes, he worked with the publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel on the Voyages extraordinaires, a series of adventure novels including Journey to the Center of the Earth (1864), Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas (1870) and Around the World in Eighty Days (1872), set mostly in the second half of the 19th century and drawing on the science and technology of the time. In the English-speaking world he was long labelled a writer of genre fiction or children's books, largely because of abridged translations. He has been the second most-translated author in the world since 1979.

entries.name: Torah
entries.desc: The Torah is the compilation of the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, also known as the Pentateuch or the Five Books of Moses. Rabbinic tradition holds that its teachings were given by God through the prophet Moses, at Mount Sinai and at the Tabernacle; in rabbinic literature the word also covers the Oral Torah, now embodied in the Talmud and Midrash. Biblical scholarship generally sees its final form as largely complete by the Persian period and based on earlier sources. Written on a scroll by a scribe, it is read publicly in synagogues, and it is also sacred to the Samaritans, in Christianity and in Islam.

entries.name: Rudyard Kipling
entries.desc: Joseph Rudyard Kipling was an English journalist, novelist, poet and short-story writer, born in Bombay in British India, which inspired much of his work. His fiction includes The Jungle Book (1894), Kim (1901), the Just So Stories (1902) and "The Man Who Would Be King" (1888); his poems include "Gunga Din" (1890), "The White Man's Burden" (1899) and "If—" (1910). Among the most popular writers in the United Kingdom of his day, in 1907 he became the first English-language recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature. His reputation has changed with the political climate, and critics such as Douglas Kerr see him as a controversial interpreter of how empire was experienced.

entries.name: Al-Ghazali
aka: Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad Ghazālī Ṭūsi
entries.desc: Al-Ghazali was a Shafi'i Ash'ari Sunni Muslim scholar and polymath, one of the most influential jurists, philosophers, theologians and mystics in Islamic history. Born about 1058 in Tus in Khorasan, he became head of the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, but after a spiritual crisis in 1095 he left Baghdad and spent some ten years away from his post, when many of his major works were written, among them The Revival of the Religious Sciences. His The Incoherence of the Philosophers advanced a critique of Aristotelian science. Sunni Muslims consider him the mujaddid of the 11th century and call him the "Proof of Islam". He returned to teach at Nishapur in 1106 and died in 1111.

entries.name: Florence Nightingale
entries.desc: Florence Nightingale was an English social reformer and statistician, regarded as the founder of modern nursing. Born in Florence, she came to prominence during the Crimean War, arriving at the Selimiye Barracks in Scutari in November 1854 to manage nurses caring for wounded British soldiers, and reduced death rates by improving hygiene. In 1860 she established a nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in London, the first secular nursing school in the world. She wrote Notes on Nursing (1859) and presented her analysis in graphical forms such as the polar area diagram.

entries.name: James Prescott Joule
entries.desc: James Prescott Joule was an English physicist from Salford who studied the nature of heat and discovered its relationship to mechanical work. The son of a wealthy brewer, he managed the family brewery and pursued science as a serious hobby, discovering Joule's first law in 1841. In 1843 he estimated the mechanical equivalent of heat, a direct challenge to the caloric theory, and his work led to the law of conservation of energy and the first law of thermodynamics. With Lord Kelvin he developed an absolute temperature scale. He died at home in Sale, and the SI unit of energy, the joule, is named after him.

entries.name: Synagogue
entries.desc: A synagogue is a place of worship for Jews or Samaritans, used for prayer, study, assembly and the reading of the Torah. It holds a main sanctuary with the Torah ark where the scrolls are kept and a stage called the bema. Its origins are obscure: scholars have dated it to Josiah's reform of 622/1 BCE, to the Babylonian exile after the Temple's destruction in 587/6 BCE, or to Ezra's public reading of the Torah, and Lee I. Levine argues it developed gradually between the 5th and 1st centuries BCE. Jewish law holds that communal worship can be held wherever a minyan of at least 10 adults gathers.

entries.name: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
entries.desc: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres was a French Neoclassical painter born in Montauban who studied in the studio of Jacques-Louis David. He won the Prix de Rome in 1802 and worked in Rome and Florence from 1806 to 1824, supporting himself as a portrait painter while critics in Paris found his style bizarre and archaic. The Vow of Louis XIII brought acclaim at the Salon of 1824, and he later directed the French Academy in Rome from 1835. He finished The Turkish Bath at the age of 83. His portraits are recognised as his chief legacy, and his distortions of form influenced Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso.

entries.name: Adam
entries.desc: Adam is the name given in Genesis 1–5 to the first human, a figure in Judaism, Christianity, Gnosticism, Islam and the Baháʼí Faith. In Genesis 2 God forms Adam out of the dust of the ground, places him in the Garden of Eden and forms a woman, Eve, as his companion; after they eat from the tree of knowledge, God condemns Adam to labour on the earth. According to Christianity, this sin introduced death and sin into the world. In Islam, Adam is considered Khalifa on earth, and the Quran tells that he was forgiven by God when he repented.

entries.name: Ancient history
entries.desc: Ancient history is the period from the beginning of writing and recorded human history through late antiquity, covering all inhabited continents from about 3000 BCE to 500 CE. Recorded history, roughly 5,000 years long, begins with the development of Sumerian cuneiform script. The three-age system divides the past into the Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age, with recorded history usually counted from the Bronze Age, though the ages begin and end at different times in different regions. The world population is estimated to have risen from 45 million in 3000 BCE to 209 million by 500 CE.

entries.name: Paul Cézanne
entries.desc: Paul Cézanne was a French Post-Impressionist painter from Aix-en-Provence whose work formed the bridge between late 19th-century Impressionism and early 20th-century Cubism. The son of a banker, he was a school friend of Émile Zola. Through close study of Impressionist forms he arrived at a new pictorial language, building up complex fields from planes of colour and small brushstrokes and emphasising the underlying structure of objects. His paintings at first met ridicule, until Ambroise Vollard gave him a first solo exhibition in Paris in 1895. He died of pneumonia in Aix on 22 October 1906.

credit.artist: Unknown; Cézanne was born in 1839 and died in 1906

entries.name: George Bernard Shaw
entries.desc: George Bernard Shaw was an Irish playwright, critic, polemicist and political activist, born in Dublin, who moved to London in 1876. He became a theatre and music critic and the most prominent pamphleteer of the Fabian Society, and after his first public success, Arms and the Man in 1894, wrote more than sixty plays, among them Man and Superman, Pygmalion and Saint Joan. He was awarded the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature. His views were often contentious: he promoted eugenics and opposed vaccination, and later expressed admiration for Benito Mussolini and Joseph Stalin.

entries.name: Virginia Woolf
entries.desc: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and modernist author who helped to pioneer stream of consciousness narration. Born in South Kensington, London, the daughter of Leslie Stephen, she moved to Bloomsbury after his death in 1904 and became a founding member of the Bloomsbury Group. She married Leonard Woolf in 1912, and in 1917 they established the Hogarth Press. Her novels include Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927) and Orlando (1928), and her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became central to feminist criticism. On 28 March 1941 she drowned herself in the River Ouse near her home.

entries.name: Joseph Fourier
entries.desc: Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier was a French mathematician and physicist from Auxerre, best known for initiating the study of Fourier series and their use in problems of heat transfer and vibrations. Orphaned at nine, he took part in the French Revolution and was briefly imprisoned during the Terror. He accompanied Napoleon Bonaparte on the Egyptian expedition in 1798 as secretary of the Institut d'Égypte, and in 1801 was appointed Prefect of Isère in Grenoble, where he began his experiments on the propagation of heat. He is also generally credited with the discovery of the greenhouse effect.

entries.name: Du Fu
entries.desc: Du Fu was a Chinese poet and government official of the Tang dynasty who, with his older friend Li Bai, is one of the principal poets of Tang poetry; nearly 1,500 poems attributed to him survive. Born near Luoyang, he failed the Imperial examination around 735 and pursued an official career, briefly serving as a remonstrance official at court. The An Lushan rebellion, which began in 755, displaced him and his family, and he lived in Qinzhou and Chengdu before travelling the middle Yangtze. Later critics called him the Poet-Historian and the Poet-Sage. Accounts differ on the place and cause of his death in 770.

entries.name: Thomas Mann
entries.desc: Paul Thomas Mann was a German novelist, short story writer and essayist, born to a Hanseatic family in Lübeck, who won the 1929 Nobel Prize in Literature. He portrayed his family and class in his first novel, Buddenbrooks (1901), and went on to write Death in Venice (1912), The Magic Mountain (1924), the tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers and Doctor Faustus (1947). When Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933 he fled to Switzerland, and in 1939 he moved to the United States, becoming one of the best-known writers of German literature in exile. He returned to Switzerland in 1952 and died in Zürich in 1955.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.desc: Francis Bacon, 1st Viscount St Alban, was an English philosopher and statesman who served as Attorney General and Lord Chancellor of England under King James I. Educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, he argued for scientific knowledge based on inductive reasoning and careful observation, and has been called the father of empiricism; his Novum Organum appeared in 1620. He was created Baron Verulam in 1618 and Viscount St Alban in 1621, but was impeached on corruption charges, found guilty, briefly imprisoned and barred from public office. He died of pneumonia at Highgate on 9 April 1626.

credit.artist: Paul van Somer I / Formerly attributed to Frans Pourbus the Younger

entries.name: Martin Heidegger
entries.desc: Martin Heidegger was a German philosopher from Meßkirch whose work was central to the development of phenomenology, hermeneutics and existentialism. In Being and Time (1927) he introduced the concept of Dasein to describe human existence and sought to reawaken the question of being, and his later work turned to technology, language, art and poetry. In April 1933 he was elected rector of the University of Freiburg and joined the Nazi Party, remaining a member until 1945. After the war he was banned from teaching, a ban lifted in 1949. His commitment to Nazism remains a subject of scholarly controversy.

entries.name: Antoni Gaudí
entries.desc: Antoni Gaudí i Cornet was a Spanish architect and designer and the principal exponent of Catalan Modernisme, with most of his works in Barcelona. Born in Reus, or possibly Riudoms, the son of a coppersmith, he combined crafts such as ceramics, stained glass, wrought iron and carpentry, introduced trencadís, which used waste ceramic pieces, and worked from three-dimensional models rather than detailed plans. His magnum opus is the still-incomplete Sagrada Família. Struck by a tram in Barcelona, he died on 10 June 1926. Between 1984 and 2005 seven of his works were declared UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

entries.name: Brahmagupta
entries.desc: Brahmagupta was an Indian mathematician and astronomer, born, by his own statement, in 598 CE at Bhillamāla in Gurjaradesa, modern Bhinmal in Rajasthan. An astronomer of the Brahmapaksha school, he composed the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta in 628, a treatise of 24 chapters and 1008 verses covering astronomy, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, and later moved to Ujjaini, where he wrote the practical manual Khandakhadyaka in 665. He is credited as the first to formalise the concept of zero in mathematics and with the first clear description of the quadratic formula. He is presumed to have died in Ujjain in 668.

entries.name: Alexandre Dumas
entries.desc: Alexandre Dumas, also known as Alexandre Dumas père, was a French novelist and playwright born in Villers-Cotterêts. His father, General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, was born in Saint-Domingue to a French nobleman and Marie-Cessette Dumas, an enslaved woman. Dumas began his career writing plays and became one of the most widely read French authors with historical novels of adventure first published as serials, including The Count of Monte Cristo and The Three Musketeers. In the 1840s he founded the Théâtre Historique in Paris. He died on 5 December 1870 and was buried at his birthplace.

entries.name: T. S. Eliot
entries.desc: Thomas Stearns Eliot was a poet, essayist and playwright, a leading figure of modernist poetry in the English language. Born in St. Louis, Missouri, to a Boston Brahmin family, he studied at Harvard and moved to the United Kingdom in 1914, becoming a British subject in 1927 and converting to Anglicanism. He drew attention with The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock (1915), followed by The Waste Land (1922) and Four Quartets (1943), and wrote seven plays, including Murder in the Cathedral (1935). He was awarded the 1948 Nobel Prize in Literature and died of emphysema in Kensington in 1965.

credit.artist: Thomas Stearns Eliot with his sister and his cousin by Lady Ottoline Morrell.jpg : Lady Ottoline Morrell (1873–1938) derivative work: Octave

entries.name: Selma Lagerlöf
entries.desc: Selma Ottilia Lovisa Lagerlöf was a Swedish writer, born at Mårbacka in Värmland, who was the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, awarded in 1909. She trained in Stockholm and worked as a schoolteacher in Landskrona from 1885 to 1895, where she began her first novel, Gösta Berling's Saga, published when she was 33. Asked by the National Teachers' Association to write a geography book for children, she wrote The Wonderful Adventures of Nils. In 1914 she became the first woman granted membership of the Swedish Academy, and she bought back the family estate of Mårbacka with her prize money.

entries.name: Émile Zola
entries.desc: Émile Édouard Charles Antoine Zola was a French novelist, journalist and playwright, the best-known practitioner of the literary school of naturalism. Born in Paris and raised in Aix-en-Provence, where Paul Cézanne was his childhood friend, he worked as a clerk and for the publisher Hachette before his novel Thérèse Raquin (1867). More than half of his novels belong to the twenty-volume Les Rougon-Macquart cycle, the history of one family under Napoléon III. His newspaper opinion J'Accuse...! helped exonerate the falsely convicted officer Alfred Dreyfus. He died of carbon monoxide poisoning in 1902.

entries.name: Robert Koch
entries.desc: Robert Koch was a German physician and microbiologist who is regarded as one of the main founders of modern bacteriology. As a private physician he identified the anthrax bacterium in 1876; he announced the tuberculosis bacterium on 24 March 1882 and isolated the cholera bacterium in Calcutta in 1884. His culture method using agar and glass plates, later developed into the Petri dish by his assistant Julius Richard Petri, and the principles known as Koch's postulates gave the germ theory of disease its proofs. His tuberculin, announced as a cure in 1890, proved ineffective and damaged his standing. He won the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine and died in Baden-Baden in 1910.

entries.name: Alexander Fleming
entries.desc: Sir Alexander Fleming was a Scottish physician and microbiologist, born at Lochfield farm near Darvel in Ayrshire, who spent his career at St Mary's Hospital in London. Serving in the Royal Army Medical Corps in World War I, he showed that antiseptics often worsened deep wounds, and in 1922 he discovered the enzyme lysozyme. In 1928 he found that the mould Penicillium rubens produced a substance later named benzylpenicillin, the first antibiotic substance discovered. He was knighted in 1944 and shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain. He died of a heart attack at his home in London in 1955, and his ashes are buried in St Paul's Cathedral.

entries.name: H. G. Wells
entries.desc: Herbert George Wells was an English writer, born in Bromley, who wrote more than forty novels and dozens of short stories besides works of social commentary and history. A student of biology under Thomas Henry Huxley, he made his name with science fiction: The Time Machine (1895), The Island of Doctor Moreau (1896), The Invisible Man (1897) and The War of the Worlds (1898) imagined time travel, alien invasion and invisibility before these were common in the genre. Novels such as Kipps (1905) and Tono-Bungay (1909) described English society. An outspoken socialist, he was for much of his adult life an advocate of eugenics, a view he had largely recanted by 1940. He died in London in 1946.

entries.name: Maxim Gorky
entries.desc: Maxim Gorky, born Alexei Maximovich Peshkov in Nizhny Novgorod, was a Russian and Soviet writer and journalist who took his pen name, meaning bitter, in 1892. An orphan at eleven, he later travelled across the Russian Empire; his stories of people on the margins of society, the play The Lower Depths (1902) and the novel Mother (1906) made his name. He supported the Bolsheviks but condemned their political repressions after the October Revolution and lived long in exile. He returned to the USSR on Joseph Stalin's invitation in 1928, was declared the founder of Socialist Realism. He died in 1936, officially of pneumonia; several historians hold that he was poisoned on Stalin's orders.

entries.name: Pierre Curie
entries.desc: Pierre Curie was a French physicist and chemist, born in Paris, who was a pioneer in crystallography, magnetism and radioactivity. In 1880 he and his older brother Jacques demonstrated piezoelectricity, and his doctoral work on magnetism gave his name to Curie's law and the Curie temperature. With his wife, Maria Skłodowska-Curie, he worked to isolate polonium and radium, and the couple were the first to use the term radioactivity; they shared one half of the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics, the first married couple to win a Nobel Prize. In 1906 he slipped while crossing the Rue Dauphine in Paris and was killed under a horse-drawn cart.

entries.name: Neanderthal
entries.desc: Neanderthals are an extinct group of archaic humans who inhabited Europe and Western and Central Asia during the Middle to Late Pleistocene. They had a long and low skull, a heavy brow ridge, strong teeth and jaws, a wide chest and short limbs. They made Mousterian stone tools, maintained fire, hunted big game and buried their dead. The first recognised fossil, Neanderthal 1, was found in the Neander Valley in Germany in 1856. They are generally considered to have died out in Asia and most of Europe by 40,000 years ago, perhaps because early modern humans came to Europe, and the sequencing of their genome in 2010 showed that they interbred with modern humans.

entries.name: Trinity
entries.desc: The Trinity is the Christian doctrine that one God exists in three divine persons, God the Father, God the Son (Jesus Christ) and God the Holy Spirit, held to be coeternal and to share one essence. Early Christians and the fathers of the Church developed it from the late 2nd century onwards, and the First Council of Nicaea and the First Council of Constantinople in the 4th century established it as part of the creed. Most major Christian denominations today are Trinitarian. Those who reject the doctrine are called nontrinitarians, and their positions include Unitarianism, binitarianism and modalism; many Trinitarians regard them as heretical.

entries.name: Aphrodite
entries.desc: Aphrodite is the ancient Greek goddess associated with love and beauty, whose main cult centres were Cythera, Cyprus, Corinth and Athens. In Homer's Iliad she is the daughter of Zeus and Dione, while in Hesiod's Theogony she is born from the sea foam produced by the severed genitals of Uranus. In the Odyssey she is married to Hephaestus and takes Ares as her lover, and with Athena and Hera she was one of the three goddesses whose feud led to the Trojan War. Her origins are debated: proposed influences include Near Eastern love goddesses, an indigenous Cypriot goddess and a Proto-Indo-European dawn goddess. The Romans identified her with their goddess Venus.

credit.artist: Copy of Praxiteles; restorer: Ippolito Buzzi (Italian, 1562–1634)

entries.name: Castle
entries.desc: A castle is a type of fortified structure built during the Middle Ages and usually regarded by scholars as the private fortified residence of a lord or noble. European-style castles arose in the 9th and 10th centuries after the fall of the Carolingian Empire, when lords built them to control the land around them; they were also centres of administration and symbols of power. Many were first built of earth and timber and later given stone defences, and from the late 12th century towers and concentric defences spread. Once artillery could break stone walls in the 15th century, castles declined and gave way to star forts and country houses. The word comes from the Latin castellum.

entries.name: Honoré de Balzac
entries.desc: Honoré de Balzac was a French novelist and playwright who is regarded as one of the founders of realism in European literature. He had his first success under his own name with Les Chouans (1829). In 1832 he conceived a series of books portraying all aspects of society, which became La Comédie humaine, a panorama of post-Napoleonic French life that includes Le Père Goriot (1835); it was unfinished at his death. His complex characters and his portrayal of Paris influenced writers such as Émile Zola, Charles Dickens, Marcel Proust and Fyodor Dostoevsky. He married Ewelina Hańska in Berdychiv in March 1850 and died five months later.

entries.name: Helen Keller
entries.desc: Helen Keller was an American deafblind author, disability rights advocate and political activist, born in Tuscumbia, Alabama. An illness at 19 months old left her blind and deaf, and from the age of seven she was taught language, including reading and writing, by Anne Sullivan, her lifelong companion. She attended Radcliffe College and became the first deafblind person in the United States to earn a college diploma. She wrote 14 books, among them The Story of My Life (1903), and campaigned for people with disabilities and for women's suffrage, labor rights and world peace. She joined the Socialist Party of America in 1909 and was a founding member of the American Civil Liberties Union.

entries.name: Ada Lovelace
aka: Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace
entries.desc: Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician and writer known for her work on Charles Babbage's proposed mechanical general-purpose computer, the analytical engine. The only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron and Anne Isabella Milbanke, she met Babbage in 1833. She translated an article on the engine by Luigi Menabrea and added seven long notes, one of which described a method of calculating Bernoulli numbers that is often called the first published computer program. She was the first to point out that such a machine could encode more than numbers, such as music. She died of cervical cancer in 1852, aged 36.

entries.name: Paleolithic
entries.desc: The Paleolithic, or Old Stone Age, is the period of human prehistory marked by the first development of stone tools, extending from their earliest known use by hominins about 3.3 million years ago to the end of the Pleistocene about 11,650 years before the present. People lived in small bands and subsisted by gathering plants, fishing, and hunting or scavenging wild animals, using knapped stone tools. From about 50,000 years ago artifacts became more varied and the first art appeared, and humans reached Australia, Japan, Siberia and finally the Americas. The term was coined by John Lubbock in 1865.

entries.name: Giordano Bruno
entries.desc: Giordano Bruno, born Filippo Bruno in Nola in the Kingdom of Naples, was an Italian philosopher, Dominican friar and priest, poet and cosmological theorist. He entered the Dominican Order in Naples at 17. He took up the Copernican model and argued that the universe is infinite and has no centre, and that the stars are distant suns with planets of their own that might foster life. Tried for heresy by the Roman Inquisition for denying Catholic doctrines including the Trinity and transubstantiation, he was burned at the stake in Rome's Campo de' Fiori in 1600. Later commentators regarded him as a martyr for science, though historians disagree whether his cosmology caused his trial.

entries.name: Arab–Israeli conflict
entries.desc: The Arab–Israeli conflict is the conflict between Israel and the surrounding Arab countries that has existed since the declaration of Israel's establishment in 1948. It grew from the clash between Zionism, which sought a Jewish state in Palestine, and Arabs who saw Palestine as Arab land; Britain ruled Mandatory Palestine from 1920. After the United Nations adopted the Partition Plan for Palestine in 1947, civil war turned into the 1948 Palestine war, which ended with the 1949 Armistice Agreements; further wars followed in 1956, 1967, 1973 and 1982. Egypt signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1979 and Jordan in 1994, and the Abraham Accords of 2020 calmed relations further.

entries.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
entries.desc: Arthur Schopenhauer was a German philosopher and writer, born in Danzig, known for The World as Will and Representation (1818, expanded in 1844), which describes the world of appearances as the manifestation of a blind and irrational will. Building on the transcendental idealism of Immanuel Kant, he developed an atheistic, metaphysical and ethical system that rejected the German idealism of his day, and he was among the first Western philosophers to affirm tenets of Indian philosophy such as asceticism and denial of the self. His work drew little attention during his lifetime. He settled in Frankfurt in 1833 and lived there until his death in 1860.

entries.name: Pentecost
entries.desc: Pentecost is a Christian holiday held on the 49th day after Easter (the 50th by inclusive counting), commemorating the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles and other followers of Jesus in Jerusalem during the Feast of Weeks, as described in the Acts of the Apostles. Its name comes from the Koine Greek pentēkostē, fiftieth, a word the Septuagint used for Shavuot, the Jewish harvest festival held on the fiftieth day after Passover. It is called the birthday of the Church. As its date depends on Easter it is a moveable feast; it is one of the Great feasts of the Eastern Orthodox Church and a Solemnity of the Catholic Church, and the Monday after it is a legal holiday in many countries.

entries.name: Trimurti
