entries.desc: The Trimurti is the triple deity of supreme divinity in Hinduism, in which the cosmic functions of creation, preservation and destruction are personified as three gods, typically Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer. R. C. Majumdar saw the idea as the chief expression of the harmony between orthodox and sectarian forms in the Puranic period (4th–12th centuries CE). The Vishnu Purana and the Kūrma Purāṇa present the three as one being. Brahma never gained an ascendancy like that of Shiva or Vishnu, and the sects often took the three as forms of their own god. The Tridevi are their goddess consorts.

entries.name: Lewis Carroll
entries.desc: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, an English author, poet, mathematician, photographer and Anglican deacon, born at Daresbury in Cheshire. He studied at Christ Church, Oxford, where he lived for most of his life. His Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) and its sequel Through the Looking-Glass (1871) are among the most important works of Victorian literature, and his poems Jabberwocky and The Hunting of the Snark (1876) belong to literary nonsense. Alice Liddell, a daughter of Henry Liddell, the Dean of Christ Church, is widely identified as the inspiration for Alice, though Carroll always denied it. He died of pneumonia in Guildford in 1898.

entries.name: Antoine Lavoisier
entries.desc: Antoine Lavoisier was a French nobleman and chemist central to the 18th-century chemical revolution and made chemistry quantitative. He showed the role of oxygen in combustion against the phlogiston theory, named oxygen in 1778 and recognised hydrogen as an element in 1783, and his precise measurements confirmed the conservation of mass. He wrote the first extensive list of elements, helped reform chemical nomenclature and construct the metric system with his wife Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier and set out his chemistry in the Traité élémentaire de chimie (1789). An administrator of the Ferme générale, he was charged with tax fraud during the French Revolution and guillotined in 1794.

entries.name: Carl Benz
entries.desc: Carl Benz was a German engine designer and automotive engineer whose Benz Patent-Motorwagen of 1885 is considered the first practical, modern automobile. Born in Mühlburg, now part of Karlsruhe, he studied at Karlsruhe's polytechnical school and founded workshops in Mannheim, where he patented a two-stroke engine in 1880. He received a patent for the motorcar in 1886 and began selling it in 1888, the year his wife Bertha Benz drove one 104 km from Mannheim to Pforzheim. His firm Benz & Cie. merged with Daimler Motoren Gesellschaft in 1926 to form Daimler-Benz. He died at Ladenburg in 1929.

entries.name: Armenian genocide
entries.desc: The Armenian genocide was the systematic destruction of the Armenian people and identity in the Ottoman Empire during World War I, led by the ruling Committee of Union and Progress (CUP). On 24 April 1915 the authorities arrested and deported hundreds of Armenian intellectuals and leaders from Constantinople; at the orders of Talaat Pasha an estimated 800,000 to 1.2 million Armenians were then sent on death marches to the Syrian desert, where they were robbed, raped and massacred. Around one million were killed, and 100,000 to 200,000 women and children were forcibly converted to Islam. The Turkish government denies that the deportations were genocide.

entries.name: Nikolai Gogol
entries.desc: Nikolai Gogol was a Russian novelist, short-story writer and playwright of Ukrainian origin, born in Sorochyntsi in the Poltava Governorate. His early stories, Evenings on a Farm Near Dikanka (1831–1832), drew on Ukrainian folklore, while The Government Inspector and Dead Souls satirised corruption in Russia. He used the grotesque in stories such as "The Nose" and "The Overcoat", and from 1836 to 1848 lived mostly abroad, above all in Rome. Deeply depressed, he burned most of the second part of Dead Souls on the night of 24 February 1852 and died nine days later.

entries.name: Federico García Lorca
entries.desc: Federico García Lorca was a Spanish poet, playwright and theatre director, born at Fuente Vaqueros near Granada, and a member of the Generation of '27. He rose to fame with the poems of Romancero gitano (Gypsy Ballads, 1928), which drew on Andalusian life, and after a stay in New York City from 1929 to 1930 wrote his best-known plays, Blood Wedding (1932), Yerma (1934) and The House of Bernarda Alba (1936). At the start of the Spanish Civil War he was arrested in Granada and killed by Nationalist forces in August 1936. His remains have never been found, and the motive is still disputed.

entries.name: Nagarjuna
entries.desc: Nāgārjuna was a philosopher and Mahāyāna Buddhist monk from South India, considered the founder of the Madhyamaka (Middle Way) school. Very little is reliably known of his life: most scholars place him in South India between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE, and an association with the Sātavāhana dynasty conventionally dates him to around 150–250 CE. His Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (Root Verses on Madhyamaka) argues that all things are empty of svabhāva, or inherent existence, joining emptiness to dependent origination. Tibetan Buddhism calls him the "second Buddha", and his writings shaped Indian, East Asian and Tibetan Buddhist thought.

entries.name: Eve
entries.desc: Eve is a figure of the Book of Genesis who, according to the origin story of the Abrahamic religions, was the first woman created by God and the wife of Adam. Her Hebrew name, Ḥawwāh, is most commonly taken to mean "living one" or "source of life". In the second chapter of Genesis she is made from Adam's rib; after a serpent persuades her, she and Adam eat the forbidden fruit and are expelled from the Garden of Eden. Genesis names her sons Cain, Abel and Seth. Some Christian writers, among them Tertullian, blamed women through her, and Christian art most often shows her as the temptress of Adam.

entries.name: Noah
entries.desc: Noah appears as the last of the Antediluvian patriarchs in the traditions of the Abrahamic religions, in the Book of Genesis (chapters 5–9), the Quran and Baha'i writings. In the Genesis flood narrative God decides to destroy the world by flood because of humanity's evil, and Noah builds the Ark, saving his family and the land animals; afterwards God makes a covenant with him, marked by the rainbow, never again to flood the earth. Genesis presents him as the first to cultivate the vine and says he died at the age of 950. Most scholars hold that the account drew on earlier Mesopotamian flood traditions such as the Epic of Gilgamesh.

entries.name: Arthur Rimbaud
entries.desc: Arthur Rimbaud was a French poet, born in Charleville, whose transgressive and surreal themes prefigured surrealism and who contributed to symbolism. He ran away to Paris during the Franco-Prussian War, had a violent relationship of nearly two years with the poet Paul Verlaine, and wrote almost all his work in his late teens, including A Season in Hell and Illuminations; he stopped writing at about 20. He then worked as a merchant and explorer, from 1880 in Aden and Harar, trading in coffee and firearms. Cancer cost him his right leg in 1891, and he died in Marseille that November, aged 37.

entries.name: Charles Baudelaire
entries.desc: Charles Baudelaire was a French poet, essayist, translator and art critic, born in Paris. His collection Les Fleurs du mal (The Flowers of Evil), published in 1857, dealt with sex, death and the changing city; he, his publisher and the printer were prosecuted for an offence against public morals, six poems were suppressed, and the judgment was reversed only in 1949. He translated stories by Edgar Allan Poe, coined the term modernité for the fleeting experience of urban life, and influenced Paul Verlaine, Arthur Rimbaud and Stéphane Mallarmé. After a stroke in Brussels in 1866 he was left paralysed and died in Paris in 1867.

entries.name: C. V. Raman
entries.desc: Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman was an Indian physicist, born in Tiruchirappalli, known for his work on the scattering of light. While working as an accountant in the Indian Finance Service in Calcutta, he did research at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science, and in 1917 became the first Palit Professor of Physics. On 28 February 1928 he and his student K. S. Krishnan discovered that light passing through a transparent material changes its wavelength, the Raman effect, which won him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930. He became the first Indian director of the Indian Institute of Science in 1933 and later founded the Raman Research Institute.

entries.name: J. J. Thomson
entries.desc: Sir Joseph John Thomson was a British physicist, born at Cheetham Hill in Manchester, who in 1897 showed that cathode rays were made of previously unknown negatively charged particles, now called electrons: the first subatomic particle to be discovered. Appointed Cavendish Professor of Physics at Cambridge in 1884, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906 for his work on the conduction of electricity by gases. In 1912 he found the first evidence for isotopes of a stable element, work with Francis William Aston that led to the mass spectrograph. Seven of his students won Nobel Prizes, and he was Master of Trinity College from 1918 until his death in 1940.

entries.name: Alessandro Volta
entries.desc: Alessandro Volta was an Italian chemist and physicist from Como, credited as the inventor of the electric battery and the discoverer of methane, which he found in the marshes of Angera on Lake Maggiore in 1776. He invented the voltaic pile in 1799 and reported it in a letter to the president of the Royal Society, published in 1800, showing that electricity could be generated chemically; the invention led to the field of electrochemistry. He held the chair of experimental physics at the University of Pavia for almost 40 years and was honoured by Napoleon. The SI unit of electric potential, the volt, is named after him.

entries.name: Existentialism
entries.desc: Existentialism is a family of philosophical views that explore the individual's struggle to lead an authentic life despite the apparent absurdity of existence, stressing personal freedom, responsibility and choice. Its 19th-century forerunners include Søren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche and Fyodor Dostoevsky, who criticised rationalism. The term was coined by Gabriel Marcel in the mid-1940s, and Jean-Paul Sartre adopted it in a lecture in Paris in 1945, published as Existentialism Is a Humanism. The label is most associated with Sartre, Martin Heidegger, Simone de Beauvoir, Karl Jaspers and, more controversially, Albert Camus, and it influenced theology, drama, literature and psychology.

entries.name: Kahlil Gibran
entries.desc: Kahlil Gibran was a Lebanese-American writer, poet and visual artist, born in Bsharri in the Ottoman-ruled Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate to a Maronite Christian family. He emigrated with his mother and siblings to Boston in 1895, studied art in Paris from 1908 to 1910 with the help of Mary Haskell, and settled in New York in 1911. Some of his writings were banned by the Ottoman authorities for their anti-clericalism and calls for rebellion. His book The Prophet, first published in 1923, has been translated into more than 100 languages. He re-founded the Pen League with fellow Mahjari poets in 1920 and died at 48; his body was taken to Bsharri.

entries.name: Knut Hamsun
entries.desc: Knut Hamsun was a Norwegian writer, born Knud Pedersen in Lom Municipality, who received the 1920 Nobel Prize in Literature for his novel Growth of the Soil. Novels such as Hunger (1890), Mysteries (1892) and Pan (1894) pioneered a psychological literature of stream of consciousness and interior monologue that influenced Thomas Mann, Franz Kafka and Ernest Hemingway. He openly supported Adolf Hitler and Nazi Germany, gave his Nobel Prize medal to Joseph Goebbels and backed the Quisling regime. Charged with treason after the war, he was not convicted but was heavily fined in 1948. He died at Grimstad in 1952, aged 92.

entries.name: Claude Debussy
entries.desc: Claude Debussy was a French composer, born in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, who is sometimes seen as the first Impressionist composer, a term he rejected. Admitted to the Conservatoire de Paris at ten, he reached international fame in 1902 with Pelléas et Mélisande, the only opera he completed. His orchestral works include Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune (1894), Nocturnes and La mer (1903–1905), and his piano works 24 Préludes and 12 Études. Influenced by the Symbolist poets and by Russian and Far Eastern music, he reacted against Wagner and the German tradition. He died of cancer at his home in Paris in 1918, aged 55.

entries.name: André-Marie Ampère
entries.desc: André-Marie Ampère was a French physicist and mathematician, born in Lyon, and one of the founders of classical electromagnetism, which he called electrodynamics. He educated himself in his father's library, lost his father to the guillotine in 1793 during the Jacobin purges and later taught at the École polytechnique and the Collège de France. After Hans Christian Ørsted's discovery that an electric current deflects a magnetic needle was shown in Paris in September 1820, Ampère showed that two parallel wires carrying currents attract or repel each other. He coined the term solenoid, and the SI unit of electric current, the ampere, is named after him.

entries.name: John Milton
entries.desc: John Milton was an English poet, polemicist and civil servant, born in Bread Street, London, and educated at Christ's College, Cambridge. His Areopagitica (1644) argued against pre-publication censorship, and after the Civil War he defended the regicide in The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates and Eikonoklastes (1649) while serving the Commonwealth's Council of State as Secretary for Foreign Tongues. By 1652 he was totally blind and dictated his work to amanuenses, among them Andrew Marvell. His epic Paradise Lost (1667), in blank verse, tells of the fall of man. After the Restoration of 1660 he lost his public platform, and he died impoverished in 1674.

entries.name: Theodor Mommsen
entries.desc: Theodor Mommsen was a German classical scholar, historian, jurist and politician, born in Garding in the Duchy of Schleswig, then part of Denmark. After studying Roman law at Kiel, he taught at Leipzig, Zurich and Breslau and from 1861 was professor of Roman History at the University of Berlin. He planned and led the Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum, a collection of all known Latin inscriptions checked against the originals, and pioneered the study of epigraphy. His Römische Geschichte (History of Rome) won him the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1902, and he sat in the Prussian and German parliaments. He published over 1,500 works.

entries.name: Henri Becquerel
entries.desc: Antoine Henri Becquerel was a French experimental physicist, born in Paris into a family of physicists, who discovered radioactivity. While investigating phosphorescence after Wilhelm Röntgen's discovery of X-rays, he found in early 1896 that uranium salts left in a dark cabinet still exposed photographic plates, and by May he concluded that the radiation came from the uranium itself. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Marie and Pierre Curie, and also identified beta particles as high-speed electrons. He died at Le Croisic in 1908, aged 55, with serious burns on his skin reported, likely from radioactive materials. The SI unit of radioactivity is named after him.

entries.name: Walt Whitman
entries.desc: Walt Whitman was an American poet, essayist and journalist, often called the father of free verse. Born in West Hills, New York, on Long Island, he left formal schooling at 11 and worked as a printer, journalist, teacher and government clerk. In 1855 he published Leaves of Grass at his own expense; some called its open sensuality obscene, and he kept expanding and revising it until his death. During the American Civil War he cared for the wounded in the hospitals of Washington, D.C., and after the assassination of Abraham Lincoln he wrote poems including "O Captain! My Captain!". After a stroke in 1873 he moved to Camden, New Jersey, where he died in 1892.

entries.name: Ivan Pavlov
entries.desc: Ivan Petrovich Pavlov was a Russian and Soviet experimental neurologist and physiologist, known for the discovery of classical conditioning through experiments with dogs. Born in Ryazan to a village Russian Orthodox priest, he attended the local theological seminary before turning to science. In 1891 he was invited to organise and direct the Department of Physiology at the Institute of Experimental Medicine in St. Petersburg, where he studied the digestive glands, work for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1904. With his assistant Ivan Tolochinov he developed in 1901 the concept of the conditioned reflex, which he called the conditional reflex.

entries.name: Francis of Assisi
entries.desc: Francis of Assisi, born Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone, was an Italian mystic, poet and Catholic friar who founded the Franciscans. The son of a wealthy family of Assisi, he turned as a young man to poverty and devotion, repairing chapels and caring for the sick, and after a journey to Rome to meet Pope Innocent III he received approval for the Order of Friars Minor. In 1219 he travelled to Egypt in an attempt to convert the sultan Al-Kamil and end the conflict of the Fifth Crusade, and at Greccio he arranged the first live nativity scene. According to Christian tradition he received the stigmata in 1224; he died in 1226 and was canonised by Pope Gregory IX in 1228.

entries.name: Pierre-Simon Laplace
entries.desc: Pierre-Simon Laplace was a French scholar whose work shaped physics, astronomy, mathematics, statistics and philosophy. Born in Beaumont-en-Auge in Normandy, he summarised and extended his predecessors' work in the five-volume Mécanique céleste (1799–1825), which recast classical mechanics in the terms of calculus. He formulated Laplace's equation, pioneered the Laplace transform, developed mainly the Bayesian interpretation of probability and restated the nebular hypothesis of the origin of the Solar System. He examined Napoleon at the École Militaire in 1785, became a Count of the Empire in 1806 and was named a marquis in 1817, after the Bourbon Restoration.

entries.name: Ferdowsi
entries.desc: Ferdowsi, the pen name of Abul-Qāsem Mansur bin Hasan Tosi, was a Persian poet and the author of the Shahnameh ("Book of Kings"), one of the longest epic poems created by a single poet. He was born in 940 into a family of dehqans, Persian landowners, in the village of Paj near Tus in Khorasan, then under the Samanid Empire. Drawing on the Abu-Mansuri Shahnameh, he finished a first version in the 990s; when the Ghaznavids overthrew the Samanids, he rewrote sections to praise Sultan Mahmud and completed the epic in 1010. How well Mahmud rewarded him is disputed and became the subject of legends. The poem joins the culture of pre-Islamic Iran to that of Islamic Iran.

entries.name: Guy de Maupassant
aka: Henri René Albert Guy de Maupassant
entries.desc: Guy de Maupassant was a 19th-century French author, a master of the short story associated with the naturalist school, who depicted human lives and social forces in disillusioned and often pessimistic terms. A protégé of Gustave Flaubert, he wrote 300 short stories, six novels, three travel books and one volume of verse, many of the stories set in the Franco-Prussian War. His first published story, "Boule de Suif" (1880), is often considered his best-known work, and his novel Bel-Ami (1885) had thirty-seven printings in four months. After trying to take his own life in 1892, he was committed to an asylum at Passy in Paris, where he died of syphilis in 1893.

entries.name: Anna Akhmatova
entries.desc: Anna Akhmatova, the pen name of Anna Andreyevna Gorenko, was a Russian and Soviet poet born at Bolshoy Fontan near Odessa, whose verse is marked by economy and restraint. Her work runs from short lyrics to cycles such as Requiem (1935–40), on the Stalinist terror. Her first husband, Nikolai Gumilev, was executed by the Cheka, and her son Lev Gumilev and her common-law husband Nikolay Punin spent years in the Gulag, where Punin died. She chose not to emigrate; in 1946 a campaign ordered by Stalin condemned her work, and Andrei Zhdanov banned her poetry. She was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1965 and 1966 and died in 1966.

entries.name: Émile Durkheim
entries.desc: Émile Durkheim was a French sociologist who formally established the academic discipline of sociology. Born in Épinal into a family of devout Alsatian Jews, he taught the first social science course at the University of Bordeaux from 1887. There he published The Division of Labour in Society (1893) and The Rules of Sociological Method (1895), set up the first European department of sociology, wrote Le Suicide (1897) and founded the journal L'Année sociologique in 1898. He moved to the Sorbonne in 1902 and published The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life in 1912. His son André died at the front in 1915, and Durkheim died after a stroke in Paris in 1917.

entries.name: Hendrik Lorentz
entries.desc: Hendrik Antoon Lorentz was a Dutch theoretical physicist, born in Arnhem, who in 1878 was appointed to the newly established chair of theoretical physics at Leiden University. He shared the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pieter Zeeman for the discovery and theoretical explanation of the Zeeman effect. He derived the Lorentz transformation of the special theory of relativity and the Lorentz force, which acts on a charged particle in an electromagnetic field. In 1912 he became curator of the Physical Cabinet at Teylers Museum in Haarlem, and from 1925 until his death in 1928 he chaired the International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation, the forerunner of UNESCO.

entries.name: Temple
entries.desc: A temple is a place of worship, a building used for rituals such as prayer and sacrifice. The word comes from the Latin templum: in Ancient Rome, a sacred precinct marked out on the ground by a priest, or augur. By convention English uses the word for the places of worship of most ancient religions, such as the Ancient Egyptian and Ancient Greek religions, and of Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism, Shinto and others, but not usually for Christian churches, mosques or synagogues. Believers often regard a temple as the house of one or more deities, where offerings are made and a group of clergy keeps the rituals, and parts of it, or the whole main building, may be open to the clergy alone.

entries.name: Five Pillars of Islam
entries.desc: The Five Pillars of Islam are the fundamental practices of Islam, held to be obligatory acts of worship for all Muslims: the shahada (profession of faith), salah (prayer), zakat (almsgiving), sawm (fasting during Ramadan) and hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca). Each is alluded to in the Quran, and the Hadith gives further detail. Comparable practices existed in pre-Islamic Arabia and among Jews and Christians, but the Quran and Hadith gave them a monotheistic centre and tied them to the life of Muhammad. The pillars are particularly emphasised in Sunni Islam; Shia Muslims also recognise them, though their classification differs, and some communities such as the Alevis reject them.

entries.name: Luigi Pirandello
entries.desc: Luigi Pirandello was an Italian dramatist, novelist, poet and short story writer, best known for his plays. Born in Girgenti (now Agrigento) in Sicily to a family that had fought for unification, he moved to Rome in 1887 to study. He wrote novels, hundreds of short stories and about 40 plays, some in Sicilian; Six Characters in Search of an Author, staged in Rome in 1921, divided its first audience. A supporter of Italian fascism, he asked Benito Mussolini in 1924 to admit him to the National Fascist Party and in 1925 took over the Teatro d'Arte di Roma. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1934, and his tragic farces are often seen as forerunners of the Theatre of the Absurd.

entries.name: John Dalton
entries.desc: John Dalton was an English chemist, physicist and meteorologist whose work laid the foundations of modern atomic theory. Born into a Quaker family in Eaglesfield, Cumberland he settled in Manchester and joined its Literary and Philosophical Society in 1794. He proposed that each element consists of identical atoms of characteristic weight, which combine in fixed whole-number proportions, and set out the model in A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808). He kept daily weather records for over fifty years, formulated the law of partial pressures and gave the first scientific description of colour blindness, still called Daltonism in several languages.

entries.name: Venus
entries.desc: Venus is a Roman goddess whose functions encompass love, beauty, desire, sex, fertility, prosperity and victory. In Roman mythology she was the ancestor of the Roman people through her son Aeneas, who survived the fall of Troy and fled to Italy, and Julius Caesar claimed her as his own ancestor, dedicating a Temple of Venus Genetrix ("Venus the Mother") in 46 BCE. She was worshipped under many cult titles; Venus Erycina was a Punic statue of Astarte captured from Eryx in Sicily. The Romans adapted the myths and imagery of her Greek counterpart Aphrodite, and in the later classical tradition of the West she became the embodiment of love and sexuality, usually shown nude.

entries.name: King Arthur
entries.desc: King Arthur is a king of Britain in legend and the central figure of the medieval tradition known as the Matter of Britain. Welsh sources portray him as a leader of the post-Roman Britons against the Anglo-Saxons in the late 5th and early 6th centuries, but he first appears in the Annales Cambriae and the Historia Brittonum, written about 300 years later, and most historians of the period do not consider him historical. Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th-century Historia Regum Britanniae made him a figure of international interest, adding Uther Pendragon, Merlin, Guinevere, Excalibur. Chrétien de Troyes added Lancelot and the Holy Grail and began the genre of Arthurian romance.

entries.name: Jonathan Swift
entries.desc: Jonathan Swift was an Anglo-Irish writer, satirist and Anglican cleric, born in Dublin in the Kingdom of Ireland. He published his works under pseudonyms such as Isaac Bickerstaff and M. B. Drapier, or anonymously, among them A Tale of a Tub (1704), the prose satire Gulliver's Travels (1726) and A Modest Proposal (1729), whose deadpan irony led such satire to be called "Swiftian". He joined the Whigs early on, but in 1710 the Tories recruited him as editor of The Examiner. In 1713 he was appointed dean of St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin. He died in 1745 and was buried in his cathedral beside Esther Johnson; Gulliver's Travels remains the most printed book by an Irish writer.

entries.name: Nostradamus
entries.desc: Nostradamus, the Latinised name of Michel de Nostredame, was a French astrologer, apothecary and physician, born in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence to a family of Jewish origin. He studied at Avignon and Montpellier, worked as an apothecary, fought outbreaks of plague and in 1547 settled in Salon-de-Provence with his second wife, Anne Ponsarde. After the success of his almanac for 1550 he worked as an astrologer for wealthy patrons, Catherine de' Medici among them, and in 1555 published Les Prophéties, 942 quatrains said to predict future events. Academic sources reject any real prophetic power, judging his predictions vague.

entries.name: Nefertiti
entries.desc: Nefertiti was a queen of the 18th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, the great royal wife of Pharaoh Akhenaten. With her husband she overhauled state religion, promoting Atenism, a possibly monotheistic religion centred on the sun disc. Almost nothing is known of her life before her marriage; the couple had at least six daughters, among them Meritaten and Ankhesenpaaten, later the wife of Tutankhamun. Some scholars believe that after Akhenaten's death she ruled briefly as the female pharaoh Neferneferuaten, an identification still debated. Her bust, attributed to the sculptor Thutmose and excavated from his studio in the early 20th century, is now in the Neues Museum in Berlin.

entries.name: Eleanor Roosevelt
entries.desc: Eleanor Roosevelt was an American political figure, diplomat and activist, the longest-serving first lady of the United States, during her husband Franklin D. Roosevelt's four terms from 1933 to 1945. A niece of President Theodore Roosevelt, she married Franklin in 1905. As first lady she held regular press conferences and wrote a daily newspaper column, and argued for the civil rights of African Americans and Asian Americans. Widowed in 1945, she was a United States delegate to the United Nations General Assembly until 1952, chaired the UN Commission on Human Rights and oversaw the drafting of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948. She died in 1962.

entries.name: Edward Jenner
entries.desc: Edward Jenner was an English physician and scientist, born in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, who created the smallpox vaccine, the world's first vaccine. Having observed that cowpox appeared to protect against smallpox, on 14 May 1796 he inoculated James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener, with pus from the cowpox blisters of the milkmaid Sarah Nelmes. In 1798 he described the method in his Inquiry into the Variolae vaccinae known as the Cow Pox, and the words vaccine and vaccination come from his term for cowpox. He was appointed physician to King George IV in 1821 and was among the first to describe the brood parasitism of the cuckoo.

entries.name: Bernhard Riemann
entries.desc: Bernhard Riemann was a German mathematician, born in 1826 at Breselenz in the Kingdom of Hanover, who made contributions to analysis, number theory and differential geometry. The son of a poor Lutheran pastor, he went to the University of Göttingen in 1846 to study theology but turned to mathematics under Carl Friedrich Gauss. He gave the first rigorous formulation of the integral, introduced Riemann surfaces, and in an 1859 paper on the prime-counting function stated the Riemann hypothesis; his lectures of 1854 founded Riemannian geometry, later the mathematics of general relativity. He died of tuberculosis at Selasca in Italy in 1866.

entries.name: Emily Dickinson
entries.desc: Emily Dickinson was an American poet, born in 1830 in Amherst, Massachusetts, to a prominent family, who was largely unpublished and unknown during her lifetime. She studied at the Amherst Academy for seven years and briefly at the Mount Holyoke Female Seminary, and from about 1867 rarely left the family Homestead. Of her nearly 1,800 poems, written in short lines with lean descriptions and slant rhyme and dealing mainly with nature and mortality, only 10 were published while she lived. Her sister Lavinia found the poems after her death; a selection of 1890 altered them heavily, and Thomas H. Johnson's complete edition of 1955 restored them closer to her intention.

entries.name: Abel Tasman
entries.desc: Abel Tasman was a Dutch seafarer and explorer in the service of the Dutch East India Company (VOC), likely born in 1602 or 1603 in Lutjegast. On his voyage of 1642 he reached the west coast of Tasmania on 24 November, naming it Van Diemen's Land after his patron Anthony van Diemen, and then became the first European to reach New Zealand, which he named Staten Landt. Off what is now Golden Bay, Māori in a waka attacked a boat's crew and four sailors were killed, and Tasman named the place Murderers' Bay. A second voyage in 1644 mapped the north coast of Australia, but the company judged his explorations a disappointment. He died at Batavia in 1659.

entries.name: William Herschel
entries.desc: William Herschel was a German–British astronomer and composer, born in the Electorate of Hanover, who followed his father into the military band of Hanover and emigrated to Britain in 1757. While working as an organist and director of concerts in Bath he took up astronomy in 1766 and built his own telescopes, and on 13 March 1781 he noted an object in Gemini that was confirmed as a new planet, later named Uranus, the first discovered since antiquity. George III appointed him Court Astronomer. He worked closely with his sister Caroline Herschel, published catalogues of nebulae in 1802 and 1820, and discovered infrared radiation and moons of Uranus and Saturn. He died in 1822.

entries.name: Hades
entries.desc: Hades is, in ancient Greek religion and mythology, the god of the dead and of riches and the king of the underworld, with which his name became synonymous. The eldest son of Cronus and Rhea, he and his brothers Zeus and Poseidon overthrew the Titans and shared the cosmos, Hades receiving the underworld, Zeus the sky and Poseidon the sea. His most important myth is the abduction of Persephone, told in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter of most likely the early 6th century BCE: having eaten a pomegranate seed, she was to spend a third of each year with him. Greeks of around the 5th century BCE began to call him Plouton, and Roman mythographers merged him with Dis Pater and Orcus as Pluto.

entries.name: Cathedral
entries.desc: A cathedral is a church that contains the cathedra, the seat of a bishop, and so serves as the central church of a diocese, mainly in churches with an episcopal hierarchy such as the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican and some Lutheran churches. Churches serving as cathedrals first appeared in Italy, Gaul, Spain and North Africa in the 4th century; among the earliest with visible remains is the complex below the Cathedral of Aquileia, dated between 313 and 319. They became universal in the Western Catholic Church by the 12th century, and after the Reformation many in presbyterian lands kept the title without a bishop.

entries.name: Homo erectus
entries.desc: Homo erectus is an extinct species of archaic human of the Pleistocene, spanning nearly 2 million years, and the first human species with a humanlike body plan and gait, the first to leave Africa for Asia and Europe, and the first to wield fire. It evolved in Africa from a population of H. habilis; the oldest identified specimen is a skull from Drimolen, South Africa, 2.04 million years old, and the earliest records outside Africa, in Georgia, Indonesia and China, date to between 1.6 and 1.85 million years ago. It invented the Acheulean tool industry, and its last known occurrence is 108,000 to 117,000 years ago in Southeast Asia.

entries.name: Ivan Bunin
entries.desc: Ivan Bunin was a Russian writer, born in Voronezh in 1870 into an old noble family, who in 1933 became the first Russian writer awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. He carried on the classical traditions of Russian prose and poetry, and is best known for the short novels The Village (1910) and Dry Valley (1912), the autobiographical novel The Life of Arseniev and the stories of Dark Avenues (1946). Hostile to Bolshevism, he settled in 1920 in Paris and Grasse, where his diary of 1918–1920, Cursed Days, began to appear in 1925; during the German occupation he sheltered fugitives, among them Jews, in his house in Grasse. He died in Paris in 1953.

entries.name: Kurt Gödel
entries.desc: Kurt Gödel was a logician, mathematician and philosopher, born in 1906 into a German-speaking family in Brünn, Austria-Hungary (now Brno). At the University of Vienna he proved his completeness theorem in 1929, and in 1931 he published his incompleteness theorems, which imply that a formal axiomatic system meeting certain conditions cannot decide every statement about the natural numbers or prove its own consistency. He also showed that the axiom of choice and the continuum hypothesis cannot be disproved from Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory. In 1939 he left Vienna for the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. He starved to death in 1978, believing his food was poisoned.

entries.name: Spanish flu
entries.desc: The Spanish flu was a global influenza pandemic of 1918–1920 caused by the H1N1 subtype of the influenza A virus. The earliest probable cases were documented in March 1918 in Haskell County, Kansas; within two years an estimated 500 million people, nearly a third of the global population, had been infected, and estimates of deaths range from 17 million to 50 million, possibly as high as 100 million. The name is misleading: wartime censors suppressed news of the outbreak while newspapers in neutral Spain reported it freely. A second wave from August 1918 was far deadlier than the first, the historian David Arnold estimating at least 12 million dead in India, and a third wave followed in 1919.

credit.artist: Otis Historical Archives, National Museum of Health and Medicine

entries.name: Pierre-Auguste Renoir
entries.desc: Pierre-Auguste Renoir was a leading French Impressionist painter, born in Limoges in 1841, the son of a tailor whose family moved to Paris in 1844. He left school at thirteen for an apprenticeship at a porcelain factory, began studying under Charles Gleyre in 1862, where he met Alfred Sisley, Frédéric Bazille and Claude Monet, and had his first success at the Salon of 1868 with Lise with a Parasol. His works include Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette (1876) and Luncheon of the Boating Party. Around 1892 he developed rheumatoid arthritis but went on painting, and he died at Cagnes-sur-Mer in 1919; his sons included the actor Pierre Renoir and the filmmaker Jean Renoir.

credit.artist: Unknown Unknown Musée d'Orsay, Dist. RMN-Grand Palais / Patrice Schmidt

entries.name: André Gide
entries.desc: André Gide was a French author, born in Paris in 1869 into a middle-class Protestant family, who wrote more than 50 books and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1947. His first novel, The Notebooks of André Walter, appeared in 1891, and his fiction and autobiographical works explored the conflict between Protestant austerity and his sexuality. His journey through French Equatorial Africa in 1926–1927 produced Travels in the Congo, which likened French companies' exploitation of African workers to slavery and fed the anti-colonial movement in France. Sympathetic to Communism in the early 1930s, he turned against Stalin after visiting the USSR in 1936. He died in Paris in 1951.

entries.name: Edwin Hubble
entries.desc: Edwin Hubble was an American astronomer, born in Marshfield, Missouri, in 1889, who helped establish extragalactic astronomy and observational cosmology. After studying at the University of Chicago and at Oxford, he joined the Mount Wilson Observatory in 1919. Using the 100-inch Hooker Telescope to find Cepheid variables, he showed in 1924 that the Andromeda and Triangulum nebulae lay far beyond the Milky Way and were galaxies in their own right. In 1929 he confirmed that a galaxy's recessional velocity increases with its distance, the relation known as Hubble's law, which implies that the universe is expanding. He died in 1953, and the Hubble Space Telescope is named after him.

entries.name: Charles Babbage
entries.desc: Charles Babbage was an English mathematician, philosopher, inventor and mechanical engineer who originated the concept of a digital programmable computer. Most likely born in London in 1791, he was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge from 1828 to 1839. From 1822 he worked on the difference engine, made to compute values of polynomial functions, and later designed the analytical engine, to be programmed with punched cards as on the Jacquard loom. He wrote programs for it from 1837 to 1840, but died at Marylebone in 1871 before his engines were completed; a functioning difference engine built from his plans in 1991 showed that the design would have worked.

entries.name: Jacob
entries.desc: Jacob, later given the name Israel, is the third Hebrew patriarch in Judaism, described in the Book of Genesis as a son of Isaac and Rebecca and the twin brother of Esau. According to Genesis he bought Esau's birthright and deceived his aging father into blessing him instead of Esau, then went to his uncle Laban in Haran, seeing on the way a vision of a ladder to heaven at Bethel. He married Laban's daughters Leah and Rachel, and his sons were each the forefather of one of the Twelve Tribes of Israel. Genesis has him die in Egypt at the age of 147; mainstream archaeologists agree that no evidence establishes him as a historical figure.

entries.name: Monastery
entries.desc: A monastery is a building or complex of buildings housing monastics, monks or nuns, whether living in communities or alone as hermits, with a place reserved for prayer such as a chapel, church or temple. The word comes from the Greek monasterion, from monazein, 'to live alone'. Buddhist monasteries, called vihara, grew from the retreat monks and nuns kept during the South Asian wet season. According to tradition, Christian monasticism began in Egypt with Anthony the Great, and Pachomius the Great developed communal life under one roof; Benedict of Nursia founded Monte Cassino in Italy in 529, the seed of Roman Catholic monasticism.

entries.name: Mesolithic
entries.desc: The Mesolithic, from the Greek for 'middle stone', is the Old World archaeological period between the Upper Paleolithic and the Neolithic, the final period of hunter-gatherer cultures in Europe and the Middle East between the end of the Last Glacial Maximum and the Neolithic Revolution. In Europe it spans roughly 15,000 to 5,000 BP and in the Middle East roughly 20,000 to 10,000 BP, ending with the introduction of farming. Its people moved from group hunting of large animals to a broader hunter-gatherer way of life, using small composite stone tools called microliths, and their more permanent settlements lay near the sea or inland waters. Hodder Westropp proposed the term in 1866.

entries.name: Auguste Rodin
entries.desc: Auguste Rodin was a French sculptor, born in Paris in 1840 into a working-class family, who is considered a founder of modern sculpture. Rejected three times by the École des Beaux Arts, he trained at the Petite École and in studios and workshops, and after a visit to Italy in 1875, where he studied Donatello and Michelangelo, made The Age of Bronze, so naturalistic that critics accused him of casting it from a living model. His works include The Gates of Hell, with the figure later known as The Thinker, The Kiss, The Burghers of Calais and the Monument to Balzac. Camille Claudel was his student and lover; he married his companion Rose Beuret in 1917 and died that year at Meudon.

entries.name: Jack London
entries.desc: Jack London was an American novelist, journalist and activist, one of the first American authors to become an international celebrity and earn a large fortune from writing. After leaving the University of California, Berkeley, in 1897 he joined the Klondike Gold Rush, where he developed scurvy; the north became the setting of The Call of the Wild, White Fang and the story To Build a Fire. A member of the radical literary group The Crowd in San Francisco, he advocated socialism and workers' rights in works such as The Iron Heel and The People of the Abyss. In 1905 he bought a ranch at Glen Ellen in Sonoma County, where he died in 1916, suffering from uremia and late-stage alcoholism.

credit.artist: published by L C Page and Company Boston 1903

entries.name: Ivan Turgenev
entries.desc: Ivan Turgenev was a Russian novelist, short story writer, poet, playwright and translator, born in Oryol in 1818 to noble parents, who also made Russian literature known in the West. His collection A Sportsman's Sketches (1852) was a milestone of Russian realism and, like his story Mumu, took aim at the cruelties of serfdom. An obituary of Nikolai Gogol in 1852 brought him a month in prison and exile to his country estate. He moved to Western Europe in 1854, living mostly at Baden-Baden or Paris near the opera singer Pauline Viardot, and his novel Fathers and Sons (1862) is regarded as one of the major works of 19th-century fiction. He died at Bougival near Paris in 1883.

entries.name: Walter Scott
entries.desc: Sir Walter Scott was a Scottish novelist, poet and historian, born in Edinburgh, who worked as an advocate, Clerk of Session and Sheriff-Depute of Selkirkshire alongside his writing. He first won readers with narrative poems such as Marmion (1808) and The Lady of the Lake (1810). His Waverley novels (1814–1831) were for nearly a century among the most widely read novels in Europe, and they established the historical novel as a genre of European Romanticism. He was president of the Royal Society of Edinburgh from 1820 to 1832 and became a baronet of Abbotsford in 1820.

entries.name: Syrian civil war
entries.desc: The Syrian civil war was an armed conflict that grew out of the Syrian revolution of March 2011, when the Ba'athist regime of Bashar al-Assad met pro-democracy protests with lethal force and the uprising turned into civil war. Iran, Russia and Hezbollah backed Assad, while Qatar, Turkey and a United States-led program armed rebel groups; in 2014 the Islamic State seized eastern Syria. Chemical weapons were used predominantly by government forces. By the end of the decade the war had caused an estimated 470,000–610,000 violent deaths. It culminated in December 2024, when Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham took Aleppo, Hama and Homs and Assad fled to Moscow.

entries.name: John Keats
entries.desc: John Keats was an English poet of the second generation of Romantic poets, with Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley, born in Moorgate, London. His poems had been in publication for less than four years when he died of tuberculosis in Rome at the age of 25, and they were indifferently received in his lifetime; Blackwood's Magazine attacked Endymion. His fame grew rapidly after his death, and by the end of the century he was placed in the canon of English literature. His odes, among them "Ode to a Nightingale" and "Ode on a Grecian Urn", and medievalist poems such as "The Eve of St. Agnes" influenced the Pre-Raphaelite movement.

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.desc: Henri Bergson was a French philosopher, born in Paris, who argued that immediate experience and intuition matter more than abstract rationalism and science for understanding reality. His four principal works were Time and Free Will (1889), Matter and Memory (1896), Creative Evolution (1907) and The Two Sources of Morality and Religion (1932). He held the chair of Greek and Roman philosophy and then that of modern philosophy at the Collège de France, where the public attended his open courses in large numbers. He received the 1927 Nobel Prize in Literature, and his popularity caused controversy in France, where his views were seen as opposed to the Republic's secular and scientific attitude.

entries.name: Ferdinand de Saussure
entries.desc: Ferdinand de Saussure was a Swiss linguist, semiotician and philosopher, born in Geneva, who is widely considered one of the founders of 20th-century linguistics and, with Charles Sanders Peirce, of semiotics. At 21, after beginning graduate work at the University of Leipzig, he published a dissertation on the primitive vowel system of the Indo-European languages. He lectured at the University of Paris and from 1892 taught Sanskrit and Indo-European at the University of Geneva. He published little in his lifetime; his most influential work, the Course in General Linguistics, was published in 1916 by his former students Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye from notes on his Geneva lectures.

entries.name: Freemasonry
entries.desc: Freemasonry consists of fraternal groups that trace their origins to the medieval guilds of stonemasons and is considered the oldest existing secular fraternal organisation, with documents and traditions dating back to the 14th century. Its basic unit is the lodge, supervised regionally by independent Grand Lodges, of which the United Grand Lodge of England, dating from June 1717, is the oldest. Members pass through three degrees, Entered Apprentice, Fellow of the craft and Master Mason, taught through symbols and allegory. The Catholic Church and some Protestant denominations have opposed it, and Freemasons have been persecuted by authoritarian states.

entries.name: Soviet–Afghan War
entries.desc: The Soviet–Afghan War was fought in Afghanistan from December 1979 to February 1989 between the Soviet Union and the Afghan Armed Forces and the Afghan mujahideen, whose external support came mostly from Pakistan, the United States, the United Kingdom, China, Iran and the Arab states of the Persian Gulf. Soviet troops held the major cities while the mujahideen fought a guerrilla war in the countryside, and the Soviets laid millions of landmines and levelled villages. Between one and three million Afghans died. Under Mikhail Gorbachev the Soviet army withdrew, its last column leaving on 15 February 1989.

entries.name: Iraq War
entries.desc: The Iraq War was an armed conflict in Iraq from 2003 to 2011 that began in March 2003 with an invasion by a United States-led coalition, joined by the UK, Australia and Poland, which overthrew the Ba'athist government of Saddam Hussein. The invasion rested chiefly on false claims that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction and supported al-Qaeda; no stockpiles were found, and Kofi Annan declared it illegal under international law. An insurgency and a sectarian civil war between Shia and Sunni followed. US forces withdrew in 2011, and the war caused an estimated 150,000 to over a million deaths.

entries.name: James Chadwick
entries.desc: Sir James Chadwick was a British experimental physicist, born in Cheshire, who studied under Ernest Rutherford at Manchester and later served as his assistant director of research at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge. Interned at Ruhleben in Germany through World War I, he went on to discover the neutron and measure its mass, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935. That year he moved to the University of Liverpool, where he installed a cyclotron. In 1941 he wrote the final draft of the MAUD Report, and he headed the British team on the Manhattan Project; he was knighted in 1945.

entries.name: Henri Poincaré
entries.desc: Henri Poincaré was a French mathematician, theoretical physicist, engineer and philosopher of science, born in Nancy, who has been called "The Last Universalist" because he excelled in all fields of mathematics as it existed in his lifetime. In research on the three-body problem he discovered the first chaotic deterministic system, laying the foundations of chaos theory, and he is regarded as the creator of algebraic topology. He presented the Lorentz transformations in their modern symmetrical form, an important step towards special relativity, and formulated the Poincaré conjecture, solved by Grigori Perelman in 2002–2003. He was president of the French Academy of Sciences in 1906.

entries.name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
entries.desc: Srinivasa Ramanujan was an Indian mathematician, born in Erode in British-ruled India, who made substantial contributions to mathematical analysis, number theory, infinite series and continued fractions. Working at first in isolation, he began a correspondence in 1913 with G. H. Hardy at the University of Cambridge, who arranged for him to travel there. He independently compiled nearly 3,900 results, most since proven correct, and became one of the youngest Fellows of the Royal Society and the first Indian Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. Ill health forced his return to India in 1919, and he died in 1920 at the age of 32; his "lost notebook" was rediscovered in 1976.

entries.name: Joseph Smith
entries.desc: Joseph Smith Jr. was an American religious and political leader, born in Sharon, Vermont, who founded Mormonism and the Latter Day Saint movement. He said that in 1823 an angel directed him to buried golden plates, and in 1830 he published the Book of Mormon as their translation and organised the Church of Christ. His followers gathered in Kirtland, Ohio, and Independence, Missouri, and later founded Nauvoo, Illinois, which grew into the second-largest city in Illinois. In 1844, after he and the city council ordered the press of the Nauvoo Expositor destroyed, he surrendered to Illinois authorities and was killed by a mob that stormed the jailhouse in Carthage.

entries.name: Mary, Queen of Scots
entries.desc: Mary, Queen of Scots was Queen of Scotland from 1542, when she inherited the throne at six days old on the death of James V, until her forced abdication in 1567. Brought up in France, she married the Dauphin Francis in 1558 and was queen consort of France until his death in 1560, then returned to Scotland as the Catholic monarch of a Protestant kingdom. After the murder of Lord Darnley in 1567 and her marriage to the Earl of Bothwell, an uprising forced her to abdicate in favour of her son James VI. She fled to England, where Elizabeth I kept her for eighteen and a half years; found guilty of plotting to assassinate Elizabeth, she was beheaded at Fotheringhay Castle in 1587.

entries.name: Robert Hooke
entries.desc: Robert Hooke was an English polymath, born at Freshwater on the Isle of Wight, who was active as a physicist, astronomer, geologist, meteorologist and architect. He began as an assistant to Robert Boyle, building the vacuum pumps for his experiments, and from 1662 was the first Curator of Experiments of the Royal Society. His book Micrographia (1665), drawn from work with a compound microscope he designed, coined the term cell. He inferred that gravity obeys an inverse square law, which led to a rivalry with Isaac Newton, and identified the organic origin of fossils. After the Great Fire of London in 1666 he performed more than half of the property line surveys for its reconstruction.

entries.name: Hephaestus
entries.desc: Hephaestus is the Greek god of artisans, blacksmiths, craftsmen, fire, metalworking, sculpture and volcanoes. In Greek mythology he was the son of Hera, either on her own, as in Hesiod's Theogony, or by Zeus, and he was cast off Mount Olympus because of his lameness, by Hera in one account and by Zeus in another. As the blacksmith of the gods he made all their weapons, and his symbols are the smith's hammer, the anvil and a pair of tongs. His cult was based on Lemnos, and he was worshipped in the manufacturing centres of Greece, particularly Athens; a Linear B name found at Knossos probably attests his worship. In Rome he was equated with Vulcan.

entries.name: Ra
entries.desc: Ra, also called Re, was the ancient Egyptian god of the Sun, order, kings and the sky. By the Fifth Dynasty, in the 25th and 24th centuries BCE, he had become one of the most important gods of Egyptian religion, identified primarily with the noon-day Sun. According to Egyptian myth he carried the Sun across the sky in his solar barque by day and sailed through the Duat, the underworld, by night, defeating the serpent Apophis before returning at dawn. He was usually shown as a man with a falcon's head crowned by a solar disc, and he was merged with Horus as Ra-Horakhty and, in the New Kingdom, with Amun as Amun-Ra.

entries.name: Human evolution
entries.desc: Human evolution is the evolutionary history of Homo sapiens, a species of the hominid family of primates, studied through physical and evolutionary anthropology, paleontology and genetics. Primates diverged from other mammals about 85 million years ago, and the extinct biped ancestors of humans separated from the genus Pan, which includes chimpanzees and bonobos, 4–7 million years ago. The genus Homo is evidenced by the appearance of H. habilis, and anatomically modern humans emerged in Africa approximately 300,000 years ago. Over this history humans developed bipedalism, dexterity and complex language, and modern humans interbred with archaic humans such as Neanderthals and Denisovans.

entries.name: François Rabelais
entries.desc: François Rabelais was a French writer, humanist of the French Renaissance and Greek scholar who has been called the first great French prose author. Born, by tradition, at La Devinière near Chinon in Touraine, he left the Franciscans for the Benedictine Order, studied medicine at Montpellier and from 1532 worked as a doctor at the Hôtel-Dieu de Lyon. His books on the giants Gargantua and Pantagruel, the first of them Pantagruel, satirised medieval scholasticism and the abuses of powerful princes and popes, and drew opposition from John Calvin and from the hierarchy of the Catholic Church. His work gave the language the adjective Rabelaisian.

entries.name: Clara Zetkin
entries.desc: Clara Zetkin was a German Marxist theorist, communist activist and advocate for women's rights, born in Wiederau in Saxony. After the ban placed on socialist activity by Otto von Bismarck in 1878, she went into exile in Zürich and Paris, and from 1891 to 1917 she edited the Social Democratic Party's women's newspaper Die Gleichheit. With Käte Duncker and others she proposed an annual women's day in Copenhagen in 1910, and a conference she chaired in Moscow in 1921 set International Women's Day on 8 March. She joined the Spartacist League, later the Communist Party of Germany, and represented it in the Reichstag from 1920 to 1933.

entries.name: Kali
entries.desc: Kali is a major goddess in Hinduism, associated primarily with time, death and destruction, and the first of the ten Mahavidyas, goddesses who provide liberating knowledge. Her origins can be traced to pre-Vedic and Vedic goddess worship in the Indian subcontinent, and her first major appearance in Sanskrit literature is in the sixth-century CE Devi Mahatmya, where she defeats the demon Raktabija by sucking his blood before it can reach the ground. She is the preeminent deity of the Hindu tantric and Kalikula traditions and is worshipped as the Divine Mother, most widely in Bengal, where devotional songs extol her motherly nature.

entries.name: Nobility
entries.desc: Nobility is a social class found in many societies that have an aristocracy, normally appointed by and ranked immediately below royalty. The term derives from the Latin nobilitas; in the Roman Republic the nobiles were the families, patrician or plebeian, descended from someone who had held the consulship. In feudal Europe the nobility were generally those who held a fief, often land or office, in exchange for allegiance and mainly military services to a suzerain, and it became a hereditary caste with fiscal and other privileges, as in pre-revolutionary France. By the 21st century noble status had become a largely honorary dignity in most societies.

entries.name: Schutzstaffel
entries.desc: The Schutzstaffel (SS) was a major paramilitary organisation under Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party in Nazi Germany. Formed from a small bodyguard unit, it officially marked its foundation on 9 November 1925, and under Heinrich Himmler, its leader from 1929 to 1945, it became the foremost agency of security, mass surveillance and state terrorism. Its branches included the Allgemeine SS, the Waffen-SS and the SS-Totenkopfverbände, which ran the concentration and extermination camps. The SS was the organisation most responsible for the genocide of an estimated 6 million Jews and millions of other victims in the Holocaust, and at Nuremberg it was judged a criminal organisation.

entries.name: Adam Mickiewicz
entries.desc: Adam Mickiewicz was a Polish poet, dramatist, essayist, publicist, translator and political activist, a principal figure of Polish Romanticism and regarded as a national poet in Poland, Lithuania and Belarus. Born in 1798 at or near Navahrudak, in lands of the former Grand Duchy of Lithuania then under Russian rule, he spent five years exiled to central Russia and left the Russian Empire in 1829, living in Rome and then Paris, where he lectured on Slavic literature at the Collège de France. His poetic drama Dziady (Forefathers' Eve) and the epic Pan Tadeusz inspired uprisings against the partitioning powers. He died, probably of cholera, at Istanbul in 1855 during the Crimean War.

entries.name: Herman Melville
entries.desc: Herman Melville was an American writer of the American Renaissance period, born in New York City in 1819. He went to sea in 1839 and in 1841 sailed on the whaler Acushnet, jumped ship in the Marquesas Islands, and drew on his encounters with the islanders for his first books, Typee (1846) and Omoo (1847). Moby-Dick (1851) found no audience, and after publishing short fiction such as Benito Cereno in magazines he turned to poetry and worked as a United States customs inspector in New York. Little known when he died in 1891, he was the subject of a revival from the centennial of his birth in 1919, and Moby-Dick came to be considered one of the Great American Novels.

entries.name: Georg Cantor
entries.desc: Georg Cantor was a mathematician, born in Saint Petersburg in 1845 and educated in Germany and Switzerland, who did much to create set theory. He established the importance of one-to-one correspondence between the members of two sets, defined infinite and well-ordered sets, proved that the real numbers are more numerous than the natural numbers, and defined the cardinal and ordinal numbers and their arithmetic. His theory of transfinite numbers met resistance from contemporaries such as Leopold Kronecker and Henri Poincaré, and he suffered recurring bouts of depression from 1884 until his death in 1918. In 1904 the Royal Society awarded him its Sylvester Medal.

entries.name: Pierre de Coubertin
aka: Charles Pierre de Frédy, Baron de Coubertin
entries.desc: Pierre de Coubertin was a French educator and historian, co-founder of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and its second president, known as the father of the modern Olympic Games. Born in Paris in 1863 into an aristocratic family, he studied law and public affairs at Sciences Po and was particularly active in promoting sport in French schools. A congress he organised at the Sorbonne in Paris on 23 June 1894 set the first modern Olympic Games for Athens in 1896 and the second for Paris in 1900. He became president of the IOC in 1896 and was succeeded in 1925 by Henri de Baillet-Latour. He died of a heart attack in Geneva in 1937 and was buried in Lausanne.
