entries.name: Chalcolithic
entries.desc: The Chalcolithic, also called the Copper Age and the Eneolithic, was an archaeological period marked by the increasing use of smelted copper, following the Neolithic and preceding the Bronze Age. It came at different times in different areas and was absent in some, such as Russia. The site of Belovode in Serbia has the world's oldest securely dated evidence of copper smelting at high temperature, from c. 5,000 BCE. In the Ancient Near East it began in the late 5th millennium BCE and lasted about a millennium; in Britain it was a short period between about 2,500 and 2,200 BCE. The Hungarian scientist Ferenc Pulszky proposed the concept of a Copper Age in the 1870s.

entries.name: Allies of World War II
entries.desc: The Allies, formally referred to as the United Nations from 1942, were the international military coalition formed during World War II (1939–1945) to oppose the Axis powers; its principal members were the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union, the United States and China. When the war broke out on 1 September 1939 the coalition consisted of the United Kingdom, France and Poland with their dependencies. The Soviet Union joined after the German invasion of June 1941 and the United States after the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941. The Declaration by United Nations of 1 January 1942, signed by 26 countries, formalised the alliance, which became the basis of the modern United Nations.

entries.name: Mikhail Bulgakov
entries.desc: Mikhail Bulgakov was a Russian and Soviet novelist and playwright, born in Kiev in 1891, the son of a professor at the Kiev Theological Academy. He studied medicine in Kiev and wrote the novel The White Guard and the plays The Days of the Turbins, Flight and Ivan Vasilievich. Several of his works were banned by the Soviet government and personally by Joseph Stalin, although Stalin reportedly attended The Days of the Turbins at least 15 times. He died in 1940; after his novel The Master and Margarita was published in 1966–67, his work was reassessed, and he is now widely regarded as one of the great Russian authors of the 20th century.

entries.name: Thomas Hardy
entries.desc: Thomas Hardy was an English novelist, poet and architect, born in 1840 at Higher Bockhampton near Dorchester in Dorset, the son of a stonemason. Apprenticed to a local architect at sixteen, he worked in London from 1862 before turning to writing. His novels, among them Far from the Madding Crowd (1874), The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891) and Jude the Obscure (1895), concern tragic characters struggling against their passions and social circumstances, most of them set in the semi-fictional region of Wessex. He regarded himself primarily as a poet, though his first collection appeared only in 1898, and younger poets viewed him as a mentor. He died in 1928.

entries.name: Stendhal
entries.desc: Stendhal was the pen name of Marie-Henri Beyle, a French writer born in Grenoble in 1783, best known for the novels The Red and the Black (1830) and The Charterhouse of Parma (1839) and considered one of the early practitioners of realism. He served in Napoleon's administration and was part of the army in the 1812 invasion of Russia, where he witnessed the burning of Moscow and the winter retreat. After the fall of Napoleon he settled in Milan until 1821, and from 1830 he was French consul at Trieste and Civitavecchia. His book De l'amour introduced the concept of crystallization in passionate love. He died in 1842.

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.desc: Ralph Waldo Emerson was an American essayist, lecturer, philosopher, minister, abolitionist and poet who led the transcendentalist movement of the mid-19th century. Born in Boston in 1803, the son of a Unitarian minister, he entered Harvard College in 1817 and set out the philosophy of Transcendentalism in his 1836 essay Nature. His 1837 speech The American Scholar was called America's intellectual Declaration of Independence by Oliver Holmes. He wrote most of his essays as lectures, among them Self-Reliance and The Over-Soul, collected in Essays: First Series and Essays: Second Series. He was a mentor and close friend of Henry David Thoreau, and died in 1882.

entries.name: Ibn al-Haytham
aka: Abū ʿAlī al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn al-Haytham
entries.desc: Ibn al-Haytham, Latinized as Alhazen, was a mathematician, astronomer and physicist of the Islamic Golden Age, born in Basra around 965, who spent most of his productive life in the Fatimid capital, Cairo. His Book of Optics (Kitāb al-Manāẓir), written during 1011–1021, argued that vision is intromissive and occurs in the brain, gave a complete statement of the law of reflection, and in its Latin edition was cited by Galileo, Descartes, Kepler and Huygens. He held that a hypothesis must be supported by experiments or mathematical reasoning. He is said to have been forced into hiding by the caliph Al-Hakim until 1021, and he died in Cairo around 1040.

entries.name: Edmond Halley
entries.desc: Edmond Halley was an English astronomer, mathematician and physicist who in 1720 succeeded John Flamsteed as the second astronomer royal in Britain. From an observatory he built on Saint Helena in 1676–77 he catalogued the southern celestial hemisphere and recorded a transit of Mercury, realising that a transit of Venus could be used to find the distances between Earth, Venus and the Sun. He encouraged and helped fund the publication of Isaac Newton's Principia (1687), and in his 1705 Synopsis of the Astronomy of Comets used Newton's law of gravitation to compute the periodicity of the comet named after him on its return in 1758. In 1718 he discovered the proper motion of the fixed stars.

entries.name: Samuel Morse
entries.desc: Samuel Morse was an American inventor and painter, born in Charlestown near Boston in 1791, the son of a Congregational minister. After graduating from Yale College in 1810 he studied painting in England and gained admittance to the Royal Academy, and he made his reputation as a portrait painter. In middle age he contributed to the invention of a single-wire telegraph system based on European telegraphs and was co-developer and namesake of Morse code in 1837. The line was officially opened on 24 May 1844, when Morse sent the words "What hath God wrought", and he went on to help develop the commercial use of telegraphy. He died in 1872.

entries.name: Empiricism
entries.desc: Empiricism is an epistemological view in philosophy which holds that true knowledge or justification comes only or primarily from sensory experience and empirical evidence. Historically it was associated with the tabula rasa, the mind held to be blank at birth. Early forms appear in the Vaisheshika school of Hindu philosophy, between 600 and 200 BCE, and in the empiric school of Greek physicians founded in 330 BCE. In the late 17th and the 18th centuries John Locke, George Berkeley and David Hume became its leading exponents. In the philosophy of science it holds that hypotheses must be tested against observations of the natural world.

entries.name: 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami
entries.desc: The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami was a magnitude 9.0–9.1 undersea megathrust earthquake that struck on 11 March 2011 in the Pacific Ocean, 72 km east of the Oshika Peninsula of the Tōhoku region of Japan, and the tsunami it caused. It was the most powerful earthquake ever recorded in Japan, and its waves may have reached 40.5 m at Miyako and travelled up to 10 km inland in the Sendai area. Official figures released in 2021 reported 19,759 deaths, 6,242 injured and 2,553 missing. The tsunami caused the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster, with meltdowns of three reactors, and the economic damage, estimated at over $300 billion, made it the costliest natural disaster in history.

entries.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
entries.desc: Percy Bysshe Shelley was an English writer considered one of the major English Romantic poets, born in 1792 at Field Place, Warnham, Sussex, the eldest son of a Whig Member of Parliament. A radical in his poetry and in his political and social views, he faced a backlash against his avowed atheism and went into permanent self-exile in Italy in 1818. His works include Ozymandias (1818), The Mask of Anarchy (1819), Ode to the West Wind (1819), Prometheus Unbound (1820) and Adonais (1821). His second wife, Mary Shelley, was the author of Frankenstein. He died in a boating accident in 1822, aged 29, and his poems later found admirers in Owenist, Chartist and radical circles.

entries.name: Gioachino Rossini
entries.desc: Gioachino Rossini was an Italian composer and conductor of the late Classical and early Romantic eras, best known for his 39 operas. Born in Pesaro in 1792 to musician parents, he saw his first opera performed in Venice in 1810, and between 1810 and 1823 he wrote 34 operas for the Italian stage, among them the comic operas L'italiana in Algeri, The Barber of Seville and La Cenerentola and the serious Tancredi, Otello and Semiramide. Contracted by the Opéra in Paris in 1824, he wrote his last opera, Guillaume Tell, in 1829, and then withdrew from opera for the last 40 years of his life, for reasons never fully explained. He died at Passy in 1868.

entries.name: Abdul Hamid II
entries.desc: Abdul Hamid II was the 34th sultan of the Ottoman Empire, from 1876 to 1909, and the last sultan to exert effective control over the fracturing state. Elevated to power after the 1876 coup, he promulgated the empire's first constitution but suspended it and the parliament in 1878, ruling as an autocrat for three decades with a secret police and censorship regime and asserting his title of Caliph. His reign saw a lost war with Russia (1877–78), the building of the Hejaz Railway and many new schools, and massacres of Armenians by the Hamidiye regiments. Forced to restore the constitution in the Young Turk Revolution of 1908, he was deposed after the 31 March incident.

entries.name: Erwin Rommel
entries.desc: Erwin Rommel was a German field marshal of World War II, born in Heidenheim in the Kingdom of Württemberg, who became known as the Desert Fox. Awarded the Pour le Mérite on the Italian Front in World War I, he published Infantry Attacks in 1937, commanded the 7th Panzer Division in the 1940 invasion of France and led German and Italian forces in the North African campaign. In June 1944 he commanded the German forces opposing the Allied invasion of Normandy. Implicated in the 20 July plot against Adolf Hitler, he was given a choice between suicide and a trial, and took a cyanide pill. Historians dispute the postwar picture of him as an apolitical commander, which some call the Rommel myth.

entries.name: Hans Christian Ørsted
entries.desc: Hans Christian Ørsted was a Danish chemist and physicist, born in Rudkøbing, who discovered that electric currents create magnetic fields. After a doctorate on the works of Kant in 1799 and three years of travel across Europe, he became a professor at the University of Copenhagen in 1806. In 1820 he published his finding that a nearby electric current deflected a compass needle, for which the Royal Society of London awarded him the Copley Medal; the discovery led to André-Marie Ampère's work on electrodynamics and to the electric telegraph. He also discovered aluminium, which he presented in 1825, and was a leader of the Danish Golden Age. He died in Copenhagen in 1851.

entries.name: Ernst Haeckel
entries.desc: Ernst Haeckel was a German zoologist, naturalist, physician and artist, born in Potsdam, who was professor of zoology at the University of Jena from 1862 to 1909. He named thousands of new species, nearly 700 radiolarians on one trip to the Mediterranean, mapped a genealogical tree relating all life forms and coined terms such as ecology, phylum and phylogeny. He promoted Charles Darwin's work in Germany and developed the recapitulation theory, now disproven, which he supported with incorrectly drawn images of human embryos. The illustrations of his Kunstformen der Natur influenced Art Nouveau, and he also promoted scientific racism and Social Darwinism.

entries.name: Joseph-Louis Lagrange
entries.desc: Joseph-Louis Lagrange was an Italian and naturalized French mathematician, physicist and astronomer, born Giuseppe Luigi Lagrangia and educated at the University of Turin. In 1766 he succeeded Leonhard Euler as director of mathematics at the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin, where he wrote the Mécanique analytique (1788), which turned Newtonian mechanics into a branch of analysis. He was one of the creators of the calculus of variations, proved that every natural number is a sum of four squares and in 1772 found the solutions now known as Lagrangian points. Moving to Paris in 1787, he became the first professor of analysis at the École Polytechnique in 1794 and died in Paris in 1813.

entries.name: Rationalism
entries.desc: Rationalism is the view in philosophy that regards reason as the chief source and test of knowledge, in contrast to faith, tradition or sensory experience. Since the Enlightenment it has been associated with the mathematical methods that René Descartes, Baruch Spinoza and Gottfried Leibniz brought into philosophy. Rationalists held that certain principles of logic, mathematics, ethics and metaphysics are so true that denying them leads to contradiction, and that some knowledge is gained independently of sense experience. In the Enlightenment it was opposed to empiricism, held by John Locke and dominant in Britain, though the distinction was drawn later and is not clear-cut.

entries.name: Deism
entries.desc: Deism is the belief that a Supreme Being created the universe and that reason and observation of the natural world alone are sufficient to establish the existence of this creator, without prophecy, revelation or religious texts. Many deists hold that God does not intervene in the world after creating it, and the position stresses natural theology, in which God's existence is revealed through nature. Deists set out this critique of organized religion from the 17th century, especially in 18th-century England, France and North America. Deism saw a revival in early-19th-century Great Britain and North America, and several of its tenets continued in movements such as Unitarianism.

entries.name: Anubis
entries.desc: Anubis is the god of funerary rites, protector of graves and guide to the underworld in ancient Egyptian religion, usually depicted as a canine or as a man with a canine head; Anubis is the Greek form of his Egyptian name, Anpu or Inpu. A jackal god, probably Anubis, appears in stone inscriptions of First Dynasty pharaohs such as Hor-Aha and Djer, and in the Old Kingdom he was the most important god of the dead, a role Osiris took over in the Middle Kingdom. He was also an embalmer and attended the scale at the Weighing of the Heart, which decided whether a soul could enter the realm of the dead. He was depicted in black, a colour of regeneration and of the soil of the Nile.

entries.name: Sphinx
entries.desc: A sphinx is a mythical creature with the head of a human and the body of a lion, in some traditions with the wings of an eagle. In Greek tradition the sphinx is a merciless female being who asks those she meets a riddle and kills and eats those who fail, as in the myth and drama of Oedipus. In Egyptian mythology the sphinx is usually male and wingless, a benevolent image of strength, often of a pharaoh; the largest is the Great Sphinx of Giza, whose head most Egyptologists take to bear the likeness of Khafre, dating it to between 2600 and 2500 BCE. Statues of sphinxes guarded the entrances of temples and tombs, and the figure revived in European decorative art during the Renaissance.

entries.name: Prometheus
entries.desc: Prometheus is a Titan of Greek mythology who defied the Olympian gods by stealing fire and giving it to humanity; in several versions he also created humans from clay. The oldest record of him is in the late 8th-century BCE poet Hesiod's Theogony, where he is a son of the Titan Iapetus and a brother of Atlas and Epimetheus. Zeus punished him by binding him to a rock, where an eagle ate his liver, which grew back overnight; in several versions, most notably Hesiod's, the hero Heracles eventually freed him. His cult centred mainly on Athens, and in the Romantic era he came to stand for the lone genius, as in The Modern Prometheus, the alternate title of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818).

entries.name: Normans
entries.desc: The Normans were a people of the medieval Duchy of Normandy who arose from the intermingling of Norse Viking settlers with the inhabitants of West Francia. Their settlement was legitimized when the Viking leader Rollo swore fealty to King Charles III after the siege of Chartres in 911, and the settlers adopted the language, religion and customs of the West Franks. Under their duke William the Conqueror they conquered England at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, while Norman adventurers took southern Italy and Malta and helped found the Kingdom of Sicily under Roger II; Bohemond I founded the Principality of Antioch. In 1204 Philip II of France seized mainland Normandy.

entries.name: Maurice Ravel
entries.desc: Maurice Ravel was a French composer, pianist and conductor, born in the Basque town of Ciboure near Biarritz, who is often associated with Impressionism alongside Claude Debussy, though both rejected the term. At the Paris Conservatoire he was not well regarded by its conservative establishment, whose biased treatment of him caused a scandal, and he went on to develop a style of great clarity drawing on modernism, baroque, neoclassicism and later jazz. His works include Gaspard de la nuit (1908), Daphnis et Chloé (1912), two piano concertos and his best-known piece, Boléro (1928), and his 1922 orchestration of Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition. He died in 1937.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.desc: Henry David Thoreau was an American essayist, poet and philosopher, born in Concord, Massachusetts, and a leading transcendentalist. From July 1845 he spent two years in a small house he had built on land owned by Ralph Waldo Emerson by Walden Pond, the experiment in simple living he recounted in Walden (1854). His essay Civil Disobedience, first published as Resistance to Civil Government, argued for disobedience to an unjust state and later influenced Leo Tolstoy, Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. A lifelong abolitionist, he attacked the fugitive slave law and defended John Brown, and his writings on natural history anticipated ecology. He died of tuberculosis in 1862.

entries.name: Georgy Zhukov
entries.desc: Georgy Zhukov was a Soviet military leader and Marshal of the Soviet Union who served as deputy commander-in-chief of the armed forces under Joseph Stalin in World War II. After fighting in World War I and the Russian Civil War, he defeated Japanese forces at the Battles of Khalkhin Gol in 1939. Against Germany he took part in the actions at Leningrad, Moscow, Stalingrad and Kursk, and in 1945 his 1st Belorussian Front led the Vistula–Oder Offensive and he oversaw the Soviet victory at the Battle of Berlin, after which he accepted the German Instrument of Surrender. Stripped of his positions by Stalin after the war, he became Defence Minister in 1955 but was forced to retire in 1957.

entries.name: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
aka: Jean-Baptiste Pierre Antoine de Monet, chevalier de Lamarck
entries.desc: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was a French naturalist, biologist and soldier, born in Bazentin in Picardy, who was an early proponent of the idea that biological evolution occurred according to natural laws. After fighting in the Seven Years' War he turned to botany, published Flore française in 1778 and became a professor of zoology at the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle on its founding in 1793. He coined the term invertebrates, and in 1802 he was one of the first to use the word biology in its modern sense. His Philosophie zoologique (1809) set out the first cohesive theory of biological evolution, now remembered for the inheritance of acquired characteristics.

entries.name: Alfred Russel Wallace
entries.desc: Alfred Russel Wallace was an English naturalist and explorer, born in Llanbadoc, Monmouthshire, who independently conceived the theory of evolution through natural selection. His 1858 paper on the subject was published alongside extracts from Charles Darwin's writings, which spurred Darwin to write the abstract published in 1859 as On the Origin of Species. After fieldwork in the Amazon River basin he worked in the Malay Archipelago, where he identified the faunal divide now called the Wallace Line, and he is sometimes called the father of biogeography. He also became a socialist and an advocate of spiritualism, and described his travels in The Malay Archipelago (1869).

entries.name: Jean Le Rond d'Alembert
entries.desc: Jean Le Rond d'Alembert was a French mathematician, physicist, philosopher and music theorist who was co-editor of the Encyclopédie with Denis Diderot until 1759. Born in Paris as the natural son of the writer Claudine Guérin de Tencin, he was left by his mother on the steps of the church of Saint-Jean-le-Rond, after which he was named, and raised by the wife of a glazier. He was elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1741 and in 1743 published his Traité de dynamique, in which he set out his own laws of motion. He wrote over a thousand articles for the Encyclopédie, including its Preliminary Discourse, and is known for the wave equation and the formula that solves it.

entries.name: Joseph
entries.desc: Joseph is a figure of the Bible's Book of Genesis, the first of the two sons of Jacob and Rachel and the founder of the Tribe of Joseph among the Israelites. According to Genesis, his envious brothers sold him into slavery in Egypt, where he was imprisoned until he correctly interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh, rose to second-in-command and saved Egypt during a famine. Jacob's family then settled in the Land of Goshen, so that his story explains Israel's residence in Egypt. Scholars differ on its historical background and on the date and development of its composition. In Islam, as Yusuf, he is regarded as a prophet, and Christian tradition often reads him as a precursor of Jesus.

entries.name: Avesta
entries.desc: The Avesta is the corpus of religious texts of Zoroastrianism, composed in the Avestan language and containing the oldest texts in any Iranian language. Its texts were oral compositions made over several centuries, possibly between the 15th and the 4th century BCE, and fall into an Old Avestan layer and a later Young Avestan one, which forms most of what survives. They were first written down in the Sasanian era (224 to 651 CE), when the Avestan alphabet was created and a multi-volume Sasanian Avesta compiled. That edition was lost after the Islamic conquest of Iran; the surviving manuscripts, the oldest from 1323 CE, hold ritual texts such as the Yasna, Visperad and Vendidad.

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.desc: Michel de Montaigne was a writer of the French Renaissance who popularised the essay as a literary genre, born on his wealthy family's estate, the Château de Montaigne near Bordeaux, and brought up by his father's plan with Latin as his first language. After giving up his magistracy in Bordeaux, he retired by 1571 to the tower of his château, where among some 1,500 volumes he wrote the Essais, first published in 1580, which merge anecdote and autobiography with reflection. Elected mayor of Bordeaux in 1581, he was admired in his lifetime more as a statesman than as an author, and he is best known for his sceptical remark What do I know? He died at his château in 1592.

entries.name: Mikhail Lermontov
entries.desc: Mikhail Lermontov was a Russian Romantic writer, poet and painter, born in Moscow and raised by his grandmother at Tarkhany, who became the most important Russian poet after the death of Alexander Pushkin in 1837. After the Moscow University's boarding school he joined the Life-Guard Hussar regiment in Saint Petersburg. His poem Death of the Poet, written after Pushkin's death, brought him fame and his first exile to the Caucasus, a region that shaped much of his work and earned him the name the poet of the Caucasus. His novel A Hero of Our Time, printed in full in 1840, helped found the tradition of the Russian psychological novel. He was killed in a duel with Nikolai Martynov in 1841.

entries.name: Georges Bizet
entries.desc: Georges Bizet was a French composer of the Romantic era, born in Paris in 1838, whose final opera, Carmen, became one of the most frequently performed works in the opera repertoire. A student at the Conservatoire de Paris, he won the Prix de Rome in 1857, but the Paris opera theatres preferred the established repertoire, and he lived mainly by arranging the music of others. Neither Les pêcheurs de perles nor La jolie fille de Perth was an immediate success, though his suite from the music for Alphonse Daudet's L'Arlésienne was. Carmen opened on 3 March 1875; Bizet, convinced it had failed, died of a heart attack three months later.

entries.name: Baháʼu'lláh
entries.desc: Baháʼu'lláh, born Ḥusayn-ʻAlí to an aristocratic family in Iran, was the religious leader who founded the Baháʼí Faith. At 27 he accepted the claim of the Báb and became an outspoken supporter of Bábism; imprisoned in the Síyáh-Chál dungeon, he was banished from Iran, and in 1863, in Ottoman Iraq, he first announced his claim to a revelation from God. The Ottoman authorities held him under house arrest in Edirne for four years and then in the prison-city of Acre, and his last years were spent at the Mansion of Bahjí outside Acre. He wrote at least 1,500 letters, among them the Hidden Words, the Kitáb-i-Íqán and the Kitáb-i-Aqdas.

entries.name: Abu Bakr al-Razi
aka: Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakariyyāʾ al-Rāzī
entries.desc: Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, known in Latin as Rhazes, was a Persian Muslim physician, philosopher and alchemist of the Islamic Golden Age, born in the city of Ray. He studied medicine in Baghdad and served as chief physician of hospitals in Baghdad and Ray, and with Thābit ibn Qurra he was among the first physicians to distinguish clinically between smallpox and measles. He is credited with more than 200 works; his medical encyclopaedia Ḥāwī (Continens), completed by his pupils, was translated into Latin in 1279 and printed five times between 1488 and 1542, shaping medieval European medicine. In philosophy he gave reason a high place and was critical of prophethood and revelation.

entries.name: Mikhail Lomonosov
entries.desc: Mikhail Vasilyevich Lomonosov was a Russian polymath, scientist and writer, born in the village of Mishaninskaya in the far north of Russia, the son of a peasant fisherman turned ship owner. In 1730 he walked to Moscow and entered the Slavic Greek Latin Academy, and from 1736 he studied in Germany, at the University of Marburg under Christian Wolff and then at Freiberg. Among his discoveries were the atmosphere of Venus and the law of conservation of mass in chemical reactions, and he worked in chemistry, physics, mineralogy, history and philology. In 1755 he joined Count Ivan Shuvalov in founding Moscow University and, as a poet, shaped the modern Russian literary language.

entries.name: Évariste Galois
entries.desc: Évariste Galois was a French mathematician and political activist who in his teens found a necessary and sufficient condition for a polynomial to be solvable by radicals, a problem open for 350 years. After failing the entrance examination of the École Polytechnique he entered the École normale; his memoirs on equation theory were never published in his lifetime. A staunch Republican active around the French Revolution of 1830, he was arrested repeatedly and served one sentence of several months. Soon after his release he died of wounds from a duel fought on 30 May 1832, for reasons that remain obscure. His work laid the foundations for Galois theory and group theory.

entries.name: Gnosticism
entries.desc: Gnosticism is an umbrella term used by modern scholars for religious and philosophical ideas and systems that fully developed by the mid-second century among sects of early Christianity and other faiths. Gnostic groups set personal spiritual knowledge (gnosis) above religious authority and typically distinguished a hidden supreme being from a flawed demiurge who created the material world. Among them were the Sethians, Valentinians, Basilideans and Marcionists. Early Church Fathers denounced Gnostic ideas as heresy, and efforts to destroy Gnostic texts were largely successful; the 1945 discovery of the Nag Hammadi library in Egypt renewed their study. Gnosticism survives through Mandaeism.

entries.name: Yalta Conference
entries.desc: The Yalta Conference, held 4–11 February 1945 near Yalta in Crimea, was the World War II meeting of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Prime Minister Winston Churchill and General Secretary Joseph Stalin on postwar Germany and Europe. The three agreed that Germany and Berlin would be split into occupation zones, with a fourth for France, and that Poland's eastern border would follow the Curzon Line, with compensation in the west from Germany. Stalin pledged that the Soviet Union would enter the Pacific War three months after the defeat of Germany and join the United Nations. With the Cold War dividing Europe, the conference became a subject of intense controversy.

entries.name: Béla Bartók
entries.desc: Béla Bartók was a Hungarian composer, pianist and ethnomusicologist, born in 1881 in Nagyszentmiklós in the Kingdom of Hungary, now Sânnicolau Mare in Romania. He studied at the Royal Academy of Music in Budapest, where he met Zoltán Kodály, and after hearing Lidi Dósa sing folk songs in 1904 he devoted himself to folk music, whose collection and study made him one of the founders of comparative musicology, later known as ethnomusicology. His works include the opera Bluebeard's Castle, the ballet The Miraculous Mandarin, the Concerto for Orchestra and six string quartets. He emigrated to the United States in October 1940 and died in New York City on 26 September 1945.

entries.name: Thomas Robert Malthus
entries.desc: Thomas Robert Malthus was an English economist, Anglican cleric and scholar of political economy and demography. In An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798) he argued that gains in food production were temporary because they led to population growth, which brought the lower class hardship, want, war, famine and disease, a view later called the Malthusian trap. He criticised the Poor Laws, supported the Corn Laws, and from 1805 was Professor of History and Political Economy at the East India Company College in Hertfordshire. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace read his work, while his failure to predict the Industrial Revolution was a frequent criticism of his theories.

entries.name: Saint George
entries.desc: Saint George, also George of Lydda, was an early Christian martyr venerated as a saint. According to holy tradition he was a soldier of Cappadocian Greek origin in the Roman army and a member of the Praetorian Guard of the emperor Diocletian, sentenced to death during the Diocletianic Persecution for refusing to recant his faith. Very little is known of his life; the oldest tradition of his legend is a Coptic manuscript dated between 350 and 500, found at Qasr Ibrim in 1964. Venerated especially as a military saint since the Crusades and known from the legend of Saint George and the Dragon, he has been claimed as patron saint by England, Portugal, Georgia, Ethiopia and many other places.

entries.name: Fritz Haber
entries.desc: Fritz Haber was a German chemist, born in Breslau into a Jewish family, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918 for the Haber process, which synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen for fertilizers and explosives. During World War I he developed chlorine and other poisonous gases as weapons and proposed the use of chlorine gas at the Second Battle of Ypres, which earned him the name father of chemical warfare. His work was later used, without his involvement, to develop the Zyklon B pesticide used to kill more than 1 million Jews in the Holocaust. He resigned his post after the Nazis came to power in 1933 and died in Basel in 1934.

entries.name: Witchcraft
entries.desc: Witchcraft is the use of magic by a person called a witch, traditionally to inflict supernatural harm or misfortune on others. Belief in witches is attested from ancient Mesopotamia and has been found in a great many societies, which shunned, banished, punished or killed alleged witches. In medieval and early modern Europe the accused were usually women believed to have used maleficium against their own community, and the witch-hunts and witch trials of the early modern period led to tens of thousands of executions. European belief dwindled during and after the Age of Enlightenment; modern witch-hunting takes place in parts of Africa and Asia.

entries.name: Ayurveda
entries.desc: Ayurveda is an alternative medicine system with historical roots in the Indian subcontinent, its name meaning knowledge of life and longevity. Its terms and concepts appear in the Buddhist Canon from the middle of the first millennium BCE, and its main classical texts, among them the Sushruta Samhita, date in their present form to the first centuries CE. They describe three doshas, vāta, pitta and kapha, whose balance means health, divide medicine into eight components, and teach surgery including rhinoplasty. Its theory and practice are pseudoscientific, and many of its preparations contain toxic levels of lead, mercury and arsenic; it is heavily practised in India and Nepal.

entries.name: Classical antiquity
entries.desc: Classical antiquity is the period of European cultural history between the 8th century BCE and the 5th century CE, comprising the interwoven civilizations of ancient Greece and Rome, the Greco-Roman world. It is conventionally taken to begin with the earliest recorded epic poetry of Homer and to end with the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476. Greek culture, with some influences from the ancient Near East, was the basis of art, philosophy, society and education in the Mediterranean until the Roman imperial period, and the Romans spread it throughout Europe. Surviving fragments of classical culture helped produce the revival beginning in the 14th century later known as the Renaissance.

entries.name: Moors
entries.desc: Moor is a European exonym chiefly for the Muslim populations of North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula during the Middle Ages. The Moors were not a single or self-defined people: Europeans applied the name to Arabs, Berbers, Muslim Europeans and black peoples, and the word, with its racial connotations, has fallen out of fashion among scholars since the mid-20th century. It goes back through the Latin Mauri to the Berbers of Mauretania and was applied to the inhabitants of al-Andalus after Muslim Berbers and Arabs conquered the Iberian Peninsula in 711. After the fall of the Emirate of Granada in 1492, its Muslims were known as Moriscos until their expulsion from Spain in 1609.

entries.name: Hieronymus Bosch
entries.desc: Hieronymus Bosch, born Jheronimus van Aken, was a Dutch painter from Brabant and one of the most notable representatives of the Early Netherlandish painting school. He spent most of his life in 's-Hertogenbosch, which gave him his surname. His works, generally oil on oak wood, mainly illustrate religious concepts and narratives, with macabre depictions of hell, and were collected in the Netherlands, Austria and Spain in his lifetime. Only about 25 paintings and eight drawings are confidently identified as his; his most acclaimed works are three triptych altarpieces, particularly The Garden of Earthly Delights. Pieter Bruegel the Elder was his best-known follower.

entries.name: Jacques-Louis David
entries.desc: Jacques-Louis David was a French painter in the Neoclassical style, born in Paris in 1748, whose history paintings of the 1780s turned taste from Rococo toward classical austerity. A pupil of Joseph-Marie Vien, he won the Prix de Rome in 1774 and painted the Oath of the Horatii in Rome in 1784. A supporter of the French Revolution and a friend of Maximilien Robespierre, he voted in the National Convention for the death of Louis XVI and painted The Death of Marat; imprisoned after Robespierre's fall, he later served Napoleon, painting Napoleon Crossing the Alps and The Coronation of Napoleon. After the Bourbon revival he exiled himself to Brussels, where he remained until his death.

entries.name: Otto Hahn
entries.desc: Otto Hahn was a German chemist, born in Frankfurt am Main, who pioneered radiochemistry and is called the father of nuclear chemistry. After working under William Ramsay and Ernest Rutherford, he became head in 1912 of the Radioactivity Department of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry, where with Lise Meitner he discovered isotopes of radium, thorium, protactinium and uranium. In 1938 Hahn, Meitner, Otto Frisch and Fritz Strassmann discovered nuclear fission, for which Hahn alone received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. An opponent of Nazism, he still worked on the German nuclear weapons program; he was founding president of the Max Planck Society from 1948 to 1960.

entries.name: Perseus
entries.desc: In Greek mythology, Perseus is the founder of the Perseid dynasty and, with Cadmus and Bellerophon, the chief Greek hero and slayer of monsters before the days of Heracles. The son of Zeus and the mortal Danaë, he was cast into the sea with his mother by her father, King Acrisius of Argos, whom an oracle had warned he would be killed by his grandson, and was raised on Seriphos by the fisherman Dictys. He beheaded the Gorgon Medusa for King Polydectes and saved Andromeda from the sea monster Cetus. In one account he later killed Acrisius by accident with a quoit, fulfilling the oracle, and Pausanias asserts that the Greeks believed Perseus founded Mycenae.

entries.name: Australopithecus
entries.desc: Australopithecus is an extinct genus of early hominins that lived in Africa during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene, from some of whose species the genera Homo, Paranthropus and Kenyanthropus evolved. Its earliest known member, A. anamensis, lived in eastern Africa around 4.2 million years ago, and the genus became extinct 1.9 million years ago. Its species, among them A. afarensis, A. africanus and A. sediba, combined a small brain with developed bipedality, which upset the theory that large brain size had preceded bipedalism. The first specimen, the skull of the Taung Child, was found in 1924 at Taung, South Africa, and named Australopithecus africanus by Raymond Dart.

entries.name: Xia dynasty
entries.desc: The Xia dynasty is the first dynasty in traditional Chinese historiography, said to have been founded by Yu the Great after Shun, the last of the Five Emperors, gave him the throne. No contemporaneous records of the Xia survive; the earliest mentions are in the oldest chapters of the Book of Documents, from the early Western Zhou period. Traditional chronology places it between 2205 and 1766 BCE, while the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project proposed 2070 to 1600 BCE. Many Western historians consider it unsubstantiated, but most Chinese archaeologists identify it with the Erlitou culture. Tradition holds that its last king, Jie, was overthrown by Tang, founder of the Shang dynasty.

entries.name: Eastern Front (World War II)
entries.desc: The Eastern Front, also known as the Great Patriotic War or the German–Soviet War, was the theatre of the Second World War fought between the European Axis powers and the Allies, including the Soviet Union and Poland, from 22 June 1941 to 9 May 1945. It began with Operation Barbarossa, the Axis invasion of the Soviet Union, which came close to Moscow. Soviet victories at Stalingrad and Kursk and Operation Bagration turned the war, which ended with the capture of Berlin. Nazi Germany waged a war of annihilation, with mass deportations, starvation and massacres; around 30 million of the war's deaths occurred on this front.

entries.name: Rainer Maria Rilke
aka: René Karl Wilhelm Johann Josef Maria Rilke
entries.desc: Rainer Maria Rilke was an Austrian poet, born René Rilke in Prague, who became a significant writer in the German language and also wrote in French. He changed his first name to Rainer at the urging of Lou Andreas-Salomé, with whom he travelled twice to Russia. In 1912, at Duino Castle near Trieste, he began the Duino Elegies, which he completed in February 1922 at the Château de Muzot in Switzerland, where he also wrote the Sonnets to Orpheus. His other works include the novel The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge and the posthumous Letters to a Young Poet. He died of leukemia in December 1926.

entries.name: August Strindberg
entries.desc: August Strindberg was a Swedish playwright, novelist, poet, essayist and painter, born in Stockholm, who wrote more than 60 plays and more than 30 works of fiction, autobiography, history and politics. His The Red Room (1879) has often been described as the first modern Swedish novel. In The Father (1887), Miss Julie (1888) and Creditors (1889) he wrote naturalistic dramas. After a series of apparent psychotic attacks between 1894 and 1896, his so-called Inferno crisis, he turned to dream plays such as To Damascus and A Dream Play (1902), a precursor of expressionism and surrealism. From 1907 he helped run the Intimate Theatre in Stockholm.

entries.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
entries.desc: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was an English poet, literary critic, philosopher and theologian, born at Ottery St Mary in Devon, who was a founder of the Romantic Movement in England and one of the Lake Poets with his friend William Wordsworth. He wrote The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and Kubla Khan, and the prose work Biographia Literaria. His criticism of William Shakespeare was influential, he helped introduce German idealist philosophy to England, and he coined the phrase suspension of disbelief. Treated with laudanum for anxiety, depression and ill health, he had a lifelong opium addiction. He influenced Ralph Waldo Emerson and American transcendentalism.

entries.name: Leopold II of Belgium
entries.desc: Leopold II was the second king of the Belgians from 1865 to 1909 and sovereign of the Congo Free State from 1885 to 1908. Born in Brussels, the son of Leopold I, he commissioned so many buildings and public works that Belgians call him the Builder King. With the help of Henry Morton Stanley he claimed the Congo, which the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 granted him as his own colony. He ruled it through the mercenary Force Publique, first for ivory and then for rubber harvested by forced labour, with torture, murder and the cutting off of hands. Estimates of the Congolese population decline under his rule range from 1 million to 15 million.

entries.name: Medusa
entries.desc: In Greek mythology, Medusa was one of the three Gorgons, usually described as daughters of Phorcys and Ceto, and the only one of them who was mortal. She is generally described as a woman with living snakes for hair, whose appearance turned anyone who looked upon her to stone. The hero Perseus beheaded her while looking at her reflection in a mirrored shield from Athena, and the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor sprang from her body. Perseus used the head as a weapon before giving it to Athena for her shield. In a late version by the Roman poet Ovid, she was a beautiful maiden whom the goddess punished by turning her hair into snakes.

entries.name: Migration Period
entries.desc: The Migration Period, also known as the Barbarian Invasions, was a period of European history and late antiquity, from about 300 to 600, marked by large-scale migrations that saw the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the founding of post-Roman kingdoms on its former lands. It is traditionally dated from the invasion of Europe by the Huns in about 375 to the Lombards' conquest of Italy in 568. Among the peoples who moved were the Goths, Vandals, Burgundians, Alemanni, Alans, Franks, Anglo-Saxons, early Slavs, Avars and Bulgars. Modern estimates suggest that between roughly 500,000 and over 1,000,000 people migrated into Roman territory in all.

entries.name: Nathaniel Hawthorne
entries.desc: Nathaniel Hawthorne was an American novelist and short story writer, born in Salem, Massachusetts, whose works often focus on history, morality and religion. After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 he published the novel Fanshawe in 1828, which he later tried to suppress, and collected his stories as Twice-Told Tales in 1837. He worked at the Boston Custom House and joined the transcendentalist community of Brook Farm before marrying Sophia Peabody in 1842. The Scarlet Letter appeared in 1850. Much of his fiction centres on New England and belongs to dark romanticism; he also wrote a campaign biography of his college friend Franklin Pierce.

entries.name: Harriet Beecher Stowe
entries.desc: Harriet Beecher Stowe was an American author and abolitionist, born in Litchfield, Connecticut, the daughter of the Calvinist preacher Lyman Beecher. In 1832 she moved to Cincinnati, where she met African Americans who had suffered in attacks on the city's Black residents, and in 1836 she married Calvin Ellis Stowe. Her novel Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852), which depicts the harsh conditions of enslaved African Americans, reached millions as a novel and play, energising anti-slavery forces in the North and provoking anger in the South. She wrote over 30 books and met President Abraham Lincoln in 1862. She died in Hartford, Connecticut.

entries.name: Pope Leo I
entries.desc: Pope Leo I, also known as Leo the Great, was a Roman aristocrat who served as Bishop of Rome from 29 September 440 until his death in 461. He developed ideas of papal authority, grounding them in the apostolic succession of the bishop of Rome from Saint Peter. In 452 he met Attila the Hun and persuaded him to turn back from his invasion of Italy, though scholars debate how large a part his authority played. At the Council of Chalcedon his Tome of Leo set out the union of Christ's divine and human natures in one person. Pope Benedict XIV named him a Doctor of the Church.

entries.name: Lord Kelvin
entries.desc: William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin, was a British mathematician, mathematical physicist and engineer, born in Belfast, who was professor of Natural Philosophy at the University of Glasgow for 53 years. He helped formulate the first and second laws of thermodynamics and determined the value of absolute zero as about −273.15 degrees Celsius; the kelvin unit of temperature is named in his honour. For his work on the transatlantic telegraph he was knighted in 1866, and in 1892 he became the first scientist raised to the House of Lords. He served as president of the Royal Society from 1890 to 1895 and died at Largs in 1907.

entries.name: Henry Cavendish
entries.desc: Henry Cavendish was an English experimental and theoretical chemist and physicist, born in Nice, a grandson of William Cavendish, 2nd Duke of Devonshire, who was known for his reclusive personality and the precision of his research. In a 1766 paper, On Factitious Airs, he described hydrogen, which he called inflammable air, and its forming water on combustion; Antoine Lavoisier later gave the element its name. In 1797–1798 at Clapham Common he used a torsion balance built by John Michell to measure the density of the Earth, finding it 5.48 times that of water, in what is now called the Cavendish experiment. He died one of the wealthiest men in Britain.

entries.name: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov
entries.desc: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov was a Russian composer and a member of the group known as The Five, whose orchestral works Capriccio Espagnol, the Russian Easter Festival Overture and Scheherazade remain staples of the classical repertoire, along with parts of his fifteen operas. He served as an officer in the Imperial Russian Navy and later as Inspector of Naval Bands. From 1871 he was professor at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory, where he taught himself Western methods and trained a generation of composers. He prepared works by The Five, including Modest Mussorgsky's, for performance, and his style influenced Maurice Ravel, Claude Debussy and Ottorino Respighi.

entries.name: John D. Rockefeller
entries.desc: John D. Rockefeller was an American businessman and philanthropist, born in Upstate New York, who founded the Standard Oil Company in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1870 and ran it until 1897. By 1900 Standard Oil controlled about 90% of the nation's oil production. The company, criticised by writers such as Ida Tarbell, was ordered dismantled by the Supreme Court in 1911 and broken into 34 entities. Rockefeller became the country's first billionaire in 1916. In retirement he funded medicine, education and research through foundations, which helped nearly eradicate hookworm in the American South, and founded the University of Chicago and Rockefeller University.

entries.name: Santiago Ramón y Cajal
entries.desc: Santiago Ramón y Cajal was a Spanish neuroscientist, pathologist and histologist, born in Petilla de Aragón in Navarre, whose studies of the microscopic structure of the brain made him a pioneer of modern neuroscience. After studying medicine at the University of Zaragoza he served as an army medical officer in Cuba in 1874–1875. In Barcelona from 1887 he improved Golgi's staining method and drew neurons of many species, work that supported the neuron doctrine. In 1906 he and Camillo Golgi received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, making him the first Spaniard to win a scientific Nobel Prize. His drawings are still used in teaching.

entries.name: 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami
entries.desc: The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami began on 26 December 2004, when an undersea megathrust earthquake of magnitude 9.2–9.3 struck off the west coast of Aceh in northern Sumatra, Indonesia, along the boundary between the Burma plate and the Indian plate. It had the longest fault rupture ever observed, 1,200 to 1,300 kilometres, and caused a tsunami with waves up to 30 m high. The tsunami killed an estimated 227,898 people in 14 countries, especially in Aceh, Sri Lanka, Tamil Nadu and Khao Lak in Thailand, the deadliest tsunami in history. Donations to the humanitarian response totalled more than US$14 billion.
