entries.name: Ilya Repin
entries.desc: Ilya Repin was a Ukrainian-born Russian painter, born in Chuguev, who became one of the best-known artists in Russia in the 19th century. After study at the Imperial Academy of Arts in Saint Petersburg, a commission from Grand Duke Vladimir Alexandrovich for Barge Haulers on the Volga (1873) launched his career. His works include Religious Procession in Kursk Province, Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan (1885), which caused a scandal, and Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks, and portraits of Modest Mussorgsky and Leo Tolstoy. In 1898 he built a country house, the Penates, at Kuokkala in Finland, where he died in 1930.

entries.name: Johann Strauss II
entries.desc: Johann Strauss II was an Austrian composer of light music and a violinist, born near Vienna, the son of the composer Johann Strauss I, who wrote over 500 waltzes, polkas, quadrilles and marches, several operettas and a ballet. Known in his lifetime as The Waltz King, he did much to popularise the waltz in the 19th century. He made his debut, against his father's wishes, at Dommayer's Casino in Hietzing in October 1844. His best-known works include The Blue Danube, the Emperor Waltz and Tales from the Vienna Woods, and the operettas Die Fledermaus and Der Zigeunerbaron. He died in Vienna in 1899 while composing the ballet Aschenbrödel.

entries.name: Ramakrishna
entries.desc: Ramakrishna was an Indian Hindu mystic, born in Kamarpukur in the Bengal Presidency, who became a priest at the Dakshineshwar Kali Temple in Calcutta at around the age of twenty. A devotee of the goddess Kali, he also followed practices of Vaishnavism, Tantric Shaktism and Advaita Vedanta, as well as Christianity and Sufi Islam, and taught through parables that the world's religions are paths to one goal. In 1859 he married Sarada Devi, and in 1865 the monk Tota Puri initiated him into sannyasa. He founded the monastic Ramakrishna Order and died of throat cancer in 1886; his followers regard him as an avatar.

entries.name: George Boole
entries.desc: George Boole was an English mathematician and philosopher, born in Lincoln in 1815, who transformed logic from a philosophical study of language into a mathematical system of algebraic equations. The son of a shoemaker, he was largely self-taught, began teaching at 16 and ran his own schools before becoming in 1849 the first professor of mathematics at Queen’s College, Cork. His Mathematical Analysis of Logic and The Laws of Thought (1854) set out Boolean algebra, which Claude Shannon and Victor Shestakov later applied to relay circuits, leading to digital computers. He died in 1864 after developing pneumonia.

entries.name: Icon
entries.desc: An icon is a religious work of art, most often a painting on a wood panel in egg tempera, in the cultures of the Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, Catholic and Lutheran churches. Its usual subjects are Jesus, Mary, saints and angels, though the term also covers narrative scenes from the Bible and the lives of saints. Orthodox tradition holds that Christian images go back to the earliest days of the faith, while modern art history traces the tradition only to the 3rd century. The widespread destruction of images in the Byzantine Iconoclasm of 726–842 settled the question of their use, and icons have since kept a great continuity of style and subject.

entries.name: Fertile Crescent
entries.desc: The Fertile Crescent is a crescent-shaped region of the Middle East spanning modern Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine and Syria, together with northern Kuwait, south-eastern Turkey and western Iran. It is believed to be the first region where settled farming emerged, and it was home to the eight Neolithic founder crops, among them emmer wheat, einkorn, barley and lentil, and to four of the five most important domesticated animals. Early civilisations such as Sumer in Mesopotamia flourished there, and irrigation, writing, the wheel and glass first appeared in the region. The archaeologist James Henry Breasted popularised the term in 1914 and 1916.

entries.name: Nuremberg trials
entries.desc: The Nuremberg trials were international criminal trials held by France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States against leaders of defeated Nazi Germany for invasions and atrocities in the Second World War. Between 20 November 1945 and 1 October 1946 the International Military Tribunal tried 22 of the most important surviving Nazi leaders and six German organisations; twelve defendants, among them Göring, Ribbentrop and Keitel, were sentenced to death. The United States held twelve further trials of lower-level perpetrators. Controversial for criminalising aggression retroactively, the trials are considered the beginning of international criminal law.

entries.name: Rwandan genocide
entries.desc: The Rwandan genocide, also known as the genocide against Tutsi, took place from 7 April to 19 July 1994, during the Rwandan Civil War: Hutu militias systematically killed members of the Tutsi ethnic group as well as some moderate Hutu and Twa. Most scholarly estimates put the Tutsi dead at between 500,000 and 662,000, with 250,000 to 500,000 cases of rape. It began after the assassination of President Juvénal Habyarimana on 6 April 1994. The international community failed to intervene; the Rwandan Patriotic Front ended the genocide by capturing all government-controlled territory, and the flight of the génocidaires into Zaire contributed to the First Congo War in 1996.

entries.name: Nicolas Poussin
entries.desc: Nicolas Poussin was a leading painter of the classical French Baroque style who spent most of his working life in Rome. Born near Les Andelys in Normandy, he went to Paris around 1612 and in 1624 travelled to Rome, where he studied Renaissance and Baroque painters, above all Raphael, and found patrons such as Cardinal Francesco Barberini and Cassiano dal Pozzo. He returned to France in 1640 as First Painter to the King but went back to Rome after little more than a year. His religious, mythological and later landscape paintings favour line over colour, and he inspired Jacques-Louis David, Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres and Paul Cézanne. He died in Rome in 1665.

entries.name: Lesya Ukrainka
entries.desc: Lesya Ukrainka, born Larysa Petrivna Kosach in Novohrad-Volynskyi in 1871, was one of the foremost writers of Ukrainian literature, best known for her poems and plays, and an activist for political, civil and women's rights. The daughter of the writer Olena Pchilka and niece of Mykhailo Drahomanov, she grew up in a household where only Ukrainian was spoken and wrote her first poem at eight. Her works include the collections On the Wings of Songs (1893) and Thoughts and Dreams (1899) and the plays Cassandra, In the Catacombs (1905) and Forest Song (1911). Ill with tuberculosis from childhood, she died on 1 August 1913.

entries.name: Adi Shankara
entries.desc: Adi Shankara, also called Adi Shankaracharya, was an Indian Vedic scholar-monk, philosopher and teacher of Advaita Vedanta who lived in the 8th century CE. He wrote commentaries on the Brahma sutras, ten principal Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita, centred on the liberating knowledge that the individual self is Ātman-Brahman. Reliable information on his life is scant: the oldest hagiographies place his birth at Kaladi in Kerala, and the Shankara of legend who toured the subcontinent defeating opponents in debate and founding four mathas was created in the 14th century. Over 300 texts are attributed to him, most likely by others, and the title Shankaracharya derives from his name.

entries.name: Francis I of France
entries.desc: Francis I was King of France from 1515 until his death in 1547, the son of Charles, Count of Angoulême, and Louise of Savoy, and the successor of his father-in-law Louis XII. A patron of the arts, he drew Italian artists to France, among them Leonardo da Vinci, and promoted the French Renaissance and the French language. His reign saw the growth of central power, the spread of humanism and Protestantism, and the voyages of Jacques Cartier to the Americas. He continued the Italian Wars against Emperor Charles V, was captured at the Battle of Pavia and afterwards formed a Franco-Ottoman alliance with the Ottoman sultan Suleiman.

entries.name: Yom Kippur
entries.desc: Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the holiest day of the year in Judaism, held on the 10th of Tishrei, in late September or early October. Its main observances are a full fast and asceticism, with extended prayer services, usually in synagogue, and confessions of sin; with Rosh Hashanah it makes up the High Holy Days and closes the Ten Days of Repentance. The Torah commands it in Leviticus and Numbers, and while the Temple in Jerusalem stood the day had an elaborate sacrificial service, in which one of two goats was sent to Azazel, the origin of the term scapegoat.

entries.name: Heraldry
entries.desc: Heraldry is the discipline of the design, display, study and transmission of armorial bearings: a coat of arms on a shield, with helmet, crest and such devices as supporters, badges and mottoes, formally described in a blazon. Devices marking people and groups go back to antiquity, but regular hereditary designs developed only in the High Middle Ages; seals dating from between 1135 and 1155 show heraldic devices in England, France, Germany, Spain and Italy. In 1484 England's royal heralds were incorporated into the College of Arms. Heraldry outlived the abandonment of armour in the seventeenth century and is still used by people, towns and organisations.

entries.name: Ögedei Khan
entries.desc: Ögedei Khan was the second khan of the Mongol Empire and the third son of Genghis Khan, whose expansion he continued. He made his military reputation in the invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire, capturing Gurganj in 1221, and was elected khan in 1229 after a two-year regency under his brother Tolui. His reign saw the start of the Mongol invasions of Korea in 1231, the conquest of the Jin dynasty in 1234 and campaigns under Batu Khan and Subutai that defeated Poland and Hungary. With officials such as Yelü Chucai he organised taxation and regional bureaucracies, and he founded the capital Karakorum in the 1230s. He died in 1241 and was succeeded by his son Güyük.

entries.name: Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Frederick II was King of Sicily from 1198, King of Germany from 1212, Holy Roman Emperor from 1220 and King of Jerusalem from 1225 to 1228, the son of Emperor Henry VI of the Hohenstaufen dynasty and Constance I of Sicily. In the Kingdom of Sicily he built an early absolutist state run by a secular bureaucracy, and his court in Palermo fostered the Sicilian School of poetry. Frequently at war with the papacy, he was excommunicated four times, and Pope Innocent IV called him the forerunner of the Antichrist. Known as Stupor mundi, he died of dysentery at Castel Fiorentino in Apulia in 1250, and the House of Hohenstaufen soon came to an end.

entries.name: Joseph Priestley
entries.desc: Joseph Priestley was an English chemist, natural philosopher, Unitarian theologian and political theorist who published over 150 works. He is credited with the independent discovery of oxygen, which he isolated in 1774 and called dephlogisticated air, and with the invention of carbonated water but was isolated by his defence of phlogiston theory. He argued for equal rights for religious Dissenters, helped found Unitarianism in England and wrote the Essay on the First Principles of Government (1768). In 1791, after a mob burned down his Birmingham home and church, he fled to London and then to the United States, settling in Northumberland, Pennsylvania.

entries.name: Paracelsus
entries.desc: Paracelsus, born Theophrastus Bombast von Hohenheim at Einsiedeln in 1493, was a Swiss physician, alchemist, lay theologian and philosopher of the German Renaissance. He studied medicine at the University of Basel and in Vienna, took his doctorate at the University of Ferrara, and between 1517 and 1524 travelled widely across Europe, serving as an army surgeon. A pioneer of the medical revolution of the Renaissance, he stressed observation alongside received wisdom and is credited as the father of toxicology. His Prognostications were studied by Rosicrucians in the 17th century, and the medical movement inspired by his works is known as Paracelsianism. He died in Salzburg in 1541.

entries.name: Pilgrimage
entries.desc: A pilgrimage is a journey, often on foot, to a holy place of special significance to the followers of a religion, after which the pilgrim returns to daily life; the word pilgrim comes from the Latin peregrinus, one who has come from afar. The practice predates Christianity: the faiths of ancient Egypt, India, China and Japan knew it, in Greece people consulted the oracles at Dodona and Delphi, and early Hebrew pilgrims travelled to Shiloh, Dan, Bethel and Jerusalem. The Holy Land is a focus for Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and the Hajj, obligatory for Muslims who are able, draws two or three million people a year. Hindu pilgrims gather at holy cities, rivers and the Kumbh Mela.

entries.name: Heresy
entries.desc: Heresy is any belief or theory strongly at variance with established beliefs or customs, particularly the accepted beliefs or religious law of a religious organisation; its proponent is a heretic. The word comes from the Greek haíresis, choice. In Christianity Irenaeus gave it wide currency in his 2nd-century Against Heresies, and its first known legal use came in 380 with the Edict of Thessalonica of Theodosius I, which made Christianity the state church of the Roman Empire. Priscillian, condemned in 386, was the first Christian heretic to be executed. In Judaism, Christianity and Islam heresy has been met with censure ranging from excommunication to death.

entries.name: Thebes
entries.desc: Thebes, known to the ancient Egyptians as Waset, was a city on the Nile about 800 kilometres south of the Mediterranean, whose ruins lie within the modern city of Luxor. The main city of the fourth Upper Egyptian nome, it was the capital of Egypt for long periods of the Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom and a leading religious centre, known from the end of the New Kingdom as the City of Amun. The temples of Karnak and Luxor stand on the east bank, and the west bank holds a necropolis of royal and private tombs. The Greeks called it Diospolis, and Homer's Iliad Thebes of the Hundred Gates. Its ruins became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.

entries.name: Latin Empire
entries.desc: The Latin Empire, officially the Empire of Romania, was a feudal Crusader state founded by the leaders of the Fourth Crusade on lands captured from the Byzantine Empire, which lasted from 1204 to 1261. After the crusaders plundered Constantinople in April 1204, they chose Baldwin IX of Flanders as emperor and divided Byzantine territory into vassal states, with a Catholic emperor in place of the Orthodox one. Challenged by the Byzantine rump states of Nicaea, Trebizond and Epirus and at constant war with Bulgaria, it declined steadily, and in 1261 the Nicene Empire recovered Constantinople under Michael VIII Palaiologos. The last emperor, Baldwin II, went into exile.

entries.name: Christopher Wren
entries.desc: Sir Christopher Wren was an English architect, astronomer, mathematician and physicist, born at East Knoyle in Wiltshire in 1632 and known for his work in the English Baroque style. After the Great Fire of 1666 he was given responsibility for rebuilding 52 churches in the City of London, among them St Paul's Cathedral, completed in 1710, though the main creative work on several is now often attributed to others in his office, notably Nicholas Hawksmoor. He also designed the Royal Hospital Chelsea, the Old Royal Naval College at Greenwich and the south front of Hampton Court Palace. A founder of the Royal Society, he was its president from 1680 to 1682.

entries.name: Henry V of England
entries.desc: Henry V was King of England, Lord of Ireland and Duke of Aquitaine from 1413 until his death in 1422. The eldest son of Henry IV, he gained military experience in Wales against the Glyndŵr rebellion and fought at the Battle of Shrewsbury when only 16. In 1415 he renewed the war with France, besieged Harfleur and won at Agincourt, then from 1417 set out to conquer Normandy. The Treaty of Troyes of 1420 made him regent and heir to Charles VI, but Henry died in August 1422, seven weeks before Charles, and was succeeded by the infant Henry VI.

entries.name: Freyja
entries.desc: In Norse mythology Freyja, whose name means lady in Old Norse, is a goddess associated with love, beauty, fertility, war, gold and seiðr, a magic for seeing and influencing the future. A member of the Vanir with her twin brother Freyr and her father Njörðr, she owns the necklace Brísingamen, rides a chariot pulled by two cats and receives half of those who die in battle in her field Fólkvangr. She is attested in the Poetic Edda, in the Prose Edda and Heimskringla, composed by Snorri Sturluson, in sagas and in skaldic poetry, and rural Scandinavians still acknowledged her into the 19th century.

entries.name: Roman Kingdom
entries.desc: The Roman Kingdom was the earliest period of Roman history, when the city and its territory by the river Tiber in central Italy were ruled by kings. According to tradition it began with the founding of the city c. 753 BCE and ended with the overthrow of the kings and the establishment of the Roman Republic c. 509 BCE. The traditional account, handed down by Livy, Plutarch and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, names seven kings, the last being Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, who is said to have ruled as a tyrant. No contemporary records survive, and the later accounts are thought to rest largely on oral tradition.

entries.name: 2010 Haiti earthquake
entries.desc: The 2010 Haiti earthquake was a magnitude 7.0 earthquake that struck Haiti on 12 January 2010, with its epicentre near the town of Léogâne, about 25 kilometres west of the capital, Port-au-Prince. An estimated three million people were affected; estimates of the dead range from 100,000 to about 160,000, while the Haitian government gave 220,000 to 316,000, figures that are disputed. The Presidential Palace, the National Assembly building and the Port-au-Prince Cathedral were damaged or destroyed, and the collapse of the headquarters of the United Nations Stabilization Mission in Haiti killed its chief, Hédi Annabi.

entries.name: Anthony van Dyck
entries.desc: Sir Anthony van Dyck was a Flemish Baroque artist who became the leading court painter in England after success in the Spanish Netherlands and Italy. Born in Antwerp, he became a master in the Guild of Saint Luke there in 1617 and worked in the studio of Peter Paul Rubens. He stayed in Italy, mostly in Genoa, until 1627, was court painter to the Archduchess Isabella from 1630, and in 1632 returned to London as the main court painter of Charles I, who knighted him. Best known for his portraits of the aristocracy, he was the dominant influence on English portrait-painting for over 150 years and was buried in St Paul's Cathedral.

entries.name: George Gershwin
entries.desc: George Gershwin was an American composer and pianist whose works spanned jazz, popular and classical music. Born in Brooklyn to Jewish immigrants from the Russian Empire, he began as a song plugger and wrote Broadway theatre works with his brother Ira Gershwin. His works include Rhapsody in Blue (1924), An American in Paris (1928), the songs Swanee and I Got Rhythm, and the opera Porgy and Bess (1935), written with Ira and DuBose Heyward, which was at first a commercial failure. His Of Thee I Sing (1931) was the first musical to win the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. He moved to Hollywood to compose film scores and died of a brain tumor in 1937, aged 38.

entries.name: Andrew Carnegie
entries.desc: Andrew Carnegie was a Scottish-American industrialist and philanthropist who led the expansion of the American steel industry in the late 19th century. Born in Dunfermline, he emigrated with his parents in 1848, worked in a cotton mill and as a telegrapher, and invested in railroads, bridges and oil derricks. He built the Carnegie Steel Company in Pittsburgh and sold it to J. P. Morgan in 1901, when it formed the basis of U.S. Steel. In his 1889 article The Gospel of Wealth he called on the rich to use their wealth to improve society, and in the last 18 years of his life he gave away around $350 million, funding libraries, Carnegie Hall and the Peace Palace in The Hague.

entries.name: Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor
entries.desc: Francis II was the last Holy Roman Emperor, from 1792 to 1806, and as Francis I the first Emperor of Austria, from 1804 to 1835. Born in Florence, the son of Leopold II and Maria Luisa of Spain, he succeeded his father during the French Revolutionary Wars and led Austria against Napoleon through a series of defeats. After Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine he abdicated as Holy Roman Emperor in 1806, which in effect dissolved the empire, and after the defeat of the Fifth Coalition he had to marry his daughter Marie Louise to Napoleon. From 1813 he helped defeat Napoleon, and he was the first president of the German Confederation from 1815.

entries.name: Robert Baden-Powell
entries.desc: Robert Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell, was a British Army officer and writer who founded The Boy Scouts Association and, with his sister Agnes, The Girl Guides Association. He served in the army in India and Africa from 1876 until 1910, and during the Second Boer War in 1899 he defended the town in the Siege of Mafeking. In August 1907 he held an experimental camp on Brownsea Island to test his ideas for training boys, and in 1908 he published Scouting for Boys, which helped the rapid growth of the Scout Movement. He retired from guiding the two associations in 1937 and died in Nyeri, Kenya, in 1941.

credit.artist: File:General Baden-Powell, Bain news service photo portrait.jpg : James Russell & Sons [ 1 ] derivative work: Robertus Pius

entries.name: Louis Daguerre
entries.desc: Louis Daguerre was a French artist, scenic designer and photographer, known for inventing the daguerreotype process of photography. Born in Cormeilles-en-Parisis, he trained under the panorama painter Pierre Prévost and invented the diorama, which opened in Paris in July 1822. In 1829 he partnered with Nicéphore Niépce, and after Niépce's death in 1833 he developed a process in which a faint latent image on an iodised silver-plated copper sheet was chemically developed. The French Government acquired his rights in exchange for lifetime pensions and on 19 August 1839 presented the invention as a gift free to the world. He died at Bry-sur-Marne in 1851.

entries.name: Early modern period
entries.desc: The early modern period is a historical period of about 1500 to about 1800, defined chiefly from the history of Europe as the time after the Middle Ages and before the advent of modernity; its boundaries are not agreed. Proposed starting points include the Renaissance, the printing revolution of the 1440s, the Fall of Constantinople in 1453, the Age of Discovery and the Reformation, and its end is tied to the Industrial, American and French Revolutions. Historians have stressed the spread of globalization, mercantilism and the Scientific Revolution. The medieval historian Lynn Thorndike first proposed the term for a distinct period in 1926.

entries.name: Modern era
entries.desc: The modern era, or modern period, is considered the current period of human history. First applied in European history to what came after classical antiquity and the Middle Ages, often from around 1500, the term is now more often used for events from the 19th century onwards, the centuries before being called the early modern period, while the time since 1945 can also be called contemporary history. It is commonly associated with the French Revolution and the Industrial Revolution, with colonization by the European powers, and with individualism, capitalism, socialism and urbanization; postmodernism and postcolonial theory have criticised its belief in progress and Western dominance.

entries.name: Space exploration
entries.desc: Space exploration is the physical investigation of outer space by uncrewed robotic space probes and through human spaceflight, made possible by large rockets in the mid-twentieth century. Its early era was driven by a Space Race between the Soviet Union and the United States: the Soviet Sputnik 1 became the first human-made object to orbit Earth on 4 October 1957, Yuri Gagarin made the first human spaceflight aboard Vostok 1 in 1961, and the American Apollo 11 mission made the first Moon landing on 20 July 1969. From the 1970s the focus moved to reusable hardware such as the Space Shuttle and to cooperation, above all the International Space Station, built between 1998 and 2011.

entries.name: Benedict of Nursia
entries.desc: Benedict of Nursia, often known as Saint Benedict, was an Italian monk regarded as the founder of the Order of Saint Benedict. The son of a Roman noble of Nursia, he was sent to Rome to study but left it, and he founded twelve communities for monks at Subiaco before founding the monastery of Monte Cassino in 530. His Rule of Saint Benedict, influenced by John Cassian and close to the earlier Rule of the Master, was adopted by most religious communities founded in the Middle Ages and became one of the most influential in Western Christendom. The only ancient account of his life is in the Dialogues of Pope Gregory I; according to tradition he died on 21 March 547.

entries.name: Muhammad al-Bukhari
aka: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Bukhārī
entries.desc: Muhammad al-Bukhari was a 9th-century Muslim muhaddith from Bukhara, widely regarded as the most important hadith scholar in the history of Sunni Islam. He began studying hadith at the age of ten, travelled throughout the Abbasid Caliphate and is said to have examined more than 200,000 hadiths. His principal collection, the Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, compiled in 846, selected 7563 narrations including repetitions and arranged them by subject in ninety-seven books. With the Ṣaḥīḥ of his student Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj it is regarded by Sunnis as the principal compilation of reliable hadith. Near the end of his life he was exiled from Nishapur and moved to Khartank, near Samarkand.

entries.name: Ludwig Boltzmann
entries.desc: Ludwig Boltzmann was an Austrian mathematician and theoretical physicist whose chief achievements were the development of statistical mechanics and the statistical explanation of the second law of thermodynamics. Born in Erdberg, a suburb of Vienna, he studied at the University of Vienna under Josef Stefan and taught at Graz and Vienna. In 1877 he gave the current definition of entropy as a measure of the statistical disorder of a system, and Max Planck named the constant in it the Boltzmann constant. In his last years he defended his atomic theories against critics such as Ernst Mach, and he died by suicide at Duino, near Trieste, in 1906.

entries.name: Hungarian Revolution of 1956
entries.desc: The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was a countrywide revolt against the government of the Hungarian People's Republic and its subordination to the Soviet Union. It began in Budapest on 23 October 1956, when students marched to the Parliament and ÁVH police fired on protesters at the radio building; militias and workers' councils then took control in many places. The new government of Imre Nagy disbanded the ÁVH, declared Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact on 1 November and pledged free elections. Soviet troops moved in on 4 November and crushed the uprising; about 2,000 Hungarians and 700 Soviet soldiers were killed, and some 200,000 Hungarians fled abroad, mostly to Austria.

entries.name: J. M. W. Turner
entries.desc: Joseph Mallord William Turner was an English Romantic painter whose renditions of light, atmosphere and colour in landscape inspired the early impressionists Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro. Born in Covent Garden, London, the son of a barber, he was accepted at the Royal Academy of Arts at 14 and became a Royal Academician at 27. He produced about 550 oil paintings and over 2,000 watercolours, and his later, more abstract landscapes, such as Rain, Steam and Speed of 1844, were not well received at the time. He died a rich man in 1851 and bequeathed around 100 finished and 200 unfinished oil paintings to the nation, now shown at the National Gallery and Tate Britain.

entries.name: Willem Barentsz
entries.desc: Willem Barentsz was a Dutch navigator, cartographer and Arctic explorer, born around 1550 on the island of Terschelling. He led three expeditions in search of a Northeast passage to China: in 1594 and 1595 he reached Novaya Zemlya and the Kara Sea but was turned back by ice. On the third, in 1596, his crew discovered Bear Island and Spitsbergen, then became trapped by ice off Novaya Zemlya and wintered in a lodge built from driftwood and ship's timber, Het Behouden Huys. In June 1597 the survivors set out in two open boats, and Barentsz died on 20 June. The Barents Sea is named after him, and the lodge was found in 1871.

entries.name: Gottlob Frege
entries.desc: Gottlob Frege was a German philosopher, logician and mathematician who taught mathematics at the University of Jena and is regarded by many as the father of analytic philosophy. Born in Wismar, he developed modern logic in his Begriffsschrift of 1879 and argued in The Foundations of Arithmetic (1884) that arithmetic is a branch of logic. As the second volume of his Basic Laws of Arithmetic went to press in 1903, Bertrand Russell wrote to him showing that a paradox could be derived from its Basic Law V. Largely ignored in his lifetime, his work, including the paper On Sense and Reference, reached later philosophers through Peano, Russell and Wittgenstein.

entries.name: Thomas Young
entries.desc: Thomas Young was a British polymath, born in 1773 into a Quaker family of Milverton, Somerset, who made contributions to the study of vision, light, solid mechanics, energy, physiology, language, musical harmony and Egyptology. A physician by training, he lectured at the Royal Institution from 1801. With the ripple tank and a predecessor of the double-slit experiment he demonstrated interference, supporting Christiaan Huygens' wave theory of light against Isaac Newton's view of light as particles. He described Young's modulus in 1807, and from 1813 worked on the Rosetta Stone, where several scholars see his true contribution in the decipherment of the demotic script.

entries.name: Peter Abelard
entries.desc: Peter Abelard was a French philosopher, logician, theologian and poet, born at Le Pallet near Nantes, who became a popular lecturer in Paris and around 1115 master of the cathedral school of Notre Dame. His affair with his student Héloïse d'Argenteuil, their secret marriage and his castration by men sent by her uncle Fulbert drove him into the Abbey of Saint-Denis as a monk. His teaching on the Trinity was condemned at a synod at Soissons in 1121 and again at the council at Sens in 1141, after charges pressed by Bernard of Clairvaux, and Pope Innocent II excommunicated him. Peter the Venerable of Cluny took him in, and he died at the priory of St Marcel near Chalon-sur-Saône in 1142.

entries.name: Sri Aurobindo
entries.desc: Sri Aurobindo, born Aurobindo Ghosh in Calcutta in 1872, was an Indian philosopher, yogi and nationalist. After study at King's College, Cambridge, he served the princely state of Baroda from 1893 and moved into nationalist politics in Bengal, advocating complete autonomy from British rule. Arrested in May 1908 in the Alipore Bomb Case, he was acquitted on 6 May 1909 after a year of isolated incarceration, and in April 1910 withdrew to Pondicherry, then a French colony. There he developed the spiritual practice he called Integral Yoga, wrote The Life Divine, The Synthesis of Yoga and the epic poem Savitri, and in 1926 founded the Sri Aurobindo Ashram with Mirra Alfassa.

entries.name: John Logie Baird
entries.desc: John Logie Baird was a Scottish inventor and electrical engineer, born in Helensburgh in 1888. On 26 January 1926 he gave the first public demonstration of television images, for members of the Royal Institution and a reporter from The Times, in his laboratory at 22 Frith Street in Soho, London. In 1928 his company made the first transatlantic television transmission, from London to Hartsdale, New York, and he demonstrated colour transmission. The BBC broadcast with his 30-line system from 1929 to 1935, and in February 1937 it dropped his later system in favour of EMI's. He showed a fully electronic colour television display in 1944 and died at Bexhill-on-Sea in 1946.

entries.name: Mormonism
entries.desc: Mormonism is the theology and religious tradition of the Latter Day Saint movement of Restorationist Christianity, begun by Joseph Smith in Western New York in the 1820s and 1830s. Smith said he received a vision in the spring of 1820, and in 1830 he published the Book of Mormon, which he said he had translated from golden plates, and organised the Church of Christ. After Smith was killed by a mob at Nauvoo, Illinois, in 1844, the largest group followed Brigham Young to what became the Utah Territory and practised plural marriage until the 1890 Manifesto. One source estimated that over 400 denominations have sprung from the movement, differing chiefly over polygamy and the Trinity.

entries.name: 2008 financial crisis
entries.desc: The 2008 financial crisis was a worldwide financial crisis that began in the United States with the subprime mortgage crisis of early 2007, when mortgage-backed securities tied to U.S. real estate collapsed in value. It spread to global institutions and climaxed with the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 which triggered a stock market crash and bank runs in several countries. Governments answered with bailouts such as the $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program and with monetary and fiscal policy. Some 8.7 million American jobs were lost, and the crisis worsened the Great Recession and contributed to crises in Iceland and the eurozone.

entries.name: Invasion of Poland
entries.desc: The invasion of Poland, also known as the September Campaign, was the joint attack on the Republic of Poland by Nazi Germany, the Slovak Republic and the Soviet Union that marked the beginning of World War II. German and Slovak forces invaded on 1 September 1939, a week after the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact was signed, and on 3 September the United Kingdom and France declared war on Germany. After the Polish defeat in the Battle of the Bzura, the Red Army invaded eastern Poland on 17 September under the pact's secret protocol. The campaign ended on 6 October after the Battle of Kock, with Germany and the Soviet Union dividing the whole of Poland, which never formally surrendered.

entries.name: John Donne
entries.desc: John Donne was an English poet, scholar, soldier and secretary, born into a recusant Roman Catholic family, who later became a cleric of the Church of England and Dean of St Paul's Cathedral in London from 1621 to 1631. He fought with the Earl of Essex at Cádiz in 1596 and the Azores in 1597 and became chief secretary to Sir Thomas Egerton, but his secret marriage to Egerton's niece Anne More in 1601 cost him his post and a spell in Fleet Prison, and years of poverty followed. Ordained in 1615 at the king's insistence, he became known for his sermons and for the Devotions upon Emergent Occasions of 1624. He is considered the preeminent representative of the metaphysical poets.

entries.name: Edward Gibbon
entries.desc: Edward Gibbon was a British essayist, historian and politician, born at Putney, Surrey, in 1737. Removed from Magdalen College, Oxford, after his conversion to Roman Catholicism in 1753, he was sent to Lausanne, Switzerland, and later wrote that the idea of his history first came to him among the ruins of the Capitol in Rome in October 1764. The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire appeared in six volumes between 1776 and 1789, known for the quality and irony of its prose, its use of primary sources and its polemical criticism of organised religion. He sat in the House of Commons for Liskeard and died in 1794 at Fletching, East Sussex, while staying with Lord Sheffield.

entries.name: John Chrysostom
entries.desc: John Chrysostom, John the Golden-mouthed, was a Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople, born in Antioch in Roman Syria around 347. Ordained a deacon in 381 and a priest after 388, he preached in Antioch from 386 to 397, known for his homilies on the Bible and his concern for the poor; there too he delivered eight homilies denouncing Jews and the Christians who took part in Jewish festivals. Made archbishop of Constantinople in 397, he made enemies of Theophilus I of Alexandria and the empress Aelia Eudoxia and was banished. He died at Comana Pontica on 14 September 407 on his way to further exile, and is honoured as a saint in the Catholic and Eastern churches.

entries.name: Thomas Henry Huxley
entries.desc: Thomas Henry Huxley was an English biologist and anthropologist, born in Ealing in 1825, who specialised in comparative anatomy and became known as Darwin's Bulldog for his advocacy of Charles Darwin's theory of evolution. Virtually self-taught, he sailed as assistant surgeon on HMS Rattlesnake to New Guinea and Australia from 1846 and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society on his return in 1850. His 1860 Oxford debate with Samuel Wilberforce became a key moment in the acceptance of evolution, though some historians think parts of the surviving story are a later fabrication. He concluded that birds evolved from small carnivorous dinosaurs, coined the term agnosticism in 1869.

entries.name: Amaterasu
entries.desc: Amaterasu Ōmikami is the goddess of the sun in Japanese mythology, often considered the chief deity of the Shinto pantheon. Japan's earliest literary texts, the Kojiki (c. 712 CE) and the Nihon Shoki (720 CE), portray her as a daughter of the creator god Izanagi, sister of the moon deity Tsukuyomi and the storm god Susanoo, and ruler of the heavenly realm Takamagahara. In the best-known myth, Susanoo's misdeeds drove her into the cave Ame-no-Iwayato, plunging heaven and earth into darkness until the gods lured her out. As the mythical ancestress of the Imperial House of Japan through her grandson Ninigi, she is worshipped chiefly at the Grand Shrine of Ise.

credit.artist: Utagawa Kunisada (歌川国貞; b. 1786, d. 1865)

entries.name: Daniel
entries.desc: Daniel is the main character of the Book of Daniel, which tells of a noble Jewish youth of Jerusalem taken into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon, who served the king and his successors until the time of the Persian conqueror Cyrus while remaining true to the God of Israel. In its tales he interprets dreams and the message written on a wall at the feast of Belshazzar; in its visions he sees the future of the world and of Israel. Most scholars hold that he was not a historical figure, that the tales date from the 3rd or early 2nd century BCE and the visions from between 167 and 164 BCE, alluding to Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Six cities claim his tomb, the best known at Susa in Iran.

entries.name: Libyan Civil War
entries.desc: The Libyan Civil War of 2011 was an armed conflict in Libya between forces loyal to Colonel Muammar Gaddafi and rebel groups attempting to oust his government. It began with protests in Benghazi on 15 February 2011, inspired by the Arab Spring, which grew into a rebellion whose leaders formed the National Transitional Council. On 17 March United Nations Security Council Resolution 1973 created a no-fly zone, which turned into a NATO bombing campaign against Gaddafi's forces. Rebels captured Tripoli in August, the UN recognised the council on 16 September, and Gaddafi was captured and killed in Sirte on 20 October; the war was declared over on 23 October.

entries.name: Unification of Germany
entries.desc: The unification of Germany was the process that built the first nation-state for Germans on the model of Lesser Germany, without Habsburg Austria, led by the Kingdom of Prussia. It began on 18 August 1866 with the treaty establishing the North German Confederation, after the Second War of Schleswig in 1864 and the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, and was completed during the Franco-Prussian War. On 18 January 1871 the German princes and military commanders proclaimed Wilhelm German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, at the head of a German Empire of 25 member states. Historians debate whether Otto von Bismarck, Minister President of Prussia, had a master plan for it.

entries.name: William Hogarth
entries.desc: William Hogarth was an English painter, engraver, cartoonist and satirist, born in London in 1697. Apprenticed to the engraver Ellis Gamble, he became known for his series of modern moral subjects, A Harlot's Progress (1731), A Rake's Progress (1733–1735) and Marriage A-la-Mode (1743–1745), sold widely as prints. Their pirating led him to lobby for the Engravers' Copyright Act of 1735, the first copyright law to deal with visual works. Later prints such as Beer Street and Gin Lane (1751) and The Four Stages of Cruelty attacked drink and cruelty, and in The Analysis of Beauty (1753) he set out his Line of Beauty. He died in 1764 and was buried at Chiswick.

entries.name: Hermann von Helmholtz
entries.desc: Hermann von Helmholtz was a German physicist and physician, born in Potsdam in 1821, whose work ranged across physiology, psychology, physics and philosophy. His 1847 treatise on the conservation of energy is credited as the first formulation of the principle in its most general form. In 1849, at Königsberg, he measured the speed of the signal along a nerve fibre, and in 1851 he invented the ophthalmoscope for examining the inside of the eye; his Sensations of Tone (1863) influenced musicologists into the twentieth century. After chairs at Bonn and Heidelberg he became professor of physics in Berlin in 1871, where his students included Heinrich Rudolf Hertz.

entries.name: Pre-Socratic philosophy
entries.desc: Pre-Socratic philosophy, also known as early Greek philosophy, is the ancient Greek philosophy before Socrates, which began in the 6th century BCE with the three Milesians, Thales, Anaximander and Anaximenes. Its thinkers were mostly interested in cosmology and the beginning and substance of the universe, and sought explanations based on natural law rather than the actions of gods: the Milesians named water, apeiron and air as the arche of the world, and Heraclitus fire. Parmenides of the Eleatic school claimed that only one thing exists and nothing can change, while Leucippus and Democritus taught atomism. Their writings are almost entirely lost and are known from fragments and testimonia.

entries.name: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa
entries.desc: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa was a Japanese writer of the Taishō period, born in Tokyo in 1892, regarded as the father of the Japanese short story. Raised by the family of his maternal uncle, from whom he took the name Akutagawa, he studied English literature at Tokyo Imperial University and won fame with Hana (The Nose, 1916), which Natsume Sōseki praised. Many of his 150 short stories reinterpret classical tales, among them Rashōmon and Yabu no naka (In a Grove, 1922), which Akira Kurosawa retold in his 1950 film Rashōmon. After years of hallucinations and the fear that he had inherited his mother's mental disorder, he took his own life in 1927 at 35; the Akutagawa Prize is named after him.

entries.name: Biafra
entries.desc: Biafra, officially the Republic of Biafra, was a partially recognised state in West Africa that declared independence from Nigeria and existed from 1967 to 1970. It covered the former Eastern Region of Nigeria, predominantly inhabited by the Igbo, and was established on 30 May 1967 by the region's governor, Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu, after military coups and the 1966 anti-Igbo pogrom. The Nigerian attack of 6 July 1967 began the Nigerian Civil War; Gabon, Haiti, Côte d'Ivoire, Tanzania and Zambia recognised Biafra. Almost two million Biafran civilians died, most from starvation under Nigeria's blockade, before Ojukwu fled to the Ivory Coast and Philip Effiong oversaw the surrender.

entries.name: Basil of Caesarea
entries.desc: Basil of Caesarea, also called Saint Basil the Great, was an early Christian prelate who served as Bishop of Caesarea Mazaca in Cappadocia from 370 until his death in 379. An influential theologian, he supported the Nicene Creed and opposed Arianism and Apollinarianism. He founded the Basileias before the gates of Caesarea, a poorhouse, hospital and hospice believed to be one of the earliest Christian hospitals for the poor, and set guidelines for monastic life built on community life, liturgical prayer and manual labor. With his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus he is counted among the Cappadocian Fathers.

entries.name: Carl von Clausewitz
entries.desc: Carl von Clausewitz was a Prussian army officer and military theorist who stressed the moral, in modern terms psychological, and political aspects of waging war. He entered Prussian service at the age of twelve, was captured at the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt in 1806, helped Gerhard von Scharnhorst reform the Prussian army, and served at Ligny and Wavre in 1815 before directing the Kriegsakademie until 1830. He died of cholera on 16 November 1831, leaving Vom Kriege (On War) unfinished; his widow Marie published it in 1832. It is considered a seminal treatise on military strategy.

entries.name: Tarot
entries.desc: Tarot, first known as trionfi and later as tarocchi or tarocks, is a set of playing cards that first appeared in Ferrara and Milan in northern Italy, where the Fool and 21 trumps were added to the standard Italian pack of four suits. From at least the mid-15th century it was used to play trick-taking card games, which spread to most of Europe and are still played, among them French Tarot and Austrian Königrufen. Its use for divination came later: the earliest evidence is a manuscript from around 1750, and French occultists of the late 18th century made unsubstantiated claims about the cards' history and meaning, from which decks made for cartomancy arose.

entries.name: Cro-Magnon
entries.desc: Cro-Magnons, or European early modern humans, were the first surviving expansion of Homo sapiens into Europe and Siberia, possibly present from as early as 56,800 years ago. They interacted and interbred with the Neanderthals and produced the Upper Palaeolithic cultures of Europe, from the Aurignacian through the Gravettian, Solutrean and Magdalenian, which gave way to Mesolithic cultures as the Last Glacial Period drew to a close. They hunted big game and made cave paintings, Venus figurines and bone flutes. The name comes from the Cro-Magnon rock shelter at Les Eyzies, Dordogne, where Louis Lartet found human remains in 1868.

entries.name: Patanjali
entries.desc: Patanjali is the name of one or more authors, mystics and philosophers of ancient India to whom several Sanskrit works are attributed. The best known of them is the Yoga Sutras, a classical yoga text whose author may have lived between the 2nd century BCE and the 5th century CE. A Patanjali also wrote the Mahābhāṣya, a treatise on Sanskrit grammar firmly datable to the 2nd century BCE, and medical texts are credited to the name. No known text before the time of Bhoja in the 11th century conflates the two authors, and Western scholars now generally accept that they were different people; in Hindu tradition Patanjali is regarded as an avatar of Adi Sesha.

entries.name: Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot
entries.desc: Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot was a French military engineer and physicist who developed the first successful theory of the maximum efficiency of heat engines. The son of Lazare Carnot, he graduated from the École polytechnique and served as an officer in the engineering arm of the French Army. In June 1824 he published Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, his only publication, which drew little attention until Émile Clapeyron explained it in 1834. William Thomson used it to develop an absolute thermodynamic temperature scale and Rudolf Clausius to define entropy. Carnot died of cholera in 1832, aged 36.

entries.name: Joseph Pulitzer
entries.desc: Joseph Pulitzer was a Hungarian-American politician and newspaper publisher of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch and the New York World. Born in Makó, he arrived in Boston in 1864 and fought for the Union in the American Civil War, then settled in St. Louis, where he formed the Post-Dispatch in 1878; he bought the World in 1883. In the 1890s its rivalry with William Randolph Hearst's New York Journal produced the sensational methods of yellow journalism. He served one term in Congress. His will endowed Columbia University, whose School of Journalism opened in 1912 and whose Pulitzer Prizes were established in 1917.

entries.name: Oriental Orthodox Churches
entries.desc: The Oriental Orthodox Churches are a communion of Eastern Christian churches that adhere to Miaphysite Christology and recognise only the first three ecumenical councils. They shared communion with the imperial Roman church until the Council of Chalcedon in 451, separating chiefly over Christology. The communion comprises six autocephalous churches, among them the Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria, the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch, the Armenian Apostolic Church and the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The name was formally adopted at the Conference of Addis Ababa in 1965, and in 2020 the churches had an estimated 72 million members.

entries.name: European colonization of the Americas
entries.desc: The European colonization of the Americas took place mainly between the late 15th century and the early 19th century, after the voyages of Christopher Columbus; the Norse had earlier settled Greenland and, around 1000, briefly a site near the northern tip of Newfoundland. Spain, Portugal, Great Britain, France, Russia, the Netherlands, Denmark and Sweden claimed land and resources, and the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 divided the world between Portugal and Spain. Colonization brought the displacement, enslavement and genocide of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas and the founding of settler colonial states.

entries.name: Khanate of Kazan
entries.desc: The Khanate of Kazan was a Tatar state on the Middle Volga, in the lands of the former Volga Bulgaria, with its capital at Kazan. One of the successor states of the Golden Horde, it is dated by historians either to 1437 or 1438, when Ulugh Muhammad took power in Kazan, or to 1445, when his son Maxmud began to rule there. Sunni Islam was the state religion, and real power lay with the diwan, an assembly of the highest aristocracy. From 1487 to 1521 it was in effect a Muscovite protectorate. The forces of Ivan the Terrible took Kazan in 1552 after a siege of more than 40 days, and the population was massacred.

entries.name: War on terror
entries.desc: The war on terror, officially the Global War on Terrorism, is a global military campaign begun by the United States in response to the September 11 attacks in 2001. Its main targets were militant Islamist movements such as al-Qaeda and the Taliban, the Ba'athist regime in Iraq, deposed in an invasion in 2003, and later the Islamic State. President George W. Bush first used the term on 16 September 2001. The Costs of War Project estimates that the post-9/11 wars displaced 38 million people and caused more than 4.5 million deaths, direct and indirect; critics questioned the Patriot Act, torture, extraordinary rendition and drone warfare.

entries.name: Eastern Bloc
entries.desc: The Eastern Bloc, also called the Communist Bloc or Soviet Bloc, was an unofficial coalition of communist states aligned with the Soviet Union during the Cold War, from 1947 to 1991, and opposed to the capitalist Western Bloc. In Europe it meant the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact states; in Asia it included Mongolia, North Vietnam and North Korea, and in the Americas Cuba from 1961. Soviet control was tested by the Hungarian Revolution of 1956, which the Soviet Union suppressed, and the Prague Spring of 1968, ended by invasion. The bloc disintegrated after the Polish election of June 1989 and the Pan-European Picnic of 19 August 1989.

entries.name: Second Spanish Republic
entries.desc: The Second Spanish Republic was the democratic government of Spain from 1931 to 1939, proclaimed on 14 April 1931 after the deposition of King Alfonso XIII. Under Prime Minister Manuel Azaña religious orders lost control of schools, a moderate agrarian reform was carried out and Catalonia gained home rule. After the CEDA won the 1933 election, clashes between left and right grew, and an uprising in Asturias in 1934 was crushed. The Popular Front won in February 1936, and in July an army uprising began the Spanish Civil War, in which an estimated half a million people died. The Republic surrendered to Francisco Franco's Nationalists on 1 April 1939.

entries.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
entries.desc: Gregory of Nazianzus, also known as Gregory the Theologian, was an early Christian theologian and prelate who served as Archbishop of Constantinople from 380 to 381. Born near Nazianzus in Cappadocia, he studied in Athens with his friend Basil of Caesarea, and with Basil and Gregory of Nyssa he is counted among the Cappadocian Fathers. He shaped Trinitarian theology and is widely considered the most accomplished rhetorical stylist of the patristic age. Selected to lead the First Council of Constantinople in 381, he resigned when bishops disputed his position, and spent his last years at Arianzus writing poetry until his death in 390.

entries.name: Vyasa
entries.desc: Vyasa is a rishi, or sage, with a prominent role in most Hindu traditions, also known as Veda Vyasa or Krishna Dvaipayana. He is traditionally regarded as the author of the Mahābhārata, in which he also appears as a character, and Hindu tradition holds that he divided the single Veda into four and wrote the eighteen Purāṇas and the Brahma Sutras. According to the Mahabharata he was the son of Satyavati and the sage Parasara, and at Satyavati's request he fathered Pāṇḍu and Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Many Hindus regard him as a partial incarnation of Vishnu and as one of the Chiranjivis, still alive in the Kali Yuga.

entries.name: Chola dynasty
entries.desc: The Chola dynasty was a Tamil dynasty of southern India, one of the Three Crowned Kings of Tamilakam with the Chera and Pandya, whose heartland was the fertile valley of the Kaveri River. The earliest datable references to it are inscriptions of the 3rd century BCE from the reign of Ashoka. Under the Medieval Cholas, from Vijayalaya around 848, it became a maritime empire that held peninsular India south of the Tungabhadra River as one state between 907 and 1215; Rajendra I reached the Ganges and in 1025 raided the ports of Srivijaya. It was then absorbed by the Pandyan empire and ceased to exist by 1279.

credit.artist: The original uploader was Venu62 at English Wikipedia .

entries.name: Empire of Nicaea
entries.desc: The Empire of Nicaea was the largest of the three Greek rump states founded by the aristocracy of the Byzantine Empire after crusaders occupied Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade in 1204. Established by the Laskaris family in northwestern Anatolia under Theodore I Laskaris, it assumed the traditional titles of the Byzantine emperors in 1205. John III Doukas Vatatzes recovered most of Thrace and Macedonia and incorporated Thessalonica. In July 1261 the general Alexios Strategopoulos entered Constantinople, restoring the empire under Michael VIII Palaiologos. By c. 1300 nearly the whole of the former Nicene lands had been conquered by the Turks.

entries.name: Canaletto
entries.desc: Canaletto, born Giovanni Antonio Canal, was an Italian painter from the Republic of Venice who painted vedute, views of Venice, Rome and London, as well as imaginary views called capricci, and was an important etcher. The son of the painter Bernardo Canal, he began as a theatrical scene painter, and much of his early work was painted from nature, with an accuracy that led some to believe he traced it from a camera obscura, which he owned. Through the merchant Joseph Smith he found English buyers, and from 1746 he worked in England, painting London, Westminster Bridge and Warwick Castle. He was elected to the Venetian Academy in 1763 and painted until his death in 1768.

entries.name: John Dryden
entries.desc: John Dryden was an English poet, literary critic, translator and playwright, England's first Poet Laureate, who so dominated the literary life of Restoration England that the period came to be known as the Age of Dryden. He welcomed the Restoration with Astraea Redux in 1660 and wrote satires such as Mac Flecknoe and Absalom and Achitophel (1681). The Hind and the Panther (1687) celebrates his conversion to Roman Catholicism. After the Glorious Revolution he refused the oaths of allegiance to William and Mary, lost his public offices and lived by his pen, translating The Works of Virgil (1697). He died in 1700 and was reburied in Westminster Abbey.

entries.name: Mihai Eminescu
entries.desc: Mihai Eminescu, born Mihail Eminovici, was a Romanian Romantic poet, novelist and journalist from Moldavia, generally regarded as the most influential Romanian poet. His first poems appeared in 1866, when the editor Iosif Vulcan gave him the pen name Eminescu, and from 1869 to 1872 he studied at the University of Vienna. A member of the Junimea literary society, he became editor-in-chief of the newspaper Timpul in 1880 and wrote Luceafărul and Odă în metru antic. Ill from 1883, he was treated with mercury and died in a Bucharest sanatorium on 15 June 1889. His poems have been translated into over 60 languages.

entries.name: Sándor Petőfi
entries.desc: Sándor Petőfi was a Hungarian poet and liberal revolutionary, born in Kiskőrös in 1823 and considered Hungary's national poet. His poems relied on folkloric elements and song-like verse, and he wrote the long fairy-tale epic János Vitéz (1845). On 15 March 1848 he and the Youths of March led the rising in Pest, reading his Nemzeti dal (National Song) and the 12 Points to the crowds and printing them after declaring an end to censorship. He then fought in the Transylvanian army under Józef Bem and was last seen alive at the Battle of Segesvár on 31 July 1849, where he most likely died; his body was never found.

entries.name: Malik ibn Anas
entries.desc: Malik ibn Anas was a Muslim scholar, jurist and traditionalist of Medina, the eponym of the Maliki school, one of the four schools of Sunni jurisprudence. Born in Medina around 711, he studied under Hisham ibn Urwa, Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri and Ja'far al-Sadiq and became the leading hadith scholar of his day. His al-Muwatta', composed in the early Abbasid period, is one of the oldest Sunni hadith collections and law books. Accounts hold that he refused a wish of the caliph al-Mansur to impose it on the whole Islamic world. He died in Medina in 795 and was buried in the cemetery of Al-Baqi'; his school became the norm in much of North Africa and al-Andalus.

entries.name: Sturmabteilung
entries.desc: The Sturmabteilung, or SA, was the original party militia of the Nazi Party, called the Brownshirts after the colour of its uniform. Formed after Adolf Hitler rose to party leadership in 1921, it protected Nazi rallies, broke up opponents' meetings, fought the paramilitary units of the Communist and Social Democratic parties and intimidated Romani, trade unionists and especially Jews. By the end of 1933 it numbered more than 3 million men. In the Night of the Long Knives in 1934 its leader Ernst Röhm was arrested and executed, and the SS superseded it. The SA took part in the Kristallnacht pogrom of November 1938 and was disbanded and outlawed by the Allied Control Council in 1945.

entries.name: Emanuel Swedenborg
entries.desc: Emanuel Swedenborg was a Swedish scientist, engineer, anatomist, Christian theologian, philosopher and mystic. After studying at Uppsala and spending four years in London, he was appointed assessor-extraordinary on the Swedish Board of Mines by Charles XII and worked for two decades on natural science and engineering. From 1744 he described dreams and visions, and he held that Jesus Christ had appointed him to write The Heavenly Doctrine to reform Christianity. Over the last 28 years of his life he wrote 18 published theological works, among them Heaven and Hell (1758). He died in 1772, and the New Church, founded in 1787, reveres his writings as revelation.

entries.name: Ancient Greek philosophy
entries.desc: Ancient Greek philosophy arose in the 6th century BCE and dealt with astronomy, mathematics, ethics, metaphysics, logic, biology, rhetoric and politics. Aristotle regarded Thales of Miletus as the first philosopher, and the thinkers before the death of Socrates are conventionally called the pre-Socratics. Socrates, Plato and Aristotle marked a new approach, and after the wars of Alexander the Great came Hellenistic schools such as Stoicism, founded by Zeno of Citium, and Epicureanism. Greek philosophy evolved into Roman philosophy, and lines of influence run from it to early Islamic philosophy, medieval scholasticism, the Renaissance and the Enlightenment.

entries.name: Indian philosophy
entries.desc: Indian philosophy is the diverse set of philosophical traditions of the Indian subcontinent, each often called a darshan. A common classification divides the āstika schools, which accept the Vedas as a source of knowledge, from the nāstika schools, which do not: the six āstika schools are Nyāya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā and Vedanta, and the heterodox schools include the Jain, Buddhist, Ajivika, Ajñana and Charvaka. The main schools were formalised chiefly between 500 BCE and the late centuries of the Common Era. They share concepts such as dharma, karma and samsara and seek liberation from suffering; Jainism, Buddhism and Vedanta survived, while Charvaka and Ājīvika did not.

entries.name: Spring and Autumn period
entries.desc: The Spring and Autumn period was an era of Chinese history, roughly the first half of the Eastern Zhou, in which royal power eroded as local lords acted on their own. It began after a Quanrong invasion destroyed the Western Zhou capital at Haojing in 771 BCE and the court moved east to Luoyi. Its name comes from the Spring and Autumn Annals, a chronicle of the state of Lu that tradition links with Confucius. Leading states met in conferences that at times declared one ruler hegemon, the first being Duke Huan of Qi, while larger states absorbed smaller ones. The gradual Partition of Jin is generally taken to mark its end and the start of the Warring States period.

entries.name: Jusepe de Ribera
entries.desc: Jusepe de Ribera was a Spanish painter and printmaker, regarded with Zurbarán, Murillo and Velázquez as one of the major artists of Spanish Baroque painting. Baptised in Játiva in 1591, he was a member of the Accademia di San Luca in Rome by 1613 and moved in 1616 to Naples, then under Spanish rule, where he spent the rest of his life and ran a workshop with many pupils. Called Lo Spagnoletto by his contemporaries, he painted biblical and mythological scenes, brutal martyrdoms and many half-length figures of workers and beggars posed as philosophers and saints, in a stark tenebrist manner. Pope Urban VIII gave him the Cross of the Order of Christ in 1626; he died in 1652.

entries.name: Christine de Pizan
entries.desc: Christine de Pizan was a Venetian-born French court writer in prose and poetry for King Charles VI of France. Born in the Republic of Venice in 1364, she came to France as a child when her father became court astrologer to Charles V. After her husband died in 1389, she supported her mother and children by writing and has been called the first professional woman of letters in Europe. Her works, among the earliest feminist writings, include The Book of the City of Ladies and The Treasure of the City of Ladies, written while she worked for John the Fearless. In 1429 she published the Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc, celebrating Joan of Arc's victory over the English; she died around 1430.

credit.artist: photography The British Library Board, Harley 4431, f.259v

entries.name: J. P. Morgan
entries.desc: John Pierpont Morgan was an American financier and investment banker who dominated corporate finance on Wall Street in the Gilded Age and Progressive Era. Born in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1837, he worked for his father's banking houses and headed the firm that later became JPMorgan Chase & Co. He drove a wave of industrial consolidations, forming U.S. Steel, International Harvester and General Electric, and his firm held controlling interests in businesses such as Western Union and 21 railroads. During the Panic of 1907 he organised a coalition of financiers that saved the American monetary system from collapse. He died in Rome in 1913, leaving his business to his son, J. P. Morgan Jr.

entries.name: Duns Scotus
entries.desc: John Duns Scotus was a Scottish Catholic priest, Franciscan friar, philosopher and theologian, among the most important philosopher-theologians of the late medieval West. Probably from Duns in Berwickshire, he was ordained at Northampton in 1291, studied and taught at Oxford and lectured on Peter Lombard's Sentences at the University of Paris, from which he was expelled for a time for siding with Pope Boniface VIII against Philip IV. He is known for the univocity of being, the formal distinction and haecceity, and he argued for the Immaculate Conception of Mary. Called the subtle Doctor, he died in Cologne in 1308; his tradition is called Scotism, and he was beatified in 1993.

entries.name: Chinese philosophy
entries.desc: Chinese philosophy is the body of philosophical traditions that arose and developed in China. It began in earnest in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, the age of the Hundred Schools of Thought, when Confucius, Mencius, Laozi, Zhuangzi, Mozi, Han Fei and Xunzi founded Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism and Legalism. Under the Han dynasty Confucianism became the official ideology, and Indian Buddhism later fed into Neo-Confucianism in the Song and Ming dynasties. Buddhist and Neo-Confucian thought spread to Korea, Japan and Vietnam, and modern thinkers answered Western thought with the Three Principles of the People, Chinese Marxism and New Confucianism.

entries.name: Denisovans
entries.desc: The Denisovans are an extinct species or subspecies of archaic human that ranged across Asia during the Middle to Late Pleistocene, approximately 200,000 to 32,000 years ago. They were first identified in 2010 from mitochondrial DNA taken from a juvenile finger bone found in 2008 in Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains of Siberia; further remains came from the Tibetan Plateau, Laos, the Penghu channel, Harbin and Yunnan. Most of what is known of them comes from DNA, which shows close affinities with Neanderthals and interbreeding with them and with modern humans. Roughly 5% of the DNA of Melanesians, Aboriginal Australians and Filipino Negritos is Denisovan.

entries.name: Second Opium War
entries.desc: The Second Opium War was fought by the United Kingdom and France against the Qing dynasty of China between 1856 and 1860. It began after Qing officials seized the British-registered ship Arrow in October 1856 and British gunboats shelled Canton; the allies stormed Canton in December 1857, took the Taku Forts in 1858 and forced the Treaty of Tientsin. When the Xianfeng Emperor refused to ratify it, fighting resumed, and after hostages were tortured or murdered Lord Elgin had the Old Summer Palace looted and burned. Prince Gong signed the Convention of Peking in October 1860, which forced legalisation of the opium trade and ceded the Kowloon Peninsula to Britain.

entries.name: Piero della Francesca
entries.desc: Piero della Francesca was an Italian painter, mathematician and geometer of the Early Renaissance, born in Borgo Santo Sepolcro around 1415. His painting is marked by serene humanism, geometric forms and perspective, and his best-known work is the fresco cycle The History of the True Cross in the Basilica of San Francesco in Arezzo. He worked in Florence, Ferrara and Rimini and for Federico da Montefeltro at Urbino, where he painted the Flagellation and the double portrait of Federico and Battista Sforza. His treatises on the abacus, the five regular solids and perspective were later absorbed into Luca Pacioli's writing. His sight failed from about 1480, and he died in Sansepolcro in 1492.

entries.name: Mikhail Glinka
entries.desc: Mikhail Ivanovich Glinka was the first Russian composer to gain wide recognition in his own country and is often regarded as the fountainhead of Russian classical music. Born at Novospasskoye in the Smolensk Governorate in 1804, he studied in Saint Petersburg, travelled in Italy and studied composition in Berlin under Siegfried Dehn. His opera A Life for the Tsar, on the peasant hero Ivan Susanin, was a great success at its premiere in 1836, and Ruslan and Lyudmila, after Pushkin, followed in 1842. Tchaikovsky called his orchestral Kamarinskaya (1848) the acorn of later Russian symphonic music. Glinka died in Berlin in 1857 and influenced the composers known as The Five.
