entries.name: Seti I
entries.desc: Seti I was the second pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt in the New Kingdom, ruling from 1290 to 1279 BCE, the son of Ramesses I and father of Ramesses II. After the upheavals of Akhenaten's reign he worked to restore order and Egyptian power in Canaan and Syria, fought the Hittites several times and took the Syrian town of Kadesh and the land of Amurru, which soon returned to Hittite control. He built a mortuary temple at Qurna on the west bank at Thebes and began a white limestone temple at Abydos that his son completed. His tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV17, found by Giovanni Belzoni in 1817, is the longest of the New Kingdom royal tombs.

entries.name: Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon
entries.desc: Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, was a French naturalist, mathematician and cosmologist, born at Montbard in 1707. After studying law at Dijon and mathematics and medicine at Angers, he settled in Paris, where he first made his mark in mathematics by bringing calculus into probability theory. In 1739 he was appointed head of the Jardin du Roi, a post he held to the end of his life. His Histoire naturelle appeared in 36 quarto volumes from 1749 to 1788 and influenced naturalists such as Lamarck and Cuvier. The theology committee of the University of Paris forced him to recant his theories of geological history and animal evolution, which contradicted the biblical account of creation.

entries.name: Robert Fulton
entries.desc: Robert Fulton was an American engineer and inventor, born in Little Britain, Pennsylvania, in 1765, who is widely credited with developing the first commercially successful steamboat, the North River Steamboat, also known as Clermont. He lived in Europe for twenty years, working on canals and, in 1800, on a submarine for Napoleon Bonaparte, the Nautilus; he is also credited with some of the earliest naval torpedoes. In 1807 his steamboat carried passengers on the Hudson River from New York City to Albany and back, changing river traffic and trade in America. He designed the steam warship Demologos for the War of 1812 and died of tuberculosis in New York City in 1815.

entries.name: Medieval philosophy
entries.desc: Medieval philosophy is the philosophy of the Middle Ages, from the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century to the 13th and 14th centuries. As independent inquiry it began in Baghdad in the middle of the 8th century and at the court of Charlemagne in Aachen in the late 8th century. Jewish, Christian and Muslim thinkers sought to recover the learning of Greece and Rome and to reconcile sacred doctrine with secular learning, treating the relation of faith to reason, the existence of God, and the problems of universals and individuation. Its golden age in the Latin West came in the 12th, 13th and 14th centuries with the recovery of Aristotle and his Arabic commentators.

entries.name: Islamic philosophy
entries.desc: Islamic philosophy is the philosophy that emerged from the Islamic tradition, covering falsafa, which took in logic, mathematics and physics, and kalam, a rationalist form of theology. Its early phase began with al-Kindi in the early 9th century CE and declined with Ibn Rushd (Averroes) in the late 12th century, broadly the period of the Islamic Golden Age. In the east of the Islamic world it lasted much longer, in Safavid Iran, the Ottoman Empire and the Mughal Empire, through schools such as Avicennism and Illuminationism. Latin translations of Arabic texts transformed almost all philosophical disciplines in medieval Europe.

entries.name: Martin Buber
entries.desc: Martin Buber was an Austrian-Israeli philosopher, born in Vienna, best known for his philosophy of dialogue, which distinguished the I–Thou relationship from the I–It relationship. Raised by his grandfather Solomon Buber in Lemberg, he broke with Jewish custom to study philosophy and joined the Zionist movement in 1898. In 1923 he wrote Ich und Du (I and Thou), and in 1925 he began translating the Hebrew Bible into German. He resigned his professorship at Frankfurt in protest when Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933, settled in Jerusalem in 1938 and taught at Hebrew University. He died at his home in Jerusalem in 1965.

entries.name: Emilia Plater
entries.desc: Emilia Plater was a Polish-Lithuanian noblewoman who fought in the November Uprising of 1830–1831 against the Russian Empire. Born in Vilnius and raised in Polish Livonia, she joined the uprising in the former Grand Duchy of Lithuania in March 1831 and was granted the rank of captain by General Dezydery Chłapowski, though how far she actually held command remains uncertain. In July 1831 she refused to follow the withdrawing Polish forces into Prussia and tried to reach the insurgent army in Congress Poland but fell ill and died in December 1831, aged 25. Adam Mickiewicz's 1832 poem The Death of a Colonel made her a symbol of Polish independence, the Polish Joan of Arc.

entries.name: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi
aka: Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṭūsī
entries.desc: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi was a Persian polymath, philosopher, scientist and Shi'ite scholar, born in Tus in Khorasan. He worked under an Ismāʿīlī ruler at Alamūt, and when Hūlāgū Khān and the Mongols captured Alamūt in 1256 he entered Hūlāgū's service as an astrologer and helped save numerous libraries from destruction. From 1259 an observatory was built to the west of Maragheh, capital of the Ilkhanate Empire. He compiled the astronomical tables known as the Zīj al-Khānī, devised the Ṭūsī couple, criticised Ptolemaic astronomy and is often credited with making trigonometry a discipline of its own. His works include The Nasirean Ethics of 1235.

entries.name: William Gilbert
entries.desc: William Gilbert was an English physician, physicist and natural philosopher from Colchester who rejected Aristotelian philosophy and the Scholastic method of university teaching. Educated at St John's College, Cambridge, he practised medicine in London, became President of the Royal College of Physicians in 1600 and was physician to Elizabeth I from 1601 until her death in 1603. His book De Magnete, published in 1600, described experiments with a model Earth, the terrella, and concluded that the Earth itself was magnetic, which is why compasses point north. His Neo-Latin word electricus, meaning like amber, gave English the word electricity.

entries.name: Evangelicalism
entries.desc: Evangelicalism is a worldwide, interdenominational movement within Protestant Christianity that emphasises evangelism, personal conversion, often described as being born again, and the Bible as the final authority in faith. Its roots lie in the Protestant Reformation, and the modern movement is generally dated to around 1734, shaped by Pietism, Puritanism and the Moravianism of Nicolaus Zinzendorf. It gained momentum in the First Great Awakening of the 1730s and 1740s, with John Wesley and the early Methodists in central roles, and grew through revivals in Britain and the United States before spreading worldwide. The World Evangelical Alliance claims 600 million believers in 2025.

entries.name: Heian period
entries.desc: The Heian period was the last division of classical Japanese history, from 794 to 1185, beginning when Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō, modern Kyoto. Chinese influence declined and a national culture matured: the syllabaries katakana and hiragana emerged, and court ladies wrote much of the vernacular literature. Real power lay with the Fujiwara clan, who intermarried with the imperial family, while the shōen estates grew more independent of imperial control. The warrior class entered court politics with the Hōgen Rebellion of 1156, and after the Genpei War Minamoto no Yoritomo seized power in 1185, beginning the Kamakura period.

entries.name: Iconoclasm
entries.desc: Iconoclasm is the belief in the importance of destroying icons and other images or monuments, usually for religious or political reasons; it is most often the result of disputes between factions of the same religion. The term comes from the Byzantine Iconoclasm, the struggle over religious icons in the Byzantine Empire from 726 to 842 CE, begun when Emperor Leo III issued edicts between 726 and 730 against the veneration of images. Earlier, Akhenaten had ordered references to Amun cut from Egyptian tombs and temples. Later episodes include the English Reformation and the destruction of monarchist symbols during the French Revolution.

entries.name: Kumbh Mela
entries.desc: The Kumbh Mela is a Hindu pilgrimage held every four or twelve years at four places, Prayagraj, Haridwar, Nashik and Ujjain, on a cycle tied to the revolution of Jupiter. According to the Puranas, these sites received drops of the divine nectar amrita during the churning of the ocean of milk, and pilgrims bathe at the confluence of rivers as atonement for past mistakes. Before 1858 the name Kumbh was used only for the twelfth annual mela at Haridwar; after the Indian Rebellion of 1857 the Pragwal priests of Allahabad proposed an organised pilgrimage, and the first Kumbh Mela at Prayag was held in 1870. About 660 million attended in 2025.

entries.name: Khanate of Sibir
entries.desc: The Khanate of Sibir was a Siberian Tatar state in western Siberia, founded at the end of the 15th century after the break-up of the Golden Horde. The Shaybanid and Taibugid dynasties often contested its rule, and its people included Siberian Tatars, Khanty, Mansi and Selkup; it was the northernmost Muslim state in recorded history. Its capital moved from Chimgi-Tura to Iskar on the Irtysh. The Shaybanid Kuchum took power after fighting from 1556 to 1563, but a raid on the Stroganov trading posts brought an expedition of Cossacks under Yermak, who defeated him in 1582. Kuchum fled to the Nogai in 1598.

entries.name: Interwar period
entries.desc: The interwar period lasted from 11 November 1918 to 1 September 1939, from the end of World War I to the beginning of World War II. The prosperous Roaring Twenties, when automobiles, electric lighting and radio became common, were followed by the Great Depression, which severely damaged many of the largest economies. The Russian, Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian and German empires were dismantled, the Soviet Union was formed, and Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland became independent. Communism rose from the October Revolution, fascism rose in Germany and Italy, and the territorial ambitions of Japan, Italy and Germany led to the expansion of their domains.

entries.name: Wall Street crash of 1929
entries.desc: The Wall Street crash of 1929, also known as the Great Crash, was a stock market crash in the United States that began in October 1929 on the New York Stock Exchange. During the Roaring Twenties much profit had gone into speculation, pushing share prices far above their value. On Black Thursday, 24 October, a record 12.9 million shares were traded, and on Black Tuesday, 29 October, some 16.4 million. The fall continued until 8 July 1932, by when the market had lost some 90% of its value. Congress responded with the Banking Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; scholars disagree about its role in the Great Depression.

entries.name: Francesco Borromini
entries.desc: Francesco Borromini, born Francesco Castelli at Bissone in today's Ticino, was an Italian architect who, with Gian Lorenzo Bernini and Pietro da Cortona, was a leading figure of Roman Baroque architecture. The son of a stonemason, he moved to Rome in 1619 to work for his relative Carlo Maderno at St. Peter's and the Palazzo Barberini. In 1634 he received his first major commission, San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, and later works include Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza and Sant'Agnese in Agone. His buildings manipulated Classical forms with geometrical plans and symbolic meanings. Melancholic and quick-tempered, he died by suicide in 1667.

entries.name: Karl Friedrich Schinkel
entries.desc: Karl Friedrich Schinkel was a Prussian architect, city planner and painter, born in Neuruppin, and a leader of the Neoclassical and Gothic Revival movements. A student of Friedrich Gilly and David Gilly in Berlin, he earned his living as a painter and worked for the stage, creating in 1816 a backdrop for Mozart's The Magic Flute. After Napoleon's defeat he oversaw the Prussian Building Commission and reshaped Berlin as a capital for Prussia. Turning to Greek rather than Imperial Roman models, he built the Neue Wache, the Schauspielhaus at the Gendarmenmarkt and the Altes Museum on Museum Island (1823–1830). He died in Berlin in 1841.

entries.name: Nestorius
entries.desc: Nestorius was an early Christian theologian of the Catechetical School of Antioch who served as Archbishop of Constantinople from 428 to 431. He urged cautious use of the title Theotokos for Mary, so that Christ's human and divine natures not be confused, and proposed Christotokos instead, which brought him into conflict with Cyril of Alexandria. In 431 the Council of Ephesus condemned and deposed him for heresy, and in 435 Theodosius II exiled him to Upper Egypt, where he lived until about 451. The Church of the East in the Persian Empire never accepted his condemnation and reveres him as one of its three Greek Teachers.

entries.name: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj
entries.desc: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, commonly known as Imam Muslim, was an Islamic scholar of hadith from Nishapur in the Abbasid province of Khorasan. His date of birth is uncertain, usually given as 202, 204 or 206 AH, and he died in May 875. Of Arab origin, of the tribe of Banu Qushayr, he studied in the Arabian Peninsula, Egypt, Iraq and Syria before settling in Nishapur, where he became a lifelong friend of al-Bukhari. In the mid-9th century he composed Sahih Muslim, a collection of hadith he considered entirely sahih; it is one of the six canonical books of hadith in Sunni Islam and, with Sahih al-Bukhari, one of the two most authentic.

entries.name: Suebi
entries.desc: The Suebi were a large group of Germanic peoples, first reported by Julius Caesar, who originated near the Elbe River in what is now eastern Germany. Suebian groups spread across Central Europe; a powerful alliance led by the Marcomanni was crushed by the Romans in the Marcomannic Wars of the late 2nd century, and the Alemanni later took Roman territory in what became Swabia. Around 406 many Suebi moved west into Roman Gaul, and by 409 a large group entered Hispania, founding the Kingdom of the Suebi in Gallaecia, which lasted until 585 when it was absorbed by the Visigothic Kingdom.

entries.name: Mother Jones
entries.desc: Mary G. Harris Jones, known as Mother Jones from 1897, was an Irish-American labor organizer, schoolteacher and dressmaker born in Cork, whose family emigrated to Canada after the Great Famine. After her husband and four children died of yellow fever in Memphis in 1867 and her shop was destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, she organised for the Knights of Labor and the United Mine Workers of America. In 1902 she was called the most dangerous woman in America, and in 1903 she led a children's march from Philadelphia to protest weak child labor laws. She co-founded the Industrial Workers of the World and died in 1930.

entries.name: Anti-Comintern Pact
entries.desc: The Anti-Comintern Pact was an anti-communist agreement concluded between Nazi Germany and the Empire of Japan on 25 November 1936, directed against the Communist International. It was signed by Joachim von Ribbentrop and the Japanese ambassador Kintomo Mushanokōji, and a secret additional protocol set a joint policy against the Soviet Union. Italy joined in 1937, and Spain and Hungary in 1939. Japan distanced itself from Germany after the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of August 1939, and the pact was followed by the Tripartite Pact of September 1940. It was renewed in November 1941 with new members and ceased to exist with the end of World War II.

entries.name: Raja Ravi Varma
entries.desc: Raja Ravi Varma was an Indian painter, born at Kilimanoor palace in the princely state of Travancore, whose works fused European academic art with Indian iconography. Closely related to the royal family of Travancore, he received the title Raja from Lord Curzon. He won acclaim after an award at Vienna in 1873 and took three gold medals at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893. He painted Hindu deities and scenes from the Mahabharata and the Puranas, such as Nala and Damayanti. In 1894 he started a lithographic press in Ghatkopar, Mumbai, whose affordable oleographs carried his images to ordinary people.

entries.name: Tommaso Campanella
entries.desc: Tommaso Campanella was an Italian Dominican friar, philosopher, theologian, astrologer and poet from Calabria. He was drawn to the empiricism of Bernardino Telesio and opposed to the authority of Aristotle, and was prosecuted by the Roman Inquisition for heresy in 1594. Accused in 1599 of leading a conspiracy against Spanish rule in Calabria, he was tortured and spent twenty-seven years in prisons in Naples, where he wrote The City of the Sun, a utopia of a theocratic society with property held in common. Released in 1626 through Pope Urban VIII, he fled to France in 1634 and spent his last years in Paris.

entries.name: Paramahansa Yogananda
entries.desc: Paramahansa Yogananda, born Mukunda Lal Ghosh in Gorakhpur, was an Indian and American Hindu monk, yogi and guru who founded the Self-Realization Fellowship and the Yogoda Satsanga Society of India to spread the teachings of Kriya Yoga. A disciple of Swami Sri Yukteswar Giri, he arrived in Boston in 1920, toured the country as a speaker and settled in Los Angeles in 1925. In 1927 he was received at the White House by President Calvin Coolidge. His Autobiography of a Yogi, published in 1946, has sold over four million copies, and his influence on the American yoga movement led to his being called the Father of Yoga in the West.

entries.name: George Eastman
entries.desc: George Eastman was an American innovator and entrepreneur who founded the Eastman Kodak Company and brought roll film into general use. Born in Waterville, New York, he founded the Eastman Dry Plate Company in 1881 and in 1888 patented and released the Kodak camera, sold loaded with film for 100 exposures and returned to the company for developing, which made photography accessible to amateurs. Kodak became the leading supplier of film stock and faced a federal anti-trust suit for its monopolistic practices. Eastman gave $100 million to organisations such as the University of Rochester and MIT, and in 1932, in great pain from a spinal disorder, he shot himself.

credit.artist: Published by B. C. Forbes Publishing Company, New York, 1917

entries.name: Orthodox Judaism
entries.desc: Orthodox Judaism is the collective term for the traditionalist branches of contemporary Judaism, which hold that the Written and Oral Torah were revealed by God on Mount Sinai and faithfully transmitted since. It calls for strict observance of Jewish law, or halakha, interpreted only by traditional methods. Though its beliefs are old, the movement is modern: it arose from the breakdown of the autonomous Jewish community from the late 18th century, in struggle against secularisation and rivals such as Reform Judaism, and the term Orthodox Jews was first recorded in 1795. It is broadly divided into the Haredi and the Modern Orthodox, and is the largest Jewish religious group.

entries.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
entries.desc: Eastern Orthodoxy, also called Byzantine Christianity, is one of the three main branches of Chalcedonian Christianity, alongside Catholicism and certain forms of Protestantism. It spread from the eastern Mediterranean within Byzantine Greek culture and is organised into 17 mainstream autocephalous churches that choose their own primates, such as the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople and the Patriarchate of Moscow. It rejects the Filioque clause added to the Nicene Creed by the Latin Church and holds to the doctrines of the seven ecumenical councils. Roughly half of its adherents live in Russia, and it is the majority faith across much of Eastern Europe.

entries.name: Java Man
entries.desc: Java Man is an early human fossil found in 1891 and 1892 at Trinil on the Solo River in East Java, Indonesia, estimated to be between 700,000 and 1,490,000 years old. Excavated by a team led by Eugène Dubois, it consists of a tooth, a skullcap and a thighbone, which Dubois argued were the missing link between apes and humans; few accepted this, and the find caused long controversy. In 1950 Ernst Mayr placed it with Peking Man in Homo erectus, of which it remains the type specimen. Held in the Netherlands since 1900, the Dubois collection was announced in 2025 to be returned to Indonesia because of the circumstances of its acquisition.

entries.name: Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors
entries.desc: The Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors were, in Chinese mythology and traditional historiography, a series of sage rulers held to be the first emperors of China, reigning before the Xia dynasty. In myth the Three Sovereigns were demigods who helped create mankind and taught it essential skills, and the Five Emperors were sages of great moral character from a golden age. Sources name them differently: the groupings draw on figures such as Fuxi, Nüwa, Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Zhuanxu, Emperor Yao and Emperor Shun. They were credited with fire, houses, farming, medicine, the calendar and Chinese script, and once worshipped as ancestral spirits; today they are seen as culture heroes.

entries.name: Austrasia
entries.desc: Austrasia was the northeastern realm of the Frankish state in the Early Middle Ages, centred on the lands between the Meuse, Moselle, Middle Rhine and Main rivers and reaching beyond the old Roman frontier on the Rhine. It was one of the subdivisions into which the Merovingian dynasty divided their realm, alongside Neustria, Aquitaine and Burgundy, and by 561 it was ruled as a separate kingdom by Sigebert I. The Carolingian dynasty had its original power base there. The Treaty of Verdun of 843 divided it between East Francia and Middle Francia, and its western core later came to be called Lotharingia and its eastern parts Franconia.

entries.name: Neustria
entries.desc: Neustria was the western part of the Kingdom of the Franks in the Early Middle Ages, first the land between the Loire and the Silva Carbonaria, with Paris, Orléans, Tours and Soissons as its main cities. For more than two hundred years it was at war with Austrasia, the eastern Frankish realm, until Pippin of Herstal defeated the Neustrians at Tertry in 687. Under the Carolingians the name passed to a smaller kingdom between the Seine and the Loire, and in 861 Charles the Bald created the Marches of Neustria against the Bretons and the Norsemen. The family of Robert I ruled Neustria until Hugh Capet became king in 987, after which the term fell out of use.

entries.name: 1556 Shaanxi earthquake
entries.desc: The 1556 Shaanxi earthquake, one of the deadliest earthquakes in history, struck Huaxian in Shaanxi in the early morning of 23 January 1556, during the reign of the Jiajing Emperor of the Ming dynasty. Most people there lived in yaodongs, artificial caves in loess cliffs, which collapsed on those sleeping inside, and more than 97 counties in ten provinces were affected. The China Earthquake Administration puts the direct deaths at roughly 100,000, while 730,000 more migrated away or died of famine and plague, a total fall of 830,000 in the registered population. Modern estimates of its magnitude range from about Mw 8.0 down to 7.0–7.5.

entries.name: 1973 oil crisis
entries.desc: The 1973 oil crisis began in October 1973, when the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries, led by Faisal of Saudi Arabia, imposed an oil embargo on countries that had supported Israel in the Yom Kippur War, first Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States. With monthly production cuts, the price of oil rose by nearly 300%, from US$3 to nearly US$12 a barrel, before the embargo was lifted in March 1974. The shock set off a worldwide inflationary spiral and the steepest economic contraction since the Great Depression, ending the long post-war prosperity of the West. A second oil shock followed in 1979.

entries.name: Bodhidharma
entries.desc: Bodhidharma was a Buddhist monk of the 5th or 6th century CE, known mostly through later accounts mixed with legend, and traditionally credited with bringing Chan Buddhism to China and regarded as its first Chinese patriarch. Chinese sources say he came from the Western Regions and describe him as either Persian Central Asian or South Indian, and differ on when he arrived. He was mainly active in the Northern Wei, and his teaching centred on meditation, the practice of wall-gazing and the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra. Later tradition held that he faced a wall for nine years at the Shaolin Monastery, and in the 20th century he was popularly regarded as the founder of Shaolin kung fu.

entries.name: Ramana Maharshi
entries.desc: Ramana Maharshi, born Venkataraman Iyer in Tamil Nadu, was an Indian Hindu sage whom his followers and most advocates of Advaita regarded as a liberated being. In 1896, at the age of 16, he had a death-experience in which he became aware of his true self, and six weeks later he left Madurai for the holy mountain Arunachala at Tiruvannamalai, where he stayed for the rest of his life. An ashram, Sri Ramanasramam, grew up around him from 1922. He taught self-enquiry, set out in Who am I?, as the main path, with devotion or surrender. Paul Brunton's A Search in Secret India of 1934 made him known in the West, and he died in 1950 after a cancerous growth on his arm.

entries.name: Late antiquity
entries.desc: Late antiquity is the period between classical antiquity and the Early Middle Ages in the Mediterranean world, parts of Europe and the Near East, roughly from c. 250 to 750, though its exact limits are debated. It saw the end of the Western Roman Empire and the Sasanian Empire, the Arab conquests and the Rashidun Caliphate, and the rise of Christianity, Rabbinic Judaism and Islam, when the Bible and the Quran were canonised. The term was used by German-speaking historians after Alois Riegl and given currency in English by Peter Brown, whose The World of Late Antiquity of 1971 replaced the view of a declining culture with one of renewal.

entries.name: Nazi concentration camps
entries.desc: The Nazi concentration camps were a system of more than a thousand camps and subcamps that Nazi Germany built and ran in Germany and occupied Europe between 1933 and 1945. The first were set up in March 1933 after Adolf Hitler became Chancellor; from 1934 the SS ran them. Communists were the first prisoners, then habitual criminals, asocials, Jews and, after the war began, people from across occupied Europe. Prisoners were held in inhumane conditions and died of disease, malnutrition, forced labour, maltreatment and execution: of about 1.65 million registered prisoners, about a million died. From 1941 a linked system of extermination camps was built for mass murder.

entries.name: Andrea del Sarto
aka: Andrea d'Agnolo di Francesco di Luca
entries.desc: Andrea del Sarto was a Florentine painter of the High Renaissance and early Mannerism, known for his frescoes, altarpieces, portraits, drawing and colour; his name came from his father's trade as a tailor. From 1509 to 1514 he painted frescoes at the Santissima Annunziata in Florence, and he worked for years on a series in the cloister of the Scalzo. At the invitation of François I he went to the French court in 1518 but soon returned to Florence. His works include the Madonna of the Harpies of 1517 and a Last Supper at San Salvi. Called a painter without errors in his lifetime, he died of plague in Florence in 1530.

entries.name: American frontier
entries.desc: The American frontier is the history, geography and culture of the westward wave of American settlement in mainland North America, from the European colonies of the early 17th century to the admission of the last contiguous western territories as states in 1912. Encouraged after the Louisiana Purchase, it carried the idea of manifest destiny and was spurred by laws such as the Homestead Act of 1862. It was a story of conquest as well as settlement: Indian wars were fought across the West, and the Native population fell from 600,000 in 1800 to as few as 250,000 by 1890, mostly through disease. The frontier myth became a defining part of American national identity.

entries.name: Xunzi
entries.desc: Xunzi, born Xun Kuang in the state of Zhao, was a Confucian philosopher of the late Warring States period, often ranked as the third great Confucian thinker after Confucius and Mencius. He studied and taught at the Jixia Academy in Qi, later served Lord Chunshen, and taught Han Fei and Li Si. In reply to Taoist and Mohist critics he revised Confucianism into a cohesive system that shaped its flourishing under the Han dynasty. Against Mencius he held that human nature is evil and must be corrected by education and ritual. His writings, compiled as the Xunzi, were set aside from the Tang dynasty onwards and reassessed in the 20th century.

entries.name: John Wesley
entries.desc: John Wesley was an English cleric, theologian and evangelist who led Methodism, a revival movement within the Church of England. Born in Epworth and educated at Christ Church, Oxford, he led the Holy Club there and served an unsuccessful ministry in Savannah, Georgia. At a Moravian meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, on 24 May 1738 he felt his heart strangely warmed, and he then began preaching outdoors and travelling across Great Britain and Ireland, organising small groups led by unordained itinerant preachers, women and men. Methodists under him opposed slavery. Barred from many churches and persecuted at first, he was later described as the best-loved man in England.

entries.name: Herman Hollerith
entries.desc: Herman Hollerith was a German-American statistician, inventor and businessman, born in Buffalo, New York, who developed an electromechanical tabulating machine for punched cards. His first patent application was filed in 1884, and his machines were used to tabulate the 1890 United States census and then censuses in many other countries. He also invented the first automatic card-feed mechanism and the first keypunch. In 1896 he founded the Tabulating Machine Company, which in 1911 was merged with other firms into the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, renamed International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924. His punched cards remained in use for almost a century.

entries.name: Lower Paleolithic
entries.desc: The Lower Paleolithic is the earliest subdivision of the Paleolithic or Old Stone Age, spanning from around 3.3 million years ago, when the first evidence for stone tool production by hominins appears, until around 300,000 years ago. It covers the Oldowan (Mode 1) and Acheulean (Mode 2) industries; the oldest known tools come from Lomekwi 3 in Kenya, found in 2015. Early Homo is assumed to have lived largely by scavenging, while Homo erectus, which appeared by about 1.8 million years ago, moved to hunting and dispersed through Eurasia. The Middle Paleolithic, with prepared-core techniques such as the Mousterian, followed it.

entries.name: Upper Paleolithic
entries.desc: The Upper Paleolithic is the third and last subdivision of the Paleolithic or Old Stone Age, dated very broadly to between 50,000 and 12,000 years ago and, according to some theories, coinciding with the appearance of behavioral modernity in humans. It has the earliest known evidence of organized settlements, and artistic work blossomed in cave painting, petroglyphs and carvings on bone or ivory. Tool industries based on fine blades appeared, along with darts, harpoons, the fish hook, the oil lamp and the eyed needle. Modern humans peopled Europe after c. 45 ka and expanded into the Americas by about 15 ka; the period was followed by the Mesolithic.

entries.name: Northern and Southern dynasties
entries.desc: The Northern and Southern dynasties was a period of political division in the history of China from 420 to 589, following the Sixteen Kingdoms and the Eastern Jin dynasty. It began when Liu Yu seized the throne and founded the Liu Song dynasty; in the south the Liu Song was followed by the Southern Qi, Liang and Chen, while in the north the Northern Wei, founded by the Tuoba of Xianbei ethnicity, gave way to the Eastern and Western Wei, the Northern Qi and the Northern Zhou. The age saw civil war, large-scale migration of Han Chinese south of the Yangtze and the spread of Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism. It ended when Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty unified China proper in 589.

entries.name: Khanate of Bukhara
entries.desc: The Khanate of Bukhara was an Uzbek monarchy in Central Asia from 1501 to 1785, founded by the Shaybanid dynasty, a branch of the Abu'l-Khayrids. Muhammad Shaybani, grandson of Abu'l-Khayr Khan, conquered Balkh, Bukhara, Samarkand and Tashkent, but Shah Ismail I of the Safavid Empire killed him outside Merv in 1510. Abdullah Khan II made Bukhara the permanent capital by 1562, and in the 17th and 18th centuries the Janid dynasty, the last Chinggisid dynasty to rule Bukhara, held the throne. Nader Shah of Iran conquered the khanate in 1740; in 1785 Shah Murad formalized the rule of the Manghit dynasty, and it became the Emirate of Bukhara.

entries.name: 20 July plot
entries.desc: The 20 July plot was a failed attempt on 20 July 1944 to assassinate Adolf Hitler and overthrow the Nazi government, made by members of the German resistance, mainly Wehrmacht officers. Claus von Stauffenberg took a briefcase holding plastic explosive to a conference at the Wolf's Lair in eastern Prussia; the blast killed Heinz Brandt and two others, but Hitler suffered only minor injuries. The coup attempt that followed, known as Operation Valkyrie, collapsed within hours, and Stauffenberg was executed by firing squad the same night. In the following months the Gestapo arrested more than 7,000 people, 4,980 of whom were executed.

entries.name: Constantine P. Cavafy
entries.desc: Constantine P. Cavafy was a Greek poet, journalist and civil servant from Alexandria, born in 1863 to Greek parents from the Phanariot community of Constantinople. After years in England and Constantinople he returned to Alexandria in 1885 and lived there for the rest of his life, working for thirty years as a clerk in the British-run Egyptian Ministry of Public Works. His poetic canon consists of 154 poems; he refused to publish them in books, sharing them instead through newspapers, magazines and broadsheets. E. M. Forster introduced his poems to the English-speaking world in 1923. He died of cancer of the larynx on his 70th birthday in 1933.

entries.name: Unitarianism
entries.desc: Unitarianism is a nontrinitarian movement of Christianity that affirms the unitary nature of God and rejects the doctrine of the Trinity; most Unitarians respect Jesus Christ as a spiritual and moral teacher, and many as savior, but not as equal to God. It arose in the mid-16th century among the Polish Brethren in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and in the Principality of Transylvania, where Ferenc Dávid founded the Unitarian Church of Transylvania. Unitarians faced repression in 17th-century Poland and persecution in Britain, where the first Unitarian church was established on Essex Street, London, in 1774. In North America, King's Chapel in Boston accepted the faith from 1784.

entries.name: Pali Canon
entries.desc: The Pali Canon is the standard collection of scriptures of the Theravada Buddhist tradition, preserved in the Pāli language, and the most complete extant early Buddhist canon. According to Buddhist tradition its teachings were recited at the First Buddhist Council after the Buddha's death and kept orally by the Sangha, then written down on palm leaves at the Fourth Buddhist Council in 29 BCE. It falls into three pitakas or baskets: the Vinaya Piṭaka on the discipline of the sangha, the Sutta Piṭaka of discourses and sermons, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka of doctrinal treatises. The earliest fragments of canonical Pali come from the Pyu city-states in Burma, of the mid-5th to mid-6th century CE.

entries.name: Roland
entries.desc: Roland was a Frankish military leader under Charlemagne and military governor of the Breton March who became an epic hero and a principal figure of the literary cycle known as the Matter of France. His only historical attestation is in Einhard's Vita Karoli Magni, which names him among the Frankish rearguard killed by the Basques at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778. Later writers embellished his death, first in the Old French Chanson de Roland of the 11th century, then in the Italian poems Orlando Innamorato by Matteo Maria Boiardo and Orlando Furioso by Ludovico Ariosto. In poetry he is associated with his sword Durendal and his oliphant horn.

entries.name: Julio-Claudian dynasty
entries.desc: The Julio-Claudian dynasty comprised the first five Roman emperors, Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero, who ruled the Roman Empire from its formation under Augustus in 27 BCE until Nero's suicide in 68 CE. The name is a historiographical term joining the two families of the house, the Julii Caesares and the Claudii Nerones. Since Augustus, Caligula and Nero had no legitimate biological sons, the emperors used adoption to promote their chosen heirs: Augustus adopted his stepson Tiberius, and Claudius his great-nephew and stepson Nero. Within a year of Nero's death, after a brief civil war, the Flavian emperors succeeded the dynasty.

entries.name: Arab Revolt
entries.desc: The Arab Revolt was an armed uprising by the Hashemite-led Arabs of the Hejaz against the Ottoman Empire in the Middle Eastern theatre of World War I. On the basis of the McMahon–Hussein Correspondence, Hussein bin Ali launched it at Mecca on 10 June 1916, aiming at an independent, unified Arab state from Aleppo to Aden that Britain had promised to recognize. With British backing and officers such as T. E. Lawrence, the Sharifian Army drove the Ottomans from much of the Hejaz and Transjordan, and by 1918 had captured Damascus and proclaimed the Arab Kingdom of Syria under Faisal I. Most Arabs in the Ottoman territories did not join it, and its forces played a limited supporting role.

entries.name: Ivan Vazov
entries.desc: Ivan Vazov was a Bulgarian poet, novelist and playwright, often called the Patriarch of Bulgarian literature, born in Sopot in the Rose Valley, then part of the Ottoman Empire. He joined the struggle for Bulgarian independence in 1874 and, after the failure of the April Uprising of 1876, fled again to Galaţi among the exiled revolutionaries, having earlier met Hristo Botev in Romania. His 1888 novel Under the Yoke, which depicts the Ottoman oppression of Bulgaria, has been translated into over 30 languages. He served as Education and People Enlightenment Minister from 1897 to 1899 and died in 1921.

entries.name: Guillaume Du Fay
entries.desc: Guillaume Du Fay was a composer and music theorist of early Renaissance music, variously described as French or Franco-Flemish, and considered the leading European composer of his time. Educated at Cambrai Cathedral, he worked across Europe, joining the papal choir in Rome in 1428 and later serving Amadeus VIII, Duke of Savoy. In 1436 he wrote the motet Nuper Rosarum Flores for the consecration of Filippo Brunelleschi's dome for the Florence Cathedral. After settling in Cambrai in 1458 he turned to cyclic masses based on cantus firmus, among them the Missa L'Homme armé, and influenced younger musicians including Johannes Ockeghem.

credit.artist: Master of the Missal of Paul Beye

entries.name: French and Indian War
entries.desc: The French and Indian War was a conflict in North America from 1754 to 1763 between Great Britain and France and their Indigenous allies, generally seen as part of the Seven Years' War. It grew from a dispute over the Forks of the Ohio and began in May 1754, when Virginia militia under George Washington ambushed a French patrol at Jumonville Glen. After early defeats, among them the Braddock Expedition at the Monongahela in 1755, William Pitt increased British forces, and Britain took Quebec in 1759 and Montreal the following year. From 1755 thousands of Acadians were deported. By the Treaty of Paris of 1763 France ceded Canada and its claims east of the Mississippi River to Britain.

entries.name: Inigo Jones
entries.desc: Inigo Jones was an English architect, the first to introduce the classical architecture of Rome and the Italian Renaissance to England and the first there to employ Vitruvian rules of proportion and symmetry. Born in Smithfield, London, he first became known as a designer of costumes and scenery for masques, many with Ben Jonson, and is credited with bringing movable scenery and the proscenium arch to English theatre. Appointed Surveyor of the King's Works in 1613, he designed the Queen's House at Greenwich, the first English building in a pure classical style, the Banqueting House in Whitehall and the layout of Covent Garden. His career effectively ended with the English Civil War in 1642.

credit.artist: After Anthony van Dyck / William Hogarth

entries.name: Thomas Newcomen
entries.desc: Thomas Newcomen was an English inventor, ironmonger and Baptist preacher who created the atmospheric engine in 1712. Born in Dartmouth, Devon, he made and sold tools for the mining industry at a time when flooding in coal and tin mines was a major problem. Combining the ideas of Thomas Savery and Denis Papin, he used steam condensed in a cylinder to draw down a piston that worked a beam engine and pump, and with his partner John Calley built the first successful engine of this type at the Conygree Coalworks, Tipton. He died in 1729 and was buried at Bunhill Fields; by 1733 about 125 of his engines were operating.

entries.name: George Westinghouse
entries.desc: George Westinghouse was an American inventor, engineer and industrialist based in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, best known for the railway air brake and as a pioneer of alternating current (AC) electrical power distribution. He founded the Westinghouse Air Brake Company in 1869 and Union Switch & Signal in 1881, and developed means for the safe production and transmission of natural gas. His Westinghouse Electric Corporation, founded in 1886, competed with Thomas Edison's direct current, lit the White City at the 1893 Columbian Exposition in Chicago and opened the first large-scale AC generating plant at Niagara Falls in 1895. He received 360 patents and established 61 companies.

entries.name: Gregory of Nyssa
entries.desc: Gregory of Nyssa was an early Christian theologian, bishop of Nyssa from 372 to 376 and from 378 until his death, and with his elder brother Basil of Caesarea and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus one of the Cappadocian Fathers. Deposed by a synod in 376, he regained his see in 378 and took part in the First Council of Constantinople in 381. He contributed to the doctrine of the Trinity and the Nicene Creed, defining the Trinity as one essence in three persons, and his thought, influenced by Origen, has drawn new scholarly interest since the mid-twentieth century, particularly on universal salvation. He was the first person in recorded history to write against all forms of slavery.

entries.name: Thomism
entries.desc: Thomism is the philosophical and theological school that arose from the work and thought of Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a Dominican philosopher, theologian and Doctor of the Church. Aquinas drew on Greek, Roman, Islamic and Jewish philosophers, largely followed Aristotelian terminology and metaphysics, and held that the world can be known as it is; his Summa Theologica remains a central point of reference for the philosophy and theology of the Catholic Church. Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Aeterni Patris of 1879 spurred a revival known as Neothomism, which held sway as the dominant philosophy of the Roman Catholic Church until the Second Vatican Council.

entries.name: François Quesnay
entries.desc: François Quesnay was a French economist and physician of the Physiocratic school, born at Méré near Versailles. Apprenticed to a surgeon and qualified in Paris, he became physician in ordinary to King Louis XV and was installed in the Palace of Versailles, where the king called him his thinker. Around 1750 he and Jacques C.M.V. de Gournay became the centre of the group later known as the Physiocrates, which included the elder Mirabeau and du Pont de Nemours. His Tableau économique of 1758, perhaps the first work to describe the workings of the economy analytically, provided the foundations of their ideas, and his Le Despotisme de la Chine of 1767 supported enlightened despotism.

entries.name: Spanish colonization of the Americas
entries.desc: The Spanish colonization of the Americas began in 1493 on the Caribbean island of Hispaniola, after the 1492 voyage of the Genoese mariner Christopher Columbus under license from Queen Isabella I of Castile. The Indigenous population fell by an estimated 80% in the first century and a half, primarily through infectious diseases, while forced labor, slavery and forced resettlement were imposed and enslaved Africans were imported. An estimated 1.86 million Spaniards settled in the Americas between 1492 and 1832. The Spanish American wars of independence of the early 19th century ended Spanish rule over most of the region, and Cuba and Puerto Rico were lost to the United States in 1898.

entries.name: Islamic schools and branches
entries.desc: Islamic schools and branches are the sects, schools of jurisprudence and schools of theology into which Muslims are divided. The original schism between Kharijites, Sunnīs and Shīʿas arose over the succession to the guidance of the Muslim community after the death of Muhammad: Shīʿas hold ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib to be his true successor, Sunnīs Abu Bakr. Sunnīs, around 87-90% of all Muslims, follow four main schools of jurisprudence, the Mālikī, Ḥanafī, Shāfiʿī and Ḥanbalī; Shīʿa Islam has three major sects, the Twelvers, Ismāʿīlīs and Zaydīs. Of the Kharijite branches only the Ibadis survive.

entries.name: Middle Paleolithic
entries.desc: The Middle Paleolithic is the second subdivision of the Paleolithic, or Old Stone Age, in Europe, Africa and Asia, called the Middle Stone Age in African archeology. It broadly spanned from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, with considerable dating differences between regions, and was succeeded by the Upper Paleolithic. The earliest evidence of behavioral modernity appears in it: burials at Krapina in Croatia and the Qafzeh and Es Skhul caves in Israel, and bracelets, beads and ochre at Blombos Cave. Long-distance trade between groups appeared as early as 120,000 years ago, and people lived in small, egalitarian band societies.

entries.name: Old Chosŏn
entries.desc: Old Chosŏn, also known as Gojoseon, was the first kingdom on the Korean Peninsula. According to the Samguk yusa of the 13th century it was founded in 2333 BCE by Tan'gun, son of the heavenly prince Hwanung and the bear-woman Ungnyeo, a myth that has played an important role in Korean identity; Chinese sources tell of the Shang sage Jizi, or Kija, founding Kija Chosŏn, whose existence is debated. In 194 BCE Wiman, a refugee from Yan, overthrew its ruling dynasty and founded Wiman Joseon, which the Han dynasty under Emperor Wu conquered in 108 BCE. Its capital from at least the 2nd century BCE was Wanggeom-seong, now Pyongyang.

entries.name: Tomás de Torquemada
entries.desc: Tomás de Torquemada was a Spanish Dominican friar and the first Grand Inquisitor of the Spanish Inquisition. Prior of the monastery of Santa Cruz at Segovia, he became confessor to Isabella I and later to Ferdinand, and was named Grand Inquisitor of Spain a year after his appointment as an inquisitor in 1482. Under him the Inquisition grew from a single tribunal at Seville to a network of two dozen, and he was one of the chief supporters of the Alhambra Decree of 1492, which expelled the Jews from Spain. Because of the Inquisition's use of torture and burning at the stake, which he approved, his name became synonymous with cruelty and religious intolerance.

credit.artist: Maestro de la Virgen de los Reyes Católicos.

entries.name: Lee de Forest
entries.desc: Lee de Forest was an American inventor and electrical engineer who in 1908 invented the three-element Audion triode vacuum tube, the first practical electronic amplifier. Born in Council Bluffs, Iowa, he earned a doctorate at Yale in 1899. The Audion helped start the Electronic Age and made radio broadcasting and long-distance telephone lines possible; from 1921 he worked on Phonofilm, an optical sound-on-film process. He held over 300 patents, spent much of his income on patent lawsuits and was tried for mail fraud and acquitted. He received the 1922 IRE Medal of Honor and died in Hollywood in 1961.

credit.artist: The original uploader was Thbusch at English Wikipedia . Later versions were uploaded by Neutrality at en.wikipedia .

entries.name: Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia
entries.desc: The Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia, also known as the Kingdom of Ruthenia, was a medieval state in Eastern Europe, mostly in modern-day Ukraine, and one of the three most important powers to emerge from the collapse of Kievan Rus'. Roman the Great united the principalities of Galicia and Volhynia at the turn of the 13th century. After the Mongol invasion of 1239–1241, Prince Daniel of Galicia pledged allegiance to Batu Khan of the Golden Horde in 1246, and in 1253 he was crowned King of Ruthenia by the Pope in an attempt to create an anti-Mongol alliance. Casimir III the Great of Poland annexed Galicia in 1349, and Volhynia came under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

entries.name: Eastern Front (World War I)
entries.desc: The Eastern Front of World War I was the theater of operations along the frontier between Russia and Romania on one side and Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Germany on the other, from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea, where the fighting was more dynamic than on the Western Front. Russia's invasion of East Prussia in 1914 was defeated, and Central Powers offensives in 1915 drove it from Galicia and Poland; the Brusilov offensive of 1916 was the largest Entente victory in the war. After the February Revolution of 1917 discipline declined, the Bolsheviks took power, and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk of March 1918 took Russia out of the war.

entries.name: Nigerian Civil War
entries.desc: The Nigerian Civil War was fought from 6 July 1967 to 15 January 1970 between Nigeria and the Republic of Biafra, a secessionist state that had declared its independence. Its immediate causes were a military coup, a counter-coup and anti-Igbo pogroms in the Northern Region in 1966. Nigerian forces under General Yakubu Gowon surrounded Biafra, led by Lieutenant Colonel Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu, and a blockade led to the mass starvation of its civilians: there were approximately 100,000 military casualties, while between 500,000 and 2 million Biafran civilians died of starvation. The Biafran airlift inspired the formation of Doctors Without Borders.

entries.name: 1976 Tangshan earthquake
entries.desc: The 1976 Tangshan earthquake struck Tangshan, Hebei, China, early on 28 July 1976 local time, with a magnitude of Mw 7.6 and a maximum intensity of XI on the Mercalli scale. Its first shock began approximately 12 kilometres under the southern part of the city, on a fault running right under its center. In minutes 85 percent of the buildings in Tangshan collapsed or were rendered unusable, all services failed and most highway and railway bridges collapsed or were seriously damaged. The official count stated 242,469 deaths, while historians accepted at least 300,000, making it the deadliest earthquake in recorded history excluding the famine deaths of the 1556 Shaanxi earthquake.

entries.name: India–Pakistan war of 1971
entries.desc: The India–Pakistan war of 1971 was fought between India and Pakistan during the Bangladesh Liberation War, from 3 to 16 December 1971. It began with Pakistan's Operation Chengiz Khan, preemptive aerial strikes on eight Indian air stations, after which India declared war and joined the conflict on the side of Bengali nationalist forces. Thirteen days later the Eastern Command of the Pakistan military surrendered in Dhaka, and East Pakistan became the new nation of Bangladesh; approximately 93,000 Pakistanis were taken prisoner. Pakistani forces and the Razakars killed an estimated 300,000 to 3,000,000 civilians in Bangladesh, and eight to ten million people fled to India.

entries.name: Ignacy Łukasiewicz
entries.desc: Ignacy Łukasiewicz was a Polish pharmacist, engineer, businessman, inventor and philanthropist in the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria, then part of the Austrian Empire. Born in Zaduszniki near Mielec, he was imprisoned in Lwów from 1846 to 1847 as a member of a party preparing an uprising, and graduated in pharmaceutics from the University of Vienna in 1852. He discovered how to distill kerosene from seep crude oil, invented the modern kerosene lamp in 1853, built the world's first modern oil well in 1854 and in 1856 opened the world's first industrial oil refinery at Ulaszowice, near Jasło. He died of pneumonia at Chorkówka in 1882.

entries.name: Isaac Singer
entries.desc: Isaac Merritt Singer was an American inventor, actor and businessman who improved the design of the sewing machine and founded what became the Singer Sewing Machine Company, one of the first American multi-national businesses. After patenting a rock drill in 1839 and touring as an actor, he redesigned a sewing machine in Boston so that the shuttle moved in a straight line, with a straight needle, and patented it in 1851. In 1856 his firm joined the Sewing Machine Combination, the first patent pool, and sewing machines began to be mass-produced and marketed for home use. He settled in Paignton, Devon, in 1871 and died in 1875, leaving a $13 million fortune.

entries.name: Reform Judaism
entries.desc: Reform Judaism, also known as Liberal or Progressive Judaism, is a major Jewish denomination that emphasizes the evolving nature of Judaism, the superiority of its ethical aspects to its ceremonial ones, and a continuous revelation. It began in mid-19th-century Germany, where Rabbi Abraham Geiger and his associates formulated its principles, removing parts of the liturgy such as bodily resurrection and translating much of the prayer into German. Brought to America by German-born rabbis, it flourished there from the 1860s to the 1930s, the era of Classical Reform. The World Union for Progressive Judaism, founded in 1926, estimates it represents at least 1.8 million people in 50 countries.

entries.name: Mitochondrial Eve
entries.desc: Mitochondrial Eve, in human genetics, is the matrilineal most recent common ancestor of all living humans: the most recent woman from whom all living humans descend in an unbroken line purely through their mothers. She stands at the divergence of macro-haplogroup L into L0 and L1–7, which estimates of 2013 placed at around 155,000 years ago. The idea comes from the 1987 paper in Nature by Cann, Stoneking and Wilson, which concluded that all current human mtDNA originated from a single population from Africa, a blow to the multiregional hypothesis. She was not a first woman, nor the only woman of her time, and her position moves forward as lineages become extinct.

entries.name: Paranthropus
entries.desc: Paranthropus is a genus of extinct hominin with three widely accepted species, P. aethiopicus, P. robustus and P. boisei, also called the robust australopithecines; its validity is contested, and it is sometimes considered synonymous with Australopithecus. They lived between approximately 2.9 and at least 1.2 million years ago, had robust skulls with a gorilla-like sagittal crest and broad grinding teeth, were bipeds and had comparatively small bodies. Robert Broom erected the genus in 1938 from a braincase found at Kromdraai in South Africa, and Mary Leakey discovered P. boisei at Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, in 1959.

entries.name: Wounded Knee Massacre
entries.desc: The Wounded Knee Massacre took place on 29 December 1890 near Wounded Knee Creek on the Lakota Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota, during the U.S. Army's Pine Ridge Campaign. The 7th Cavalry Regiment had surrounded the camp of Spotted Elk's band of Miniconjou Lakota and 38 Hunkpapa Lakota, supported by four Hotchkiss mountain guns, amid settlers' fears of the Ghost Dance. During an attempt to disarm the Lakota a rifle went off, the firing became indiscriminate, and between 250 and 300 Lakota were killed, along with 25 soldiers. In 1990 both houses of Congress expressed deep regret for the massacre.

entries.name: Information Age
entries.desc: The Information Age is a historical period that began in the mid-20th century, marked by a rapid shift from the traditional industries of the Industrial Revolution to an economy centered on information technology. Its onset has been linked to the first working transistor, invented in 1947 by John Bardeen and Walter Houser Brattain under William Shockley at Bell Labs, which led the way to more compact digital computers. The digital revolution converted technology from analog to digital format, so that identical copies could be made; a message was sent over the ARPANET in 1969, and in the 1980s compact discs replaced vinyl records and cassette tapes.

entries.name: Kellogg–Briand Pact
aka: General Treaty for Renunciation of War as an Instrument of National Policy
entries.desc: The Kellogg–Briand Pact, or Pact of Paris, is an international agreement of 1928 in which the signatory states renounced war as an instrument of national policy and promised to settle their disputes only by pacific means. Named after the United States Secretary of State Frank B. Kellogg and the French foreign minister Aristide Briand, it was first signed in Paris on 27 August 1928 and took effect on 24 July 1929, with 57 state parties by 1929. It had no mechanism for enforcement and could not prevent the Second World War, but it served as the legal basis for the crime against peace tried by the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals. It remains in effect.

entries.name: Angolan Civil War
entries.desc: The Angolan Civil War was fought in Angola, with interludes, from 1975, just after independence from Portugal, until 2002. It was a power struggle between two former anti-colonial movements, the communist People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA) and the anti-communist National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA). With Cuban soldiers and Soviet support the MPLA won the first phase and became the de facto government, while UNITA, backed by the United States and South Africa, fought on. Widely considered a Cold War proxy conflict, it ended with the MPLA's victory in 2002, after government troops killed Jonas Savimbi; between 500,000 and 800,000 people had died.

entries.name: Second Congo War
entries.desc: The Second Congo War was a conflict in the Democratic Republic of the Congo that began on 2 August 1998, after President Laurent-Désiré Kabila turned against the Rwandan and Ugandan allies who had helped him seize power. It drew in nine African nations and about 25 armed groups. Rwandan troops and RCD rebels overran the Kivus, while Zimbabwean and Angolan forces saved Kinshasa. After the Lusaka Peace Agreement of 1999 and Kabila's assassination in January 2001, the war officially ended on 18 July 2003, though violence persisted in the east. A 2008 report by the International Rescue Committee estimated 5.4 million deaths, mainly from disease and malnutrition.

entries.name: Great Chinese Famine
entries.desc: The Great Chinese Famine was a famine in the People's Republic of China between 1959 and 1961, though some scholars include 1958 or 1962. Estimates of deaths from starvation range from 15 to 46 million, with newer estimates around 30 to 46 million. Its main causes were the policies of the Great Leap Forward and the people's communes launched by Mao Zedong: high grain confiscation for export, poor farming techniques, the Eliminate Sparrows campaign, over-reporting of harvests and the shift of farmers to iron and steel production. Anhui, Sichuan and Guizhou were among the worst hit. In 1962 Liu Shaoqi attributed 70% of the famine to man-made errors.

entries.name: Vasil Levski
entries.desc: Vasil Levski, born Vasil Ivanov Kunchev in Karlovo, was a Bulgarian revolutionary who worked to free Bulgaria from Ottoman rule and is a national hero of Bulgaria. He became an Orthodox monk in 1858, then joined the Bulgarian Legions in Serbia and, abroad, gained the nickname Levski, "Lionlike". Instead of raising detachments abroad, he built the Internal Revolutionary Organisation, a network of secret committees inside Bulgaria centred on Lovech, and helped found the Bulgarian Revolutionary Central Committee in Romania. He envisioned a republic in which all ethnic and religious groups had equal rights. Ottoman authorities captured him near Lovech and hanged him in Sofia in 1873.

credit.artist: File:BASA-600K-1-1865-15-Vasil Levski.jpeg : Unknown author Unknown author derivative work: Iliev

entries.name: European integration
entries.desc: European integration is the process of political, legal, social and economic integration of states in or near Europe, brought about mainly through the European Union. Earlier ideas of a united Europe looked back to the Roman Empire, and in the interwar years Richard von Coudenhove-Kalergi and Aristide Briand argued for European unity. In 1951 six states, among them France, Italy and West Germany, placed coal and steel under the European Coal and Steel Community. The 1957 Treaties of Rome created the European Economic Community and Euratom, the Single European Act of 1987 set up the single market, and the Treaty of Maastricht established the European Union in 1993.

entries.name: African traditional religions
entries.desc: African traditional religions are the diverse ethnic religions of African peoples, handed down orally from one generation to the next through narratives, songs, myths and festivals rather than scripture. They include beliefs in spirits and in higher and lower gods, sometimes with a supreme creator, the veneration of ancestors, magic and traditional medicine. Most can be described as animistic, with polytheistic and pantheistic aspects. Islam and Christianity have largely displaced them, yet many Africans combine them with Abrahamic practice, and their adherents are estimated at over 100 million in 43 countries.

entries.name: Early human migrations
entries.desc: Early human migrations were the spread of archaic and modern humans across the continents, believed to have begun about 2 million years ago when Homo erectus expanded out of Africa. Homo sapiens dispersed within Africa around the time of its speciation, roughly 300,000 years ago. The recent African origin theory holds that modern humans outside Africa descend from a population that left East Africa roughly 70–50,000 years ago and reached Oceania by about 50,000 years ago and Europe about 40,000 years ago, interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans on the way. People reached the Americas about 20,000 years ago, and Polynesia was settled within the past 2,000 years.

entries.name: Macedonian Wars
entries.desc: The Macedonian Wars were a series of conflicts from 214 to 148 BCE in which the Roman Republic and its Greek allies fought the major Greek kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean. The First Macedonian War against Philip V, an ally of Hannibal, ended indecisively in 205 BCE. Rome defeated Philip at Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE, the Seleucid Empire at Magnesia in the war of 192–188 BCE, and Perseus of Macedon at Pydna in 168 BCE, after which Macedonia was split into four client republics. A fourth war against the pretender Andriscus was followed in 146 BCE by the defeat of the Achaean League and the destruction of Corinth, leaving Rome dominant over Greece.

entries.name: Mary Baker Eddy
entries.desc: Mary Baker Eddy was an American religious leader and author who in 1879 founded The Church of Christ, Scientist, the Mother Church of the Christian Science movement. Born in Bow to a Congregationalist family, she was influenced by the Mesmerist ideas of Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, and after a fall on the ice in Lynn, Massachusetts in 1866 she said she had recovered through reading the Bible. Her book Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures first appeared in 1875. She taught many students, opened a college in Massachusetts in the 1880s and founded The Christian Science Monitor in 1908. She led the movement until her death in 1910; critics view her methods of healing as harmful.

entries.name: Jade Emperor
entries.desc: The Jade Emperor is a god of Chinese myth and folk religion, one of the representations of the primordial god. In Taoist theology he is the assistant of Yuanshi Tianzun, one of the Three Pure Ones, and he is often identified with Śakra in Chinese Buddhist cosmology. In myth he was the head of the pantheon, the supreme sovereign proclaimed by gods, immortals and humans after he defeated an evil entity that had overcome the gods; one story makes him the father of Zhinü, the weaver girl. His birthday is said to fall on the ninth day of the first lunar month, when Taoist temples hold a ritual at which worshippers burn incense and make food offerings.

entries.name: Conservative Judaism
entries.desc: Conservative Judaism, also known as Masorti Judaism, is a Jewish religious movement that holds Jewish law, or Halakha, to be both binding and subject to historical development, its authority resting chiefly on the assent of the people through the generations. It regards itself as heir to the positive-historical school of Rabbi Zecharias Frankel in 19th-century Europe, but became fully institutionalized in the United States in the mid-20th century. The United Synagogue was founded in 1913, and the Jewish Theological Seminary of America is its largest seminary. In 1983 it resolved to ordain women rabbis. It is the third-largest Jewish movement, close to 1.1 million people.

entries.name: Cradle of civilization
entries.desc: A cradle of civilization is a place and culture in which one of the earliest civilizations emerged independently, a civilization being a complex society with a state, social stratification, cities and writing or graphic arts. Scholars once thought civilization began in the Fertile Crescent and spread from there; today they generally recognise six cradles: Mesopotamia, Ancient Egypt, Ancient India and Ancient China in Afro-Eurasia, and the Caral–Supe civilization of Peru and the Olmec civilization of Mexico in the Americas. All depended on agriculture, except possibly Caral–Supe. The first large cities, such as Uruk, Ur, Kish and Eridu, rose by the 31st century BCE.

entries.name: American Indian Wars
entries.desc: The American Indian Wars were conflicts fought by European colonial empires, the United States and others against American Indian tribes in North America, from the earliest colonial settlements in the 17th century to the end of the 19th century. Their most common cause was the settlers' and governments' desire for tribal lands. After the War of 1812, treaties transferred large areas to the United States, which often broke them, and the Indian Removal Act of 1830 led to forced removals such as the Trail of Tears. On the Great Plains peoples were confined to reservations; at Wounded Knee in 1890 soldiers killed up to 300 Native Americans. Some scholars call these policies genocide.

credit.artist: The United States Army and Navy, Unknown author Unknown author

entries.name: 1931 China floods
entries.desc: The 1931 China floods were a series of floods from June to August 1931 along the Yangtze and Huai rivers, which struck Wuhan, Nanjing and other cities and culminated in a dike breach along Lake Gaoyou on 25 August. After a long drought and a harsh winter, snowmelt met heavy rain and nine cyclones in July, and the waters covered about 180,000 square kilometres. Estimates of the dead vary widely: a survey led by John Lossing Buck found 150,000 drowned, Chinese historians led by Li Wenhai counted 422,420, and some Western sources claim 3.7 to 4 million from famine and disease. The Kuomintang government set up the National Flood Relief Commission under T.V. Soong.

credit.artist: 新浪博客「武汉一中老校友」（轉載讀者稿件）

entries.name: 1970 Bhola cyclone
entries.desc: The 1970 Bhola cyclone was the deadliest tropical cyclone on record, which struck East Pakistan (present-day Bangladesh) and India's West Bengal on 12 November 1970. It formed over the central Bay of Bengal on 8 November and reached winds of 185 km/h. At least 300,000 people died, possibly as many as 500,000, mostly in the storm surge that flooded the low-lying islands of the Ganges Delta; in Tazumuddin over 45% of the population was killed. The government of General Yahya Khan was criticised for its slow relief. Anger in East Pakistan helped the Awami League win a landslide in the election a month later, and the Bangladesh Liberation War followed seven months later.

entries.name: Population transfer in the Soviet Union
entries.desc: From 1930 to 1952 the government of the Soviet Union, on the orders of Joseph Stalin and under the direction of Lavrentiy Beria, forcibly transferred whole groups of people, mostly to remote and underpopulated areas. Those deported included "anti-Soviet" categories, entire ethnic groups such as the Soviet Koreans in 1937, the Chechens and Ingush and the Crimean Tatars, and labour forces. At least 6 million people were affected, among them 1.8 million kulaks in 1930–31. Soviet archives record hundreds of thousands of deaths, and Nicolas Werth places the total near 1 to 1.5 million. In 1991 a law of the Russian republic denounced the deportations as a policy of genocide.
links: Population transfer in the Soviet Union

entries.name: Al-Nawawi
entries.desc: Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi was a jurist and hadith scholar of the Shafi'i school, born at Nawa near Daraa in Syria, and best known for The Meadows of the Righteous and his Sharh Sahih Muslim. He studied in Damascus from the age of 18 under more than twenty teachers and settled there after his pilgrimage in 1253. In 1267 he became head of the Ashrafiyya Dār al-Ḥadīth in Damascus, a post he held until his death. Known for his asceticism, he never married, and he twice defied the Mamluk Sultan Baybars over taxes and endowments. He died at about 45, but his many works on hadith, theology and law are still read, and the Shafi'i school counts him and al-Rafi'i as the Two Shaykhs.

entries.name: Dōgen
entries.desc: Dōgen was a Japanese Zen Buddhist monk, writer and philosopher who founded the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan. First ordained in the Tendai School in Kyoto, he grew dissatisfied with its teaching and in 1223 crossed to Song China, where he trained under Rujing of the Caodong lineage and received Dharma transmission in 1227. Back in Japan he promoted zazen, or sitting meditation, and after tension with the Tendai community he moved in 1243 to Echizen province, where his followers built the temple he renamed Eihei-ji in 1246. His writings, above all the Shōbōgenzō, and the Eihei Shingi, the first Japanese Zen monastic code, remain central to Sōtō Zen.

entries.name: Diamond Sutra
entries.desc: The Diamond Sūtra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture of the Prajñāpāramitā, or perfection of wisdom, genre, one of the most influential sutras in East Asia and especially prominent in the Chan or Zen tradition. The date of its composition in Sanskrit is uncertain, with arguments made for the 2nd and the 5th centuries. Kumārajīva's Chinese translation, thought to date from 401, became the most widely used version. A printed copy of that translation, found among the Dunhuang manuscripts in 1900 and sold to Aurel Stein in 1907, dates to 868 CE and is now in the British Library; it is the oldest dated printed book known, made, its colophon says, for universal free distribution.

credit.artist: The colophon, at the inner end, reads: Reverently [caused to be] made for universal free distribution by Wang Jie on behalf of his two paren

entries.name: Nanyue
entries.desc: Nanyue was an ancient kingdom in what is now southern China and northern Vietnam, founded in 204 BCE by the Qin general Zhao Tuo, with its capital at Panyu. It covered Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan and central to northern Vietnam. Its rulers called themselves emperors while paying the Han dynasty only symbolic obeisance, and they brought Chinese-style administration and writing to the south while encouraging the mixing of Yue and Han cultures. When the king Zhao Xing sought union with the Han in 113 BCE, his prime minister Lü Jia killed him, and in 111 BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent 100,000 troops and ended the kingdom. The name Vietnam derives from Nam Việt.

entries.name: Dust Bowl
entries.desc: The Dust Bowl was a period of severe dust storms and drought from 1930 to 1940 that badly damaged the farming and ecology of the High Plains and North American prairies, above all western Kansas, the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southeast Colorado and northeast New Mexico. It was caused by drought, which came in three waves in 1934, 1936 and 1939–1940, and by settlers who had destroyed the topsoil without using dryland farming methods. On "Black Sunday", 14 April 1935, black blizzards swept the plains. About 3.5 million people left the Plains states, many of them, called Okies, for California. John Steinbeck, Woody Guthrie and Dorothea Lange depicted its migrants.

entries.name: Kang Youwei
entries.desc: Kang Youwei was a Chinese political thinker and reformer of the late Qing dynasty, born in Nanhai County, Guangdong, in 1858. After China's defeat by Japan in 1895 he, his student Liang Qichao and over 600 examination candidates petitioned the Guangxu Emperor against the Treaty of Shimonoseki, and in 1898 both took a leading part in the Hundred Days' Reform. When the Empress Dowager Cixi ended the reform by a coup and ordered his arrest and execution, Kang fled abroad and organised the Protect the Emperor Society. He remained an advocate of constitutional monarchy, launched a failed coup in 1917 and set out a cosmopolitan utopia in his Datong Shu. He died in Qingdao in 1927.

entries.name: Ayyavazhi
entries.desc: Ayyavazhi, the Path of the Master, is a Hindu denomination that originated in South India in the 19th century, centred on the life and preaching of Ayya Vaikundar (c. 1809 – c. 1851), whom it holds to be the Purna avatar of Narayana. Its holy texts are the Akilathirattu Ammanai and the Arul Nool. The washing penance of 1840 is taken as its origin; most early followers came from marginalised and poor sections of society, mainly of the Nadar caste, in South Travancore and South Tirunelveli, and Swamithope became its centre. Its followers, mostly in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, are estimated at 8,000,000 to 10,000,000.

entries.name: Kingdom of Germany
entries.desc: The Kingdom of Germany (Latin Regnum Teutonicum) was the original core of the Holy Roman Empire, distinct from the empire's kingdoms of Italy and Burgundy. It grew out of the eastern Frankish kingdom formed by the Treaty of Verdun in 843 and was made up of the stem duchies of Saxony, Franconia, Thuringia, Bavaria and Swabia, consolidating its hold on Lotharingia in the 10th century. After the last Carolingian, Louis the Child, died in 911, the dukes elected Conrad I king, and from 962 the kings of Germany claimed the imperial title. Its rulers stressed their imperial office, and no official royal title named Germany until 1508.

entries.name: Stab-in-the-back myth
entries.desc: The stab-in-the-back myth (German Dolchstoßlegende) was an antisemitic and anti-communist conspiracy theory, widely believed in Germany after 1918, which held that the Imperial German Army had not lost World War I on the battlefield but had been betrayed on the home front, above all by Jews, revolutionary socialists and republican politicians. Its advocates called the leaders who signed the Armistice of 11 November 1918 the November criminals. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party made it part of their official history after 1933. Historians reject the myth, pointing to the lack of further reserves and the overwhelming of German forces on the western front by more numerous Allied armies.

entries.name: Madam C. J. Walker
entries.desc: Madam C. J. Walker, born Sarah Breedlove near Delta, Louisiana, in 1867, was an American entrepreneur, philanthropist and activist who made her fortune with a line of cosmetics and hair care products for Black women. The first child of her family born into freedom, she was orphaned at seven and worked as a domestic servant and laundress before developing her own products in Denver from 1905. In 1910 she moved to Indianapolis, home of the Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company, which employed several thousand women as sales agents between 1911 and 1919. She gave to the NAACP and other causes, and at her death in 1919 was considered the wealthiest African-American businesswoman in America.

entries.name: Yan Fu
entries.desc: Yan Fu was a Chinese military officer, newspaper editor, translator and writer, born in Fuzhou in 1854, who introduced Western ideas to China in the late 19th century. A student of the Foochow Arsenal Academy, he went on to the Royal Naval College, Greenwich, in 1877–79 and later taught at the Beiyang Naval Officers' School at Tianjin. After China's defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War he became known for his translations of Thomas Huxley's Evolution and Ethics, Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, John Stuart Mill's On Liberty and Herbert Spencer's Study of Sociology, through which natural selection and survival of the fittest reached Chinese readers. He died in 1921.

entries.name: Baal Shem Tov
entries.desc: Israel ben Eliezer, known as the Baal Shem Tov or Besht, was a Jewish mystic and healer regarded as the founder of Hasidic Judaism. He was born about 1700; early Hasidic legends name Okop as his birthplace, while the historian Moshe Idel places it in Moldavia. About 1740 he settled in Medzhybizh, where Polish census records show a holy man, described as a kabbalist and later a baal shem, from 1740 to 1760. He left no books: his teachings, centred on devekut, a direct connection with the divine in every human activity, are known from the works of his disciples, and legends of his life were collected in the Shivḥei haBesht of 1815.

entries.name: Wallace Carothers
entries.desc: Wallace Hume Carothers was an American chemist, born in Burlington, Iowa, in 1896, who led organic chemistry at DuPont and is credited with the invention of nylon. After a PhD at the University of Illinois in 1924 and teaching posts that included Harvard University, he joined DuPont's new fundamental research programme at Wilmington, Delaware, where he chose polymer research. His group helped lay the groundwork for neoprene, and in 1935 Gerard Berchet, under his direction, produced polyamide 6-6, the substance later known as nylon.
