Troubled by depression since his youth, he took his own life in 1937, sixteen months before the discovery of nylon was announced.

entries.name: Samuel Crompton
entries.desc: Samuel Crompton was an English inventor and pioneer of the spinning industry, born in Bolton, Lancashire, in 1753, who invented the spinning mule. As a boy he learned to spin on James Hargreaves's spinning jenny, and about 1779, at Hall i' th' Wood, he produced a mule-jenny that spun yarn fine enough for muslin. As he lacked the means to take out a patent, he made the machine public on manufacturers' promises of payment and received no royalties, though a survey in 1812 found between 4 and 5 million mule spindles in use. Parliament awarded him £5000 in 1812, but his later businesses failed, and he died in Bolton in 1827.

entries.name: Charles Algernon Parsons
entries.desc: Sir Charles Algernon Parsons was an English mechanical engineer and inventor, born in London in 1854 as the youngest son of the astronomer William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse, who designed the modern steam turbine in 1884. At Clarke, Chapman and Co. near Newcastle he built a turbine turning at 18,000 RPM and used it to drive an electrical generator of his own design. In 1889 he founded C. A. Parsons and Company in Newcastle, and his Turbinia of 1894 was the first steamship powered by a steam turbine, changing marine propulsion. He was knighted in 1911 and died in 1931 on board the Duchess of Richmond.

entries.name: History of writing
entries.desc: The history of writing traces how writing systems developed and how their use transformed societies. Each invention of writing, the first within the last 6,000 years, grew out of proto-writing, symbols that could not fully record spoken language. Four independent inventions are most commonly recognised: in Mesopotamia about 3400–3100 BCE, in Egypt about 3250 BCE, in China before about 1250 BCE and in Mesoamerica before about 1 CE. The first alphabetic writing was developed by workers in the Sinai Peninsula about 1800 BCE, and its descendant, the Phoenician alphabet, was adapted into the Aramaic and Greek alphabets, from which most writing systems of Afro-Eurasia descend.

entries.name: Control of fire by early humans
entries.desc: The control of fire by early humans gave warmth, light, protection from predators, better hunting tools and cooked food, and so allowed humans to spread and changed their diet and behaviour. Claims for the earliest use of fire by members of Homo reach back 2.0 million years; charred bones in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, show fire use 1.79 million years ago, and heated fish teeth at the Daughters of Jacob Bridge in the Golan Heights are the oldest likely evidence of cooking, about 780,000 years ago. The oldest definitive evidence of making fire, about 400,000 years old, comes from a Neanderthal site in eastern England.
links: Control of fire by early humans

entries.name: Oprichnina
entries.desc: The oprichnina was a state policy of Tsar Ivan the Terrible in Russia from 1565 to 1572 that included mass repression of the boyars, the Russian aristocracy, with public executions and the confiscation of their land and property. During the costly Livonian War, and after Prince Andrey Kurbsky defected in 1564, Ivan announced his abdication and returned only on condition that he could prosecute traitors outside legal limits. He ruled a separate territory alone through his guard, the oprichniki, while the Boyar Council ruled the zemshchina. The oprichniki carried out a month-long terror in Novgorod, and in 1572 the two halves of the state were reunited.

entries.name: Ottoman wars in Europe
entries.desc: The Ottoman wars in Europe were a series of conflicts between the Ottoman Empire and European states from the Late Middle Ages to the early 20th century. After seizing Gallipoli in 1354 the Ottomans expanded through the Balkans and pushed into Central Europe in the 15th and 16th centuries, while their wars with Venice lasted from 1423 to 1718 and included their fleet's defeat at Lepanto in 1571. The Holy League reversed a number of Ottoman gains in the Great Turkish War of 1683–99. The final retreat began with the First Balkan War of 1912–1913 and ended in the partitioning of the empire after World War I.

entries.name: Shitao
entries.desc: Shitao, born Zhu Ruoji into the Ming imperial clan in Quanzhou County, Guangxi, in 1642, was a Chinese Buddhist monk, calligrapher and landscape painter of the early Qing dynasty. He escaped the fall of the Ming in 1644, became a Buddhist monk no later than 1651, lived in Nanjing and Yangzhou in the 1680s and sought patronage in Beijing from 1690. When no patron was found, he converted to Daoism in 1693 and returned to Yangzhou, where he died in 1707. An individualist painter, he broke with codified styles through washes, bold brushstrokes and blank space, and wrote Sayings on Painting from Monk Bitter Gourd.

entries.name: Rus' people
entries.desc: The Rus', also known as Russes, were a people of early medieval Eastern Europe whom the scholarly consensus holds to have been originally Norsemen, mainly from present-day Sweden, who settled and ruled along the river routes between the Baltic and the Black Sea from around the 8th to 11th centuries. Their first centres were Ladoga, founded in the mid-8th century, and Rurikovo Gorodische, founded in the mid-9th, at either end of the Volkhov River. In Kievan Rus' the ruling Norsemen gradually assimilated into the East Slavic population, and the elite lost Old Norse by the second half of the 11th century. They gave their name to Russia and Belarus.

entries.name: Chivalry
entries.desc: Chivalry is an informal and varying code of conduct that developed in France between 1170 and 1220, associated with the medieval Christian institution of knighthood. The word comes from the Old French chevalerie, horse soldiery, and the code arose in the Carolingian Empire from the idealisation of the cavalryman among Charlemagne's horse soldiers. Its ideals were spread by medieval literature, above all the Matter of France and the Matter of Britain, with its legend of King Arthur. By the Late Middle Ages it was a moral system combining a warrior ethos, knightly piety and courtly manners, described in works by Ramon Llull and Geoffroi de Charny.

entries.name: Russian conquest of Siberia
entries.desc: The Russian conquest of Siberia took place between 1581 and 1778, beginning traditionally with the campaign of some 540 Cossacks under Yermak Timofeyevich against the Khanate of Sibir of Kuchum Khan. Yermak entered its capital, Qashliq, in 1582 but was defeated in 1584; the Russians returned in 1586, and Kuchum Khan was beaten at the Battle of Irmen in 1598. From forts built to collect yasak, a fur tribute, the Russians pushed east and reached the Pacific Ocean in 1639. The indigenous peoples resisted, the Cossacks often committed atrocities against them, and smallpox carried away up to 80 percent of the Tungus and Yakut populations in the 1650s.

entries.name: Paleo-Indians
entries.desc: Paleo-Indians were the first peoples to enter and inhabit the Americas, towards the end of the Late Pleistocene. Traditional theories hold that big-animal hunters crossed from North Asia over the Beringia land bridge, which existed from 45,000 to 12,000 BCE, and moved south once ice-free corridors opened along the Pacific coast and valleys of North America; the dates and routes remain debated. Stone tools, above all projectile points and scrapers, are the main evidence of their lives, and the Clovis culture appeared around 11,500 BCE. As the climate stabilised from 8000 to 7000 BCE, the more sedentary Archaic Period followed.

entries.name: Bagratid Armenia
entries.desc: Bagratid Armenia was an independent Armenian state established by Ashot I of the Bagratuni dynasty in the early 880s, after nearly two centuries of Umayyad and Abbasid rule over Greater Armenia. Courted by Byzantine and Arab leaders who wanted a buffer state, Ashot was recognised by the Abbasid Caliphate as prince of princes in 862 and as king in 884 or 885. Under Ashot III, Ani became the capital and a thriving economic and cultural centre. Basil II annexed parts of the southwest, King Hovhannes-Smbat pledged in 1022 that the kingdom would pass to Byzantium, and his successor Gagik II resisted until Byzantine forces took it in 1045.

entries.name: Slavery in Africa
entries.desc: Slavery was widespread in Africa, practised as debt slavery and pawnship, the enslavement of war captives and criminals, military slavery and domestic and court service, with plantation slavery on the eastern coast and in parts of West Africa. With the trans-Saharan, Red Sea, Indian Ocean and Atlantic slave trades, many local systems began supplying captives to markets outside the continent. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database estimates that the Atlantic trade took around 12.8 million people between 1450 and 1900. Colonial rule brought abolition in the 20th century, but slavery still exists in some regions despite being illegal.

entries.name: Italian front (World War I)
entries.desc: The Italian front was one of the main theatres of World War I, a series of engagements along the border between the Kingdom of Italy and Austria-Hungary from 1915 to 1918. Italy entered the war on the Entente side to annex Trento, Trieste, South Tyrol, Istria and northern Dalmatia, promised to it in the 1915 Treaty of London. The front bogged down into trench warfare, much of it at high altitudes, and several thousand civilians died in refugee camps. Fighting ended with Italian victory and the armistice of Villa Giusti on 4 November 1918, and Italy annexed Trento, Trieste, South Tyrol and Istria.

entries.name: Ethiopian Civil War
entries.desc: The Ethiopian Civil War was fought in Ethiopia and present-day Eritrea between the military junta known as the Derg and anti-government rebels from 12 September 1974 to 28 May 1991. The Derg overthrew Emperor Haile Selassie and repressed nationalist fronts such as the EPLF, the TPLF and the OLF with large counterinsurgency campaigns and the Qey Shibir (Red Terror). The invasion by Somalia in 1977 drew a Soviet and Cuban intervention, and the 1983–1985 famine and economic decline later strengthened the rebels. The war ended when the EPRDF entered Addis Ababa and Mengistu Haile Mariam fled; at least 1.4 million people died.

entries.name: Jacobus Arminius
entries.desc: Jacobus Arminius, born Jakob Hermanszoon in Oudewater, was a Dutch Reformed minister and theologian whose views became the basis of Arminianism and the Dutch Remonstrant movement. He became an orphan while still young, and studied at Leiden from 1576 to 1582 and then under Theodore Beza at Geneva and at Basel. From 1603 he was professor of theology at the University of Leiden and wrote many books and treatises. After his death in 1609, his challenge to the Belgic Confession was debated at the Synod of Dort, which crafted the five points of Calvinism in response to his teaching.

entries.name: Naqada III
entries.desc: Naqada III is the last archaeological phase of the Naqada culture of ancient Egyptian prehistory, dated depending on the sources to approximately 3325 to 3000 BCE or c. 3350 to c. 2920 BCE. Often described as the Protodynastic Period, it was the time when state formation became highly visible, with named kings, written in serekhs, heading powerful polities; its later part is associated with Dynasty 0. Upper Egypt was reduced to the states of Thinis, Naqada and Nekhen, and the Thinite kings, buried at Abydos, came to rule all of Egypt. The Egyptian language was first recorded in hieroglyphs in this period.

entries.name: Nerva–Antonine dynasty
entries.desc: The Nerva–Antonine dynasty comprised seven Roman emperors who ruled from 96 to 192 CE: Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Lucius Verus and Commodus. The first five are popularly known as the Five Good Emperors, a term based on Niccolò Machiavelli's Discourses on Livy. In five of its six successions the reigning emperor had no male heir and adopted the candidate of his choice, a bond that Roman law made as strong as kinship. Marcus Aurelius's naming of his son Commodus as heir was considered an unfortunate choice, and the murder of Commodus in 192 ended the dynasty, followed by the Year of the Five Emperors.

entries.name: Treaty of Zaragoza
entries.desc: The Treaty of Zaragoza was a peace treaty between Castile and Portugal, signed on 22 April 1529 by King John III of Portugal and Emperor Charles V in the Aragonese city of Zaragoza. It settled the Moluccas issue, which arose in 1520 when both kingdoms claimed the Spice Islands as lying within their zones under the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas. The treaty set the border 297½ leagues, or 17°, east of the Maluku Islands, leaving them to Portugal, which paid Charles V 350,000 gold ducats. The Philippines were not mentioned, though Spain later established a trading post at Manila in 1565.

entries.name: Frederick Jackson Turner
entries.desc: Frederick Jackson Turner was an American historian, based at the University of Wisconsin until 1910 and then at Harvard University, known primarily for his frontier thesis. Born in Portage, Wisconsin, he earned his PhD at Johns Hopkins University in 1890 with a thesis on the fur trade in Wisconsin. His essay The Significance of the Frontier in American History argued that the moving western frontier shaped American democracy and character from the colonial era until 1890. He published little but trained many historians, and by his death in 1932, 60% of the major history departments in the U.S. taught frontier history.

entries.name: New Imperialism
entries.desc: New Imperialism characterises a period of colonial expansion by the major Western powers and the Empire of Japan during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its main participants were the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Russia, the United States and Japan, which conquered almost all of Africa and parts of Asia. It reflected rivalries among the great powers, the desire for new resources and markets and a civilizing mission ethos, sharpened by the Long Depression of 1873–1896; the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 set effective occupation as the test of a claim. Many of its colonies gained independence after World War II.

entries.name: Middle Eastern theatre of World War I
entries.desc: The Middle Eastern theatre of World War I saw fighting between 30 October 1914 and 30 October 1918 between the Ottoman Empire, aided by the other Central Powers, and the British, the Russians and the French with troops from their dominions and colonies. Its four main campaigns were the Sinai and Palestine, Mesopotamian, Caucasus and Gallipoli campaigns, with minor ones in Persia, South Arabia, the Arabian interior and Libya. It covered the largest territory of all theatres in the war, and included the Arab Revolt and Armenian resistance. The Ottomans accepted the Armistice of Mudros on 30 October 1918.
links: Middle Eastern theatre of World War I

entries.name: Elias Howe
entries.desc: Elias Howe Jr. was an American inventor, born in Spencer, Massachusetts, best known for creating the modern lockstitch sewing machine. On September 10, 1846, he received the first United States patent for a sewing machine using a lockstitch design, with a needle with the eye at the point, a shuttle beneath the cloth and an automatic feed. He defended his patent in a court case from 1849 to 1854 against Isaac Singer and won considerable royalties. His machine won a gold medal at the Paris Exhibition of 1867, the year he received the Légion d'honneur, and he died that year at age 48.

credit.artist: Elias_Howe-Southworth_&_Hawes.jpg : Southwarth and Hawes derivative work: TheCuriousGnome ( talk )

entries.name: Cretan War
entries.desc: The Cretan War, also known as the War of Candia, was fought from 1645 to 1669 between the Republic of Venice and its allies, chief among them the Knights of Malta, the Papal States and France, and the Ottoman Empire and the Barbary States, largely over Crete, Venice's largest and richest overseas possession. The Ottomans conquered most of the island in the first years, but the fortress of Candia resisted, and the war turned into naval battles over supplies. A final Ottoman expedition in 1666 began the bloodiest stage of the siege, and Candia was surrendered on 5 September 1669, leaving Crete under Ottoman control until 1897.

entries.name: British colonization of the Americas
entries.desc: British colonization of the Americas began in the late 16th century with failed English attempts such as the short-lived Roanoke Colony, established by Sir Walter Raleigh in 1585, and the first permanent English colony was established at Jamestown, Virginia, in 1607. Colonies followed in North America, Central America, South America and the Caribbean, among them Massachusetts in 1620, Barbados, Jamaica and Rupert's Land. In 1763 Britain took Canada and the Floridas, but many North American colonies won independence in the American Revolutionary War, which ended in 1783. Most remaining colonies gained independence between 1962 and 1983, while some remain British Overseas Territories.

entries.name: Toungoo dynasty
entries.desc: The Toungoo dynasty was the ruling dynasty of Burma (Myanmar) from the mid-16th century to 1752, in two periods: the First Toungoo Empire (1510–1599) and the Nyaungyan Restoration (1599–1752). King Mingyi Nyo founded it at Taungoo, and Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung reunified the territories of the Pagan Kingdom and brought in the Shan States, Manipur, Siam and Lan Xang. The empire collapsed after Bayinnaung's death in 1581, but Nyaungyan Min and Anaukpetlun restored a smaller kingdom based in Ava. After a Mon rebellion founded the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom in 1740, its armies captured Inwa in 1752 and ended the dynasty.

entries.name: Su Song
entries.desc: Su Song was a Chinese polymathic scientist and statesman of the Song dynasty, working in mathematics, astronomy, cartography, metallurgy, mechanical and hydraulic engineering and poetry. He was the engineer of a hydro-mechanical astronomical clock tower at Kaifeng, whose armillary sphere was the first to use a mechanical clock drive and which had the oldest known endless power-transmitting chain drive. His treatise on the tower, the Xinyi Xiangfayao, was written in 1092 and printed in 1094. As an official he became Minister of Justice in 1086 and went on a diplomatic mission to the Liao dynasty in 1077.

entries.name: Byzantine–Bulgarian wars
entries.desc: The Byzantine–Bulgarian wars were a series of conflicts between the Byzantine Empire and the Bulgarian Empire, beginning in the late 5th century and lasting through the Middle Ages. After Asparuh defeated Constantine IV, the Byzantines acknowledged the Bulgarian state in 681; Krum later inflicted crushing defeats on them, and Simeon I campaigned against them from 893 to 927. John I Tzimiskes captured Preslav in 971, and Basil II won the Battle of Kleidion and conquered Bulgaria in 1018. A revolt by Theodore Peter and Ivan Asen in 1185 restored Bulgarian rule, and relations fluctuated until the Ottoman Turks took both capitals in 1393 and 1453.

entries.name: Balkan Front (World War I)
entries.desc: The Balkan Front was a theatre of World War I fought between the Central Powers (Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, Germany and the Ottoman Empire) and the Allies (Serbia, Montenegro, France, the United Kingdom, Russia, Italy and later Greece). Three Austro-Hungarian offensives into Serbia failed in 1914, but a combined attack by Austria-Hungary, Germany and Bulgaria conquered Serbia and Montenegro in 1915. The Serbian army retreated through Albania to Corfu and joined the Allied Army of the Orient on the Macedonian front. Greece joined the Allies in 1917, and in September 1918 the Vardar Offensive broke the Bulgarian lines and forced Bulgaria to surrender.

entries.name: Mediterranean and Middle East theatre of World War II
entries.desc: The Mediterranean and Middle East theatre was a major theatre of the Second World War, in which land, naval and air campaigns were fought for the Mediterranean Sea, North Africa, the Horn of Africa, the Middle East and Southern Europe. It began on 10 June 1940 with Italy's declaration of war on the United Kingdom and France and ended on 2 May 1945 when all Axis forces in Italy surrendered. Axis forces conquered Greece and Yugoslavia in 1941, but losses in Egypt and Tunisia ended their threat in North Africa by May 1943, and the Allies invaded Italy. The theatre destroyed the Italian Empire.
links: Mediterranean and Middle East theatre of World War II

entries.name: Gaudapada
entries.desc: Gauḍapāda was an early medieval Hindu philosopher and scholar of the Advaita Vedanta school, whose biography is uncertain; estimates of his dates vary from the early 6th to the 7th century CE. He was the author or compiler of the Māṇḍūkya Kārikā, a verse explanation of the Mandukya Upanishad in 215 verses and four chapters, the fourth of which uses Buddhist terminology. According to Sarma, it is the earliest extant systematic treatise on Advaita Vedānta. Adi Shankara called him a Paramaguru, and his teacher Govinda Bhagavatpada is presumed to have been Gauḍapāda's direct disciple.

entries.name: Germanic paganism
entries.desc: Germanic paganism was the traditional religion of the Germanic peoples, spanning at least one thousand years across Scandinavia, the British Isles, modern Germany, the Netherlands and at times other parts of Europe, from the first Roman reports to the conversion to Christianity. Few sources were written by its adherents. Its peoples believed in many gods, among them *Wodanaz (Odin), *Thunraz (Thor), *Tiwaz (Tyr) and *Frijjō (Frigg), and in jötnar, dwarfs, elves and dragons. Archaeology shows rich grave goods, ship and wagon burials, carved wooden figures and sacrificial deposits in bogs and springs, as well as sacred groves and temples.

entries.name: Peopling of the Americas
entries.desc: The peopling of the Americas is believed to have begun when Paleolithic hunter-gatherers entered North America from northeastern Siberia over the Beringia land bridge, formed as sea levels fell during the Last Glacial Maximum (26,000 to 19,000 years ago). The Clovis First theory dated the earliest human presence to the Clovis culture about 13,000 years ago, but pre-Clovis sites such as Monte Verde in Chile pushed the date back. Academics generally believe that humans reached North America south of the Laurentide Ice Sheet between 15,000 and 20,000 years ago, inland or along the Pacific coast.

entries.name: Collective farming
entries.desc: Collective farming is agricultural production in which multiple farmers run their holdings as a joint enterprise, as cooperatives of member-owners or as state farms owned and run by a central government; the process of aggregating farmland is called collectivization. Older communal forms include the Aztec calpulli and the Russian peasant commune, the mir or obshchina. The Soviet Union introduced collective farms (kolkhozy) between 1927 and 1933, and after Stalin forced the peasants into collectives an estimated 5.7 to 8.7 million people died in the famine of 1932–1933. China, North Korea, Vietnam and most of the Eastern Bloc later collectivized, and the kibbutzim of Israel began in 1909.

entries.name: Cyrus McCormick
entries.desc: Cyrus Hall McCormick was an American inventor and businessman, born in Raphine, Virginia, who founded the McCormick Harvesting Machine Company. Building on his father Robert McCormick Jr.'s work, and aided by Jo Anderson, an enslaved African-American man held by the family, he demonstrated a horse-drawn mechanical reaper in 1831 and patented it in 1834, though he was one of several engineers who produced working models in the 1830s. In 1847 he and his brother Leander moved to Chicago, where by 1856 their factory made more than 4,000 reapers a year. He died in Chicago in 1884, and the company became part of the International Harvester Company in 1902.

credit.artist: Cyrus_McCormick_engraving.jpg : George Smillie [1] derivative work: — raeky ( talk | edits )

entries.name: North Yemen civil war
entries.desc: The North Yemen civil war was fought from 1962 to 1970 between partisans of the Mutawakkilite Kingdom and supporters of the Yemen Arab Republic. It began when the army under Abdullah al-Sallal dethroned the newly crowned Imam Muhammad al-Badr and declared a republic, which abolished slavery, while the Imam rallied northern Zaydi tribes from the Saudi border. Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Israel aided the royalists, and Egypt under Gamal Abdel Nasser sent as many as 70,000 troops to back the republicans, at a cost to its army in the 1967 Six-Day War. The republicans held Sana'a through a siege lifted in February 1968, and in 1970 Saudi Arabia recognized the Republic and a ceasefire took effect.

entries.name: Hasdai Crescas
entries.desc: Hasdai ben Abraham Crescas was a Spanish-Jewish philosopher and halakhist, born in Barcelona around 1340, who served as crown rabbi of Aragon and taught pupils including Joseph Albo. In 1378 he was imprisoned with his teacher Nissim of Gerona on a false accusation of host desecration, and his only son was killed in the massacre of 1391, which he described in a letter to the congregations of Avignon. His Or Adonai (The Light of the Lord) became a classical Jewish refutation of medieval Aristotelianism, and he deeply influenced Baruch Spinoza. He died in Zaragoza in 1410 or the year after.

entries.name: Ptahhotep
entries.desc: Ptahhotep was a vizier of Egypt during the reign of Djedkare Isesi in the Fifth Dynasty, holding the highest administrative office under the pharaoh and posts such as overseer of the treasury and overseer of all royal works. He is best known as the named author of The Maxims of Ptahhotep, an early work of Egyptian wisdom literature in which a father advises his son on conduct, humility, restraint in speech and respect for Maat. Its oldest surviving copies are in Middle Egyptian, and some scholars argue that it was composed in the Middle Kingdom and that its authorship is fictional. He was buried in Mastaba D62 at Saqqara.

entries.name: Andean civilizations
entries.desc: The Andean civilizations were complex societies of many indigenous peoples of South America, stretching 4,000 km along the Andes from southern Colombia through Ecuador and Peru to north Chile and northwest Argentina. The Caral or Norte Chico civilization of coastal Peru, dating back to 3500 BCE, is the oldest known civilization in the Americas; later came Chavín, Paracas, Nazca, Moche, Wari, Tiwanaku and Chimor. They had no writing, wheeled vehicles or money, recorded information on the quipu and domesticated crops such as potatoes, quinoa and coca. From 1438 the Incas united most of them in one empire, before the Spanish conquest of the 16th century.

entries.name: Pantheon
aka: Basilica of Saint Mary and the Holy Martyrs
entries.desc: The Pantheon is an ancient Roman temple in Rome, built on the site of an earlier temple commissioned by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa under Augustus and rebuilt by the emperor Hadrian, probably dedicated around 126 CE. Its exact date is uncertain because Hadrian re-inscribed it with Agrippa's original inscription. A portico of granite Corinthian columns leads to a rotunda under a coffered concrete dome with an oculus; the height to the oculus and the interior diameter are both 43 metres, and it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Since 609 it has been a church, which helped to preserve it.

entries.name: Catholic Church
entries.desc: The Catholic Church is the largest Christian denomination, made up of the Latin Church and 23 Eastern Catholic Churches organised into nearly 3,500 dioceses and eparchies. Its doctrine rests on the Nicene Creed and holds that its bishops succeed the apostles and that the pope, the bishop of Rome, succeeds Saint Peter. The Eucharist, celebrated in the Mass, stands at the centre of its seven sacraments. The church had a large role in the development of Western civilization; it separated from the Church of the East after 431, from the Oriental Orthodox after 451 and gradually from the Eastern Orthodox, and the 16th-century Reformation prompted its Counter-Reformation.

entries.name: Church Fathers
entries.desc: The Church Fathers were ancient Christian theologians and writers who laid the intellectual and doctrinal foundations of Christianity. Their age, the Patristic Era, ran roughly from the late 1st to the mid-8th century and flourished in the 4th and 5th centuries, as Christianity became the state church of the Roman Empire. The earliest, the Apostolic Fathers such as Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch and Polycarp of Smyrna, were believed to have known or been shaped by the apostles. Many denominations count their writings as part of Sacred Tradition, though some, such as Origen and Tertullian, had parts of their teaching later condemned.

entries.name: Supreme Court of the United States
entries.desc: The Supreme Court of the United States is the highest court of the federal judiciary, created under Article Three of the Constitution and organised by the Judiciary Act of 1789. It has final appellate jurisdiction over federal cases and over state cases that turn on constitutional or federal law. In 1803 it asserted the power of judicial review, the ability to strike down a statute that violates the Constitution. Nine justices, the chief justice and eight associate justices, sit for life, appointed by the president with the advice and consent of the Senate. It receives about 7,000 petitions a year and grants about 80.
links: Supreme Court of the United States

entries.name: Alexander Pope
entries.desc: Alexander Pope was an English poet, translator and satirist of the Enlightenment, a leading figure of Augustan literature in the early 18th century. Born in London to Catholic parents, he was barred by the Test Acts from university and largely taught himself from the classical and English poets, while Pott disease, a tuberculosis of the spine, affected his health from the age of 12. His works include An Essay on Criticism (1711), The Rape of the Lock (1712–1717) and The Dunciad (1728–1743), and his translations of Homer paid for his move in 1719 to a villa at Twickenham. Many of his lines entered common speech.

entries.name: Archaeological Survey of India
entries.desc: The Archaeological Survey of India is the Indian government agency responsible for archaeological research and for conserving the country's historic monuments. It grew out of earlier study by the Asiatic Society, founded in Calcutta in 1784, and James Prinsep's decipherment of the Brahmi script in 1837. Alexander Cunningham, who had excavated stupas across India, lobbied for a permanent body, and the survey was formed in 1861 by a statute under Lord Canning with Cunningham as its first Archaeological Surveyor. Suspended for lack of funds from 1865, it was revived in 1871 as a separate department with Cunningham as Director-General.

entries.name: World Heritage Site
entries.desc: A World Heritage Site is a landmark or area given legal protection under an international treaty administered by UNESCO for its cultural, historical or scientific significance. The programme began with the Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage, adopted by UNESCO's General Conference on 16 November 1972 and since ratified by 196 states. It grew from the campaign launched in 1960 to save the monuments of Nubia from the reservoir of the Aswan High Dam, which moved temples such as Abu Simbel and Philae. Sites are nominated by their host country and chosen by the World Heritage Committee of 21 states parties.

entries.name: Mount Vesuvius
entries.desc: Mount Vesuvius is a somma-stratovolcano on the Gulf of Naples in Campania, Italy, about 9 km east of Naples. Its eruption of 79 CE destroyed the Roman cities of Pompeii, Herculaneum, Oplontis and Stabiae, throwing a cloud of stones, ash and gas to a height of 33 km; more than 1,000 people are thought to have died, and the only surviving witness account is two letters of Pliny the Younger to Tacitus. The Romans held the mountain sacred to Hercules. It has erupted many times since, most recently from 1913 to 1944, and is counted among the most dangerous volcanoes in the world.

entries.name: Olympia
entries.desc: Olympia is a small town in Elis in the western Peloponnese, Greece, beside the archaeological site of the ancient sanctuary of the same name. The sacred precinct, the Altis, was dedicated mainly to Zeus, and the Olympic Games were held there every four years from the 8th century BCE to the 4th century CE, the first major games at its stadium said to date to the 720s BCE. As a Panhellenic centre it drew visitors from the whole Greek world and helped shape a shared Greek identity. The site held over 760 significant buildings, among them the Pelopion, the tomb of Pelops, and the stadium whose length set the stadion.

entries.name: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
entries.desc: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was a tomb built between 353 and 351 BCE in Halicarnassus, present-day Bodrum in Turkey, for Mausolus, a Carian satrap of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, and his sister-wife Artemisia II. Designed by the Greek architects Satyros of Paros and Pythius of Priene after the tombs of Lycia, it stood about 45 m high, with reliefs on its four sides by Leochares, Bryaxis, Scopas and Timotheus and 400 freestanding sculptures. Antipater of Sidon counted it among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Earthquakes from the 12th to the 15th century destroyed it, and its name gave the word mausoleum.

entries.name: Statue of Zeus at Olympia
entries.desc: The Statue of Zeus at Olympia was a seated figure about 12.4 m tall, made by the Greek sculptor Phidias around 435 BCE for the Temple of Zeus in the sanctuary of Olympia. Commissioned by the Eleans, custodians of the Olympic Games, it was a chryselephantine work of ivory plates and gold panels on a wooden frame, seated on a cedarwood throne adorned with ebony, ivory, gold and precious stones, and was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Pausanias described it in detail. It was lost before the end of the 6th century CE, by conflicting accounts, and is known only from descriptions, coins and gems.

entries.name: Elgin Marbles
entries.desc: The Elgin Marbles are ancient Greek sculptures from the Parthenon and other buildings of the Acropolis of Athens, most made in the 5th century BCE under the direction of Phidias. Between 1801 and 1812 agents of Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin, removed about half the surviving Parthenon sculptures from Ottoman Greece and shipped them to Britain; Elgin said he had the Ottoman officials' permission, and the legality is disputed. A parliamentary inquiry of 1816 found the acquisition legal and they passed to the British Museum. Greece formally asked for their return in 1983, and the dispute continues, each side setting out its own case.

entries.name: Roman roads
entries.desc: Roman roads were the network of routes built from about 300 BCE through the expansion of the Roman Republic and later the Roman Empire, carrying armies, officials, messages and trade overland. The main roads were often paved with stone or gravel, cambered for drainage and laid along carefully surveyed courses, with cuttings and bridges over rivers and ravines. At the empire's height 29 military highways radiated from Rome and 372 great roads linked its 113 provinces, more than 400,000 kilometres in all, over 80,500 of them paved. Many of their courses survived for millennia, some beneath modern roads.

entries.name: Circus Maximus
entries.desc: The Circus Maximus was an ancient Roman chariot-racing stadium and mass entertainment venue in the valley between the Aventine and Palatine hills in Rome. The first and largest stadium of ancient Rome, it measured 621 m in length and 118 m in width and could hold over 150,000 spectators. It was Rome's largest venue for ludi, the public games of religious festivals, with races, beast-hunts and processions, and became the model for circuses throughout the empire. The last known beast-hunt there took place in 523 and the last known races in 549. The site is now a public park.

entries.name: Domus Aurea
entries.desc: The Domus Aurea, the Golden House, was a vast landscaped palace complex built by the emperor Nero, largely on the Oppian Hill in Rome, after the great fire of 64 CE. His engineer-architects Celer and Severus nearly completed it before Nero's death in 68. Seen as a symbol of decadence, it was stripped of its marble, jewels and ivory, and the Flavian Amphitheatre, the Baths of Titus and the Baths of Trajan were built on its grounds; the Oppian wing burned under Trajan in 104. Its buried frescoes, rediscovered at the end of the 15th century, inspired the grotesque decoration of Raphael and other Renaissance artists.

entries.name: Baths of Caracalla
entries.desc: The Baths of Caracalla were the second largest public bath complex of ancient Rome, after the Baths of Diocletian. Probably begun under Septimius Severus and completed by his son Caracalla, they were inaugurated in 216 CE, heated by a hypocaust and fed by a dedicated aqueduct, and were free and open to the public. In 537, during the Gothic War, the Ostrogothic king Vitiges cut Rome's water supply, and the baths were soon abandoned. Their ruins yielded sculptures such as the Farnese Bull and the Farnese Hercules, and inspired buildings from the Basilica of Maxentius to the original Pennsylvania Station in New York.

entries.name: Ara Pacis
entries.desc: The Ara Pacis Augustae, the Altar of Augustan Peace, is an altar in Rome dedicated to the Pax Romana. The Roman Senate commissioned it in 13 BCE to honour the return of Augustus from three years in Hispania and Gaul, and it was consecrated in 9 BCE in the Campus Martius. Its marble friezes show sacrifices, plant life evoking abundance and a procession that includes the imperial household, supporting Augustus's regime and the claims of his dynasty. Buried under silt, it was recovered in fragments from 1568 onward and reassembled in 1938, in what is now the Museum of the Ara Pacis.

entries.name: Arch of Titus
entries.desc: The Arch of Titus is an honorific arch on the Via Sacra in Rome, just south-east of the Roman Forum, built in about 81 CE by the emperor Domitian after the death of his brother Titus. It commemorates Titus's deification and his victory, with their father Vespasian, over the Jewish rebellion in Judaea. Its panels show the triumphal procession of 71 CE after the fall of Jerusalem, with spoils from Herod's Temple, including the menorah. The arch became a symbol of the Jewish diaspora, its menorah the model for the emblem of the State of Israel, and it inspired later triumphal arches, among them the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

entries.name: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus
entries.desc: The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, or Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, was the most important temple of ancient Rome, on the Capitoline Hill. Traditionally dedicated in 509 BCE, the first temple, built of wood with the help of Etruscan specialists, was the largest in the Italian world, though its exact size is disputed. Roman tradition credits the kings Tarquinius Priscus and Tarquinius Superbus with its foundations and building. It burned in 83 BCE and was rebuilt by 69 BCE; after further fires the fourth temple stood until the fall of the empire. Only parts of its foundations and podium survive.

entries.name: Palatine Hill
entries.desc: The Palatine Hill is the centremost of the seven hills of Rome and one of the oldest parts of the city. Excavations show that people lived there from the 10th century BCE, and in Roman mythology it held the Lupercal cave where the she-wolf kept Romulus and Remus alive, and was where Romulus founded the city. Before imperial times the hill was mostly occupied by the houses of the rich; from Augustus onward emperors built their palaces there, and its name is the origin of the word palace. The site is now largely an open-air museum, with the Palatine Museum holding finds from its excavations.

entries.name: Pax Romana
entries.desc: The Pax Romana, the Roman Peace, was a period of roughly 200 years of relative peace, stability and prosperity in the Roman Empire, though it still saw internal revolts and external wars. It is traditionally dated from the accession of Augustus in 27 BCE to the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE. The empire reached its greatest extent under Trajan in 117, and its population is estimated to have peaked at 70 million. Historians debate its limits: Arthur M. Eckstein finds the Roman peace emerging in parts of the Mediterranean under the Republic, while Walter Goffart doubted that peace is what the period shows.

credit.artist: Carin (empereur romain). Autorité émettrice de monnaie présumée Numérien (0254?-0284 ; empereur romain). Autorité émettrice de monnaie présu

entries.name: Roman citizenship
entries.desc: Roman citizenship, civitas, was the privileged political and legal status of free individuals in ancient Rome, governing their rights in law, property and government. There were several kinds, shaped by gender, class and political ties, and citizens owed duties to the state, such as military service, and were recorded in a census every five years under the Republic. The Twelve Tables of about 449 BCE are the oldest surviving document of its rights. Citizenship was extended to the Italian allies around the Social War, and in 212 CE the Edict of Caracalla gave it to all free men of the empire, with some exceptions.

entries.name: Cursus honorum
entries.desc: The cursus honorum, the course of honours, was the sequence of public offices held by aspiring politicians of senatorial rank in the Roman Republic and the early Roman Empire. After about ten years of military service, a man could rise from quaestor, from the age of 30 after Sulla's reforms, through aedile and praetor to consul, two of whom were elected each year. Holding each office at the youngest age allowed was a mark of success. The rules were often ignored in the last century of the Republic: Gaius Marius was consul seven times, five years in a row from 104 to 100 BCE.

entries.name: Roman legion
entries.desc: The Roman legion was the largest unit of the Roman army, made up of Roman citizens serving as legionaries. In the Republic the manipular legion had 4,200 infantry and 300 cavalry in three lines of maniples; from about 100 BCE a legion of about 5,000 men was organised in ten cohorts, the first of double strength. For most of the imperial period the legions were the army's elite heavy infantry, alongside auxiliaries recruited from provincials. Many legions lasted for centuries, but by the third century CE the legion had become a smaller unit of about 1,000 to 1,500 men.

credit.artist: No machine-readable author provided. MatthiasKabel assumed (based on copyright claims).

entries.name: Praetorian Guard
entries.desc: The Praetorian Guard was the imperial guard of the Roman army, serving the emperor as bodyguard, in crowd control and in gathering intelligence. Under the Republic praetorians guarded generals, first recorded with the Scipio family around 275 BCE; in 27 BCE Augustus made them his personal escort. For three centuries they were known for palace intrigue, overthrowing emperors and proclaiming successors: their prefect Sejanus gathered great power under Tiberius, and they once put the empire up to auction to Didius Julianus. Constantine the Great disbanded the guard in 312 and destroyed its barracks, the Castra Praetoria.

entries.name: Gladiator
entries.desc: A gladiator was an armed combatant who fought other gladiators, wild animals and condemned criminals before audiences in the Roman Republic and Empire. Some were volunteers, but most were slaves, trained under harsh conditions and socially marginalised, though a gladiator who fought or died well could win admiration. The origin of the games is debated: Livy places the first Roman games in 264 BCE, when three pairs fought at a funeral in the Forum Boarium. The games lasted nearly a thousand years, peaking between the 1st century BCE and the 2nd century CE, until Honorius banned them in 399 and again in 404, at least in the West.

entries.name: Code of Justinian
entries.desc: The Code of Justinian was a compilation of imperial Roman laws, one part of the Corpus Juris Civilis ordered by Justinian I, the Eastern Roman emperor in Constantinople. In February 528 he set up a ten-man commission, headed by John the Cappadocian and including Tribonian, to review the earlier codes and gather the laws in force; its first edition was promulgated in April 529. Because new laws soon made it out of date, a second edition was published in 534. It has twelve books, covering church law, private law, crimes and administrative law.

entries.name: Nicene Creed
entries.desc: The Nicene Creed is the original statement of belief of Nicene Christianity, adopted at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 to resolve the Arian controversy over the divinity of Jesus. According to the traditional view, put forward by the Council of Chalcedon of 451, it was amended in 381 by the First Council of Constantinople; the amended form is known as the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed. It is professed by the Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, Anglican and many other churches, and is said or sung at the Eucharist.

entries.name: Benedictines
entries.desc: The Benedictines, officially the Order of Saint Benedict, are a mainly contemplative monastic order of the Catholic Church for men and women who follow the Rule of Saint Benedict. Benedict of Nursia established the monastery at Subiaco in Italy c. 529 and later founded the Abbey of Monte Cassino, though there is no evidence he meant to found an order. By the ninth century the Benedictine rule had become the standard form of monastic life across most of Western Europe. The order is a collection of autonomous monasteries, represented since 1893 by the Benedictine Confederation.

entries.name: House of Habsburg
entries.desc: The House of Habsburg, also known as the House of Austria, was a European dynasty named after Habsburg Castle, a Swabian fortress built in the 1020s in present-day Switzerland. In 1273 Rudolph was elected King of the Romans and, after his victory over Ottokar II of Bohemia in 1278, moved the family's power base to Vienna, where it ruled until 1918. The Habsburgs held the throne of the Holy Roman Empire from 1440 to 1740, and as Habsburg-Lorraines from 1765 to 1806. After Charles V abdicated in 1556 the family split into Spanish and Austrian branches, which ruled Spain, Hungary, Bohemia and much else.

entries.name: House of Windsor
entries.desc: The House of Windsor is the royal house of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms, founded in 1917 when King George V changed the name of the royal house from the German Saxe-Coburg and Gotha to Windsor, after Windsor Castle. The change came because of anti-German sentiment during the First World War, which peaked as Gotha bombers began bombing London. A royal proclamation of 17 July 1917 announced the new name. Five British monarchs have belonged to the house: George V, Edward VIII, George VI, Elizabeth II and Charles III.

entries.name: Ottoman dynasty
entries.desc: The Ottoman dynasty was the imperial House of Osman, which ruled the Ottoman Empire from c. 1299 to 1922. According to Ottoman tradition the family came from the Kayı branch of the Oghuz Turks, led by Osman I in northwestern Anatolia around Söğüt. From Orhan to Ahmed I, succession was often settled by violence among a dead sultan's sons, a practice known as fratricide. The sultan was usually an absolute monarch, though much power often passed to the Grand Vizier. The sultanate was abolished on 1 November 1922 and the family was sent into exile.

entries.name: Carolingian dynasty
entries.desc: The Carolingian dynasty was a Frankish noble family named after Charles Martel and his grandson Charlemagne, descended from the Arnulfing and Pippinid clans of the 7th century. In the 8th century the family made the office of mayor of the palace hereditary and became the real power behind the Merovingian throne. In 751 the Merovingians were overthrown and Pepin the Short was crowned king of the Franks. The dynasty reached its peak in 800 with Charlemagne's coronation as emperor; after his death in 814 the empire fragmented, leading towards the Kingdom of France and the Holy Roman Empire.

entries.name: Salian dynasty
entries.desc: The Salian dynasty was a royal dynasty of the High Middle Ages that provided four kings of Germany from 1024 to 1125, all of them crowned Holy Roman emperors. After the death of the last Ottonian emperor in 1024 the crown passed to Conrad II, who was followed by Henry III, Henry IV and Henry V. Modern historians suppose the family descended from the Widonids, nobles of Rhenish Franconia. The Salians made their monarchy a major European power and developed an administrative system based on public officials answerable to the crown.

entries.name: Stonehenge
entries.desc: Stonehenge is a prehistoric megalithic monument on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, consisting of an outer ring of sarsen standing stones topped by lintels, an inner ring of bluestones and free-standing trilithons. It was built in phases from about 3100 BCE, when the surrounding bank and ditch were dug, until about 1600 BCE; the large sarsen circle was placed between 2600 and 2400 BCE. The monument is aligned on the summer solstice sunrise and winter solstice sunset, and human bone deposits suggest it may have been a burial ground. It became a World Heritage Site in 1986.

entries.name: Colosseum
entries.desc: The Colosseum is an elliptical amphitheatre in the centre of Rome, just east of the Roman Forum, and the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built. Construction began under Emperor Vespasian in 72 and was completed in 80 under Titus, with further changes under Domitian. Built of travertine, tuff and Roman concrete, it held an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators for gladiatorial contests, animal hunts, executions and other spectacles. It ceased to be used for entertainment in the early medieval era and was later used for housing, workshops, a fortress and a quarry.

entries.name: Book of the Dead
aka: Spells of Coming Forth by Day
entries.desc: The Book of the Dead is an ancient Egyptian funerary text, generally written on papyrus and used from the beginning of the New Kingdom, around 1550 BCE, to around 50 BCE. It is a loose collection of magic spells meant to help the dead through the Duat, the underworld, and into the afterlife; its Egyptian name is translated as Spells of Coming Forth by Day. Some spells were drawn from the older Pyramid Texts and Coffin Texts. There was no single canonical version, and the papyri, such as the Papyrus of Ani in the British Museum, vary in their spells and illustrations.

entries.name: Great Sphinx of Giza
entries.desc: The Great Sphinx of Giza is a limestone statue of a resting sphinx, with a human head and a lion's body, carved from the bedrock of the Giza Plateau on the west bank of the Nile in Egypt. Archaeological evidence suggests it was made in the Old Kingdom during the reign of Khufu or Khafre, but whose face it shows remains in dispute. It is 73 m long, 20 m high and 19 m wide, the oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt. In the New Kingdom it was revered as the sun god Hor-em-akhet. Its nose was deliberately damaged, though not by Napoleon's troops.

entries.name: Abkhazia
entries.desc: Abkhazia, officially the Republic of Abkhazia, is a partially recognised state on the eastern coast of the Black Sea in the South Caucasus, which most countries recognise as part of Georgia. Within the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic it was the Abkhaz Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic. Ethnic tensions between Abkhaz and Georgians as the Soviet Union disintegrated led to the 1992–1993 War in Abkhazia, after which Georgia lost control of most of the territory and Georgians were expelled in what is described as ethnic cleansing. Russia, Venezuela, Nicaragua and Syria recognise it; Georgia maintains a government-in-exile.

entries.name: Albania
entries.desc: Albania, officially the Republic of Albania, is a country in Southeastern Europe, in the Balkans on the Adriatic and Ionian Seas. Once home to Illyrian tribes, it passed to the Roman and Byzantine empires, and in the 15th century resisted Ottoman expansion under Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg for over two decades before being incorporated into the Ottoman Empire. It declared independence in 1912. The twentieth century brought monarchy, foreign occupation in both World Wars, and a communist regime under Enver Hoxha, before a shift to an open market economy.

entries.name: Antigua and Barbuda
entries.desc: Antigua and Barbuda is an archipelagic country in the Caribbean made up of Antigua, Barbuda and dozens of smaller islands. Hunter-gatherers settled the islands long before European contact, probably arriving by canoe from Central and South America. After a failed Spanish attempt in 1520, Edward Warner founded the first successful British colony in 1632, and Barbuda was long controlled by the Codrington family. Autonomy grew slowly after emancipation in 1834, and the first democratic elections were held in 1951. Antigua and Barbuda gained full independence on 1 November 1981 and remains a Commonwealth realm.
