entries.name: Bangladesh
entries.desc: Bangladesh, officially the People's Republic of Bangladesh, is a country in South Asia on the Bay of Bengal, bordered by India and Myanmar. Its territory was part of the Bengal Sultanate and the Mughal Empire, then British India after the Battle of Plassey in 1757. At the partition of India in 1947 it became East Bengal, later East Pakistan. After years of marginalisation by the government in West Pakistan, Operation Searchlight began the Bangladesh Liberation War, during which Pakistani forces carried out the Bangladesh genocide. Bangladesh became sovereign on 16 December 1971.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Barbados
entries.desc: Barbados is an island nation in the Atlantic Ocean, the southernmost and easternmost island of the Caribbean region. Kalinago people lived there from the 13th century, but the indigenous population had mostly been sold into slavery, killed or died of disease by the time an English ship arrived on 14 May 1625. It became an English and later British colony with a plantation economy that used Irish indentured servants and then enslaved Africans. Barbados became independent on 30 November 1966 and a republic within the Commonwealth on 30 November 2021.

entries.name: Belize
entries.desc: Belize is a country on the north-eastern coast of Central America, bordered by Mexico, Guatemala and the Caribbean Sea. The Maya civilization spread into the area between 1500 BCE and 300 CE. English settlers began exploring in 1638, and Spain and Britain both claimed the land until Britain's victory at the Battle of St. George's Caye in 1798. It became a British colony in 1840 and a Crown colony in 1862, known as British Honduras until 1973. Belize achieved independence from the United Kingdom on 21 September 1981.

entries.name: Bhutan
entries.desc: Bhutan, officially the Kingdom of Bhutan, is a landlocked country in the Eastern Himalayas, bordering Tibet and India. In the 16th century Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal unified its valleys into a single state, defeating three Tibetan invasions. After the Duar War it ceded the Bengal Duars to British India, and the Wangchuck dynasty emerged as the monarchy. The Treaty of Punakha of 1910 made Bhutan effectively a British protectorate, though it was never officially colonised. A 1949 treaty with India recognised each country's sovereignty, and Bhutan joined the United Nations in 1971.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
entries.desc: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country in Southeastern Europe on the Balkan Peninsula, with a short coast on the Adriatic Sea. The Banate of Bosnia was established in the 12th century and became the Kingdom of Bosnia; the Ottoman Empire annexed the region in 1463, and Austria-Hungary ruled it from the late 19th century until World War I. After World War II it was a republic of Socialist Yugoslavia and in 1992, following the breakup of Yugoslavia, proclaimed independence. The Bosnian War that followed lasted until late 1995 and ended with the Dayton Agreement.

entries.name: Brunei
entries.desc: Brunei, officially Brunei Darussalam, is a country in Southeast Asia on the northern coast of Borneo, surrounded on land by the Malaysian state of Sarawak. Under Sultan Bolkiah (1485–1528) the sultanate is claimed to have controlled most of Borneo. It declined in the 19th century, ceding Kuching to James Brooke and Sabah to the British North Borneo Chartered Company. Brunei became a British protectorate in 1888. A 1962 rebellion was ended with British help, and the Sultan chose not to join the Malaysian Federation. The protectorate ended on 1 January 1984, when Brunei became fully sovereign.

entries.name: Burundi
entries.desc: Burundi, officially the Republic of Burundi, is a landlocked country in East Africa in the Great Rift Valley, bordered by Rwanda, Tanzania and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. A kingdom had emerged by the 16th century and was independent for more than 200 years. In 1885 it became part of German East Africa, and after the First World War was mandated to Belgium as Ruanda-Urundi. Burundi gained independence in 1962. A coup in 1966 replaced the monarchy, and a genocide of Hutu took place in 1972; the 12-year Burundian Civil War followed in 1993.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Chile
entries.desc: Chile is a country in the Southern Cone of southwestern South America, a narrow strip of land between the Andes Mountains and the Pacific Ocean. Spain conquered and colonized the region in the mid-16th century, replacing Inca rule, but failed to conquer the autonomous Mapuche people of what is now south-central Chile. Chile declared independence from Spain in 1818. It ended Mapuche resistance in the 1880s and gained its present northern territory by defeating Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific (1879–83). The coup of 11 September 1973 overthrew Salvador Allende and began a military dictatorship under Augusto Pinochet that lasted until 1990.

credit.artist: See file history below for details.

entries.name: Colombia
entries.desc: Colombia is a country in South America, with insular regions in North America, bordered by Venezuela, Brazil, Peru, Ecuador and Panama. Indigenous peoples lived there from at least 12,000 BCE. The Spanish landed in La Guajira in 1499 and by the mid-16th century had colonized much of the territory, establishing the New Kingdom of Granada. Independence was declared in 1810, and after a Spanish reconquest it was secured in 1819, when the Gran Colombia period began. The state became the Granadine Confederation (1858), the United States of Colombia (1863) and a centralised republic in 1886. Panama seceded in 1903, which gave Colombia its present borders.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Costa Rica
entries.desc: Costa Rica is a country in Central America, bordering Nicaragua to the north and Panama to the southeast, with coasts on the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Humans lived there from between 7,000 and 10,000 BCE, and various indigenous peoples were present before Spain colonized the territory in the 16th century. It was a peripheral colony of the Spanish Empire until independence in 1821 as part of the First Mexican Empire, then joined the Federal Republic of Central America in 1823 and formally declared independence from it in 1847. After a brief civil war in 1948, the constitution of 1949 granted universal suffrage and permanently abolished the army.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Djibouti
entries.desc: Djibouti is a country in the Horn of Africa, bordered by Somalia, Ethiopia and Eritrea, with a coast on the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. In the late 19th century the colony of French Somaliland was established after the ruling Dir-Somali and Afar sultans signed treaties with the French. Its railroad to Dire Dawa and later Addis Ababa let its port quickly supersede Zeila as the outlet for southern Ethiopia. The territory was renamed the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas in 1967, and a decade later the Djiboutian people voted for independence, founding the Republic of Djibouti, named after its capital. Armed conflict in the early 1990s ended in a power-sharing agreement in 2000.

entries.name: Dominica
entries.desc: Dominica is an island country in the Caribbean, part of the Windward Islands in the Lesser Antilles, between the French departments of Guadeloupe and Martinique. Arawak settlers arrived from South America in the fifth century and the Kalinago displaced them by the 15th century, calling the island Wai'tu kubuli. The French held it from 1690 to 1763 and enslaved West Africans to work coffee plantations. Great Britain took possession in 1763 after the Seven Years' War and continued forced labor, gradually making English the official language. Dominica was governed as part of the British Windward Islands until 1958, and the island gained independence as a republic in 1978.

entries.name: Ecuador
entries.desc: Ecuador is a country in northwestern South America, bordered by Colombia, Peru and the Pacific Ocean, and includes the Galápagos Islands about 1,000 kilometers west of the mainland. Several indigenous groups lived on its land and were gradually incorporated into the Inca Empire during the 15th century. The Spanish Empire colonized the territory during the 16th century. Ecuador achieved independence in 1820 as part of Gran Colombia and emerged as a sovereign state in 1830. The legacy of both empires is reflected in its ethnically diverse population, and 13 native languages, including Quechua and Shuar, are recognized beside Spanish.

credit.artist: President of the Republic of Ecuador, first uploaded by Denelson83 as Flag of Ecuador.svg, modifications by Husunqu, Zscout370

entries.name: El Salvador
entries.desc: El Salvador is a country in Central America on the Pacific coast, bounded by Guatemala and Honduras. The Olmecs, the Maya and later the Cuzcatlecs inhabited the territory before the Spanish Empire conquered it in 1524. During the colonial period it belonged to the Captaincy General of Guatemala, established in 1609. After independence from Spain in 1821 it was briefly annexed by the First Mexican Empire, then joined the Federal Republic of Central America in 1823, and became a fully sovereign republic when the federation dissolved in 1841. It joined Honduras and Nicaragua in a union from 1896 to 1898, and a civil war (1979–92) ended with the Chapultepec Peace Accords.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Equatorial Guinea
entries.desc: Equatorial Guinea is a country on the west coast of Central Africa and the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa. It consists of a mainland region, Río Muni, and islands including Bioko and Annobón. Pygmies are the first confirmed inhabitants of the area, followed by a migration of Bantu-speaking groups in antiquity. The Portuguese explorer Fernando Pó explored it in 1472, and by the 1778 Treaty of El Pardo Portugal ceded territories in the Bight of Biafra to Spain. It was declared Spanish Guinea during the Scramble for Africa and gained independence in 1968 under the dictatorship of Francisco Macías Nguema, who was overthrown in 1979 by his nephew Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Gabon
entries.desc: Gabon is a country on the Atlantic coast of Central Africa, lying on the equator and bordered by Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon and the Republic of the Congo. Its original inhabitants were the Bambenga, and Bantu migrants began settling the area in the 13th century BCE. The Kingdom of Orungu was established around 1700, and France colonised the region in the late 19th century. Gabon became independent from France in 1960. Omar Bongo came to office in 1967 and created a dynasty that held power through a client network, Françafrique. A multi-party system was introduced in the 1990s, and the Gabonese Democratic Party stayed dominant until the 2023 coup.

credit.artist: Léon Augé and Pierre Claver Eyeghe

entries.name: Grenada
entries.desc: Grenada is an archipelagic country of the eastern Caribbean, the southernmost of the Windward Islands, made up of Grenada itself, Carriacou and Petite Martinique. Kalinago people lived there when Christopher Columbus sighted it in 1498, and their resistance defeated early European attempts at colonisation until French settlement began in 1649. Between 1669 and 1808 approximately 127,600 African slaves were brought to the island by the British and French. It was ceded to Britain in 1763 and gained independence on 7 February 1974 under Eric Gairy. A coup in March 1979 brought Maurice Bishop to power, and a U.S.-led invasion followed his execution in October 1983.

credit.artist: See file history below for details.

entries.name: Guyana
entries.desc: Guyana, officially the Co-operative Republic of Guyana, is a country on the northern coast of South America, bordered by Suriname, Brazil and Venezuela. The Dutch were the first Europeans to found colonies there, among them Essequibo (1616) and Berbice (1627); Britain took control in 1796 and received the Dutch colonies in 1814; in 1831 they were united as British Guiana. The country became independent from the United Kingdom on 26 May 1966 and a republic on 23 February 1970. Venezuela has claimed the land west of the Essequibo River since its own independence in 1824.

entries.name: Honduras
entries.desc: Honduras is a country in Central America. Before Spanish colonization in the 16th century its territory held several Mesoamerican cultures, most notably the Maya, whose state at Copán declined in the 9th century. Honduras became independent from Spain in 1821, was part of the First Mexican Empire until 1823, and then of the United Provinces of Central America. It has been an independent republic with elections since 1838. In the early 20th century transnational agricultural companies dominated it, and the term "banana republic" was first coined for its politics. In 1960 the northern part of the Mosquito Coast was transferred from Nicaragua to Honduras.

entries.name: Iceland
entries.desc: Iceland is a Nordic island country in the North Atlantic. According to the Landnámabók, settlement began in 874 when the Norwegian chieftain Ingólfr Arnarson became the first permanent settler. The island was governed as an independent commonwealth under the Althing, until it acceded to Norwegian rule in the 13th century. It came under Danish rule after the Kalmar Union dissolved in 1523, and the Treaty of Kiel ceded it to Denmark in 1814. A national independence movement led to the Danish–Icelandic Act of Union, signed on 1 December 1918, which made Iceland a sovereign kingdom in personal union with Denmark. Icelanders voted in 1944 to become a republic.

credit.artist: Original: Matthías Þórðarson Vector: Árni Dagur and Magasjukur2

entries.name: Republic of Ireland
entries.desc: Ireland, also called the Republic of Ireland, is a country in Northwestern Europe consisting of 26 of the 32 counties of the island of Ireland. It shares its only land border with Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom. After the Easter Rising of 1916 and a War of Independence, the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921 led to the creation of the Irish Free State in 1922 with Dominion status. Acceptance of the treaty led to the Irish Civil War of 1922 to 1923. A new constitution of 1937 named the state Ireland and made it effectively a republic, and it was declared a republic in 1949. It joined the European Communities in 1973.

entries.name: Jordan
entries.desc: Jordan, officially the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, is a country in the Southern Levant region of West Asia, named for the Jordan River. Ammon, Moab and Edom arose there in the Iron Age and the Nabataeans later centred a kingdom on Petra, before the land passed to the Islamic caliphates and the Ottomans. After the Great Arab Revolt of 1916, former Ottoman Syria was partitioned, and the Emirate of Transjordan was established in 1921 as a British protectorate. Jordan gained independence in 1946. It annexed the West Bank during the 1948 Palestine war and lost it to Israeli occupation in 1967; it renounced its claim in 1988 and signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1994.

entries.name: Kazakhstan
entries.desc: Kazakhstan is a landlocked country in Central Asia, partly extending into Eastern Europe. After the Mongol conquest in the 13th century and the disintegration of the Golden Horde, the Kazakh Khanate arose in the 15th century. By the 18th century it had fragmented into three jüz, which the Russian Empire gradually absorbed, and by the mid-19th century all of Kazakhstan was nominally under Russian rule. It became an autonomous republic of the Russian SFSR after the Russian Revolution, and a union republic of the Soviet Union in 1936. It declared sovereignty on 25 October 1990 and full independence on 16 December 1991, the last Soviet republic to do so.

entries.name: Kenya
entries.desc: Kenya, officially the Republic of Kenya, is a country in East Africa, named after Mount Kenya. Its territory holds fossil evidence of early human evolution at Koobi Fora, and was later settled by Cushitic, Nilotic and Bantu speakers. European contact began in 1500 with the Portuguese. The modern country emerged from a British protectorate established in 1895 and the Kenya Colony, which began in 1920. The Mau Mau revolution began in 1952, and Kenya's independence was declared in 1963. After independence Kenya remained a member of the Commonwealth of Nations, and it is now a presidential representative democratic republic.

entries.name: Kuwait
entries.desc: Kuwait, officially the State of Kuwait, is a country in West Asia at the head of the Persian Gulf, bordering Iraq and Saudi Arabia. In the early 18th century its territory was under the Bani Khalid clan; it became known as the Sheikdom of Kuwait in 1752 and a British protectorate in 1899. Before oil reserves were discovered in 1938 it was a regional trade port. The protectorate agreements with the United Kingdom ended in June 1961, when Kuwait became an independent state. In 1990 Ba'athist Iraq under Saddam Hussein invaded it, installed a puppet regime and annexed it. The occupation ended on 26 February 1991, when a U.S.-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces in the Gulf War.

entries.name: Kyrgyzstan
entries.desc: Kyrgyzstan, officially the Kyrgyz Republic and formerly Kirghizia, is a landlocked country in Central Asia, lying in the Tian Shan and Pamir mountain ranges. Its lands were part of the Silk Road, and it was first established as the Yenisei Kyrgyz Khaganate. The Mongol Empire conquered it in the 13th century, and later the Dzungar Khanate invaded; Kyrgyz and Kipchaks then became part of the Kokand Khanate. In 1876 Kyrgyzstan became part of the Russian Empire, and in 1936 the Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic was formed as a constituent republic of the Soviet Union. Askar Akayev was elected president in 1990, and Kyrgyzstan declared independence on 31 August 1991.

entries.name: Latvia
entries.desc: Latvia, officially the Republic of Latvia, is a country in the Baltic region of northern Europe, one of the three Baltic states, with its capital at Riga. After centuries of Teutonic, Swedish, Polish-Lithuanian and Russian rule, the independent Republic of Latvia was established on 18 November 1918, breaking away from the Russian Empire after World War I. A coup in 1934 set up the dictatorship of Kārlis Ulmanis. At the outset of World War II it was forcibly incorporated into the Soviet Union, then occupied by Nazi Germany in 1941 and by the Soviets again in 1944, forming the Latvian SSR for 45 years. The Singing Revolution began in 1987, and independence was restored on 21 August 1991.

entries.name: Lesotho
entries.desc: Lesotho, officially the Kingdom of Lesotho, is a landlocked country in Southern Africa, entirely surrounded by South Africa. It emerged as a single polity, Basutoland, under King Moshoeshoe I in 1822, whose followers had joined to resist the Lifaqane. Encroaching Boer settlers and wars with them cost the kingdom its western lowlands, and Moshoeshoe appealed to Queen Victoria, who made Basutoland a British protectorate in 1868. It became a Crown colony in 1884 and gained independence from the United Kingdom on 4 October 1966, as the Kingdom of Lesotho.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Liechtenstein
entries.desc: Liechtenstein, officially the Principality of Liechtenstein, is a doubly landlocked microstate in the Central European Alps, between Austria and Switzerland. Its territory was formed on 23 January 1719, when Emperor Charles VI united Vaduz and Schellenberg and raised them to an imperial principality named after Anton Florian of Liechtenstein. The Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806, and the prince joined the Confederation of the Rhine and later the German Confederation. The principality became fully independent when that confederation dissolved in 1866. It has been a monarchy headed by a prince since.

entries.name: Luxembourg
entries.desc: Luxembourg, officially the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, is a landlocked country in Western Europe, bordered by Belgium, Germany and France. Its recorded history begins in 963, when Siegfried, Count of the Ardennes, acquired a castle on the Bock rock, around which the County of Luxembourg grew within the Holy Roman Empire. After French annexation, the Congress of Vienna restored it in 1815 in personal union with the Netherlands. The Treaty of London of 1839 gave it modern borders by transferring its western part to Belgium. Independence and neutrality were reaffirmed after the Luxembourg Crisis, and in 1890 it gained its own monarchy.

entries.name: Maldives
entries.desc: The Maldives, officially the Republic of Maldives, is an archipelagic country in the Indian Ocean, south-west of India and Sri Lanka, made up of 26 atolls. It has been inhabited for over 2,500 years. Its last Buddhist king, Dhovemi, converted to Islam in 1153 (or 1193) and began a series of six Islamic dynasties. The Portuguese set up a garrison in 1558, and a local revolt later ended their presence. The islands became a British protectorate in 1887, gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1965, and became a republic in 1968 after a referendum.

credit.artist: See File history , below, for details.

entries.name: Monaco
entries.desc: Monaco, officially the Principality of Monaco, is a sovereign city-state and microstate on the French Riviera, bordered by France on three sides and by the Mediterranean Sea. The Genoese built a castle on the rock in the early 1200s, and in 1297 Francesco Grimaldi and his men seized it disguised as monks. The Grimaldi family bought Monaco from the Crown of Aragon in 1419, and Honoré II began styling himself Prince in 1612. After periods under France and Sardinia, Monaco ceded Menton and Roquebrune to France, and its sovereignty was recognised by the Franco-Monégasque Treaty of 1861.

entries.name: Montenegro
entries.desc: Montenegro is a country in Southeastern Europe on the Balkan Peninsula, with a coastline on the Adriatic Sea. The name, from a Venetian rendering of Crna Gora, "Black Mountain", came into use in the late 15th century. After Ottoman rule it gained semi-autonomy in 1696 under the House of Petrović-Njegoš, and its independence was recognised by the Great Powers at the Congress of Berlin in 1878. It became a kingdom in 1910, then part of Yugoslavia, and later formed a union with Serbia. A referendum on 21 May 2006 passed with 55.5% in favour, and Montenegro declared independence in June 2006.

entries.name: Nauru
entries.desc: Nauru, also known as Naoero, is an island country in Micronesia in the South Pacific Ocean, and one of the smallest states in the world. Micronesians first settled it at least 3,000 years ago, and it had twelve traditional clans. Germany annexed it in 1888. Australia occupied it in World War I, after which it became a League of Nations mandate, and Japan occupied it from 1942. It was a United Nations trust territory after the war and became independent on 31 January 1968. Phosphate-rock mining, begun in 1900, stripped most of its interior.

entries.name: Nicaragua
entries.desc: Nicaragua, officially the Republic of Nicaragua, is a country in Central America, bordered by Honduras and Costa Rica, with coasts on the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. The Spanish Empire conquered it in the 16th century, and it gained independence from Spain in 1821. Its Caribbean coast, Mosquitia, was a kingdom under British protection until the Treaty of Managua of 1860 joined it to Nicaragua. The later history includes the American filibuster William Walker, American occupation, Sandino's guerrilla war, the Somoza family's rule from 1936 to 1979, the Nicaraguan Revolution and the Contra War of the 1980s.

entries.name: Northern Cyprus
entries.desc: Northern Cyprus, officially the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, is a de facto state occupying the northern third of the island of Cyprus. Only Turkey recognises it; the international community regards the land as territory of the Republic of Cyprus under Turkish military occupation. Cyprus became independent in 1960, but intercommunal violence followed. After a coup in July 1974 backed by the Greek military junta, Turkey invaded and took the north. The Turkish Federated State of Cyprus was declared in 1975, and independence was proclaimed on 15 November 1983. UN Security Council Resolution 541 rejected the declaration as legally invalid.

credit.artist: See File History , below for details.

entries.name: Panama
entries.desc: Panama, officially the Republic of Panama, is a country on the narrow isthmus at the southern end of Central America, bordered by Costa Rica and Colombia. Its Indigenous peoples were followed by Spanish colonists in the 16th century, and Panama City was founded in 1519. Panama broke away from Spain in 1821 and joined Gran Colombia, then remained part of Colombia after that union dissolved in 1831. With United States backing it seceded from Colombia in 1903, and the Panama Canal was built by the US Army Corps of Engineers between 1904 and 1914. The Torrijos–Carter Treaties of 1977 provided for transfer of the canal to Panama on 31 December 1999.

entries.name: Qatar
entries.desc: Qatar, officially the State of Qatar, is a country in West Asia that occupies the Qatar Peninsula on the northeastern coast of the Arabian Peninsula, with Saudi Arabia as its only land neighbour. The House of Thani has ruled it as a hereditary monarchy since Mohammed bin Thani signed an agreement with Britain in 1868, which officially recognised its separate status. After Ottoman rule it became a British protectorate on 3 November 1916, with foreign affairs and defence reserved to the United Kingdom. In 1968 Britain announced its withdrawal from the Persian Gulf, and Qatar left talks on a federation with Bahrain and the Trucial States; it became independent on 3 September 1971.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic
entries.desc: The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic is a partially recognised state in the western Maghreb that claims sovereignty over the whole of Western Sahara but controls only its easternmost portion. The Polisario Front proclaimed it on 27 February 1976 at Bir Lehlou, after Spain, Morocco and Mauritania signed the Madrid Accords in November 1975 to divide the territory without any role for the Sahrawi people. Morocco occupies the rest and calls it its Southern Provinces. The republic is a full member of the African Union, and has been recognised by some states, of which a number have since frozen or withdrawn recognition. Its government operates largely from refugee camps near Tindouf in Algeria.

credit.artist: El Uali Mustafá Sayed from Polisario Front

entries.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
aka: Federation of Saint Kitts and Nevis
entries.desc: Saint Kitts and Nevis, officially the Federation of Saint Kitts and Nevis, is an island country in the Leeward Islands of the Lesser Antilles in the Caribbean. Saint Kitts hosted the first British and French Caribbean colonies, which divided the island between them after 1625, and its slave-based sugar industry made it the richest British colony per capita in the Caribbean by the 1700s. The islands were federated with Anguilla in 1882, joined the West Indies Federation from 1958 to 1962, and became an associated state with full internal autonomy in 1967. Anguilla seceded that year, and the federation of the two remaining islands gained full independence on 19 September 1983.

entries.name: Saint Lucia
entries.desc: Saint Lucia is an island country in the eastern Caribbean, part of the Windward Islands of the Lesser Antilles. Arawaks settled it around 200 to 400 CE and the Kalinago took it over around 800 CE. France claimed it in 1650 and signed a treaty with the Caribs in 1660, and England and France then fought repeatedly over it, so that control changed often until Britain secured it in 1814. Universal suffrage came in 1951, the island belonged to the West Indies Federation from 1958 to 1962, and it became internally self-governing in 1967. Saint Lucia gained independence peacefully on 22 February 1979, remaining a Commonwealth realm.

entries.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
entries.desc: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is an archipelagic country in the southeast Windward Islands of the eastern Caribbean, made up of the island of Saint Vincent and the northern Grenadines. The Kalinago resisted European settlement, and the French were the first to colonise it, in 1719, using enslaved Africans on plantations. Britain took the island in the Seven Years' War and held it from 1783. The Garifuna fought the First Carib War of 1772 to 1773 and the Second of 1795 to 1797, after which almost 5,000 were deported to Roatán and other places. Associate statehood came in 1969 and full independence on 27 October 1979.

credit.artist: No machine-readable author provided. SKopp assumed (based on copyright claims).

entries.name: Samoa
entries.desc: Samoa, officially the Independent State of Samoa, is an island country in Polynesia in the South Pacific, consisting chiefly of the islands of Savai'i and Upolu. The Lapita people settled the islands around 3,500 years ago. Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States divided the archipelago under the Tripartite Convention of 1899, and the western islands became German Samoa until New Zealand troops occupied them in 1914. New Zealand governed them under League of Nations and United Nations arrangements, and about a fifth of the population died in the influenza epidemic of 1918 to 1919. Western Samoa became independent on 1 January 1962 and dropped the word Western on 4 July 1997.

credit.artist: Original: Malietoa Tanumafili II and Tupua Tamasese Meaʻole Vector: See the file history below for details.

entries.name: San Marino
entries.desc: San Marino, officially the Republic of San Marino, is a landlocked country in Southern Europe, completely surrounded by Italy. It claims to have been founded in 301 CE by Saint Marinus, a stonemason said to have fled persecution under Diocletian and built a chapel on Monte Titano, and to be the oldest extant sovereign state. Its borders have been unchanged since 1463. Its independence survived occupation by Cesare Borgia in 1503 and by a papal legate in 1739, and in the 19th century it sheltered supporters of Italian unification, among them Giuseppe Garibaldi. It remained neutral in both world wars, joined the Council of Europe in 1988 and the United Nations in 1992.

entries.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
aka: Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe
entries.desc: São Tomé and Príncipe, officially the Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe, is an island country in the Gulf of Guinea off the western coast of Central Africa. The islands were uninhabited when Portuguese explorers reached them in 1470. They were settled gradually in the 16th century and became a commercial centre of the Atlantic slave trade, with sugar and later coffee and cocoa grown on plantations dependent on enslaved Africans. Unrest in the 20th century included riots in 1953 in which several hundred African labourers were killed. After talks in Algiers in November 1974, the islands became independent on 12 July 1975 as a one-party communist state, which lasted until 1990.

credit.artist: See File history below for details.

entries.name: Solomon Islands
entries.desc: Solomon Islands is an archipelagic country in Melanesia, north-east of Australia, made up of six major islands and many smaller ones; its capital Honiara lies on Guadalcanal. People have lived there since at least 30,000 to 28,800 BCE. The Spanish navigator Álvaro de Mendaña was the first European to visit, in 1568. Britain declared a protectorate over the southern islands in June 1893, and the Solomon Islands campaign of 1942 to 1945 brought heavy fighting, including the Battle of Guadalcanal. Self-government came in 1976 and independence in 1978. Ethnic violence between 1998 and 2003 was ended with the arrival of the Australian-led RAMSI mission in July 2003.

entries.name: Tajikistan
entries.desc: Tajikistan, officially the Republic of Tajikistan, is a landlocked country in Central Asia, bordered by Afghanistan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and China. Parts of its territory belonged to the Sogdian and Bactrian civilisations and were ruled in turn by the Achaemenids, Alexander the Great, the Samanid Empire, the Mongols and the Khanate of Bukhara, before conquest by the Russian Empire. Its borders were drawn while it was part of Uzbekistan as the Tajik ASSR, and it became a Soviet republic on 5 December 1929. Tajikistan declared independence on 9 September 1991. A civil war followed from May 1992 to June 1997, with estimated deaths above 100,000.

entries.name: The Bahamas
entries.desc: The Bahamas is an archipelagic country in the Caribbean, within the Lucayan Archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean, north of Cuba and southeast of Florida. The islands were inhabited by the Arawak and Lucayans, whom Spain shipped to Hispaniola and enslaved, leaving the islands mostly deserted from 1513 until 1648. English colonists settled Eleuthera in 1649, and the Bahamas became a crown colony in 1718. After the American Revolutionary War, Loyalists brought slaves with them; slavery was abolished in 1834. The Bahamas became an independent Commonwealth realm in 1973, with Lynden Pindling as its first prime minister.

entries.name: Tonga
entries.desc: Tonga is an island country in Polynesia, in the southern Pacific Ocean, made up of 171 islands. It was first settled roughly 2,500 years ago by people of the Lapita culture, and later became the centre of the Tuʻi Tonga Empire, a thalassocracy that held parts of the Pacific from Fiji to Samoa and Niue. Europeans reached the islands in 1616. From 1900 to 1970 Tonga was a British protected state under a Treaty of Friendship, but it never relinquished its sovereignty, and in 1970 it joined the Commonwealth. In 2010 the absolute monarchy gave way to a semi-constitutional one.

entries.name: Transnistria
entries.desc: Transnistria is a landlocked breakaway state, internationally recognised as part of Moldova, on the strip of land between the Dniester river and the Moldova–Ukraine border. Its origins lie in the Moldavian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, formed in 1924 within the Ukrainian SSR. In 1990, as the Soviet Union dissolved, the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic was established. A military conflict with Moldova began in March 1992 and ended in a ceasefire in July that year. Its political status remains unresolved: it is unrecognised but de facto independent, with its own government, parliament and currency.

entries.name: Trinidad and Tobago
entries.desc: Trinidad and Tobago is the southernmost archipelagic country in the Caribbean, lying off the coast of Venezuela. Indigenous peoples settled Trinidad long before Christopher Columbus reached it in 1498, and its oldest known settlement, Banwari Trace, dates to about 5000 BCE. Spanish governor José María Chacón surrendered Trinidad to a British fleet in 1797, and Trinidad and Tobago were ceded to Britain in 1802 as separate states. They were unified in 1889, became independent in 1962 and a republic in 1976. Indian indentured workers came to its sugar plantations in the 19th century.

credit.artist: See File history , below, for details .

entries.name: Turkmenistan
entries.desc: Turkmenistan is a landlocked country in Central Asia, bordered by Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan, Iran and the Caspian Sea. Its written history begins with its annexation by the Achaemenid Empire. In the 8th century CE Turkic-speaking Oghuz tribes moved from Mongolia into Central Asia and formed the ethnic basis of the Turkmen. Merv, one of the oldest oasis-cities in Central Asia, was an important stop on the Silk Road. The Russian Empire annexed the territory in 1881, it became a Soviet republic in 1925, and it declared independence in 1991 after the Soviet Union dissolved.

entries.name: Benin
entries.desc: Benin is a country in West Africa, bordered by Togo, Nigeria, Burkina Faso and Niger, with its coast on the Bight of Benin. From the 17th to the 19th centuries the area held political entities including the Kingdom of Dahomey and the city-state of Porto Novo. France took over the territory in 1894 as French Dahomey, and it became independent on 1 August 1960. A Marxist–Leninist coup led to its renaming as Benin in 1975, after the Bight of Benin. The People's Republic of Benin lasted from 1975 to 1990 and was replaced in 1991 by a multi-party republic.

credit.artist: Drawn by User:SKopp , rewritten by User:Gabbe

entries.name: Israel
entries.desc: Israel is a country in the Southern Levant region of West Asia, on the Mediterranean coast, bordered by Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Egypt. Zionism, which sought a homeland for the Jewish people in Palestine, grew from European antisemitism in the late 19th century. Britain established Mandatory Palestine in 1920, and in 1947 the United Nations proposed partitioning the land between Jews and the Arab-majority population. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, and neighbouring Arab states invaded the next day. Most Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled during the Nakba, and the Israeli–Palestinian conflict persists.

credit.artist: Israel Belkind and Fanny Abramovitch (original) “The Provisional Council of State Proclamation of the Flag of the State of Israel” of 25 Tis

entries.name: Niger
entries.desc: Niger is a landlocked country in West Africa, named for the Niger River, with over 80% of its land area in the Sahara. Parts of its territory lay within states such as the Kanem–Bornu Empire, the Mali Empire, the Sultanate of Agadez and the Songhai Empire. France colonised it during the Scramble for Africa as part of French West Africa, and it became a distinct colony in 1922. It became an autonomous state within the French Community in 1958 and gained independence in 1960. Since then Niger has experienced five coups d'état and four periods of military rule.

credit.artist: Made by: Philippe Verdy User:verdy_p , see also fr:Utilisateur:verdy_p .

entries.name: Portugal
entries.desc: Portugal is a country in Southwestern Europe, on the western Iberian Peninsula, that also includes the archipelagos of Madeira and the Azores. Muslims had occupied the peninsula since 711; as a result of the Reconquista, Portugal was established as a county of the Kingdom of León in 868 and formally as a kingdom in 1179. In 1385 John of Aviz was elected king and defeated the Castilians. During the Age of Discovery the kingdom advanced nautical science and built the Portuguese Empire. It became a republic in 1910 and a dictatorship in 1926; the dictatorship was overthrown in 1974 and democracy established in 1976.

credit.artist: Original: Columbano Bordalo Pinheiro Vector: Vítor Luís Rodrigues, António Martins-Tuválkin

entries.name: Tuvalu
entries.desc: Tuvalu is an archipelagic country in Polynesia, in the Pacific Ocean midway between Hawaii and Australia, made up of three reef islands and six atolls. Polynesians were its first inhabitants, spreading out from Samoa and Tonga. Álvaro de Mendaña was the first European known to sail through the archipelago, in 1568. A British protectorate was proclaimed in 1892, and the islands joined the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony in 1916. After a referendum in 1974 the colony was divided, and Tuvalu became a separate colony on 1 January 1976. It became fully independent on 1 October 1978.

entries.name: Paul the Apostle
entries.desc: Paul, born Saul of Tarsus, was a Christian apostle who spread the teachings of Jesus in the first century CE and founded several Christian communities in Asia Minor and Europe from the mid-40s to the mid-50s. His life is known chiefly from his letters and the Acts of the Apostles. According to Acts, he was a Pharisee who persecuted the followers of Jesus until a vision of Christ on the road to Damascus led him to be baptized. Fourteen New Testament books are traditionally attributed to him, of which scholars regard seven as undisputed. His death in Rome under Nero is traditional, dated either after the fire of 64 or a few years later.

entries.name: Saint Peter
entries.desc: Peter, born Simon bar Jonah, was one of the Twelve Apostles of Jesus and one of the first leaders of the early Christian Church. A fisherman and the brother of Andrew, he appears prominently in all four gospels and in Acts, and Jesus gave him the Aramaic name Cephas, meaning rock. Catholic and Orthodox tradition treats him as the first bishop of Rome and of Antioch, and Catholic teaching holds that Jesus promised him a special position. Church Fathers attest that he spent his last years in Rome and, according to tradition, was crucified upside down under Nero. Modern scholarship generally rejects his authorship of the two New Testament letters attributed to him.

entries.name: Pontius Pilate
entries.desc: Pontius Pilate was the fifth Roman governor of Judaea, serving under Emperor Tiberius from 26/27 to 36/37 CE. The gospels, Josephus and Tacitus attribute the crucifixion of Jesus to his orders, and the gospels portray him as reluctant to carry it out. Josephus and Philo record several conflicts with the Jewish population, and Josephus reports that he was dismissed after violently putting down a Samaritan uprising at Mount Gerizim. Little survives of his rule beyond his coins and the Pilate Stone inscription, and his fate after leaving office is unknown. Historians are divided on whether he governed brutally and ineptly or with moderate competence.

entries.name: Mary Magdalene
entries.desc: Mary Magdalene was, according to the four canonical gospels, a woman who travelled with Jesus as one of his followers and witnessed his crucifixion and resurrection. Luke says that seven demons had gone out of her and that she helped support the group from her resources. Her name is usually taken to mean that she came from Magdala, a village on the Sea of Galilee. In the gospel of John she is the first to see the risen Jesus and is sent to tell the apostles, so some traditions call her the apostle to the apostles. A Western tradition, shaped by a sermon of Pope Gregory I in 591, made her a repentant prostitute, which has no basis in the gospels.

entries.name: Saint Joseph
entries.desc: Joseph, according to the canonical gospels, was a Jewish man of Nazareth in the first century who was married to Mary and was the legal father of Jesus. Matthew and Luke give him differing genealogies and infancy narratives: in Matthew an angel directs him in dreams, including the flight into Egypt, while in Luke he travels to Bethlehem for a census. He last appears when Jesus is twelve, at the Passover visit to the Temple. The gospels call him a tekton, traditionally translated as carpenter, a word that can cover other craftsmen. He is venerated as a saint in the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran traditions, and Catholics honour him as patron of workers.

entries.name: Judas Iscariot
entries.desc: Judas Iscariot was, according to the four canonical gospels, one of the Twelve Apostles of Jesus. The gospels say he betrayed Jesus to the authorities in Gethsemane with a kiss, and Matthew adds that the price was thirty pieces of silver. Luke and John suggest that Satan had entered him. Matthew says he hanged himself, while Acts gives a different account of his death, and Matthias was later chosen to replace him. The Gnostic Gospel of Judas presents his act as done at Jesus's instruction, and Irenaeus denounced that text as heresy. Most secular historians accept that he existed. His name later became a byword for betrayal and was used to justify Christian antisemitism.

entries.name: Caiaphas
entries.desc: Joseph ben Caiaphas was a high priest in the first century. The Gospels of Matthew, Luke and John present him as an organizer of the plot against Jesus and as presiding over the Sanhedrin trial. Josephus, the most reliable source outside the New Testament, says the Roman prefect Valerius Gratus appointed him in 18 CE and that the legate of Syria Lucius Vitellius later deposed him. His tenure of eighteen years suggests a working relationship with the Romans. In John he is the son-in-law of Annas and argues that it is better for one man to die than for the nation to be destroyed. A limestone ossuary found in 1990 may be his, though some scholars dispute the identification.

entries.name: James, brother of Jesus
entries.desc: James, called the Just, was according to the New Testament a brother of Jesus and the first leader of the church in Jerusalem. Paul knew him personally and mentions him in his letter to the Galatians. Accounts of his death differ: Josephus records that he was stoned in 62 CE on the order of the high priest Ananus ben Ananus, while Hegesippus places his death in 69 and says he was thrown from the Temple pinnacle and clubbed. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that the brothers of Jesus were cousins or stepbrothers, while others consider James a son of Mary and Joseph. Most agree he is not James, son of Zebedee.

entries.name: Apostles in the New Testament
entries.desc: In the New Testament the apostles, above all the Twelve, were the primary disciples of Jesus. The word comes from the Greek apostolos, meaning a messenger or envoy. The Synoptic Gospels describe Jesus commissioning the Twelve, and the gospels and Acts give four lists of them that differ slightly in names. Peter, James and John formed an inner circle. After Judas Iscariot betrayed Jesus and died, the remaining eleven chose Matthias by lot. Paul, though not one of the Twelve, called himself an apostle, and the New Testament also uses the title for others, among them Barnabas. Christian tradition holds that all the Twelve but John were martyred.

entries.name: Last Supper
entries.desc: The Last Supper is the final meal that, in the gospel accounts, Jesus shared with his apostles in Jerusalem before his crucifixion. The earliest mention is in Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, and the gospels place it in the week of Passover. During it Jesus predicts his betrayal and Peter's denial. Paul and the Synoptic Gospels relate that Jesus took bread and gave it to those present, which is the scriptural basis of the Eucharist, while John tells instead of the washing of the apostles' feet. The three Synoptic Gospels describe a Passover meal, which John seems to disagree with, and scholars propose various ways to reconcile them.

entries.name: Sermon on the Mount
entries.desc: The Sermon on the Mount is a discourse of Jesus of Nazareth found in chapters 5 to 7 of the Gospel of Matthew, summarizing his moral teachings. It is the first of five discourses in that gospel and contains the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer in its commonly recited form and the Golden Rule. In Matthew, Jesus goes up a mountain with his disciples, sits down and teaches. Christians have traditionally commemorated the Mount of Beatitudes as the site, though Mount Arbel and the Horns of Hattin have also been suggested. Some Christian traditions see the sermon as the counterpart of the giving of the Ten Commandments on Sinai, and Luke places parts of the material in a different setting.

entries.name: Crucifixion of Jesus
entries.desc: The crucifixion of Jesus was his execution by the Romans in 1st-century Judaea, most likely in 30 CE or 33 CE. The four canonical Gospels say he was arrested, tried before the Sanhedrin, then brought before Pontius Pilate, who sentenced him to be scourged and crucified at Calvary (Golgotha) between two convicted men. Paul is the earliest surviving source, and scholars hold the fact of the crucifixion to be near universally accepted, though not its details. Christians call his suffering and death the Passion and treat it as central to their doctrines of salvation and atonement.

entries.name: Resurrection of Jesus
entries.desc: The resurrection of Jesus is the Christian belief that God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day after his crucifixion. The New Testament does not describe the moment itself, only an empty tomb and appearances to his followers; Paul reports an early creed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 that scholars think predates his letter. For Christians it is the central mystery of their faith and is observed at Easter. Some historians assess the visionary experiences of his followers as the impetus for the belief, while many leave the question to faith. Islam generally teaches that Jesus was not crucified but ascended directly to God.

entries.name: Baptism of Jesus
entries.desc: The baptism of Jesus by John the Baptist is described in the three Synoptic Gospels, Matthew, Mark and Luke, and is placed at Al-Maghtas (Bethany Beyond the Jordan), in present-day Jordan. In each, the Spirit descends on Jesus and a voice from Heaven speaks, after which the Gospels place his forty days in the Judean desert. Modern biblical scholars regard the baptism as a historical event assigned a high degree of certainty, and often start from it in studying the historical Jesus. Eastern Christianity commemorates it on 6 January, the feast of Epiphany or Theophany, and Western churches recall it in the following week.

entries.name: Lord's Prayer
entries.desc: The Lord's Prayer, also called the Our Father or Pater Noster, is a central Christian prayer attributed to Jesus. It survives in two versions, in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, and the first-century Didache gives a form close to Matthew's. Most scholars regard it as deriving from the historical Jesus, though they debate how the two versions relate. Matthew's has seven petitions, the first three addressed to God and the other four to human needs, and it is the form used in most Christian worship. Some manuscripts and Protestant usage add a closing doxology, and Orthodox churches use their own.

entries.name: Calvary
entries.desc: Calvary, or Golgotha, was a site outside the walls of Roman Jerusalem where, according to the four canonical Gospels, Jesus was crucified. The names mean "place of the Skull", from the Latin Calvariae and the Aramaic Golgolta. Tradition places it within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, a site traditionally believed to have been identified by the empress Helena, mother of Constantine, on her visit to the Holy Land in 325. In the 19th century Protestant scholars proposed another location near the Garden Tomb, about 500 m to the north. It has been a pilgrimage destination since at least the early medieval period.

entries.name: Gethsemane
entries.desc: Gethsemane is a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives in East Jerusalem where, according to the four Gospels, Jesus underwent the Agony in the Garden and was arrested before his crucifixion. The name comes from Aramaic or Hebrew words meaning "oil press". Four sites near the western foot of the Mount of Olives are claimed by different denominations, among them the garden of the Catholic Church of All Nations and the Russian Orthodox orchard; modern scholarship acknowledges that the exact location is unknown. It became a focus for early Christian pilgrims, and the Pilgrim of Bordeaux visited it in 333.

entries.name: Capernaum
entries.desc: Capernaum was a fishing village on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, established under the Hasmoneans in the 2nd century BCE, with a population of about 1,500 in the 1st century CE. All four Gospels name it, and the Synoptic Gospels present it as the centre of Jesus' public ministry in Galilee, where he taught in the synagogue and healed. Excavations have found two synagogues built in succession on the same spot and a house turned into a church over the 4th and 5th centuries, which Christian tradition holds was the home of Saint Peter. The village was inhabited until the 11th century and abandoned before the First Crusade.

entries.name: Council of Jerusalem
entries.desc: The Council of Jerusalem, or Apostolic Council, is a meeting described in chapter 15 of the Acts of the Apostles and held in Jerusalem about 48–50 CE. According to Acts, it addressed whether Gentile converts had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, a question raised by the mission of Paul and Barnabas. It decided that they did not, but told them to abstain from food associated with idols, from blood and strangled meat, and from porneia; these instructions are known as the Apostolic Decree. Scholars increasingly affirm the council as historical, but disagree on whether Galatians 2 describes the same event.

entries.name: Conversion of Paul the Apostle
entries.desc: The conversion of Paul the Apostle was, according to the New Testament, the event that led Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who had intensely persecuted the followers of Jesus, to become one himself. Acts describes him travelling to Damascus with a mandate from the High Priest when a light from heaven flashed around him; Paul's own letters, including Galatians and 1 Corinthians, speak of a revelation from Jesus Christ and of seeing the risen Christ. Both sources say he had not known Jesus before the crucifixion, and Acts suggests the conversion came four to seven years after it. The accounts describe it as miraculous or revelatory in nature.

entries.name: Pauline epistles
entries.desc: The Pauline epistles are the thirteen books of the New Testament attributed to Paul the Apostle, among the earliest extant Christian documents. Most scholars believe Paul wrote seven of them: Galatians, Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philemon, Philippians and 1 Thessalonians, with consensus dates from about 48 CE for Galatians. Scholars are about evenly divided on 2 Thessalonians, Colossians and Ephesians, and many regard 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus as written in his name by others. The Epistle to the Hebrews was traditionally counted as Paul's, but few scholars now ascribe it to him. They are foundational texts for Christian theology and ethics.

entries.name: Annunciation
entries.desc: The Annunciation is the event in which, according to the Gospel of Luke, the angel Gabriel told Mary that she would conceive and bear a son, Jesus, through a virgin birth. Luke places it in Nazareth in the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy with John the Baptist; Matthew gives a separate, briefer announcement by an angel to Joseph. Many Christians observe the Feast of the Annunciation on 25 March, nine months before Christmas. Gabriel's greeting forms the first part of the Hail Mary prayer. The Annunciation was a major subject in Christian art, especially in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.

entries.name: Assumption of Mary
aka: Dormition of the Mother of God
entries.desc: The Assumption of Mary is the Catholic dogma that Mary, at the end of her earthly life, was taken body and soul into heaven. Pope Pius XII defined it on 1 November 1950 in the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus, leaving open whether she died first. Eastern Christianity holds the equivalent belief as the Dormition, or Falling Asleep, of the Mother of God, and the feast is kept on 15 August. The New Testament is silent on the end of her life; accounts appear in apocryphal Dormition narratives that scholars date from the fourth century or earlier, and the Emperor Maurice established the feast in Constantinople in 600.
links: Dormition of the Mother of God

entries.name: Khadija bint Khuwaylid
entries.desc: Khadija bint Khuwaylid was the first wife of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and a wealthy merchant of the Quraysh of Mecca. She employed Muhammad to manage a trade caravan to Syria and then offered him marriage; sources differ on her age at the time, giving about 28 or 40. Traditional Sunni accounts hold that she was the first person to accept Islam after his first revelation. Sources disagree on how many children they had, most naming six, and Sunni and some Shia views differ on her earlier marriages. She died in November 619, and the year is known as the Year of Sorrow.

entries.name: Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib
entries.desc: Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib was an uncle of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, the father of Ali, and the leader of the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh in Mecca. He took in Muhammad after the death of his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and, as clan chief, protected him when other Quraysh leaders pressed him to silence his nephew, including during a three-year boycott of the Banu Hashim. He died around 619, within a month of Khadija. His religious status at death is disputed: most Sunni scholars hold that he did not accept Islam, while Shia scholars hold that he was a believer who concealed his faith to protect Muhammad.

entries.name: Battle of Badr
entries.desc: The Battle of Badr was fought on 13 March 624 (17 Ramadan, 2 AH) near Badr, in present-day Saudi Arabia. Muhammad, with an army of about 313 men, defeated a Quraysh force of around 1300 led by Amr ibn Hisham, known to Muslims as Abu Jahl. It began when Muhammad set out to intercept a Meccan caravan under Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, which escaped by another route. About 70 Meccans were killed, including Amr ibn Hisham and Umayya ibn Khalaf, and about 70 were taken prisoner. Muslim tradition calls it a victory owed to divine intervention; other sources credit Muhammad's strategy.

entries.name: Battle of the Trench
entries.desc: The Battle of the Trench was fought in 627, when a confederate force estimated at around 10,000 men, led by the Quraysh with the exiled Banu Nadir and several Bedouin tribes, advanced on Medina. At the suggestion of Salman the Persian, Muhammad's followers dug a trench around the settlement, which held the attackers back for about two weeks until bad weather and quarrels within the confederacy led them to withdraw. Reported casualties were few. The Muslims then besieged the Banu Qurayza, who surrendered, and a judgment pronounced by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was carried out; scholars doubt Ibn Ishaq's account of the numbers killed.

entries.name: Conquest of Mecca
entries.desc: The conquest of Mecca was a campaign by Muhammad and his companions against the Quraysh-controlled city in December 629 or January 630 (10–20 Ramadan, 8 AH); sources vary on the dates. It followed an attack by the Banu Bakr, with Quraysh support, on the Banu Khuza'ah, allies of the Muslims, which breached the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb sought a renewed truce in Medina without success. Muhammad entered the city, proclaimed a general amnesty with a few exceptions, and cleared the Kaaba of its idols, which tradition numbers at 360. The fall of Mecca formally ended the conflict between the Muslims and the Quraysh.

entries.name: Isra' and Mi'raj
entries.desc: The Isra' and Mi'raj, the Night Travel and Ascension, are Islamic narratives of a night journey in which Muhammad ascends to the heavens, sees the afterlife and returns. The Quran has only brief references, in verses of Surah an-Najm and in the 17th chapter, later called Surah al-Isra'; the detailed accounts come from hadith compiled after his lifetime. In the fuller versions he is accompanied by the angels Gabriel and Michael, meets earlier prophets, and reaches the Sidrat al-Muntaha, where the fifty daily prayers required of him are reduced to five. Classical commentaries mostly read the journey as bodily, Sufism generally as spiritual, and the 27th night of Rajab is widely observed.

entries.name: Farewell Pilgrimage
entries.desc: The Farewell Pilgrimage was the Hajj that Muhammad performed in 10 AH, after the conquest of Mecca. Approximately 100,000 of his companions are said to have gathered to make it with him. He left Medina on 25 Dhu al-Qi'dah, around February 632, and performed Hajj al-Qiran, combining the Umrah and the Hajj. On the 9th of Dhu al-Hijjah, the Day of Arafah, he delivered the Farewell Sermon on Mount Arafat. Muslims believe verse 3 of Surah 5 was revealed after it. His rites on this journey were recorded by those who accompanied him and became a precedent, or sunnah, for later pilgrims.

entries.name: Jabal al-Nour
entries.desc: Jabal al-Nour, the Mountain of the Light, is a mountain of 642 m near Mecca in the Hejaz region of Saudi Arabia. Near its summit is the cave of Hira, where Muhammad is said by Islamic tradition to have received his first revelation, the opening verses of Surah al-Alaq, from the angel Gabriel; the date is traditionally placed on Laylat al-Qadr, around August 610. The cave is about 3.7 m long and lies at 270 m, reached by some 1750 steps. Most Muslims do not count a visit as part of the Hajj, though many climb it, and the mountain is closed to non-Muslims because it lies near Mecca.

entries.name: Ghadir Khumm
entries.desc: Ghadir Khumm was an event of 16 March 632, shortly before Muhammad's death, at a pond near Juhfa between Mecca and Medina, on the return from the Farewell Pilgrimage. Muhammad took Ali by the hand and said, "For whoever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla." Sunni and Shia Muslims both accept that this was said, but differ on its meaning. Shia Muslims understand mawla as authority and take it as Muhammad's designation of Ali as successor and first Imam, commemorated on 18 Dhu al-Hijjah as Eid al-Ghadir. Sunni Muslims read it as an expression of friendship and esteem rather than a designation of a successor.

entries.name: Imam Ali Shrine
entries.desc: The Imam Ali Shrine is a Shia mosque and mausoleum in Najaf, Iraq, which Shia and Sunni Muslims believe holds the tomb of Ali ibn Abi Talib, cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad. Shias regard Ali as the first Imam and Muhammad's rightful successor; Sunnis count him as the fourth caliph. The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid built the first structure over the tomb in 786 CE, and later rulers rebuilt and enlarged it, among them the Buyid emir 'Adud al-Dawla, Shah Abbas I and Nader Shah, who gilded the dome in 1742. The present building dates from the Safavid period, with a dome 42 metres high between twin minarets. Millions of pilgrims visit each year.

entries.name: Ahl al-Bayt
entries.desc: Ahl al-Bayt, Arabic for 'People of the House', refers to the family of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. Sunni and Shia Muslims both revere it but differ on its religious authority. Shias hold that Muhammad appointed Ali and his descendants, and the largest Shia branch sees the Twelve Imams as divinely guided; Sunnis honour the family without holding the Imams to be divinely appointed or infallible. The term appears in the Quran in verse 33:33, the verse of purification, and Muslims disagree over who belongs to the group. Many traditions name Muhammad, Fatima, Ali, Hasan and Husayn, while some Sunni authors include Muhammad's wives or wider kin such as the Abbasids.

entries.name: Prophet's Mosque
entries.desc: The Prophet's Mosque (al-Masjid al-Nabawi) is a mosque in Medina in the Hejaz, built by Muhammad in 622 after his arrival in the city. Muslim sources say the land belonged to two orphans, Sahl and Suhayl, and that Muhammad paid for it with money provided by Abu Ayyub al-Ansari. The first building had a roof of palm trunks, clay and palm leaves, and served as a community centre, court and school. Umar and Uthman enlarged it, and the Umayyad caliph al-Walid I carried out a large expansion in 706 or 707. It now includes the graves of Muhammad, Abu Bakr and Umar beneath the Green Dome, and it is the second holiest site in Islam after Mecca.

entries.name: Hagar
entries.desc: Hagar is an Egyptian woman in the Book of Genesis, the concubine of Abraham and the mother of his firstborn son Ishmael. Genesis says that Sarah, believing herself barren, gave her to Abraham, that tension followed, and that Hagar fled into the desert, where an angel told her to return and promised her many descendants. After Isaac's birth she and Ishmael were sent away and, according to Genesis, God showed her a well. The Quran does not name her, but Islamic tradition describes Hajar as a maid who ran seven times between Safa and Marwah and found the Zamzam well, an act recalled in the Hajj rites. Ishmael is generally taken as the ancestor of the Arabs.

entries.name: Ishmael
entries.desc: Ishmael is the first son of Abraham in the Book of Genesis, born to Hagar, the Egyptian handmaiden of Abraham's wife Sarah. Genesis says he was circumcised at 13, that after Isaac's birth he and Hagar were sent into the wilderness, and that God promised to make of him a great nation; it gives his age at death as 137. Jewish and Islamic traditions regard him as ancestor of the Arabs. Islam honours him as a prophet. Muslim tradition holds that he and Abraham raised the foundations of the Kaaba in Mecca, and that he was buried at the Hijr near it.

entries.name: Isaac
entries.desc: Isaac is the second Hebrew patriarch in Judaism and a figure of the Abrahamic religions. In the Torah he is the son of Abraham and Sarah, father of Jacob and Esau, and grandfather of the twelve tribes of Israel. His name means 'he will laugh', recalling the laughter of his parents when his birth was foretold. Genesis tells of his binding on Mount Moriah, his marriage to Rebekah, and his death at 180. Islam regards him as a prophet and names him seventeen times in the Quran. Some recent scholarship suggests he may originally have been an ancestor revered at a sanctuary in the Beersheba region.

entries.name: Sarah
entries.desc: Sarah, originally Sarai, is the wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac in the Book of Genesis, and a matriarch honoured in Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Genesis says she travelled with Abraham to Canaan, gave her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham when still childless, and, after God renamed her, bore Isaac when Abraham was a hundred. She later asked that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away. According to Genesis she died aged 127 and Abraham bought a cave near Hebron from Ephron the Hittite to bury her, the place later called the Cave of the Patriarchs. Rabbinic tradition links her death to the Binding of Isaac.
