entries.name: Binding of Isaac
entries.desc: The Binding of Isaac is the story in Genesis 22 in which, according to the text, God orders Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a sacrifice on a mountain in the region of Moriah. After Abraham has bound Isaac to an altar, an angel stops him and a ram is sacrificed instead. Jewish tradition interprets it in many ways, among them as a test of Abraham's faith, and some Christian writers saw Isaac as foreshadowing Christ. In the Quran the son is unnamed; early scholars disagreed whether he was Isaac or Ishmael, and Muslims commemorate the submission of Abraham and his son at Eid al-Adha. Some scholars suggest an older version in which Isaac was killed.

entries.name: Cave of the Patriarchs
entries.desc: The Cave of the Patriarchs, called Machpelah in Hebrew and the Ibrahimi Mosque by Muslims, is a series of caves in the Old City of Hebron in the West Bank. According to Genesis, Abraham bought the cave and its field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place for Sarah; Judaism, Christianity and Islam hold it holy as the tomb of the patriarchs and their wives. A large enclosure built under Herod the Great stands over it. A Byzantine basilica was later built there, and after the Muslim conquest the building became a mosque. Since the Six-Day War of 1967 it has been divided between a mosque and a synagogue. In February 1994 Baruch Goldstein killed 29 Palestinian Muslims there.

entries.name: Four Noble Truths
entries.desc: The Four Noble Truths are a central teaching of Buddhism: dukkha, usually rendered suffering or unsatisfactoriness; its origin in craving and attachment; its cessation, or nirvana; and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to that cessation. Buddhist tradition identifies them as the Buddha's first teaching, set out in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Some scholars hold that this identification was made later and that the formulation developed over time. Theravada tradition gave them great importance by about the 5th century CE, while Mahayana places more weight on emptiness and the bodhisattva path. Western presentations since the 19th century often present them as the central teaching of Buddhism.

credit.artist: Asia Society created the file. Artwork created by an anonymous ancient source.

entries.name: Noble Eightfold Path
entries.desc: The Noble Eightfold Path is an early summary of Buddhist practice leading to liberation from samsara, the cycle of rebirth, in nirvana. Its eight parts are right view, right resolve, right speech, right conduct, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right samadhi. It is the fourth of the Four Noble Truths. Theravada tradition also groups it as morality, meditation and insight. The Indologist Tilmann Vetter suggests that the early description of the path may have been as simple as the Middle Way, later elaborated into eight factors. In Buddhist symbolism the path is often shown as the eight spokes of the dharma wheel.

entries.name: Bodhi tree
entries.desc: The Bodhi tree is the sacred fig (Ficus religiosa) at the Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya, Bihar, India, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment beneath a Bo tree at this site and became the Buddha, around the 5th century BCE. The original tree no longer survives. Recorded episodes of destruction include its felling in the reign of Aśoka (c. 268–232 BCE) and its cutting down by King Śaśāṅka of Gauda around 600 CE, and each time it was replanted from saplings. A sapling taken to Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka survives as the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, and the present tree at Bodh Gaya was planted in 1881 from a cutting of it.

entries.name: Maya (mother of the Buddha)
entries.desc: Maya, also called Mahāmāyā and Māyādevī, was Queen of the Shakya and the mother of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha. She was the wife of King Śuddhodana. Buddhist tradition holds that she dreamed of a white elephant entering her side before the birth, and that her son was born in the gardens of Lumbini while she was travelling to her family home in Devadaha. The commentaries say she died about seven days later and was reborn in a Buddhist heaven, as is said to happen to the mothers of all Buddhas. Her sister Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī raised the child. In Buddhist art she is most often shown giving birth while holding the branch of a tree.

entries.name: Yaśodharā
entries.desc: Yaśodharā, originally called Bhaddakaccānā in Pāli, was the wife of Prince Siddhartha before he renounced the household life, and the mother of Rāhula. Buddhist texts describe her as a Koliya princess, daughter of Suppabuddha, who married Siddhartha when both were 16. Tradition holds that he left the palace on the night their son was born, when she was 29. Texts say she lived simply during his six-year absence and later asked Rāhula to go to the Buddha to ask for his inheritance. She was ordained as a bhikkhunī among the five hundred women who followed Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, is considered an arahat, and is said to have died at 78, two years before the Buddha.

entries.name: Rāhula
entries.desc: Rāhula was the son of Prince Siddhārtha, later the Buddha, and of Yaśodharā. The Pāli tradition says he was born on the day of his father's renunciation, when the prince was 29, and was named for a "fetter" on the path; the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition says he was conceived that day and born six years later. When the Buddha returned to his hometown, Yaśodharā had Rāhula ask for the throne of the Śākya clan, and the Buddha instead had him ordained as the first Buddhist novice monk. Early accounts state that Rāhula died before the Buddha, while later tradition holds that he outlived him. The earliest texts give little detail about him.

entries.name: Ānanda
entries.desc: Ānanda was the primary attendant of the Buddha and one of his ten principal disciples, remembered for his memory. In early Buddhist texts he was the Buddha's first cousin, and he became attendant twenty years into the Buddha's ministry, accompanying him for the rest of his life. He requested on behalf of Mahāpajāpati Gotamī that women be allowed to be ordained, and he was with the Buddha in his last year. Tradition holds that he became enlightened just before the First Council, where he recited the Buddha's discourses and was also reproved by Mahākassapa. Scholars are skeptical about the historicity of many events of his life. He is said to have died 20 years after the Buddha.

entries.name: Devadatta
entries.desc: Devadatta was, by tradition, a Buddhist monk, cousin and brother-in-law of Gautama Siddhārtha. Accounts of his life vary greatly. The Theravāda Vinaya says he sought to lead the Sangha, won the support of Prince Ajātashatru and tried to kill the Buddha, and it names five austerities he urged on monks, which the Buddha would not make obligatory. Pilgrims such as Faxian recorded followers of Devadatta centuries later. Scholars differ on how to read the stories: Reginald Ray regards them as a later Sthavira legend, while Bhikkhu Sujato argues the core episodes go back to the time of the Buddha. The Lotus Sūtra says that he too will become a Buddha.

entries.name: Buddhist councils
entries.desc: Buddhist councils were gatherings of the monastic community, the sangha, held to recite and correct the teachings and settle disputes of discipline. The term saṅgīti means "reciting together". Tradition places the First Council at Rājagṛha soon after the Buddha's death, where Ānanda is said to have recited the discourses and Upāli the Vinaya. The Second Council is said to have met at Vaiśālī a century later over lax practices. Theravāda sources add a Third Council under Ashoka at Pāṭaliputra and a Sri Lankan council in the 1st century BCE that wrote down the canon. Modern scholars question the historicity of several of these councils, and a Fifth Council met at Mandalay in 1871.

entries.name: Middle Way
entries.desc: The Middle Way, or Middle Path, is a Buddhist term for two aspects of the Buddha's teaching. The first is a spiritual practice that avoids both extreme asceticism and sensual indulgence, and is defined as the Noble Eightfold Path leading to awakening. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which Buddhist tradition regards as the Buddha's first teaching after his awakening, presents it this way, addressing five ascetics. The second is teaching the Dharma "by the middle", which avoids both eternalism and annihilationism in speaking of existence and personal identity. Y. Karunadasa notes it is not a compromise between the extremes.

entries.name: Parinirvana
entries.desc: In Buddhism, parinirvana is the state entered at death by someone who attained nirvana during life. It means release from samsara, karma and rebirth, and the ending of the aggregates (skandhas) that make up a being. Modern usage tends to keep "nirvana" for the awakening experience and "parinirvana" for the death. Accounts of the Buddha's parinirvana at Kuśinagara are found in the Pāli Mahāparinibbāna Sutta and its Sanskrit and Chinese parallels. Bareau judged only the death and funeral rites to be the oldest core. Some Mahāyāna scriptures, notably the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, describe it as the realm of the eternal true Self of the Tathāgata.

entries.name: Tirthankara
entries.desc: In Jainism, a Tirthaṅkara, literally a "ford-maker", is a supreme preacher of the dharma who establishes a passage across saṃsāra, the cycle of birth and death. Jains hold that after attaining kevala jñāna, or omniscience, a Tirthaṅkara teaches and organises a fourfold sangha of monks, nuns and male and female lay followers. Jain cosmology says that 24 appear in each half of the time cycle, with Rishabhanatha first in the present one and Mahavira, traditionally dated 599–527 BCE, the 24th. Academic consensus broadly accepts Parshvanatha, the 23rd, and Mahavira as historical figures. Their teachings form the basis of the Jain canons.

entries.name: Kalpa Sūtra
entries.desc: The Kalpa Sūtra is a Jain scripture containing the biographies of the Tirthankaras, notably Parshvanatha and Mahavira. It is ascribed to Acharya Bhadrabahu, which would place it in the 4th century BCE, and it states that it was written down 980 or 993 years after Mahavira's nirvana. From the mid-15th century it was frequently illustrated with miniature paintings, and the oldest surviving copies are on paper from western India in the 14th century. It is read during the eight-day festival of Paryushan, and Jain tradition regards the sound of its words as transforming the listener's soul.

entries.name: Anekantavada
entries.desc: Anekantavada, from the Sanskrit for "many-sidedness", is the Jain doctrine that ultimate truth and reality are complex and have multiple aspects and viewpoints. Jainism holds that no single statement can describe existence, and that complete knowledge (Kevala Jnana) is comprehended only by the Arihants. Jain tradition traces it to the teachings of Mahavira and his predecessors, while its details emerged in the 1st millennium CE from debates among Jain, Buddhist and Vedic scholars. Syadvada and nayavada later gave it logical structure. Jain texts illustrate it with the parable of the blind men and an elephant.

entries.name: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur
entries.desc: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur is a gurdwara in Kartarpur, in the Narowal District of Punjab, Pakistan, beside the Ravi River. It stands on the site where, in Sikh tradition, Guru Nanak settled and gathered the Sikh community after his journeys, living there for 18 years until his death in 1539. The main shrine was built in 1925 with funds from the Maharaja of Patiala, repaired in 1995 and fully restored in 2004. A new courtyard, museum and library were added in November 2018. The shrine lies near the India-Pakistan border, and the Kartarpur Corridor, opened on 9 November 2019, gave Indian pilgrims visa-free access.

entries.name: Bhai Mardana
entries.desc: Bhai Mardana was a musician born to a Mirasi Muslim family of Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib, and a lifelong companion of Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism. He played the rabab while Nanak sang his hymns, and became one of Nanak's first disciples. The Miharban Janam Sakhi says he was ten years older than Nanak and his companion from childhood. The janamsakhis portray him as the doubting traveller whose questions draw out the Guru's message. The Puratan Janam Sakhi relates that, when he fell ill at Kartarpur, Nanak told him his body could be disposed of as he pleased. Three of Nanak's shlokas addressed to him are in the Guru Granth Sahib.

credit.artist: Unknown artist. Published in sourced book. Page photographed by me (Wikimedia Commons user ThethPunjabi).

entries.name: Guru Angad
entries.desc: Guru Angad was the second of the ten Sikh gurus. Born Lehna, a Khatri and a worshipper of the goddess Durga, he met Guru Nanak at Kartarpur, served him there, and was named Angad, "my own limb", as successor in 1539. After Nanak's death on 22 September 1539 he led the community from Khadur Sahib, though few Sikhs at first accepted him because Nanak's sons also claimed the succession. He is remembered for formalising the Gurmukhi alphabet, although scholars note the script pre-dates Sikhism, and for systematising langar. He contributed 62 or 63 saloks and chose Amar Das, not his own son, as successor. He died on 29 March 1552.

credit.artist: possibly the family workshop (or atelier) of Nainsukh of Guler

entries.name: Nankana Sahib
entries.desc: Nankana Sahib is a city in central Punjab, Pakistan, about 91 km west of Lahore and the headquarters of its district. It is named for Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, who was born and lived there, and its birthplace gurdwara is among the holiest Sikh sites. A town called Rai-Bhoi-Di-Talwandi was founded there under the Delhi Sultanate by Rai Bhoi, and his great-grandson Rai Bular Bhatti renamed it after the birth of Guru Nanak. Maharaja Ranjit Singh renovated the main gurdwara in 1819–20. On 20 February 1921 the Udasi mahant ordered his men to fire on Akali protesters, an event called the Nankana massacre. The city had 130,041 people in 2023.

entries.name: Mul Mantar
entries.desc: The Mul Mantar is the opening verse of the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, a twelve-word statement in Punjabi in the Gurmukhi script. It is the best known of Sikh texts and summarises the teaching of Guru Nanak. After Ik Onkar, its words literally mean true name, the creator, without fear, without hate, timeless in form, beyond birth, self-existent, known by the grace of the Guru. Translators differ over the first two words, rendering them "There is one god" or "One reality is". The verse is repeated before many hymns. It existed in several versions in the 16th century, and Guru Arjan gave it its final form in the 17th.

entries.name: Langar
entries.desc: In Sikhism, a langar is the community kitchen of a gurdwara, serving free meals to all regardless of religion, caste, gender, economic status or ethnicity. Visitors sit on the floor and eat together, volunteers work as seva, and the food is always lacto-vegetarian. Sikh tradition credits Guru Nanak with introducing it around 1500 CE as a symbol of equality, though free kitchens existed earlier in the region, including among Sufi missionaries. Guru Angad is remembered for systematising the langar in all gurdwaras. Guru Amar Das made it prominent by requiring that people dine together regardless of caste and class.

entries.name: Aaron
entries.desc: According to the Hebrew Bible, Aaron was an Israelite prophet, high priest and elder brother of Moses; information about him comes only from religious texts. Exodus relates that he served as Moses' spokesman before Pharaoh. Part of the Law given at Sinai granted the priesthood to him and his male descendants, and the kohanim are traditionally held to descend from him. The Bible tells how he made the golden calf, while the Quran attributes it to Samiri. Numbers says he died aged 123 on Mount Hor, whereas Deuteronomy places his death at Moseroth. Many historians think Aaronide families did not control the priesthood before the Babylonian exile.

entries.name: Miriam
entries.desc: Miriam is described in the Hebrew Bible as the daughter of Amram and Jochebed and the older sister of Moses and Aaron. The Torah calls her a prophetess, and the Talmud names her among the seven major female prophets of Israel. Tradition identifies her with the unnamed sister who watched the infant Moses on the Nile. In Exodus she leads the Israelites in the Song of the Sea. In Numbers she and Aaron speak against Moses over his "Cushite" wife, and she is afflicted with a skin disease and shut out of the camp for seven days. The Torah records that she died and was buried at Kadesh. The Quran also has her follow the infant Moses.

credit.artist: Window: Edward Burne-Jones 1886; Photo: Wojciech Dittwald

entries.name: Burning bush
entries.desc: The burning bush is an event recorded in the Book of Exodus and in Islamic scripture, in which a bush burns on Mount Horeb without being consumed. In the biblical account an angel of the Lord appears in a flame from the bush, and God calls to Moses, who was grazing Jethro's flocks, telling him to take off his sandals because the place is sacred. The voice names itself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and sends Moses to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. It gives its name as Yahweh, linked to the phrase "I Am Who I Am". Some Old Testament scholars see the account as joined from Yahwist and Elohist texts.

entries.name: Plagues of Egypt
entries.desc: In the Book of Exodus, the Plagues of Egypt are ten disasters that Yahweh inflicts on the Egyptians to persuade Pharaoh to free the enslaved Israelites. They run from the Nile turned to blood, frogs, gnats and flies through the death of livestock, boils, hail, locusts and three days of darkness, to the death of the firstborn. Jews recite the plagues during the Passover Seder. Modern scholars broadly hold that the Exodus is not a historical account of the origins of the Israelites. Biblical scholars have dismissed natural explanations, such as a volcanic eruption for the darkness, because the plagues' pattern, timing and control by Moses mark them as supernatural in the text.

entries.name: Parting of the Red Sea
entries.desc: The Parting of the Red Sea is an episode of the Exodus in the Hebrew Bible. According to the Book of Exodus, the Israelites led by Moses were pursued by the Egyptian army; at God's command Moses held out his staff, the waters of the Yam Suph parted, and the Israelites crossed on dry ground. When the Egyptians followed, the waters returned and drowned them. The Quran also relates the crossing, and Muslims fast two days in Muharram to commemorate it. No archaeological evidence directly supports the account apart from the biblical text, and scholars debate where the crossing took place, since Yam Suph is literally a sea or lake of reeds.

entries.name: Golden calf
entries.desc: The golden calf is a cult image that, according to the Book of Exodus, the Israelites made while Moses was on Mount Sinai. The narrative says Aaron collected gold earrings and ornaments and fashioned the calf; Moses, on seeing it, broke the tablets, burned the calf, and the Levites killed some three thousand people. The Quran also tells of a calf made in his absence. Scholars note that bull imagery was widespread in the ancient Near East and compare Exodus 32 with the golden calves of 1 Kings 12. The apostle Paul cites the episode in 1 Corinthians as a warning against idolatry.

entries.name: Mount Nebo
entries.desc: Mount Nebo is a ridge in Jordan, about 700 metres above sea level, part of the Abarim range. According to Deuteronomy, Moses climbed it in the land of Moab, saw the Promised Land that he was not to enter, and died there; the text says his burial place was unknown. On the summit, called Syagha, excavators found a Byzantine church and monastery, first built in the second half of the 4th century to commemorate Moses' death. A pilgrim named Aetheria mentions the church in 394. Pope John Paul II and Pope Benedict XVI have visited the site.

entries.name: Tabernacle
entries.desc: According to the Hebrew Bible, the Tabernacle was the portable dwelling of Yahweh used by the Israelites from the Exodus until the conquest of Canaan. Exodus 25–31 and 35–40 describe it: a Holy of Holies containing the Ark of the Covenant, behind a veil, and an outer sanctuary with a lamp-stand, a table for showbread and an altar of incense. Those who read the books of Kings literally hold that Solomon's Temple replaced it after 480 years in the Masoretic Text or 440 in the Septuagint. Scholars compare it with tent shrines of Canaan, Babylonia and Egypt, among them a Midianite tent shrine at Timna.

entries.name: Joshua
entries.desc: Joshua, whose Hebrew name Yehoshua means 'Yahweh is salvation', was Moses' assistant in Exodus and Numbers and, in the Book of Joshua, his successor as leader of the Israelite tribes. The Bible names him as one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan, and says he led the conquest of the land, including the fall of Jericho, and allocated it to the tribes. It gives his age at death as 110. Muslims honour him as Yusha bin Nun, understood to be Moses' attendant in the Quran. Mainstream scholarship holds that the Book of Joshua is a theological narrative compiled centuries after the events it describes, and that archaeology largely contradicts its account.

entries.name: Midian
entries.desc: Midian was a region in the Tabuk Province of modern Saudi Arabia, on the east shore of the Gulf of Aqaba, mentioned in the Hebrew Bible and the Quran. The Bible makes Midian a son of Abraham and Keturah and says Moses spent forty years there, marrying Zipporah, daughter of the priest Jethro. Some scholars think the name first denoted a tribal confederation. Midianite pottery, also called Qurayyah Painted Ware, is found from the southern Levant to north-west Arabia, and a Midianite tent shrine at the copper-mining site of Timna offers a close parallel to the biblical Tabernacle.

entries.name: Zipporah
entries.desc: Zipporah appears in the Book of Exodus as the wife of Moses and a daughter of Jethro, the priest of Midian. According to Exodus, Moses defended Jethro's daughters at a well in Midian, and Jethro gave her to him. She bore two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. In an obscure passage at an inn on the road to Egypt, she circumcises her son and God spares Moses; the details are debated. Later, Jethro brings her and her sons to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. Numbers 12 mentions a Cushite wife of Moses, and interpreters differ on whether this is Zipporah.

entries.name: Gathas
entries.desc: The Gathas are the central texts of Zoroastrianism, composed in Old or Gathic Avestan and often attributed to Zarathustra himself. They comprise five poems of seventeen hymns, with 238 stanzas and 897 verses, and survive within the Yasna liturgy. They are the oldest attestation of an Iranian language. Scholars are divided on whether Zarathustra wrote them. Zoroastrian tradition places him in the 6th century BCE, but many scholars now accept a date near 1000 BCE, some as early as 1500 BCE. The texts describe a simple society of nomadic pastoralists.

entries.name: Vishtaspa
entries.desc: Vishtaspa is a figure in Zoroastrian scripture and tradition, portrayed as an early follower and patron of Zoroaster who helped spread his message. The Gathas speak of him as Zoroaster's ally, and later Avestan hymns describe his struggles against enemies of the faith. Zoroastrian tradition presents him as a righteous king ruling from Bactria. In the Sistan cycle texts, by contrast, he is a loathsome ruler of the Kayanian dynasty, and Greco-Roman writers knew prophecies written under his name. He is not attested in inscriptions, and is traditionally assumed to be historical, though obscured by later accretions.

entries.name: Amesha Spenta
entries.desc: In Zoroastrianism, the Amesha Spenta, literally 'Immortal (which is) holy', are seven divine entities emanating from Ahura Mazda, through whom, in tradition, all later creation was accomplished. The doctrine is only alluded to in the Avesta and is set out in later Middle Persian texts such as the Bundahishn. In the Gathas each represents a moral quality, such as truth or good thought, that people should strive to acquire, and each has an opposing counterpart. Each is linked to one of the seven creations. The first seven days of the Zoroastrian month are dedicated to them.

entries.name: Yasna
entries.desc: Yasna is the Avestan name both of a text of the Avesta and of the Yasna liturgy, Zoroastrianism's principal act of worship. The ceremony is meant to strengthen the ordered creation of Ahura Mazda against the destructive forces of Angra Mainyu, and culminates in the offering to the waters. A trained priest recites it in about two hours, in the morning. The text has 72 chapters composed at different times, including the oldest of the canon: the four most sacred prayers and the five Gathas, which tradition holds were composed by Zoroaster himself.

entries.name: Ahriman
entries.desc: Ahriman, in Avestan Angra Mainyu, is the destructive evil spirit of Zoroastrianism, the main adversary either of the Spenta Mainyu or directly of Ahura Mazda. In the Gathas, the oldest texts, angra mainyu is not yet a proper name but describes a destructive spirit set against the bounteous one. In the Younger Avesta and the Pahlavi texts, including the Bundahishn completed in the 12th century, he opposes Ahura Mazda's creation with his own, and Zoroastrian tradition holds that he will be defeated. Zurvanite sources make him the twin brother of Ohrmuzd. In 1862 Martin Haug proposed that he was a creature of Ahura Mazda, a view widely held by Zoroastrians today.

entries.name: Wu wei
entries.desc: Wu wei (無為) is a concept of ancient Chinese philosophy that literally means not-acting or non-doing, and is variously translated as actionlessness, inaction or effortless action. In Daoism it describes the way the Tao acts, silently and without force, and Daoists aspire to live in alignment with it. The idea appears as early as the Spring and Autumn period and also figures in the Confucian Analects and in Legalist statecraft, where it names a ruler who leaves details to his ministers. Scholars such as Herrlee G. Creel distinguished the Zhuangzi's wu wei, a detachment from human affairs, from that of the Tao Te Ching, a technique for governing.

entries.name: Tao
entries.desc: The Tao or Dao (道) is, in East Asian philosophy and religions, the source and fundamental principle of the universe. The Chinese character means way, path or road, and philosophically doctrine or principle. According to the Tao Te Ching, Tao is self-existent, formless, eternal and the source of all existence, and it is said to be beyond description; the text distinguishes the named Tao from the unnamed Tao. It describes Tao as feminine, a mother of all things, and Taoist scriptures treat the Ultra Supreme Elder Lord as an embodiment of it. Scholars distinguish its ethical use in Confucianism and religious Taoism from its more metaphysical use in philosophical Taoism.

entries.name: Yinxi
entries.desc: Yinxi is a figure of Zhou China known from later accounts, said to have been a guard at the western gate of the Zhou capital Chengzhou, present-day Luoyang, or alternatively at the western pass out of the Luo–Yi valley. He is said to have recognised the wisdom of Laozi, halted him on his way through the gate and persuaded him to compose the Tao Te Ching before letting him pass. He is later credited with a book called Guan Yi, revered by later scholars, and came to be regarded as a sage. His own work, the Perfect Classic of the Beginning of the Scripture of the Supreme Way, was lost in the Han period, and later versions were considered forgeries.

entries.name: I Ching
entries.desc: The I Ching, or Book of Changes, began as a Western Zhou divination manual of 64 hexagrams. With the Ten Wings added, it became one of the Five Classics in 136 BCE, and it has been read for centuries as divination, moral guidance and philosophy across East Asia and, since the 18th century, in the West.

entries.name: Thucydides, son of Melesias
entries.desc: Thucydides, son of Melesias, was a politician of ancient Athens and for a number of years the leader of the powerful conservative faction. Born in the deme of Alopeke to a noble family, he was a relative of Cimon, whom he succeeded as leader of the conservatives, and he opposed Pericles. He is likely related to the later historian Thucydides, son of Olorus, though the details are uncertain. His strength peaked after the First Peloponnesian War, when he had his supporters sit together in the assembly. According to Plutarch, he was ostracised for ten years in 442 BCE after Pericles answered his charge of profligacy.

entries.name: The Republic
entries.desc: The Republic is Plato's Socratic dialogue of about 375 BCE on justice, in which Socrates and others describe a hypothetical just city ruled by philosopher-kings and compare it with the soul.

entries.name: Histories of Herodotus
entries.desc: The Histories is Herodotus's Greek inquiry into the rise of the Persian Empire and the causes and course of the Greco-Persian Wars. Its reliability has been disputed since antiquity, yet it remains the primary source for much of its period and is regarded as the founding work of Western history.

entries.name: Notre-Dame de Paris
entries.desc: Notre-Dame de Paris, begun in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully and largely complete by 1260, is a Gothic cathedral known for its rib vaults, flying buttresses and rose windows.

entries.name: Sistine Chapel ceiling
entries.desc: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512 for Pope Julius II, with nine scenes from Genesis, prophets, sibyls and the ancestors of Christ.

entries.name: Mona Lisa
entries.desc: The Mona Lisa is Leonardo da Vinci's half-length oil portrait, traditionally held to show Lisa del Giocondo and begun around 1503. Leonardo may have worked on it until 1517.

entries.name: Palace of Versailles
entries.desc: The Palace of Versailles grew from Louis XIII's hunting lodge of 1623 into the vast residence Louis XIV built, and the court lived there from 1682 to 1789. After the Revolution it became a history museum and a venue of state, and it has been restored since 1892.

entries.name: Lascaux
entries.desc: Lascaux is a cave network in the Dordogne with over 600 Upper Palaeolithic paintings, mostly of large animals, usually dated to 17,000 to 22,000 years ago. Found by four teenagers in 1940 and closed to visitors in 1963 after damage, it is now protected from mould and shown through replicas.

entries.name: Gutenberg Bible
entries.desc: The Gutenberg Bible is Johannes Gutenberg's printed Latin Vulgate of the 1450s, made at Mainz with mass-produced metal type. Of a print run put at between 160 and 185 copies, 49 survive in at least substantial portion, and it marked the start of the age of printed books in the West.

entries.name: Statue of Liberty
entries.desc: The Statue of Liberty is a copper statue designed by Bartholdi, built over an iron framework by Gustave Eiffel, and given by the French people to the United States.

entries.name: Moai
entries.desc: The moai are the monolithic statues carved by the Rapa Nui on Easter Island, mostly between 1250 and 1500, chiefly as the living faces of deified ancestors. More than 900 were made, nearly half still at the Rano Raraku quarry; all the erected ones had fallen by the 19th century, and about 50 have been re-erected.

entries.name: Tomb of Tutankhamun
entries.desc: KV62, in the Valley of the Kings, was probably begun as a non-royal tomb and enlarged for Tutankhamun after his early death. Robbed twice and then buried under debris, it was found intact in 1922 by Howard Carter, and its 5,398 objects went mostly to Cairo.

entries.name: Göbekli Tepe
entries.desc: Göbekli Tepe, in the Taş Tepeler of modern Turkey, was inhabited from around 9500 BCE to at least 8000 BCE. Its circular enclosures of T-shaped, carved pillars are among the oldest known megaliths, and whether it was a ritual centre or a settlement is still debated.

entries.name: Great Mosque of Djenné
entries.desc: The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali is the largest adobe brick building in the world. A first mosque stood there from about the 13th century; the present building was raised in 1907 by the town's masons and is replastered every year by the whole community.

entries.name: Sanchi
entries.desc: Sanchi is a hilltop Buddhist complex in Madhya Pradesh whose Great Stupa, commissioned by Ashoka, was enlarged under the Shungas and given four carved gateways under the Satavahanas.

entries.name: Prambanan
entries.desc: Prambanan is a Hindu temple compound in southern Java, begun by the Mataram court in the 9th century and dedicated to Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. It was abandoned, collapsed in an earthquake and was rebuilt from the 1930s by anastylosis; it is a World Heritage Site.

entries.name: Bagan
entries.desc: Bagan, the capital of the Pagan Kingdom from 1044 to 1287, was the site of over 10,000 Buddhist monuments built mainly between the 11th and 13th centuries. Earthquakes and renovations altered it, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2019.

entries.name: Sigiriya
entries.desc: Sigiriya, the Lion Rock, is a granite column in Sri Lanka that King Kashyapa made his fortress capital from 477 CE. After his defeat in 495 it became a Buddhist monastery.

entries.name: Panchatantra
entries.desc: The Panchatantra is an ancient Indian collection of animal fables in Sanskrit, in five treatises, by an unknown author, probably composed around 300 CE. Carried through Pahlavi, Arabic and Hebrew, it reached Europe and Southeast Asia and has been called the most frequently translated literary product of India.

entries.name: The Art of War
entries.desc: The Art of War is an ancient Chinese treatise on strategy in 13 chapters, attributed to Sun Tzu and probably completed between 500 and 430 BCE. It treats war as a costly last resort, led the Seven Military Classics and has been read by commanders in East Asia and the West.

entries.name: Dream of the Red Chamber
entries.desc: Dream of the Red Chamber is Cao Xueqin's 18th-century novel of the rise and decline of the Jia clan. It circulated as 80-chapter manuscripts until a 120-chapter edition was printed in 1791 and 1792, and the authorship of its last 40 chapters is still debated.

entries.name: Journey to the West
entries.desc: Journey to the West is a Ming-dynasty Chinese novel, attributed to Wu Cheng'en, that turns the monk Xuanzang's pilgrimage to India into a fantasy led by the Monkey King.

entries.name: Himeji Castle
entries.desc: Himeji Castle in Hyōgo Prefecture was first fortified in 1333 and rebuilt on its present scale by Ikeda Terumasa from 1601 to 1609. It escaped demolition in the Meiji Period, the bombing of 1945 and the 1995 earthquake, and was registered as a World Heritage Site in 1993.

entries.name: Truganini
entries.desc: Truganini (c. 1812–1876), a Nuenonne woman from Bruny Island, guided George Augustus Robinson's expeditions in the Black War and was exiled with her people. She was wrongly called the last Aboriginal Tasmanian, a claim scholars and the Aboriginal Tasmanian community reject.

Sheikh ul-Islam was the title of the chief religious authority in the Ottoman Empire, who headed the learned hierarchy of Islamic scholars. Known as a soldier and tournament fighter, he fought long wars against the city of Nuremberg and other neighbours. In 1473 he issued the Dispositio Achillea, which ruled that Brandenburg should pass undivided to the eldest son while the Franconian lands went to younger sons.

Lorenzo de' Medici, called the Magnificent, was the effective ruler of the Republic of Florence from 1469 until his death. He survived the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478, in which his brother Giuliano was killed, and worked to keep peace among the Italian states through diplomacy. A poet and a patron of artists such as Botticelli and the young Michelangelo, he came to embody the Florentine Renaissance.

Lin Biao was a Chinese military commander and politician, ranked third among the Ten Marshals of the People's Republic of China. Pivotal to the Communist victory in the Chinese Civil War, he commanded the Liaoshen and Pingjin campaigns and led the People's Liberation Army into Beijing. Édouard Manet was a French painter, one of the first 19th-century artists to paint modern life and a pivotal figure in the transition from Realism to Impressionism. Born in Paris in 1832, he studied under the academic painter Thomas Couture from 1850 to 1856 and copied Velázquez and Titian in the Louvre. His Luncheon on the Grass (1863) and Olympia (1865) caused great controversy with critics and the Academy but were praised by progressive artists, and they are considered to mark the start of modern art. His last major work, A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, hung in the Salon in 1882; he died in Paris in April 1883, 11 days after his left foot was amputated because of gangrene.

Louis Armstrong was an American jazz trumpeter, cornetist and singer from New Orleans, among the most influential figures in jazz, who shifted the music's focus from collective improvisation to solo performance. Raised in poverty, he followed his mentor King Oliver to Chicago in 1922, and his Hot Five and Hot Seven recordings from 1925 showcased his solos. His recording of Hello, Dolly! reached No. 1 in 1964. He died in Queens, New York, in 1971.

Emperor Daigo was the 60th emperor of Japan according to the traditional order of succession, reigning from 897 to 930. The eldest son of Emperor Uda, he was born a subject named Minamoto no Korezane, because his grandfather Emperor Kōkō had demoted his sons from the imperial ranks, and became an imperial prince only in 887. The highlight of his 34-year reign was that he ruled by himself without a Fujiwara regent, though he was part Fujiwara himself; in his reign Ki no Tsurayuki presented the Kokin Wakashū. Falling ill in 930, he abdicated, became a monk and died, and was buried at Daigo-ji, which gave him his posthumous name.

A shōen was a private estate or manor in Japan from about the 8th to the 15th century, often tax-free and autonomous, whose rise undermined the power of the emperor. The estates grew from lands assigned to shrines and temples or granted by the emperor, and from fields reclaimed under laws of 723 and 743 that let reclaimers keep them, eroding the ritsuryō system. Peasants commended their land to temples, shrines and court nobles to escape taxes, and by the end of the Heian period virtually all land in Japan was shōen. The estates fostered a local military class; stewards appointed under the Kamakura shogunate weakened their lords, and the system ended as villages came under daimyō.

The White Sea–Baltic Canal is a ship canal in Russia, opened on 2 August 1933, that runs 227 kilometres from the White Sea to Lake Onega and so to the Baltic Sea. It was the first major Soviet project built with forced labour: Gulag inmates dug it in twenty months between 1931 and 1933, almost entirely by hand, and between 12,000 and 25,000 of them died according to official records. Presented as a showcase of the first five-year plan and of convicts 'reforging' themselves through labour, it was praised in a book compiled by a brigade of 120 writers and artists organised by Maxim Gorky. Yet at 3.5 metres deep it was too shallow for most seagoing ships.

The Gonbad-e Sorkh, or Red Dome, is a brick tomb tower built in 1147–48 in Maragheh, north-western Iran, under the Ahmadili rulers. Maragheh has several other medieval tomb towers of the Seljuk and Mongol periods.

The Dilwara Temples are a group of five Jain temples at Mount Abu in Rajasthan, India, famed for their intricately carved white marble interiors. Kalkar is a town on the lower Rhine in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, founded by the counts of Cleves in 1230. It prospered from the cloth trade in the late Middle Ages, when its church of St Nicolai was furnished with carved altarpieces by a renowned school of local woodcarvers. The Maitraka dynasty ruled western India from about 475 to 776 from their capital at Valabhi in Saurashtra, now Vala in Gujarat. The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World are a list of remarkable monuments drawn up by Greek writers of the Hellenistic period: the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the statue of Zeus at Olympia, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Colossus of Rhodes and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. Only the Great Pyramid survives.

Eboracum was the Roman fortress and city on the site of York, founded around 71 AD as the base of the Ninth Legion. It became the capital of the province of Britannia Inferior; the emperor Septimius Severus died there in 211, and Constantine the Great was proclaimed emperor there in 306. After Roman rule ended, the site became the Anglian royal and ecclesiastical centre of Eoforwic.

The Lament for Ur, or Lamentation over the city of Ur, is a Sumerian lament composed around the time when Ur fell to the Elamites and its Third Dynasty came to an end, about 2000 BC. The dynasty had ruled for around a hundred years. Invading Elamites raided the temple treasury, the centre of power in Sumer moved to Isin, and control of Ur's trade passed to several leading families of the city.

The Great Hymn to the Aten is the longest of several hymn-poems addressed to the Aten, the sun-disk worshipped as the supreme god under the 18th Dynasty pharaoh Akhenaten. It was composed in the middle of the 14th century BC and is attributed, depending on the version, to Akhenaten himself or to his courtiers.

"Guan ju" is the first poem of the Shi Jing, the Classic of Poetry, and one of the best-known poems in Chinese literature. It has been dated to the seventh century BC, which makes it one of China's oldest poems, though not the oldest in the anthology.

"Va, pensiero", also called the Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves, is a chorus from Giuseppe Verdi's opera Nabucco, first staged in 1842. It recalls the Babylonian captivity after the destruction of Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem in 586 BC: the exiled Hebrews sing of their homeland. The libretto is by Temistocle Solera, who drew on Psalm 137.

The Paris Commune was a French revolutionary government that seized power in Paris on 18 March 1871 and controlled parts of the city until 28 May 1871. After the French Army's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War, soldiers of the National Guard took the city and refused the authority of the Third Republic under Adolphe Thiers. The Commune separated church and state, remitted rents and abolished child labor. The army suppressed it in the semaine sanglante, the bloody week beginning on 21 May, killing in battle or executing an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 Communards; Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels saw it as the first example of the dictatorship of the proletariat.

Vatican City is a sovereign city-state, an enclave within Rome, ruled by the pope and governed by the Holy See as the administrative center of the Catholic Church. Catholic theology holds that Saint Peter was crucified on Vatican Hill in the 1st century. The Holy See ruled the Papal States, formed in 756, until the capture of Rome by the Kingdom of Italy in 1870, after which the pope declared himself a prisoner in the Vatican; the Lateran Treaty of 1929 created the modern state. With 0.49 square kilometres and about 882 people it is the smallest country by area and population, and it holds St. Peter's Basilica, the Sistine Chapel and the Vatican Library.

Chichen Itza was a large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people, whose ruins lie in Yucatán, Mexico, between Valladolid and Mérida. It was a major focal point of the Northern Maya Lowlands from the Late Classic into the early Postclassic, and in the 10th century rose to be a regional capital controlling the area from central Yucatán to the north coast. Its buildings mix central Mexican styles with the Puuc and Chenes styles of the region, among them the Temple of Kukulcán (El Castillo), the Great Ball Court and the Sacred Cenote. It declined as a regional center by 1100, and Francisco de Montejo the Younger, who tried to make it a Spanish capital, abandoned it in 1534.

The Federalist Papers are a collection of 85 articles and essays written by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay under the collective pseudonym Publius to promote the ratification of the Constitution of the United States. The first 77 appeared in New York newspapers between October 1787 and April 1788, and the whole was published in two volumes by J. & A. McLean in 1788. Among them, Madison's No. 10 argues against rule by a majority faction and for a large republic, his No. 51 for checks and balances, and Hamilton's No. 78 lays the groundwork for judicial review by federal courts. The Constitution was ratified by the required nine states on June 21, 1788.

The Great Migration was the movement of six million Black Americans out of the rural Southern United States to the urban Northeast, Midwest and West between 1910 and 1970. It was driven by racial segregation and discrimination under the Jim Crow laws and by lynchings, and drawn by labor shortages in Northern factories during World War I. Historians divide it into a first migration (1910–1940) of about 1.6 million people and a second (1940–1970) of at least five million. Most migrants settled in the largest cities, among them New York City, Chicago, Detroit and Los Angeles, where they built culturally influential communities; by 1970 more than 80% of Black Americans lived in cities.

Affranchi was a French legal term for a freedman or emancipated slave, also used pejoratively for free people of color; in English it names the class of freedmen in Saint-Domingue and other slave-holding French territories, whose legal rights stood between those of free whites and enslaved Africans. Affranchis could get some education and own land, and many owned slaves: the indigo planter Julien Raimond claimed they held a third of the colony's slaves. Colonial laws barred them from voting, administrative posts and careers as doctors or lawyers. A 1791 court decision in their favour provoked a backlash from white planters that helped bring on the Haitian Revolution.

The transatlantic telegraph cables were undersea cables laid across the Atlantic Ocean for telegraph communication between Europe and the Americas. The Atlantic Telegraph Company, led by Cyrus West Field, laid the first from Valentia Island off Ireland to Trinity Bay, Newfoundland, and it carried its first messages on August 16, 1858, among them Queen Victoria's congratulations to President James Buchanan, but it failed after three weeks. Cables laid from the SS Great Eastern in 1865 and 1866 proved durable, and since 1866 the continents have been linked, so that a message could be answered on the same day rather than after weeks by ship.

Coartación was a system of self-purchase in the slave societies of Ibero-America from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries, by which an enslaved person paid part of the price of freedom before a court and had the rest fixed, becoming a coartado. Growing from custom and slaves' petitions rather than from the Siete Partidas code, it entered Cuban law only in 1842. A new master could not raise the fixed price, and a coartado gained rights, among them to change masters without showing cause and to a share of the hire when rented out. Women, urban and American-born slaves gained freedom this way most often; it helped create a large population of free people of color in Spanish America.

Helen Keller was an American deafblind author, disability rights advocate and political activist, born in Tuscumbia, Alabama. An illness at 19 months old left her blind and deaf, and from the age of seven she was taught language, including reading and writing, by Anne Sullivan, her lifelong companion. She attended Radcliffe College and became the first deafblind person in the United States to earn a college diploma. She wrote 14 books, among them The Story of My Life (1903), and campaigned for people with disabilities and for women's suffrage, labor rights and world peace. She joined the Socialist Party of America in 1909 and was a founding member of the American Civil Liberties Union.

Basil of Caesarea, also called Saint Basil the Great, was an early Christian prelate who served as Bishop of Caesarea Mazaca in Cappadocia from 370 until his death in 379. An influential theologian, he supported the Nicene Creed and opposed Arianism and Apollinarianism. He founded the Basileias before the gates of Caesarea, a poorhouse, hospital and hospice believed to be one of the earliest Christian hospitals for the poor, and set guidelines for monastic life built on community life, liturgical prayer and manual labor. With his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus he is counted among the Cappadocian Fathers.

Mary G. Harris Jones, known as Mother Jones from 1897, was an Irish-American labor organizer, schoolteacher and dressmaker born in Cork, whose family emigrated to Canada after the Great Famine. After her husband and four children died of yellow fever in Memphis in 1867 and her shop was destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, she organised for the Knights of Labor and the United Mine Workers of America. In 1902 she was called the most dangerous woman in America, and in 1903 she led a children's march from Philadelphia to protest weak child labor laws. She co-founded the Industrial Workers of the World and died in 1930.

The Spanish colonization of the Americas began in 1493 on the Caribbean island of Hispaniola, after the 1492 voyage of the Genoese mariner Christopher Columbus under license from Queen Isabella I of Castile. The Indigenous population fell by an estimated 80% in the first century and a half, primarily through infectious diseases, while forced labor, slavery and forced resettlement were imposed and enslaved Africans were imported. An estimated 1.86 million Spaniards settled in the Americas between 1492 and 1832. The Spanish American wars of independence of the early 19th century ended Spanish rule over most of the region, and Cuba and Puerto Rico were lost to the United States in 1898.

The Eastern Front of World War I was the theater of operations along the frontier between Russia and Romania on one side and Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Germany on the other, from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea, where the fighting was more dynamic than on the Western Front. Russia's invasion of East Prussia in 1914 was defeated, and Central Powers offensives in 1915 drove it from Galicia and Poland; the Brusilov offensive of 1916 was the largest Entente victory in the war. After the February Revolution of 1917 discipline declined, the Bolsheviks took power, and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk of March 1918 took Russia out of the war.

The 1976 Tangshan earthquake struck Tangshan, Hebei, China, early on 28 July 1976 local time, with a magnitude of Mw 7.6 and a maximum intensity of XI on the Mercalli scale. Its first shock began approximately 12 kilometres under the southern part of the city, on a fault running right under its center. In minutes 85 percent of the buildings in Tangshan collapsed or were rendered unusable, all services failed and most highway and railway bridges collapsed or were seriously damaged. The official count stated 242,469 deaths, while historians accepted at least 300,000, making it the deadliest earthquake in recorded history excluding the famine deaths of the 1556 Shaanxi earthquake.

The Information Age is a historical period that began in the mid-20th century, marked by a rapid shift from the traditional industries of the Industrial Revolution to an economy centered on information technology. Its onset has been linked to the first working transistor, invented in 1947 by John Bardeen and Walter Houser Brattain under William Shockley at Bell Labs, which led the way to more compact digital computers. The digital revolution converted technology from analog to digital format, so that identical copies could be made; a message was sent over the ARPANET in 1969, and in the 1980s compact discs replaced vinyl records and cassette tapes.

Elias Howe Jr. was an American inventor, born in Spencer, Massachusetts, best known for creating the modern lockstitch sewing machine. On September 10, 1846, he received the first United States patent for a sewing machine using a lockstitch design, with a needle with the eye at the point, a shuttle beneath the cloth and an automatic feed. He defended his patent in a court case from 1849 to 1854 against Isaac Singer and won considerable royalties. His machine won a gold medal at the Paris Exhibition of 1867, the year he received the Légion d'honneur, and he died that year at age 48.

Dominica is an island country in the Caribbean, part of the Windward Islands in the Lesser Antilles, between the French departments of Guadeloupe and Martinique. Arawak settlers arrived from South America in the fifth century and the Kalinago displaced them by the 15th century, calling the island Wai'tu kubuli. The French held it from 1690 to 1763 and enslaved West Africans to work coffee plantations. Great Britain took possession in 1763 after the Seven Years' War and continued forced labor, gradually making English the official language. Dominica was governed as part of the British Windward Islands until 1958, and the island gained independence as a republic in 1978.

The Burgundians were an East Germanic people who crossed the Rhine in the early 5th century and founded a kingdom as Roman allies around 411, traditionally centred on Worms. After its destruction by Hunnic troops in Roman service in 436, the survivors were settled in Sapaudia around Geneva in 443, where they built a new kingdom in the Rhône and Saône valleys. The Franks conquered it in 534, and its name lives on in Burgundy.

The Bharatas were an Indo-Aryan tribe of the early Vedic period, prominent in the Rigveda, where their king Sudas defeats a coalition of tribes in the Battle of the Ten Kings. They later merged with the Purus to form the Kuru tribe of the upper Ganges–Yamuna region. Their name lives on in Bharat, the official Sanskrit name of India.

Atropates was a Persian noble who served as satrap of Media under the Achaemenid king Darius III and fought at Gaugamela in 331 BCE. Alexander the Great later restored him as satrap, and after Alexander's death he made the northern part of Media an independent kingdom, Media Atropatene, named after him. The name lives on in Azerbaijan.

Ming Rui was a Manchu general of the Qing dynasty, a relative by marriage of the Qianlong Emperor, who commanded the third Qing invasion of Burma in 1767–1768. After advancing towards Ava, his army was cut off and destroyed by Burmese forces near Maymyo in early 1768, and he took his own life rather than be captured. He had earlier served in the Qing campaigns in Xinjiang.

A thing was a governing assembly of the free people of a community in early Germanic societies, presided over by a lawspeaker and held regularly at prominent places. Tacitus gave the first detailed description in 98 CE, and the oldest written reference is a pillar at Housesteads on Hadrian's Wall dedicated to Mars Thincsus, the Mars of the Thing. In the Viking Age things served as parliaments and courts at local, regional and wider levels, settling disputes, electing chieftains and kings and judging by the law the lawspeaker recited. As royal power grew they became mainly courts, but the name lives on in the Icelandic Althing, the Norwegian Storting and the Manx Tynwald.

Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist and inventor known for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating current (AC) electricity supply system. Born in Smiljan in the Austrian Empire, he migrated to the United States in 1884 and worked briefly at the Edison Machine Works before setting up his own laboratories in New York. His AC induction motor and polyphase patents, licensed by Westinghouse Electric in 1888, became the cornerstone of the polyphase system. His Wardenclyffe Tower project for wireless communication and power ran out of funding. He died in New York City in 1943; in 1960 the SI unit of magnetic flux density was named the tesla.

Frank Lloyd Wright was an American architect, designer, writer and educator who designed more than 1,000 structures over a creative period of 70 years. Raised in rural Wisconsin, he apprenticed in Chicago with Louis Sullivan at Adler & Sullivan, opened his own practice in 1893 and became a pioneer of the Prairie School movement. He called his philosophy of designing in harmony with humanity and the environment organic architecture, exemplified in Fallingwater (1935), and developed the Usonian home within Broadacre City, his vision for urban planning. In 2019 a selection of his work became a World Heritage Site as The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright.

The Torah is the compilation of the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, also known as the Pentateuch or the Five Books of Moses. Rabbinic tradition holds that its teachings were given by God through the prophet Moses, at Mount Sinai and at the Tabernacle; in rabbinic literature the word also covers the Oral Torah, now embodied in the Talmud and Midrash. Biblical scholarship generally sees its final form as largely complete by the Persian period and based on earlier sources. Written on a scroll by a scribe, it is read publicly in synagogues, and it is also sacred to the Samaritans, in Christianity and in Islam.

Giordano Bruno, born Filippo Bruno in Nola in the Kingdom of Naples, was an Italian philosopher, Dominican friar and priest, poet and cosmological theorist. He entered the Dominican Order in Naples at 17. He took up the Copernican model and argued that the universe is infinite and has no centre, and that the stars are distant suns with planets of their own that might foster life. Tried for heresy by the Roman Inquisition for denying Catholic doctrines including the Trinity and transubstantiation, he was burned at the stake in Rome's Campo de' Fiori in 1600. Later commentators regarded him as a martyr for science, though historians disagree whether his cosmology caused his trial.

Frederick II was King of Sicily from 1198, King of Germany from 1212, Holy Roman Emperor from 1220 and King of Jerusalem from 1225 to 1228, the son of Emperor Henry VI of the Hohenstaufen dynasty and Constance I of Sicily. In the Kingdom of Sicily he built an early absolutist state run by a secular bureaucracy, and his court in Palermo fostered the Sicilian School of poetry. Frequently at war with the papacy, he was excommunicated four times, and Pope Innocent IV called him the forerunner of the Antichrist. Known as Stupor mundi, he died of dysentery at Castel Fiorentino in Apulia in 1250, and the House of Hohenstaufen soon came to an end.

Isaac is the second Hebrew patriarch in Judaism and a figure of the Abrahamic religions. In the Torah he is the son of Abraham and Sarah, father of Jacob and Esau, and grandfather of the twelve tribes of Israel. His name means 'he will laugh', recalling the laughter of his parents when his birth was foretold. Genesis tells of his binding on Mount Moriah, his marriage to Rebekah, and his death at 180. Islam regards him as a prophet and names him seventeen times in the Quran. Some recent scholarship suggests he may originally have been an ancestor revered at a sanctuary in the Beersheba region.

In Buddhism, parinirvana is the state entered at death by someone who attained nirvana during life. It means release from samsara, karma and rebirth, and the ending of the aggregates (skandhas) that make up a being. Modern usage tends to keep "nirvana" for the awakening experience and "parinirvana" for the death. Accounts of the Buddha's parinirvana at Kuśinagara are found in the Pāli Mahāparinibbāna Sutta and its Sanskrit and Chinese parallels. Bareau judged only the death and funeral rites to be the oldest core. Some Mahāyāna scriptures, notably the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, describe it as the realm of the eternal true Self of the Tathāgata.

"Cielito Lindo" (roughly "Lovely Sweet One") is a Mexican folk song, or copla, popularized in 1882 by the Mexican author Quirino Mendoza y Cortés (c. 1862–1957). It is widely known by words from its refrain, "Canta y no llores", or as the "Ay, Ay, Ay, Ay song". Its verses follow the seguidilla, a classical Castilian stanza of seven lines of alternating seven and five syllables, and singers add and drop verses freely.

The Investiture Controversy, or Investiture Contest, was a conflict between the Church and the state in medieval Europe over the ability to choose and install bishops, abbots and the Pope himself. It began in 1076 as a power struggle between Pope Gregory VII and Henry IV, then King and later Holy Roman Emperor, and led to nearly 50 years of conflict. It ended in 1122 with the Concordat of Worms, agreed by Pope Callixtus II and Emperor Henry V: bishops swore fealty to the monarch, while the church kept the right to invest them with sacred authority, symbolized by a ring and staff. A struggle between Pope Paschal II and Henry I of England ended in the similar Concordat of London.

Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. Born in rural Missouri, he fought in France as an artillery captain in World War I, was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1934 and, as vice president, succeeded Franklin D. Roosevelt on his death in April 1945. He authorized the first and only use of nuclear weapons in war, against Hiroshima and Nagasaki, set up the Marshall Plan, established the Truman Doctrine and supported the founding of NATO to contain Soviet communism. He presided over the onset of the Cold War, the Berlin Airlift and the Korean War, and issued Executive Order 9981, which desegregated the armed forces.

The Muslim Brotherhood is a transnational Sunni Islamist organization founded in Egypt in 1928 by the scholar and schoolteacher Hassan al-Banna. It began as a religious and social movement that preached, taught the illiterate and set up hospitals, then entered politics against British colonial rule; its stated aim is a state ruled by Sharia under a caliphate. Members assassinated the prime minister Mahmoud El Nokrashy Pasha in 1948, and Sayyid Qutb promoted takfirism in Milestones (1964); the group abandoned violence in the 1970s. Its candidate Mohamed Morsi became Egypt's first democratically elected president in 2012, but was overthrown in 2013, after which the group was banned in Egypt.

The Dead Sea Scrolls are a set of ancient Jewish manuscripts from the Second Temple period, discovered between 1946 and 1956, mostly in the Qumran Caves near the Dead Sea in the West Bank. Dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE, they include the oldest surviving manuscripts of entire books later included in the Jewish and Christian biblical canons, texts never canonized, and sectarian writings such as the Community Rule and the War Scroll. Most are in Hebrew, some in Aramaic and a few in Greek; researchers have assembled 981 different manuscripts from 11 caves. Almost all are held in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

The Young Ottomans were a secret society established in 1865 by Ottoman intellectuals who believed the Tanzimat reforms did not go far enough. They sought to preserve and modernize the Empire through constitutional government on the European model, kept rooted in Islam; among them were the writers İbrahim Şinasi, Namık Kemal, Ali Suavi and Ziya Pasha. In 1876 Midhat Pasha conspired with them to overthrow Sultan Abdul Aziz, and Abdul Hamid II reluctantly promulgated the Ottoman constitution of 1876, opening the First Constitutional Era. Abdul Hamid suspended it in 1878, but the Young Turks later repeated their efforts in the Young Turk Revolution of 1908.

Biblical Hebrew, also called Classical Hebrew, is an archaic form of the Hebrew language, of the Canaanitic branch of the Semitic languages, spoken by the Israelites in the Land of Israel. It is attested in inscriptions from about the 10th century BCE, when it was almost identical to Phoenician, and persisted as a spoken first language through the Second Temple period, which ended in 70 CE, before developing into Mishnaic Hebrew. It was first written in the Paleo-Hebrew alphabet, displaced after the Babylonian captivity by the Imperial Aramaic alphabet, and its vowel marks, the Tiberian vocalization, were added by the Masoretes in the Middle Ages.

Vedic Sanskrit, also called the Vedic language, is the earliest attested form of the Sanskrit and Prakrit languages, of the Indo-Aryan subgroup of the Indo-European family. It is attested in the Vedas and related literature compiled from the mid-2nd to the mid-1st millennium BCE, and was preserved orally, predating the local advent of writing by several centuries. The oldest hymns of the Rigveda are generally estimated to roughly 1500 BCE. The late form of the language was formalized as Classical Sanskrit in Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, and its literature has been a major source for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European and Proto-Indo-Iranian history.

The Egyptian Feminist Union was the first nationwide feminist movement in Egypt, founded on 6 March 1923 at the home of Huda Sha'arawi, who led it until her death in 1947. Formed out of dissatisfaction with an independence movement that put women's rights second, it campaigned for women's suffrage, education for girls, an end to legalized prostitution and reform of the personal status law, publishing the periodical L'Egyptienne from 1925. Primary education became compulsory for girls in 1925, but its campaign to reform family law failed. In 1944 it convened the congress that founded the Arab Feminist Union. Women won the vote in 1956, the year the Nasser regime dissolved the union.

On Liberty is an essay by the English philosophers Harriet Taylor Mill and John Stuart Mill, published in 1859 under the latter's name. It applies their ethical system of utilitarianism to society and the state, proposing standards for the relationship between authority and liberty. Its harm principle holds that power may rightfully be used over a member of a civilized community against his will only to prevent harm to others. The essay stresses the importance of individuality and warns that democratic ideals may result in the tyranny of the majority. Greatly influential, it has remained in print since its first publication.

Betty Friedan was an American feminist writer and activist, born Bettye Naomi Goldstein in Peoria, Illinois, whose 1963 book The Feminine Mystique is often credited with sparking the second wave of American feminism. The book grew from a survey of college graduates she made for her 15th college reunion in 1957 and depicted the role of the full-time homemaker, which she deemed stifling. In 1966 she co-founded the National Organization for Women (NOW) and was elected its first president. In 1970 she organized the nationwide Women's Strike for Equality, and in 1971 she helped establish the National Women's Political Caucus. She died in Washington, D.C., in 2006.

The United Arab Republic was a sovereign state in the Middle East from 1958 to 1971, formed as a political union of Egypt and Syria under the presidency of Gamal Abdel Nasser. It was established on 1 February 1958 at the urging of Syrian leaders, as a first step towards a larger pan-Arab state, and referendums on 21 February approved the merger and Nasser as president. Nasser demanded the dismantling of Syria's political parties, squeezed Syrians out of positions of influence and in 1961 nationalized banks and heavy industry; the backlash led to the Syrian coup of 28 September 1961 and Syria's secession. Egypt kept the name until Anwar Sadat formally dissolved it in September 1971.

Hassan al-Banna was an Egyptian schoolteacher and imam who founded the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the largest and most influential Islamist movements. Born in Mahmudiyya in the Nile Delta, he trained at Dar al-Ulum in Cairo and taught at a primary school in Ismailia, where in March 1928 six workers of the Suez Canal Company made him their leader. He held Islam to be a comprehensive system of life and criticized Western materialism and British imperialism. By the late 1930s the Brotherhood had branches in every Egyptian province, and a decade later 500,000 active members. After the government outlawed it in December 1948, he was shot in Cairo and died on 12 February 1949.

Hamza ibn Ali ibn Ahmed was an 11th-century Persian Isma'ili missionary and the founding leader of the Druze. Born in Zuzan in Greater Khorasan, he preached a heterodox strand of Isma'ilism in Cairo under the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, teaching from a mosque on the Raydan Canal that God had become incarnate in al-Hakim. Despite opposition from the Isma'ili clergy he set up a parallel hierarchy of missionaries in Egypt and Syria. Born in Zuzan in Greater Khorasan, he preached a heterodox strand of Isma'ilism in Cairo under the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, teaching from a mosque on the Raydan Canal that God had become incarnate in al-Hakim. Despite opposition from the Isma'ili clergy he set up a parallel hierarchy of missionaries in Egypt and Syria. After al-Hakim's disappearance, most likely his assassination, in February 1021, Hamza's followers were persecuted and he disappeared; his disciple Baha al-Din al-Muqtana resumed the mission in 1027–1042 and finalised the doctrines of the Druze faith.

Amy Ashwood Garvey was a Jamaican Pan-Africanist activist, born in Port Antonio, who with Marcus Garvey founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) in 1914 and organized its women's section. In the United States she was secretary of the UNIA's New York branch and in 1919 became one of the first directors of the Black Star Line; she married Garvey that year, and he divorced her in 1922. In London she opened the Florence Mills Social Club with Sam Manning in 1934, and in 1945 she helped organize the 5th Pan-African Congress in Manchester. After the 1958 Notting Hill race riots she co-founded the Association for the Advancement of Coloured People.

Juan José Linz was a German-born Spanish sociologist and political scientist of comparative politics, best known for his work on authoritarian regimes and democratization. Born in Bonn, he went with his mother to Spain in 1932 and took a doctorate at Columbia University in 1959; he taught at Columbia from 1961 and at Yale from 1969 for the rest of his life. His study of Francisco Franco's Spain classed it as an authoritarian regime, when regimes tended to be called either democratic or totalitarian. His works include Totalitarian and Authoritarian Regimes (1975), The Perils of Presidentialism (1990) and, with Alfred Stepan, Problems of Democratic Transition and Consolidation (1996).

Blackwater Draw is an intermittent stream channel about 140 km long that runs from Roosevelt County, New Mexico, south-eastward across the Llano Estacado towards Lubbock, Texas, and holds Blackwater Locality No. 1, the type site of the Clovis culture. Ridgley Whiteman first recognized the site in 1929, and the first large excavation came in 1932. Its stratified levels, from Clovis and Folsom to the historic period, hold fluted Clovis points and other tools with the remains of extinct Late Pleistocene animals such as mammoth, camel, bison and dire wolf. Two of its points were used in the 1930s to define Clovis technology, and its Clovis layers date to around 11,290 years before the present.

Thomas Becket was an English cleric and statesman who served as Lord Chancellor from 1155 to 1162 and as Archbishop of Canterbury from 1162 until his murder in 1170. Born in London to a Norman family, he rose in the household of Archbishop Theobald of Bec, who recommended him to Henry II. As archbishop he resisted the king's attempt to reassert royal prerogatives over the Church; convicted in 1164 of contempt of royal authority, he spent six years in exile under the protection of Louis VII of France. Soon after his return in 1170 four knights loyal to Henry killed him in Canterbury Cathedral. Pope Alexander III canonized him in 1173, and he is venerated as a saint and martyr.

Copán is an archaeological site of the Maya civilization in the Copán Department of western Honduras, near the border with Guatemala. Occupied for more than two thousand years, it was the capital of a major Classic period kingdom from the 5th to the 9th century CE, refounded in 426 by a dynasty with its origins at Tikal; at its Late Classic peak the kingdom had at least 20,000 people. In 738 its king Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil was captured and beheaded by his former vassal, the king of Quiriguá. The population later declined and the city was abandoned in the early 10th century. Known for its sculpture and Hieroglyphic Stairway, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.

Philaret, born Vasily Mikhaylovich Drozdov, was Metropolitan of Moscow and Kolomna and the most influential figure in the Russian Orthodox Church from 1821 to 1867. Born in Kolomna to a clerical family, he taught at the Troitse-Sergiyeva Lavra and the academy of the Alexander Nevsky Lavra, became Archbishop of Tver in 1819, moved to Moscow in 1821 and became metropolitan in 1826. A leading preacher and author of many theological works, he worked toward a Russian translation of the Bible and is said to have prepared Alexander II's proclamation freeing the serfs; he also had Old Believer churches sealed and their clergy imprisoned. He was canonized in 1994.

Plaçage was a recognized extralegal system in the French slave colonies of North America and the Caribbean in which European men entered into unions with women of African, Native American and mixed-race descent, known as placées. The unions, called left-handed marriages among free people of colour, were often settled by contracts that gave property to the woman and her children, and sometimes freedom if they were enslaved. It developed first in Saint-Domingue amid a shortage of European women, was most widely practised in New Orleans and reached its height between 1769 and 1803. Emily Clark sees it as a broad range of relationships rather than a contractual system.

Álvaro III Nimi a Mpanzu was king, or manikongo, of the Kingdom of Kongo from August 1615 to 4 May 1622. A son of King Álvaro II and formerly Duke of Mbamba, he was the fourth ruler of the royal house of Kwilu founded by Álvaro I. Around 1619 he formalized the construction of a Jesuit college in São Salvador. Relations with the Dutch soured in the 1610s after the closure of a Dutch factory in Soyo, but he revived them as a check on Portuguese expansion, and Dutch factories reopened at Soyo in 1621. He died in 1622 while his son was too young to rule, and the nobles elected the Duke of Mbamba, beginning the short House of Nsundi.

Military settlements were an organization of the Russian army from 1810 to 1857 that combined military service with farming, introduced by Alexander I to create an inexpensive reserve of trained troops. Alexei Arakcheyev set up the first in the Mogilev Governorate in 1810–1812 and headed all of them from 1817; by 1825 they made up almost a quarter of the army by some accounts. Life was strictly regulated, corporal punishment was common, and drill left the farm work late. Settlers rose in the Chuguyev regiment in 1819 and near Staraya Russa in July 1831, when the rebels executed their superiors; both risings were harshly put down, and all the settlements were abolished in 1857.

Robert Francis Kennedy was an American politician and lawyer who served as the 64th United States attorney general from 1961 to 1964 and as a senator from New York from 1965 until his assassination in 1968. He managed the campaigns of his brother John F. Kennedy and was his closest adviser, and as attorney general he supported the civil rights movement and fought organized crime. As a senator he opposed US involvement in the Vietnam War and sponsored legislation against poverty. A leading candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1968, he was shot by Sirhan Sirhan shortly after winning the California primary and died 25 hours later.

Canassatego was a leader of the Onondaga nation who became a prominent diplomat and spokesman of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy in the 1740s. He first appears in the records at a treaty conference in Philadelphia in 1742, and he was involved in several controversial land sales to British colonial officials. He is best known for a speech at the Treaty of Lancaster in 1744, in which he recommended that the British colonies form a confederacy as the Haudenosaunee had done. He was reportedly assassinated in 1750, perhaps by sympathizers or agents of New France.

George C. Marshall was an American soldier and diplomat. He rose to become Chief of Staff of the United States Army under Franklin D. Roosevelt and Harry S. Truman, and Winston Churchill called him the organizer of victory for his leadership in the Second World War. He then tried without success to end the Chinese Civil War, and served Truman as Secretary of State and Secretary of Defense. As Secretary of State he advocated an American commitment to Europe's recovery after the war, the Marshall Plan that bore his name, and he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953.

A bayonet is a knife, dagger, sword or spike mounted on the barrel of a musket or rifle, so that the gun can be used as a spear in close combat. The first recorded bayonet proper is the 'gun-knife' of the son-and-mother gun in the Chinese military treatise Binglu of 1606, a plug bayonet pushed into the barrel. Jean Martinet standardized plug bayonets for new French fusilier regiments in 1671; because they stopped the gun from firing, socket bayonets that fitted around the barrel replaced them, and by the mid-18th century most European armies had adopted these for massed infantry charges.

A lithium-ion battery is a rechargeable battery that stores energy by moving lithium ions in and out of electronically conducting solids. M. Stanley Whittingham conceived intercalation electrodes in the 1970s and made the first rechargeable lithium-ion battery, with a titanium disulfide cathode, though safety problems kept it from being commercialized. John Goodenough used lithium cobalt oxide as a cathode in 1980, and Akira Yoshino developed the first prototype of the modern battery, with a carbonaceous anode, in 1985. A Sony and Asahi Kasei team led by Yoshio Nishi brought it to market in 1991, and the three inventors shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The "Hymn to the Nile", also called the "Hymn to Hapy", was created and sung by the ancient Egyptians about the flooding of the Nile. The Greek historian Herodotus called Egypt the "Gift of the Nile", because ancient Egyptian civilization shaped its culture around the river and depended on its resources.
