Dekulakization was a campaign of repression in the Soviet Union against the so-called kulaks, a loosely defined category of supposedly wealthy or exploitative peasants, begun after Stalin announced the liquidation of the kulaks as a class on 27 December 1929. It aimed to break resistance to collectivization and to supply forced labour for Siberia, the Urals, Kazakhstan and the North. Between 2.1 and 2.3 million people were deported to special settlements in 1930–1933 and 20,000 to 30,000 executed by troiki; Manfred Hildermeier estimates 530,000 to 600,000 deaths, excluding the famine. The deportations became central to the Gulag and helped bring about the famine of 1930–1933.

Dongzhi is the 22nd solar term of the Chinese calendar, marking the winter solstice, and the festival that Chinese people observe at that time, around 21 to 23 December. Its origins are traced to the philosophy of yin and yang, the lengthening days representing positive energy. The festival was first celebrated during the Zhou dynasty (1045 BCE–256 BCE) and declared an official celebration during the Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE), when people took a break from work, worshipped heaven and honoured their ancestors. Families still gather to eat tangyuan, balls of glutinous rice that symbolize reunion, and dumplings; in Korea, where the day is called Dongji, porridge is made with red beans.

Stendhal was the pen name of Marie-Henri Beyle, a French writer born in Grenoble in 1783, best known for the novels The Red and the Black (1830) and The Charterhouse of Parma (1839) and considered one of the early practitioners of realism. He served in Napoleon's administration and was part of the army in the 1812 invasion of Russia, where he witnessed the burning of Moscow and the winter retreat. After the fall of Napoleon he settled in Milan until 1821, and from 1830 he was French consul at Trieste and Civitavecchia. His book De l'amour introduced the concept of crystallization in passionate love. He died in 1842.

Joseph-Louis Lagrange was an Italian and naturalized French mathematician, physicist and astronomer, born Giuseppe Luigi Lagrangia and educated at the University of Turin. In 1766 he succeeded Leonhard Euler as director of mathematics at the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin, where he wrote the Mécanique analytique (1788), which turned Newtonian mechanics into a branch of analysis. He was one of the creators of the calculus of variations, proved that every natural number is a sum of four squares and in 1772 found the solutions now known as Lagrangian points. Moving to Paris in 1787, he became the first professor of analysis at the École Polytechnique in 1794 and died in Paris in 1813.

Deism is the belief that a Supreme Being created the universe and that reason and observation of the natural world alone are sufficient to establish the existence of this creator, without prophecy, revelation or religious texts. Many deists hold that God does not intervene in the world after creating it, and the position stresses natural theology, in which God's existence is revealed through nature. Deists set out this critique of organized religion from the 17th century, especially in 18th-century England, France and North America. Deism saw a revival in early-19th-century Great Britain and North America, and several of its tenets continued in movements such as Unitarianism.

The Normans were a people of the medieval Duchy of Normandy who arose from the intermingling of Norse Viking settlers with the inhabitants of West Francia. Their settlement was legitimized when the Viking leader Rollo swore fealty to King Charles III after the siege of Chartres in 911, and the settlers adopted the language, religion and customs of the West Franks. Under their duke William the Conqueror they conquered England at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, while Norman adventurers took southern Italy and Malta and helped found the Kingdom of Sicily under Roger II; Bohemond I founded the Principality of Antioch. In 1204 Philip II of France seized mainland Normandy.

Fritz Haber was a German chemist, born in Breslau into a Jewish family, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918 for the Haber process, which synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen for fertilizers and explosives. During World War I he developed chlorine and other poisonous gases as weapons and proposed the use of chlorine gas at the Second Battle of Ypres, which earned him the name father of chemical warfare. His work was later used, without his involvement, to develop the Zyklon B pesticide used to kill more than 1 million Jews in the Holocaust. He resigned his post after the Nazis came to power in 1933 and died in Basel in 1934.

Classical antiquity is the period of European cultural history between the 8th century BCE and the 5th century CE, comprising the interwoven civilizations of ancient Greece and Rome, the Greco-Roman world. It is conventionally taken to begin with the earliest recorded epic poetry of Homer and to end with the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476. Greek culture, with some influences from the ancient Near East, was the basis of art, philosophy, society and education in the Mediterranean until the Roman imperial period, and the Romans spread it throughout Europe. Surviving fragments of classical culture helped produce the revival beginning in the 14th century later known as the Renaissance.

The early modern period is a historical period of about 1500 to about 1800, defined chiefly from the history of Europe as the time after the Middle Ages and before the advent of modernity; its boundaries are not agreed. Proposed starting points include the Renaissance, the printing revolution of the 1440s, the Fall of Constantinople in 1453, the Age of Discovery and the Reformation, and its end is tied to the Industrial, American and French Revolutions. Historians have stressed the spread of globalization, mercantilism and the Scientific Revolution. The medieval historian Lynn Thorndike first proposed the term for a distinct period in 1926.

The modern era, or modern period, is considered the current period of human history. First applied in European history to what came after classical antiquity and the Middle Ages, often from around 1500, the term is now more often used for events from the 19th century onwards, the centuries before being called the early modern period, while the time since 1945 can also be called contemporary history. It is commonly associated with the French Revolution and the Industrial Revolution, with colonization by the European powers, and with individualism, capitalism, socialism and urbanization; postmodernism and postcolonial theory have criticised its belief in progress and Western dominance.

Mary G. Harris Jones, known as Mother Jones from 1897, was an Irish-American labour organizer, schoolteacher and dressmaker born in Cork, whose family emigrated to Canada after the Great Famine. After her husband and four children died of yellow fever in Memphis in 1867 and her shop was destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, she organised for the Knights of Labor and the United Mine Workers of America. In 1902 she was called the most dangerous woman in America, and in 1903 she led a children's march from Philadelphia to protest weak child labour laws. She co-founded the Industrial Workers of the World and died in 1930.

The Upper Paleolithic is the third and last subdivision of the Paleolithic or Old Stone Age, dated very broadly to between 50,000 and 12,000 years ago and, according to some theories, coinciding with the appearance of behavioral modernity in humans. It has the earliest known evidence of organized settlements, and artistic work blossomed in cave painting, petroglyphs and carvings on bone or ivory. Tool industries based on fine blades appeared, along with darts, harpoons, the fish hook, the oil lamp and the eyed needle. Modern humans peopled Europe after c. 45 ka and expanded into the Americas by about 15 ka; the period was followed by the Mesolithic.

It has the earliest known evidence of organised settlements, and artistic work blossomed in cave painting, petroglyphs and carvings on bone or ivory. Tool industries based on fine blades appeared, along with darts, harpoons, the fish hook, the oil lamp and the eyed needle. Modern humans peopled Europe after c. 45 ka and expanded into the Americas by about 15 ka; the period was followed by the Mesolithic.

The Khanate of Bukhara was an Uzbek monarchy in Central Asia from 1501 to 1785, founded by the Shaybanid dynasty, a branch of the Abu'l-Khayrids. Muhammad Shaybani, grandson of Abu'l-Khayr Khan, conquered Balkh, Bukhara, Samarkand and Tashkent, but Shah Ismail I of the Safavid Empire killed him outside Merv in 1510. Abdullah Khan II made Bukhara the permanent capital by 1562, and in the 17th and 18th centuries the Janid dynasty, the last Chinggisid dynasty to rule Bukhara, held the throne. Nader Shah of Iran conquered the khanate in 1740; in 1785 Shah Murad formalized the rule of the Manghit dynasty, and it became the Emirate of Bukhara.

The Arab Revolt was an armed uprising by the Hashemite-led Arabs of the Hejaz against the Ottoman Empire in the Middle Eastern theatre of World War I. On the basis of the McMahon–Hussein Correspondence, Hussein bin Ali launched it at Mecca on 10 June 1916, aiming at an independent, unified Arab state from Aleppo to Aden that Britain had promised to recognize. With British backing and officers such as T. E. Lawrence, the Sharifian Army drove the Ottomans from much of the Hejaz and Transjordan, and by 1918 had captured Damascus and proclaimed the Arab Kingdom of Syria under Faisal I. Most Arabs in the Ottoman territories did not join it, and its forces played a limited supporting role.

Reform Judaism, also known as Liberal or Progressive Judaism, is a major Jewish denomination that emphasizes the evolving nature of Judaism, the superiority of its ethical aspects to its ceremonial ones, and a continuous revelation. It began in mid-19th-century Germany, where Rabbi Abraham Geiger and his associates formulated its principles, removing parts of the liturgy such as bodily resurrection and translating much of the prayer into German. Brought to America by German-born rabbis, it flourished there from the 1860s to the 1930s, the era of Classical Reform. The World Union for Progressive Judaism, founded in 1926, estimates it represents at least 1.8 million people in 50 countries.

Conservative Judaism, also known as Masorti Judaism, is a Jewish religious movement that holds Jewish law, or Halakha, to be both binding and subject to historical development, its authority resting chiefly on the assent of the people through the generations. It regards itself as heir to the positive-historical school of Rabbi Zecharias Frankel in 19th-century Europe, but became fully institutionalized in the United States in the mid-20th century. The United Synagogue was founded in 1913, and the Jewish Theological Seminary of America is its largest seminary. In 1983 it resolved to ordain women rabbis. It is the third-largest Jewish movement, close to 1.1 million people.

A cradle of civilization is a place and culture in which one of the earliest civilizations emerged independently, a civilization being a complex society with a state, social stratification, cities and writing or graphic arts. Scholars once thought civilization began in the Fertile Crescent and spread from there; today they generally recognise six cradles: Mesopotamia, Ancient Egypt, Ancient India and Ancient China in Afro-Eurasia, and the Caral–Supe civilization of Peru and the Olmec civilization of Mexico in the Americas. All depended on agriculture, except possibly Caral–Supe. The first large cities, such as Uruk, Ur, Kish and Eridu, rose by the 31st century BCE.

New Imperialism characterises a period of colonial expansion by the major Western powers and the Empire of Japan during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its main participants were the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Russia, the United States and Japan, which conquered almost all of Africa and parts of Asia. It reflected rivalries among the great powers, the desire for new resources and markets and a civilizing mission ethos, sharpened by the Long Depression of 1873–1896; the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 set effective occupation as the test of a claim. Many of its colonies gained independence after World War II.

Collective farming is agricultural production in which multiple farmers run their holdings as a joint enterprise, as cooperatives of member-owners or as state farms owned and run by a central government; the process of aggregating farmland is called collectivization. Older communal forms include the Aztec calpulli and the Russian peasant commune, the mir or obshchina. The Soviet Union introduced collective farms (kolkhozy) between 1927 and 1933, and after Stalin forced the peasants into collectives an estimated 5.7 to 8.7 million people died in the famine of 1932–1933. China, North Korea, Vietnam and most of the Eastern Bloc later collectivized, and the kibbutzim of Israel began in 1909.

The North Yemen civil war was fought from 1962 to 1970 between partisans of the Mutawakkilite Kingdom and supporters of the Yemen Arab Republic. It began when the army under Abdullah al-Sallal dethroned the newly crowned Imam Muhammad al-Badr and declared a republic, which abolished slavery, while the Imam rallied northern Zaydi tribes from the Saudi border. Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Israel aided the royalists, and Egypt under Gamal Abdel Nasser sent as many as 70,000 troops to back the republicans, at a cost to its army in the 1967 Six-Day War. The republicans held Sana'a through a siege lifted in February 1968, and in 1970 Saudi Arabia recognized the Republic and a ceasefire took effect.

The Andean civilizations were complex societies of many indigenous peoples of South America, stretching 4,000 km along the Andes from southern Colombia through Ecuador and Peru to north Chile and northwest Argentina. The Caral or Norte Chico civilization of coastal Peru, dating back to 3500 BCE, is the oldest known civilization in the Americas; later came Chavín, Paracas, Nazca, Moche, Wari, Tiwanaku and Chimor. They had no writing, wheeled vehicles or money, recorded information on the quipu and domesticated crops such as potatoes, quinoa and coca. From 1438 the Incas united most of them in one empire, before the Spanish conquest of the 16th century.

The Catholic Church is the largest Christian denomination, made up of the Latin Church and 23 Eastern Catholic Churches organised into nearly 3,500 dioceses and eparchies. Its doctrine rests on the Nicene Creed and holds that its bishops succeed the apostles and that the pope, the bishop of Rome, succeeds Saint Peter. The Eucharist, celebrated in the Mass, stands at the centre of its seven sacraments. The church had a large role in the development of Western civilization; it separated from the Church of the East after 431, from the Oriental Orthodox after 451 and gradually from the Eastern Orthodox, and the 16th-century Reformation prompted its Counter-Reformation.

Belize is a country on the north-eastern coast of Central America, bordered by Mexico, Guatemala and the Caribbean Sea. The Maya civilization spread into the area between 1500 BCE and 300 CE. English settlers began exploring in 1638, and Spain and Britain both claimed the land until Britain's victory at the Battle of St. George's Caye in 1798. It became a British colony in 1840 and a Crown colony in 1862, known as British Honduras until 1973. Belize achieved independence from the United Kingdom on 21 September 1981.

Chile is a country in the Southern Cone of southwestern South America, a narrow strip of land between the Andes Mountains and the Pacific Ocean. Spain conquered and colonized the region in the mid-16th century, replacing Inca rule, but failed to conquer the autonomous Mapuche people of what is now south-central Chile. Chile declared independence from Spain in 1818. It ended Mapuche resistance in the 1880s and gained its present northern territory by defeating Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific (1879–83). The coup of 11 September 1973 overthrew Salvador Allende and began a military dictatorship under Augusto Pinochet that lasted until 1990.

Colombia is a country in South America, with insular regions in North America, bordered by Venezuela, Brazil, Peru, Ecuador and Panama. Indigenous peoples lived there from at least 12,000 BCE. The Spanish landed in La Guajira in 1499 and by the mid-16th century had colonized much of the territory, establishing the New Kingdom of Granada. Independence was declared in 1810, and after a Spanish reconquest it was secured in 1819, when the Gran Colombia period began. The state became the Granadine Confederation (1858), the United States of Colombia (1863) and a centralised republic in 1886. Panama seceded in 1903, which gave Colombia its present borders.

Costa Rica is a country in Central America, bordering Nicaragua to the north and Panama to the southeast, with coasts on the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Humans lived there from between 7,000 and 10,000 BCE, and various indigenous peoples were present before Spain colonized the territory in the 16th century. It was a peripheral colony of the Spanish Empire until independence in 1821 as part of the First Mexican Empire, then joined the Federal Republic of Central America in 1823 and formally declared independence from it in 1847. After a brief civil war in 1948, the constitution of 1949 granted universal suffrage and permanently abolished the army.

Ecuador is a country in northwestern South America, bordered by Colombia, Peru and the Pacific Ocean, and includes the Galápagos Islands about 1,000 kilometers west of the mainland. Several indigenous groups lived on its land and were gradually incorporated into the Inca Empire during the 15th century. The Spanish Empire colonized the territory during the 16th century. Ecuador achieved independence in 1820 as part of Gran Colombia and emerged as a sovereign state in 1830. The legacy of both empires is reflected in its ethnically diverse population, and 13 native languages, including Quechua and Shuar, are recognized beside Spanish.

Honduras is a country in Central America. Before Spanish colonization in the 16th century its territory held several Mesoamerican cultures, most notably the Maya, whose state at Copán declined in the 9th century. Honduras became independent from Spain in 1821, was part of the First Mexican Empire until 1823, and then of the United Provinces of Central America. It has been an independent republic with elections since 1838. In the early 20th century transnational agricultural companies dominated it, and the term "banana republic" was first coined for its politics. In 1960 the northern part of the Mosquito Coast was transferred from Nicaragua to Honduras.

Paul, born Saul of Tarsus, was a Christian apostle who spread the teachings of Jesus in the first century CE and founded several Christian communities in Asia Minor and Europe from the mid-40s to the mid-50s. His life is known chiefly from his letters and the Acts of the Apostles. According to Acts, he was a Pharisee who persecuted the followers of Jesus until a vision of Christ on the road to Damascus led him to be baptized. Fourteen New Testament books are traditionally attributed to him, of which scholars regard seven as undisputed. His death in Rome under Nero is traditional, dated either after the fire of 64 or a few years later.

Joseph ben Caiaphas was a high priest in the first century. The Gospels of Matthew, Luke and John present him as an organizer of the plot against Jesus and as presiding over the Sanhedrin trial. Josephus, the most reliable source outside the New Testament, says the Roman prefect Valerius Gratus appointed him in 18 CE and that the legate of Syria Lucius Vitellius later deposed him. His tenure of eighteen years suggests a working relationship with the Romans. In John he is the son-in-law of Annas and argues that it is better for one man to die than for the nation to be destroyed. A limestone ossuary found in 1990 may be his, though some scholars dispute the identification.

The Sermon on the Mount is a discourse of Jesus of Nazareth found in chapters 5 to 7 of the Gospel of Matthew, summarizing his moral teachings. It is the first of five discourses in that gospel and contains the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer in its commonly recited form and the Golden Rule. In Matthew, Jesus goes up a mountain with his disciples, sits down and teaches. Christians have traditionally commemorated the Mount of Beatitudes as the site, though Mount Arbel and the Horns of Hattin have also been suggested. Some Christian traditions see the sermon as the counterpart of the giving of the Ten Commandments on Sinai, and Luke places parts of the material in a different setting.
